root.title: Parameterized Exact Algorithm Synthesis
root.top_down_role: Exact algorithms for computationally hard discrete problems, parameter-sensitive tractability, structural algorithm design, preprocessing, and their conditional or unconditional limitations. General complexity theory, graph theory, approximation, integer programming, matroid optimization, and finite-model theory remain external dependencies.

children.title: The Parameterized Viewpoint
children.top_down_role: Problem representations, parameter choices, tractability regimes, and multivariate comparisons required by later algorithmic and hardness branches.

children.title: Parameterized Decision Problems
children.top_down_role: Yes-or-no formulations indexed by a designated parameter.

assumptions_latex: The instance alphabet \(\Sigma\) is finite.
The parameterization \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) is computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((L,\kappa)\) is the parameterized decision problem whose yes-instances are exactly the strings in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard language-plus-parameter formulation.

source_refs.locator: Decision Problems: The Classes P and NP p. 24

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized decision problem is a pair \((L,\kappa)\), where \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) is a language and \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) is a computable parameterization. On input \(x\in\Sigma^*\), the required output is \(1\) precisely when \(x\in L\), and \(0\) otherwise. It is fixed-parameter tractable when some algorithm decides membership in time \(f(\kappa(x))|x|^{O(1)}\) for a computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized decision problem asks whether an instance belongs to a language while separately tracking a computable integer parameter, often seeking running time arbitrary in the parameter but polynomial in input length.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Decision Problems

source_witnesses.locator: Decision Problems: The Classes P and NP p. 24

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but the cited section supports classical decision problems rather than the parameterized pair or FPT running-time claim. A parameterized-complexity source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Parameterized Search Problems
children.top_down_role: Witness-producing formulations indexed by a designated parameter.

assumptions_latex: The instance alphabet \(\Sigma\) and witness alphabet \(\Gamma\) are finite.
The parameterization \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) is computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relation \(R\) specifies all valid outputs, with \(R(x)=\varnothing\) exactly when no solution exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines total output behavior, including infeasible instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized search problem is a pair \((R,\kappa)\), where \(R\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\Gamma^*\) is a computably recognizable relation and \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) is computable. For \(x\in\Sigma^*\), write \(R(x)=\{y\in\Gamma^*:(x,y)\in R\}\). The task is to output some \(y\in R(x)\), or the distinguished symbol \(\bot\) when \(R(x)=\varnothing\). An FPT search algorithm runs in time \(f(\kappa(x))|x|^{O(1)}\), including verification and output time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized search problem must produce a valid witness, or report that none exists, within a resource bound expressed using the instance parameter and input length.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Search Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but no source supports this particular relation-based search model, its infeasibility output convention, or the stated FPT resource bound. Recognizability of the relation alone also does not guarantee that infeasibility can be decided.

children.title: Decision-to-Search Reductions
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions under which decision access supports witness recovery.

assumptions_latex: A decision oracle recognizes whether \(R(z)\neq\varnothing\).
Every feasible instance admits a witness of length at most \(p(|x|)\).
Each prefix restriction is computable and has parameter at most \(g(\kappa(x))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most \(|\Gamma|p(|x|)+1\) oracle calls recover a witness or correctly output \(\bot\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to prefix-self-reducible witness relations with controlled parameter growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\), first query \(D(x)\); if the answer is no, output \(\bot\). Otherwise initialize \(u=\epsilon\). For each position \(i=1,\ldots,p(|x|)\), test symbols \(a\in\Gamma\) by querying the restricted instance asking whether some \(y\in R(x)\) has prefix \(ua\). Choose a symbol receiving yes and set \(u\leftarrow ua\); stop when \((x,u)\in R\). The procedure makes at most \(|\Gamma|p(|x|)+1\) oracle calls, and an FPT oracle yields FPT total time when restricted parameters are bounded by \(g(\kappa(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a self-reducible problem, repeatedly ask the decision oracle whether a solution extends each candidate prefix; successful answers determine a witness with polynomially many parameter-controlled oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision-to-Search Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A direct self-reduction source is required. The restricted instances and their relationship to the oracle's input domain are not formally defined, and the procedure fails to check whether the empty string is already a witness before extending the prefix.

assumptions_latex: Each instance \(x\) has a finite feasible set \(F(x)\).
The objective \(c_x:F(x)\to\mathbb Z\) and parameter \(\kappa(x)\) are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The required output is an optimizer and its value, or \(\bot\) when \(F(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the minimization form; maximization follows by reversing the order.

source_refs.locator: 4.7 Optimization problems p. 42
Section 1.3. Linear Optimization Problems p. 8

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized minimization problem assigns to every instance \(x\in\Sigma^*\) a finite feasible set \(F(x)\), an objective \(c_x:F(x)\to\mathbb Z\), and a parameter \(\kappa(x)\in\mathbb N\). If \(F(x)\neq\varnothing\), its value is \(\operatorname{opt}(x)=\min\{c_x(y):y\in F(x)\}\), and the output is a pair \((y,\operatorname{opt}(x))\) with \(y\in F(x)\) and \(c_x(y)=\operatorname{opt}(x)\). If \(F(x)=\varnothing\), the output is \(\bot\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized optimization problem returns a feasible solution attaining the best objective value, while complexity is measured using both input length and a designated parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Forms

source_witnesses.locator: 4.7 Optimization problems p. 42
Section 1.3. Linear Optimization Problems p. 8

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited optimization sections can support the underlying optimization form, but they do not establish the parameterized formulation. Moreover, the plain statement discusses parameterized complexity although the LaTeX statement defines no complexity bound.

assumptions_latex: For every instance \(x\), the solution set \(F(x)\) is finite.
The parameterization \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) is computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The required output is the exact integer \(\#F(x)\), including zero for infeasible instances.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts distinct encoded solutions exactly, without quotienting by symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized counting problem is a pair \((F,\kappa)\) in which each instance \(x\in\Sigma^*\) has a finite set \(F(x)\) of valid solutions and \(\kappa(x)\in\mathbb N\) is computable. The required output is \(\#F(x)=|F(x)|\). The problem is fixed-parameter tractable in the output-bit model if an algorithm returns the binary encoding of \(\#F(x)\) in time \(f(\kappa(x))|x|^{O(1)}\), which necessarily includes the time used to write that encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized counting problem returns the exact number of valid solutions, with running time measured against the parameter, input length, and the binary output representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Counting Forms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-counting definition fits the leaf, but no cited source supports the parameterized counting formulation or the stated output-bit FPT convention. A source should also specify the encoding or length conditions governing finite solution sets.

assumptions_latex: For every instance \(x\), the solution set \(F(x)\) is finite.
Solutions possess a fixed canonical encoding.
The parameterization \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) is computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs each member of \(F(x)\) exactly once and then halts.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses total-FPT enumeration and canonical solution encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized enumeration problem assigns to each instance \(x\in\Sigma^*\) a finite solution set \(F(x)\) and a parameter \(\kappa(x)\). A correct enumerator emits every \(y\in F(x)\) exactly once, emits no other string, and halts after its final output. It is total-FPT if, writing \(N=|F(x)|\), its complete running time is bounded by \(f(\kappa(x))|x|^{O(1)}+O\!\left(\sum_{y\in F(x)}|y|\right)\), so the unavoidable cost of writing all solutions is explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized enumeration problem outputs every valid solution exactly once; total-FPT complexity separates parameterized computation from the unavoidable cost of writing all solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Enumeration Forms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The enumeration task fits the leaf, but the claimed total-FPT terminology and output-sensitive bound require a direct source; this bound is not universally called total-FPT in parameterized enumeration literature.

children.title: Solution-Size Parameters
children.top_down_role: Parameters measuring the size of a sought solution or witness.

assumptions_latex: Each instance \(x\) has a finite family \(F(x)\) of feasible combinatorial objects.
The parameterization is derived from the cardinality of a feasible or optimal object.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A solution-size parameter is \(k(x)=\min\{|S|:S\in F(x)\}\), or a supplied threshold \(k\) bounding \(|S|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers cardinality parameters for minimization and threshold decision forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)\subseteq 2^{U_x}\) be the feasible solutions of instance \(x\), where \(U_x\) is a finite ground set. For a minimization problem, the solution-size parameter is \(k(x)=\min\{|S|:S\in F(x)\}\), with \(k(x)=\infty\) when \(F(x)=\varnothing\). In the threshold decision form, \(k\in\mathbb N\) is part of the input and the question is whether some \(S\in F(x)\) satisfies \(|S|\le k\). Parameterized complexity then measures nonpolynomial dependence in \(k\), rather than in \(|U_x|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution-size parameter records the cardinality of an optimal feasible object, or a threshold that bounds the size of the sought object.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Size Parameters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record blends parameterization by an optimum value with parameterization by an input threshold, which are distinct forms. It also assigns infinity to an infeasible instance although parameterizations ordinarily map into natural numbers. A direct source is needed to determine the intended convention.

children.title: Dual Solution-Size Parameters
children.top_down_role: Complementary parameters measuring distance from the corresponding full-size choice.

assumptions_latex: The finite ground set \(U_x\) has size \(n(x)\).
Every primal solution \(S\) has a designated complementary dual object \(U_x\setminus S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual solution-size parameter is \(k^\star(x)=n(x)-k(x)\) whenever optimum solutions correspond by complementation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses combinatorial complementation, not linear-programming dual variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U_x\) be a finite ground set and suppose the primal and dual feasible families are related by complementation: \(F^\star(x)=\{U_x\setminus S:S\in F(x)\}\). If the primal parameter is \(k(x)=\min\{|S|:S\in F(x)\}\), define the complementary dual solution-size parameter by \(k^\star(x)=\max\{|T|:T\in F^\star(x)\}\). Then \(k^\star(x)=|U_x|-k(x)\). Equivalently, a primal threshold \(|S|\le k\) corresponds to a dual threshold \(|T|\ge |U_x|-k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For solution families paired by complementation, the dual size counts the elements outside a primal solution and therefore equals ground-set size minus primal size.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Solution-Size Parameters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complement identity is correct under the stated bijection, but calling the complementary cardinality a dual solution-size parameter is context-dependent and potentially confusable with optimization duality. The exact terminology and scope require a source.

children.title: Primal–Dual Parameter Relations
children.top_down_role: Comparability, translation, and separation between primal and dual parameterizations.

assumptions_latex: Primal and dual feasible objects are complements in a ground set of size \(n\).
The reduction between the two encodings is polynomial-time computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parameters satisfy \(k^\star=n-k\), but this does not generally constitute an FPT parameter transformation between \(k\) and \(k^\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates numerical complementation from parameter-preserving reducibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under a complement bijection \(S\mapsto U\setminus S\) on a ground set \(U\) of size \(n\), primal and dual cardinalities obey \(k^\star=n-k\). Hence either of the pairs \((n,k)\) and \((n,k^\star)\) determines the other. However, parameterization solely by \(k\) and parameterization solely by \(k^\star\) are not automatically FPT-equivalent: an FPT parameter transformation requires a computable bound \(k^\star\le h(k)\), or conversely \(k\le h^\star(k^\star)\), independent of the unbounded quantity \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary primal and dual sizes sum to the ground-set size, yet smallness of one need not imply smallness of the other without an additional bound on ground-set size.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Parameter Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The numerical complement relation and warning about parameter equivalence are plausible and fit the property leaf, but the criterion for an FPT parameter transformation needs a direct parameterized-complexity source and a precise reduction convention.

children.title: Decomposition-Width Parameters
children.top_down_role: Parameters arising from tree-like, path-like, branch-like, or related decompositions.

assumptions_latex: For each graph \(G\), \(\mathcal D(G)\) is a nonempty family of admissible decompositions.
Every decomposition \(D\) has finite pieces \(B\) whose sizes are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposition-width parameter is the minimum, over admissible decompositions, of the largest local piece size minus one.

notation.meaning: pieces or bags of decomposition D

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A generic template encompassing bag-based widths after admissibility is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a decomposition scheme assigning each finite graph \(G\) a nonempty set \(\mathcal D(G)\) of admissible decompositions. For \(D\in\mathcal D(G)\), let \(\mathcal B(D)\) be its finite family of pieces or bags and define \(w(D)=\max\{|B|-1:B\in\mathcal B(D)\}\). The associated decomposition-width parameter is \(w_{\mathrm{dec}}(G)=\min\{w(D):D\in\mathcal D(G)\}\). The admissibility axioms distinguish particular parameters; for example, tree-decomposition axioms specialize this template to treewidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition width minimizes the largest local piece over all admissible decompositions of a graph; different admissibility axioms produce different width parameters.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Width Parameters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic bag-minimization template fits some decomposition widths, notably treewidth, but not every parameter normally classified as decomposition width. A taxonomic source must delimit the covered schemes and justify the minus-one convention.

children.title: Layout-Width Parameters
children.top_down_role: Parameters derived from linear layouts, cuts, or vertex orderings.

assumptions_latex: A layout is a bijection from the vertices of a finite graph to consecutive positions.
A nonnegative cut-cost function \(\rho_G\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The layout-width parameter minimizes the maximum cut cost encountered along a vertex ordering.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A generic cut-based template; the cut-cost function selects the concrete width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite graph with \(n=|V(G)|\). A layout is a bijection \(\pi:V(G)\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and its \(i\)-th prefix is \(L_i^\pi=\{v\in V(G):\pi(v)\le i\}\). Given a nonnegative cut-cost function \(\rho_G(X,V(G)\setminus X)\), define the width of \(\pi\) by \(w_\rho(\pi)=\max_{0\le i\le n}\rho_G(L_i^\pi,V(G)\setminus L_i^\pi)\). The corresponding layout-width parameter is \(w_\rho(G)=\min_\pi w_\rho(\pi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layout width chooses a vertex ordering and measures its worst prefix cut; the graph parameter is the smallest such worst-cut value over all orderings.
knowledge_statements.title: Layout-Width Parameters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordering-and-cut template is coherent and fits the leaf, but no source supports it as the intended taxonomy. Conditions on the cut-cost function and the treatment of endpoint cuts must be sourced for the claimed family definition.

children.title: Structural Graph Parameters
children.top_down_role: Graph-structure measures not primarily expressed as decomposition width.

assumptions_latex: Graphs are finite and considered up to isomorphism.
The parameter value is a computable nonnegative integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A structural graph parameter is an isomorphism-invariant map \(p\) used to index graph instances independently of their encoding.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the common invariant property, not a particular structural measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A structural graph parameter is a computable function \(p:\mathcal G\to\mathbb N\) on finite graphs satisfying \(G\cong H\Rightarrow p(G)=p(H)\). Thus \(p\) depends only on graph structure and not on vertex names or the chosen input encoding. In parameterized optimization on a graph instance \(G\), the running time is expressed as \(f(p(G))|G|^{O(1)}\). Typical structural parameters measure obstruction, sparsity, density, or distance to a designated graph class; each concrete choice requires its own defining predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural graph parameter is a computable integer invariant under graph isomorphism and used to isolate the graph feature governing an exact algorithm's nonpolynomial dependence.
knowledge_statements.title: Structural Graph Parameters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Isomorphism invariance defines a graph parameter generally, not specifically a structural graph parameter; the proposed definition would include essentially every computable graph invariant. A source is needed to establish the intended boundary from width, size, and other parameter families.

children.title: Width–Structure Comparability
children.top_down_role: Dominance, incomparability, and transfer relations among graph parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Width–Structure Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domination and equivalence of graph-structure parameters on a fixed instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be an instance class and let \(p,q:\mathcal I\to\mathbb N\) be structural parameters. Parameter \(p\) is dominated by \(q\), written \(p\preceq q\), if there exists a computable nondecreasing function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(p(I)\le f(q(I))\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\). The parameters are comparable if \(p\preceq q\) or \(q\preceq p\), equivalent if both relations hold, and incomparable if neither holds. A family on which \(q\) is bounded and \(p\) is unbounded certifies \(p\npreceq q\); analogous families in both directions therefore suffice to certify incomparability, but need not be necessary when the bounding functions are required to be computable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural parameters are comparable when one computably bounds the other, equivalent when both do, and incomparable when neither does. Opposing bounded-versus-unbounded families are sufficient certificates of incomparability.
assumptions_latex: \(p,q:\mathcal I\to\mathbb N\) are defined on the same instance class.
Bounding functions are computable and nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\preceq q\iff (\exists f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\text{ computable and nondecreasing})(\forall I\in\mathcal I)\;p(I)\le f(q(I))\).

notation.meaning: Parameter p is functionally dominated by q.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: functional domination is a standard comparison relation for parameterizations

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-to-Tractability Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance measured by admissible modifications into a polynomial-time solvable instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be an instance class, let \(\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal I\) be a tractable subclass, and let \(\mathcal O\) be a specified set of elementary modifications. For instances \(I,J\), let \(d_{\mathcal O}(I,J)\) be the minimum number of modifications from \(\mathcal O\) transforming \(I\) into \(J\), with value \(\infty\) if no transformation exists. The distance-to-tractability parameter is \(k_{\mathcal T,\mathcal O}(I)=\min_{J\in\mathcal T}d_{\mathcal O}(I,J)\). The modification model and tractable target class are part of the parameter definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The parameter is the fewest permitted modifications needed to transform an instance into a specified tractable class.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) admits polynomial-time solution for the problem under consideration.
\(\mathcal O\) fixes the allowed modification operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k_{\mathcal T,\mathcal O}(I)=0\iff I\in\mathcal T\), provided zero modifications preserve the instance.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distance to a tractable class is conventionally defined by a minimum modification set
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the topic, but no inspectable citation supports the modification-distance formulation.

children.title: Numeric-Magnitude Parameters
children.top_down_role: Parameters tied to values, weights, capacities, or encoded magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Numeric-Magnitude Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameters measuring coefficient or capacity magnitude rather than binary encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\) containing an integer data vector \(a(I)=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\), a numeric-magnitude parameter is a specified function of the numerical values, commonly \(M(I)=\max\{1,\lVert a(I)\rVert_\infty\}\). Under a standard binary representation, these integers require \(O(m\log(M(I)+1))\) bits, apart from representation metadata. Consequently, dependence polynomial in \(M(I)\) may be exponential in the binary input length. The parameter definition must identify the included data, such as weights, costs, capacities, or right-hand sides, and the convention for zero or absent values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numeric-magnitude parameter measures values such as maximum weight or capacity, which can be exponentially larger than the number of bits used to encode them.
assumptions_latex: The selected numerical input data are integers encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(I)=\max\{1,\max_{1\le i\le m}|a_i|\}\), and the selected integers use \(O(m\log(M(I)+1))\) bits.

notation.meaning: Selected integer data of the instance.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: maximum coefficient magnitude is a standard numerical parameter

children.title: Dimension Parameters
children.top_down_role: Parameters measuring geometric, algebraic, logical, or representation dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameters counting independent coordinates, variables, constraints, or other problem dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each instance \(I\) specify a finite-dimensional model with variable index set \(V(I)\), constraint index set \(C(I)\), or ambient space \(\mathbb R^{d(I)}\). A dimension parameter is one explicitly selected count, for example \(k(I)=|V(I)|\), \(k(I)=|C(I)|\), or \(k(I)=d(I)\). These choices are distinct parameterizations and must not be conflated. An exact algorithm is fixed-parameter tractable in the chosen dimension when its running time is \(f(k(I))|I|^{O(1)}\) for a computable function \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension parameter is a specified count of variables, constraints, coordinates, or another independent modeling dimension.
assumptions_latex: Each instance has the selected finite index set or finite-dimensional ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k(I)\in\{|V(I)|,|C(I)|,d(I)\}\) only after one choice is fixed as the parameterization.

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of the instance.

source_refs.locator: Hulls, Independence, Dimension p. 3

review_flags: locator supports dimension terminology but parameterized-complexity formulation needs dedicated sourcing

source_witnesses.locator: Hulls, Independence, Dimension p. 3

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the cited locator supports geometric dimension terminology rather than the stated parameterized-complexity formulation. A dedicated source is needed.

children.title: Domain-Size Parameters
children.top_down_role: Parameters measuring the cardinality of an underlying value or label domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Size Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameters bounding the number of admissible values per decision variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance \(I\) have variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), where variable \(x_i\) ranges over a finite explicitly specified domain \(D_i(I)\). The maximum domain-size parameter is \(q(I)=\max_{1\le i\le n}|D_i(I)|\); alternatively, a uniform-domain formulation may use \(q(I)=|D(I)|\). Domain size is distinct from the number of variables and from the bit length needed to name domain elements. Any parameterized analysis must state whether domains are explicit, implicit, or accessible through an oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The domain-size parameter is the largest number of allowed values for any variable, under a specified domain representation.
assumptions_latex: Every variable has a finite domain.
The representation of each domain is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(I)=\max_{1\le i\le n}|D_i(I)|\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: maximum finite-domain cardinality is the conventional domain-size parameter
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-domain definition is precise and appropriate, but it has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Encoding-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Boundaries created by unary, binary, explicit, or succinct representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating dependence on numerical values from dependence on their encoded length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(I)\) be a positive integer appearing in a binary-encoded instance and let \(L(I)=\lceil\log_2(M(I)+1)\rceil\). A running-time bound \(|I|^{O(1)}M(I)^{O(1)}\) is pseudopolynomial rather than necessarily polynomial in the binary input length. For the family \(M(I)=2^{L(I)}-1\), every fixed positive power of \(M(I)\) is exponential in \(L(I)\). Thus tractability expressed through numeric magnitude does not automatically imply tractability expressed through encoding length. Unary encoding removes this particular exponential separation because representing \(M(I)\) then requires length proportional to \(M(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial dependence on a binary-encoded value can be exponential in its bit length, which is the pseudopolynomial boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(M(I)\) is a positive integer encoded in binary unless stated otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(I)=2^{L(I)}-1\Rightarrow M(I)^c=(2^{L(I)}-1)^c=2^{\Theta(L(I))}\) for every constant \(c>0\).

notation.meaning: Binary length of the magnitude under the declared convention.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the binary-value versus bit-length separation is the standard pseudopolynomial boundary

children.title: Above-Guarantee Parameters
children.top_down_role: Parameters measuring improvement beyond a guaranteed baseline.

knowledge_statements.title: Above-Guarantee Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterization of an integer-valued maximization threshold by improvement over a guaranteed baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an integer-valued maximization problem with optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\in\mathbb Z\) and a polynomial-time computable integer-valued guarantee \(g(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). For an integer target \(t\ge g(I)\), the above-guarantee parameter is \(k=t-g(I)\in\mathbb N\). The associated decision question asks whether \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge g(I)+k\). The guarantee is part of the parameterization; if a nonintegral bound is used, its rounding rule must first produce a valid integer-valued guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integer-valued maximization problem, the parameter is the requested improvement above a computable integral lower guarantee on the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(I),g(I),t\in\mathbb Z\).
\(g(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every instance.
\(g(I)\) is polynomial-time computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k=t-g(I)\in\mathbb N\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge t\iff\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge g(I)+k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: above-guarantee parameterization uses target minus a valid maximization guarantee

children.title: Below-Guarantee Parameters
children.top_down_role: Parameters measuring shortfall relative to a guaranteed or extremal reference.

knowledge_statements.title: Below-Guarantee Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterization of an integer-valued minimization threshold by improvement below a guaranteed baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an integer-valued minimization problem with optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\in\mathbb Z\) and a polynomial-time computable integer-valued guarantee \(g(I)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). For an integer target \(t\le g(I)\), the below-guarantee parameter is \(k=g(I)-t\in\mathbb N\). The associated decision question asks whether \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le g(I)-k\). The guarantee is part of the parameterization; if a nonintegral bound is used, its rounding rule must first produce a valid integer-valued guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integer-valued minimization problem, the parameter is the requested improvement below a computable integral upper guarantee on the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(I),g(I),t\in\mathbb Z\).
\(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le g(I)\) for every instance.
\(g(I)\) is polynomial-time computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k=g(I)-t\in\mathbb N\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le t\iff\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le g(I)-k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: below-guarantee parameterization uses a valid minimization guarantee minus the target

children.title: Guarantee Selection
children.top_down_role: Choice of baseline and its effect on parameterized structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Guarantee Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity conditions for a baseline used in guarantee-relative parameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer-valued optimization problem on an instance class \(\mathcal I\), a function \(g:\mathcal I\to\mathbb Z\) is admissible as a guarantee-relative baseline when it is polynomial-time computable from the instance alone, is fixed uniformly over \(\mathcal I\), and has the correct direction: \(g(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for maximization or \(g(I)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for minimization. For an allowed integer target \(t\), define \(k(I,t)=t-g(I)\) in the maximization case and \(k(I,t)=g(I)-t\) in the minimization case, with the target restricted so that \(k(I,t)\ge0\). A target-dependent expression is not a baseline under this convention, and any proposed baseline whose evaluation requires solving a computationally hard optimization task fails the polynomial-time computability condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected baseline must be uniform, target-independent, polynomial-time computable, valid in the correct direction, and produce a nonnegative integral gap for allowed targets.
assumptions_latex: The optimization direction, integer objective convention, and allowed targets are fixed over \(\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\text{ admissible}\Rightarrow g\in\mathrm{FP}\text{ and }k(I,t)\in\mathbb N\) for every allowed \((I,t)\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative target-to-guarantee gap in the applicable optimization direction.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: validity, computability, uniformity, and target independence are natural conditions for a guarantee-relative baseline

children.title: Baseline Degeneracy Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where a weak, unstable, or inaccessible baseline destroys useful parameter sensitivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Baseline Degeneracy Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by baselines that collapse a hard parameterized problem or conceal hard computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\) be NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions and let \(k:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) be a parameter. If \(k(x)=0\) for every input \(x\), then an algorithm for \(Q\) with running time \(f(k(x))|x|^{O(1)}\) would run in polynomial time; hence such a parameterization is not fixed-parameter tractable unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Separately, a target-dependent expression is not an instance-only baseline under the guarantee-selection convention, while a baseline whose evaluation requires solving an NP-hard optimization task violates the required polynomial-time computability condition unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter is degenerate when it collapses an NP-hard problem to a constant value; target-dependent expressions and computationally hard baselines violate separate baseline-selection conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
The parameter and any selected baseline are required to be polynomial-time computable from the parameterized input under the adopted convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall x)\;k(x)=0\ \land\ Q\in\mathrm{FPT}[k]\Rightarrow\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: Parameter value assigned to input x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: an NP-hard constant parameter slice excludes FPT unless P equals NP

children.title: Combined Parameter Tuples
children.top_down_role: Multivariate parameterizations retaining several coordinates explicitly.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Parameter Tuples
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector parameterization retaining every selected component value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given parameter functions \(k_1,\ldots,k_r:\mathcal I\to\mathbb N\) for fixed \(r\), their combined parameter is the tuple \(\boldsymbol{k}(I)=(k_1(I),\ldots,k_r(I))\in\mathbb N^r\), ordered componentwise when comparisons are required. A problem is fixed-parameter tractable for this tuple if some computable function \(f:\mathbb N^r\to\mathbb N\) and constant \(c\) yield running time \(f(\boldsymbol{k}(I))|I|^c\). The tuple retains each component and therefore permits arbitrary computable joint dependence without committing to an aggregation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A combined parameter is the vector of selected component parameters; FPT permits arbitrary computable dependence on the whole vector.
assumptions_latex: The number \(r\) of component parameters is fixed independently of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\boldsymbol{k}(I)=(k_1(I),\ldots,k_r(I))\quad\text{and}\quad T(I)\le f(\boldsymbol{k}(I))|I|^c\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: multidimensional parameterizations are represented by fixed-length tuples
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-length tuple definition and vector-valued FPT bound fit the leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Aggregate Parameters
children.top_down_role: Scalar parameterizations formed by combining several measurements.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar parameterization obtained by aggregating several component parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k_1,\ldots,k_r:\mathcal I\to\mathbb N\) be component parameters and let \(h:\mathbb N^r\to\mathbb N\) be a fixed computable aggregation function. The associated aggregate parameter is \(a(I)=h(k_1(I),\ldots,k_r(I))\). Typical choices include \(\sum_{i=1}^r k_i(I)\) and \(\max_{1\le i\le r}k_i(I)\). Unlike the tuple, an aggregate may identify distinct component vectors. A sufficient condition for every computable tuple-dependent FPT bound to be expressible as an aggregate-dependent bound is that, for each component, there is a computable function \(\phi_i\) satisfying \(k_i(I)\le\phi_i(a(I))\) for all \(I\in\mathcal I\). A particular algorithm may transfer under weaker conditions when its dependence ignores information lost by the aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An aggregate parameter compresses several component values into one scalar. Computable bounds on every component are sufficient for transferring arbitrary tuple-based FPT dependence, though particular algorithms may need less information.
assumptions_latex: \(r\) is fixed and \(h\) is computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a(I)=h(k_1(I),\ldots,k_r(I))\), and \((\forall i)(\exists\phi_i\text{ computable})(\forall I)\;k_i(I)\le\phi_i(a(I))\) is a sufficient transfer condition.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scalar composition by a computable aggregation function is a standard aggregate construction

children.title: Aggregation Functions
children.top_down_role: Maximum, sum, product, lexicographic, and related aggregation choices.

assumptions_latex: The instance domain is a decidable set \(X\subseteq\Sigma^*\).
The component parameters are total computable maps \(\kappa_i:X\to\mathbb N\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\).
The aggregation map \(g:\mathbb N^d\to\mathbb N\) is total and computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composite map \(\kappa_g=g\circ(\kappa_1,\ldots,\kappa_d)\) is a parameterization of \(X\).

notation.meaning: Aggregation function and induced aggregate parameter

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines scalar aggregation of a finite parameter tuple; monotonicity is optional and must be imposed separately when required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\Sigma^*\), let \(\kappa_i:X\to\mathbb N\) be total computable parameters for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\), and let \(g:\mathbb N^d\to\mathbb N\) be total and computable. The aggregation function \(g\) induces the scalar parameter
\[
\kappa_g(x)=g\bigl(\kappa_1(x),\ldots,\kappa_d(x)\bigr)\qquad(x\in X).
\]
If comparisons of componentwise larger tuples must never decrease the aggregate, one additionally requires \(u_i\le v_i\) for every \(i\) to imply \(g(u)\le g(v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computable function combines a finite tuple of computable parameters into one scalar parameter; componentwise monotonicity is an additional, application-dependent requirement.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the aggregation convention or the optional monotonicity distinction.

children.title: Information-Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where aggregation conceals parameter interactions needed for useful analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Loss Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when scalar aggregation loses the boundedness information needed to transfer parameter-dependent guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\Sigma^*\), let \(\boldsymbol\kappa:X\to\mathbb N^d\), and let \(g:\mathbb N^d\to\mathbb N\) be total and computable, with \(\lambda=g\circ\boldsymbol\kappa\). Coordinate \(i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\) is bounded by the aggregate if there exists a function \(h:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(\kappa_i(x)\le h(\lambda(x))\) for every \(x\in X\). An information-loss boundary for coordinate \(i\) occurs when there exists \(t\in\mathbb N\) such that the set \(g^{-1}(t)\cap\boldsymbol\kappa(X)\) has unbounded \(i\)-th coordinate; in that case no such function \(h\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregation loses boundedness information about a coordinate when one aggregate value represents realizable parameter tuples with unbounded values in that coordinate; the coordinate then cannot be bounded from the aggregate alone.
assumptions_latex: The instance domain is \(X\subseteq\Sigma^*\).
The parameter tuple is \(\boldsymbol\kappa:X\to\mathbb N^d\).
The scalar aggregation is \(\lambda=g\circ\boldsymbol\kappa\) for a total computable map \(g:\mathbb N^d\to\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If some realizable fiber \(g^{-1}(t)\cap\boldsymbol\kappa(X)\) has unbounded \(i\)-th coordinate, then no function \(h:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) satisfies \(\kappa_i(x)\le h(\lambda(x))\) for every \(x\in X\).

assumptions_latex: The parameterized decision problem is \((L,\kappa)\), where \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) and \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) is total and computable.
Running time is measured on a deterministic machine as a function of input length \(n=|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is fixed-parameter tractable precisely when it is decidable in time \(f(\kappa(x))n^c\) for some computable \(f\) and constant \(c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard uniform deterministic definition of the class FPT for decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A parameterized decision problem \((L,\kappa)\), with \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) and total computable \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\), is fixed-parameter tractable if there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\), a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), and a constant \(c\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every \(x\in\Sigma^*\), algorithm \(A\) decides whether \(x\in L\) within time
\[
f(\kappa(x))\,|x|^c.
\]
The algorithm and exponent are uniform over all parameter values; only the multiplicative factor may depend arbitrarily, but computably, on \(\kappa(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem is fixed-parameter tractable when one uniform algorithm solves it in parameter-dependent time times a polynomial whose exponent is independent of the parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Parameter Tractability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a mathematically standard uniform deterministic definition of FPT and fits the container, but it has no cited authoritative source or locator.

assumptions_latex: The parameterized problem is \((L,\kappa)\), with slices \(L_k=\{x\in L:\kappa(x)=k\}\).
Each slice is considered as an ordinary language over \(\Sigma^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Slice-wise polynomial tractability requires each \(L_k\) to be decidable in polynomial time, while allowing its algorithm and polynomial degree to depend on \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the literal nonuniform slice-by-slice notion, weaker than the standard uniform definition of XP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\in\mathbb N\), define the slice \(L_k=\{x\in L:\kappa(x)=k\}\). The parameterized problem \((L,\kappa)\) is slice-wise polynomially tractable if, for every fixed \(k\), there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_k\) and constants \(a_k,c_k\in\mathbb N\) such that \(A_k\) decides membership in \(L_k\) within time \(a_k|x|^{c_k}\). No effective procedure producing \(A_k\), \(a_k\), or \(c_k\) from \(k\) is required. Consequently, both the algorithm and polynomial degree may vary noncomputably across slices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every fixed-parameter slice has some polynomial-time decision algorithm, but the algorithms, constants, and degrees need not be generated uniformly from the parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Slice-Wise Polynomial Tractability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record consistently defines a nonuniform slice-by-slice notion, but the title is not universally standardized and may be confused with uniform XP. A source must establish the intended terminology and quantifiers.

children.title: Uniform Parameterized Regimes
children.top_down_role: Algorithm families represented by a single effective procedure across parameter values.

assumptions_latex: The parameterized problem is \((L,\kappa)\).
A resource bound \(R(n,k)\) is fixed for the regime under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniformity requires one effective algorithm to meet \(R(|x|,\kappa(x))\) simultaneously for every input and parameter value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines uniformity independently of the particular time or space bound used by a parameterized regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a resource measure and a bound \(R:\mathbb N^2\to\mathbb N\). A parameterized regime for \((L,\kappa)\) is uniform if there exists one finite deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that, for every \(x\in\Sigma^*\), \(A\) decides whether \(x\in L\) using at most \(R(|x|,\kappa(x))\) units of the resource. The same transition rules operate for all parameter values, and every parameter-dependent function appearing in an effective bound must be computable. Thus uniformity concerns effective global realization, not merely the existence of a suitable algorithm on each fixed slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized regime is uniform when one effective algorithm handles every parameter value within the stated parameter-dependent resource bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Parameterized Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the uniform-regime leaf, but no source or exact locator supports this resource-independent formulation, including its computability requirement for parameter-dependent bounds.

children.title: Nonuniform Parameterized Regimes
children.top_down_role: Slice-specific algorithm families lacking a shared effective construction.

assumptions_latex: The slices are \(L_k=\{x\in L:\kappa(x)=k\}\).
A family of slice bounds \(R_k:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) is specified existentially.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonuniform membership permits a separate algorithm \(A_k\) for each slice without requiring an effective map \(k\mapsto A_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates existential slice algorithms from any effective procedure that constructs them from the parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized regime for \((L,\kappa)\) is nonuniform when its membership condition has the form: for every \(k\in\mathbb N\), there exists a finite algorithm \(A_k\) deciding the slice \(L_k=\{x\in L:\kappa(x)=k\}\) within the prescribed bound \(R_k(|x|)\). The definition does not require the map \(k\mapsto A_k\), or the constants encoded in \(R_k\), to be computable. Hence all slices may satisfy the same qualitative resource restriction even though no single effective algorithm realizes the family over arbitrary \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonuniform regime gives each parameter slice its own bounded-resource algorithm without requiring those algorithms or their constants to be computably obtainable from the parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniform Parameterized Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantifier structure clearly describes a nonuniform slice family and fits the leaf, but the generic prescribed-bound convention needs an authoritative source and exact locator.

children.title: Uniformity Transfer Conditions
children.top_down_role: Conditions supporting passage from slice-wise behavior to a uniform algorithmic regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniformity Transfer Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives sufficient effectivity conditions for converting a slice-indexed algorithm family into one uniform algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) and let \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) be total and computable. For each \(k\in\mathbb N\), let \(A_k\) decide the slice \(L_k=\{x\in L:\kappa(x)=k\}\). The family \((A_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) admits a uniform realization if there is a total computable compiler \(C\) such that \(C(k)\) encodes \(A_k\), the slice resource bounds have a computable common envelope \(R:\mathbb N^2\to\mathbb N\), and universal simulation in the fixed machine model has computably bounded overhead. Under these conditions, one algorithm computes \(k=\kappa(x)\), obtains \(C(k)\), and simulates \(A_k\) on \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slice-indexed algorithm family becomes uniform when the parameter is computable, the slice algorithms and their resource envelope are computably obtainable from it, and universal-simulation overhead is computably controlled.
assumptions_latex: The language is \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\), and \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) is total and computable.
For every \(k\in\mathbb N\), an algorithm \(A_k\) decides the slice \(L_k=\{x\in L:\kappa(x)=k\}\).
There is a total computable compiler \(C\) with \(C(k)\) encoding \(A_k\).
The slice resource bounds admit a computable common envelope \(R:\mathbb N^2\to\mathbb N\), and the fixed universal simulator has computably bounded overhead.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists one uniform decider for \(L\), with resource use bounded by a computable function of \(R(|x|,\kappa(x))\), \(|C(\kappa(x))|\), and the fixed simulator overhead.

children.title: Effectivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits caused by unavailable, noncomputable, or excessively costly slice information.

knowledge_statements.title: Effectivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete undecidability construction separates nonuniform slice tractability from effective uniform decidability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb N\) be undecidable. Fix an effective encoding \(e:\mathbb N\to\Sigma^*\) whose range \(X=e(\mathbb N)\) is decidable, and define \(\kappa(e(k))=k\) and \(L_S=\{e(k):k\in S\}\subseteq X\). For every fixed \(k\in\mathbb N\), the domain slice \(X_k=\{x\in X:\kappa(x)=k\}=\{e(k)\}\) admits a constant-output decider for membership in \(L_S\). Nevertheless, no single algorithm decides \(L_S\) on all of \(X\). Thus existentially trivial slice algorithms need not form an effective uniform family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undecidable set can index singleton domain slices, each having a constant-output membership algorithm, while no uniform algorithm decides the resulting language across all slices.
assumptions_latex: The set \(S\subseteq\mathbb N\) is undecidable.
The map \(e:\mathbb N\to\Sigma^*\) is an effective encoding with decidable range \(X=e(\mathbb N)\).
The parameter is \(\kappa(e(k))=k\), and the language is \(L_S=\{e(k):k\in S\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every domain slice \(X_k\) has a constant-output membership decider for \(L_S\cap X_k\), but no uniform algorithm decides \(L_S\) on \(X\).

notation.meaning: Language induced by the index set
Parameter map on the instance domain

assumptions_latex: The parameterized problem is \((L,\kappa)\), and \(n=|x|\).
Workspace excludes the read-only input and output tapes under the standard deterministic-machine convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parameterized space regimes are classified by bounds \(s(n,k)\), notably \(f(k)+O(\log n)\), \(f(k)\log n\), and \(f(k)n^{O(1)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records common deterministic workspace forms without assigning potentially nonstandard class names.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deterministic parameterized space regime consists of problems \((L,\kappa)\) decidable by one algorithm whose work-tape usage on input \(x\) is at most \(s(|x|,\kappa(x))\). Common bounds include parameterized logarithmic space \(f(\kappa(x))+O(\log |x|)\), multiplicative parameterized logspace \(f(\kappa(x))\log |x|\), and fixed-parameter polynomial space \(f(\kappa(x))|x|^c\), where \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) is total computable and \(c\) is constant. The machine convention must specify whether input, output, and auxiliary parameter storage are counted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameterized space complexity bounds workspace jointly by input length and parameter, with additive logspace, multiplicative logspace, and fixed-parameter polynomial-space forms among common regimes.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Space Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record appropriately describes space regimes rather than assigning class names, but the asserted list of common bounds and workspace conventions varies across the literature and needs an authoritative source with an exact locator.

children.title: Parameter Dominance
children.top_down_role: Functional control of one parameter by another over a problem class.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses functional domination: the dominating parameter computably bounds the dominated parameter on the stated instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\Sigma^*\) and let \(p,q:X\to\mathbb N\) be parameterizations. Parameter \(q\) dominates \(p\) on \(X\), written \(p\preceq_X q\), if there exists a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(p(x)\le f(q(x))\) for every \(x\in X\). Under this convention, \(\preceq_X\) is the computable functional-domination preorder on parameters over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter q dominates p on X when a total computable function of q bounds p on every instance in X; this defines the selected functional-domination preorder.
assumptions_latex: The instance class is \(X\subseteq\Sigma^*\).
The maps \(p,q:X\to\mathbb N\) are parameterizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parameter \(q\) dominates \(p\) on \(X\) exactly when there exists a total computable \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) satisfying \(p(x)\le f(q(x))\) for every \(x\in X\).

children.title: Parameter Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Mutual control supporting comparable parameterized classifications.

assumptions_latex: The instance class is \(X\subseteq\Sigma^*\).
The maps \(p,q:X\to\mathbb N\) are parameterizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parameters \(p\) and \(q\) are equivalent on \(X\) exactly when each computably bounds the other.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines equivalence as mutual computable domination on a fixed instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For parameterizations \(p,q:X\to\mathbb N\), define \(p\equiv_X q\) if both \(p\preceq_X q\) and \(q\preceq_X p\). Equivalently, there exist total computable functions \(f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that
\[
p(x)\le f(q(x))\quad\text{and}\quad q(x)\le g(p(x))
\]
for every \(x\in X\). This is the equivalence relation induced by the domination preorder. Parameters in the same equivalence class carry the same computable boundedness information, although their numerical values and the resulting explicit running-time functions may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two parameters are equivalent when each is bounded by a computable function of the other on the same instance class.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Equivalence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Mutual computable domination is a coherent definition of parameter equivalence and fits the leaf, but it inherits the unresolved orientation convention and has no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Parameter Incomparability
children.top_down_role: Instance families witnessing the absence of mutual parameter control.

assumptions_latex: The instance class is \(X\subseteq\Sigma^*\).
The maps \(p,q:X\to\mathbb N\) are parameterizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parameters \(p\) and \(q\) are incomparable on \(X\) when neither \(p\preceq_X q\) nor \(q\preceq_X p\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses failure of computable domination in both directions on the full stated instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Parameterizations \(p,q:X\to\mathbb N\) are incomparable on \(X\) if neither dominates the other: there is no total computable \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) satisfying \(p(x)\le f(q(x))\) for all \(x\in X\), and there is no total computable \(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) satisfying \(q(x)\le g(p(x))\) for all \(x\in X\). Equivalently, for every total computable \(f\) some instance violates the first bound, and for every total computable \(g\) some instance violates the reverse bound. Comparability may reappear after restricting \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two parameters are incomparable when neither can be bounded by any computable function of the other across the full instance class.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Incomparability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and its explicit quantifiers correctly express incomparability relative to the stated preorder, but the underlying dominance convention and terminology require a cited source with an exact locator.

children.title: Restricted-Class Comparability
children.top_down_role: Parameter relations that hold only on designated structural subclasses.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Class Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of integer-valued parameters only on a specified instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an instance set, let \(\mathcal C\subseteq I\), and let \(\kappa,\lambda:I\to\mathbb N\) be computable parameters. Define \(\kappa\preceq_{\mathcal C}\lambda\) when there exists a computable nondecreasing function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(\kappa(x)\leq f(\lambda(x))\) for every \(x\in\mathcal C\). The parameters are comparable on \(\mathcal C\) when \(\kappa\preceq_{\mathcal C}\lambda\) or \(\lambda\preceq_{\mathcal C}\kappa\). This comparison need not extend to instances outside \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One parameter is bounded by another on a restricted class if a computable monotone function transforms the latter into a uniform upper bound for the former.
assumptions_latex: \(\kappa,\lambda:I\to\mathbb N\) are computable.
\(\mathcal C\subseteq I\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa\preceq_{\mathcal C}\lambda\iff (\exists f)(\forall x\in\mathcal C)\,\kappa(x)\leq f(\lambda(x))\).

notation.meaning: parameter domination restricted to the class C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator supports this particular restricted domination convention.

children.title: Parameter Tuple Design
children.top_down_role: Selection of complementary coordinates for multivariate analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Tuple Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility conditions for a multivariate parameterization used in exact running-time bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For instances \(x\in I\), a parameter tuple is a computable map \(K=(\kappa_1,\ldots,\kappa_r):I\to\mathbb N^r\), where \(r\) is fixed independently of \(x\). It is admissible for an exact algorithm \(A\) when every coordinate is computable in time polynomial in \(|x|\) and there exist a computable function \(F:\mathbb N^r\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) and a constant \(c\) such that \(A\) solves every \(x\in I\) in time at most \(F(K(x))|x|^c\). Coordinate order and interpretation are fixed throughout the analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter tuple has fixed dimension, polynomial-time computable coordinates, and supports a uniform multivariate fixed-parameter running-time bound.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is an encoded instance class.
\(A\) is an exact algorithm on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_A(x)\leq F(\kappa_1(x),\ldots,\kappa_r(x))|x|^c\) for every \(x\in I\).

notation.meaning: running time of algorithm A on x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits parameter-tuple design, but polynomial-time coordinate computability and the stated admissibility convention require a supporting source.

children.title: Parameter Substitution
children.top_down_role: Replacement of one coordinate by another under explicit control relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Substitution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of a multivariate running-time bound through coordinatewise parameter bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:I\to\mathbb N^r\) and \(L:I\to\mathbb N^s\) be parameter tuples. Suppose an exact algorithm has running time \(T(x)\leq F(K(x))|x|^c\), where \(F\) is coordinatewise nondecreasing. If computable functions \(g_i:\mathbb N^s\to\mathbb N\) satisfy \(\kappa_i(x)\leq g_i(L(x))\) for every \(x\in I\) and every \(i\), then substitution yields \(T(x)\leq F(g_1(L(x)),\ldots,g_r(L(x)))|x|^c\). Thus fixed-parameter tractability transfers whenever the composed bound is computable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinatewise bounds permit one parameter tuple to replace another inside any monotone multivariate running-time bound.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb N^r\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) is coordinatewise nondecreasing.
\(\kappa_i(x)\leq g_i(L(x))\) holds uniformly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(x)\leq (F\circ(g_1,\ldots,g_r))(L(x))|x|^c\).

notation.meaning: bound replacing the ith original coordinate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotone substitution argument is precise and the content kind fits, but the record has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Pareto Parameter Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Running-time or preprocessing tradeoffs with no uniformly superior parameter choice.

knowledge_statements.title: Pareto Parameter Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto order on attainable resource bounds indexed by a fixed parameter tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a parameter domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb N^r\) and resource bounds \(R_A:D\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}^q\) for exact algorithms \(A\) solving the same problem. Algorithm \(A\) weakly dominates \(B\) on \(D\) when \(R_A(z)\leq R_B(z)\) coordinatewise for every \(z\in D\). It strictly dominates \(B\) when weak dominance holds and the inequality is strict in at least one resource coordinate for some \(z\in D\). An attainable bound is Pareto-optimal if no other attainable bound strictly dominates it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource bound is Pareto-optimal when no competing exact algorithm is uniformly no worse and somewhere strictly better over the chosen parameter domain.
assumptions_latex: All compared algorithms solve the same problem exactly.
Resources use a common parameter domain and cost model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_A\) is Pareto-optimal iff no attainable \(R_B\) strictly dominates \(R_A\) on \(D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto definition is internally consistent and locally appropriate, but no source supports its parameterized-algorithm formulation.

children.title: Tradeoff Regime Changes
children.top_down_role: Instance regions where the preferred parameter combination changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Tradeoff Regime Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Switching loci in the lower envelope of competing parameter-dependent bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1,\ldots,T_m:D\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) be valid running-time bounds on a parameter domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb N^r\). The best available bound is the lower envelope \(T_*(z)=\min_{1\leq j\leq m}T_j(z)\). The regime of algorithm \(j\) is \(D_j=\{z\in D:T_j(z)=T_*(z)\}\). A tradeoff regime change between algorithms \(i\) and \(j\) can occur only on the switching locus where \(T_i(z)=T_j(z)=T_*(z)\); crossing that locus changes which bound attains the minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Competing parameterized bounds form a lower envelope; regime changes occur where two minimizing bounds coincide and exchange which one is smaller.
assumptions_latex: \(T_1,\ldots,T_m\) use the same computation model.
\(D\) is the common parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_*(z)=\min_jT_j(z)\), with switching possible only where \(T_i(z)=T_j(z)=T_*(z)\).

notation.meaning: regime where bound j attains the envelope

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-envelope representation fits the leaf and is mathematically coherent, but it lacks an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Degenerate Parameterizations
children.top_down_role: Parameters that collapse, remain constant, or encode little useful instance variation.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Parameterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameters whose bounded slices or induced running-time claims carry no useful structural restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance class \(I\), call a computable parameter \(\kappa:I\to\mathbb N\) degenerate for structural algorithm analysis if either \(\kappa\) is bounded by a constant on all of \(I\), or every slice \(I_t=\{x\in I:\kappa(x)leq t\}\) eventually contains unrestricted instances of arbitrarily large encoding length. In the first case an \(f(\kappa)|x|^{O(1)}\) bound collapses to polynomial time on all instances; in the second, bounded parameter values do not isolate the intended structural restriction. Any tractability claim must therefore be interpreted against the complexity of these slices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter is degenerate when fixing it imposes no intended structural restriction, so the resulting parameterized classification is trivial or misleading.
assumptions_latex: \(\kappa:I\to\mathbb N\) is computable.
Complexity is measured on parameter slices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded values of \(\kappa\) fail to define informative restricted instance families.

notation.meaning: instances whose parameter value is at most t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Arbitrarily large instances in every bounded slice do not imply degeneracy; meaningful parameters such as treewidth can have that property. The phrase 'unrestricted instances' is undefined, and the slice formula contains malformed LaTeX. The proposed failure boundary therefore cannot be repaired mechanically without replacing its mathematical criterion.

children.title: Input-Size Parameters
children.top_down_role: Parameter choices that merely reproduce unrestricted input-size dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Input-Size Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why parameterizing solely by total input length gives a vacuous fixed-parameter classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n(x)=|x|\) be the encoding length of an instance. Every decidable problem with running time \(T(n)\) is formally fixed-parameter tractable under the parameter \(\kappa(x)=n(x)\): choose \(f(k)=T(k)\), giving \(T(|x|)=f(\kappa(x))|x|^0\). Hence parameterization by total input size distinguishes no decidable problems and supplies no algorithmic information beyond ordinary input-size complexity. It is therefore a failure boundary for claims intended to expose tractability caused by a secondary structural quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using total input length as the parameter makes every decidable problem formally fixed-parameter tractable and therefore yields no structural classification.
assumptions_latex: The problem is decidable by an algorithm with worst-case time \(T(n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(|x|)=f(\kappa(x))\) for \(f(k)=T(k)\), so the parameterized classification is vacuous.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vacuity claim for parameterization by total encoding length is standard and correctly scoped, but no parameterized-complexity source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Answer-Encoding Parameters
children.top_down_role: Parameters whose values directly conceal the desired outcome or witness.

knowledge_statements.title: Answer-Encoding Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameters derived from a solution encoding can conceal the computational work needed to find that solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an encoded instance class, let \(y^*:I\to Y\) select a canonical optimal solution, and define \(\kappa(x)=|\operatorname{enc}(y^*(x))|\). Although this map can define a mathematical parameter, it is not operationally available from the input when evaluating \(\kappa(x)\) requires recovering \(y^*(x)\) or solving a computationally equivalent search or optimization task. Consequently, a bound \(f(\kappa(x))|x|^{O(1)}\) does not by itself make \(\kappa\) usable for preprocessing, instance selection, or empirical prediction. A short solution encoding also does not imply a small search space or low verification cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter based on the unknown answer may be unusable operationally because evaluating it can require solving the original problem.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is an encoded instance class.
\(y^*:I\to Y\) selects a canonical optimal solution.
\(\operatorname{enc}:Y\to\{0,1\}^*\) is a fixed encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If computing \(\kappa(x)\) requires recovering \(y^*(x)\) or solving an equivalent task, then answer length is not an operationally available input parameter.

notation.meaning: encoding length of the canonical optimal solution

children.title: Promise-Driven Misclassification
children.top_down_role: Apparently favorable classifications caused by overly restrictive or unstable instance promises.

knowledge_statements.title: Promise-Driven Misclassification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tractability obtained only after restricting instances by a promise absent from the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an unrestricted instance class, let \(P\subsetneq I\) be a promised subclass, and let \(\kappa:I\to\mathbb N\) be a parameter. If an algorithm is required to be correct only for inputs \(x\in P\), with its behavior on \(I\setminus P\) unrestricted, then an \(f(\kappa(x))|x|^c\) running-time guarantee classifies only the parameterized promise problem on \(P\). It does not establish fixed-parameter tractability on all of \(I\). Extension to the unrestricted problem requires correctness and the same form of running-time bound for every \(x\in I\setminus P\) as well.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPT result under a promise classifies only the promise problem, not the unrestricted problem, unless correctness and complexity extend outside the promise.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subsetneq I\) is the promised input class.
\(\kappa:I\to\mathbb N\) is a parameter.
The stated guarantee is proved only for \(x\in P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-parameter tractability on \(P\) does not imply fixed-parameter tractability on \(I\).

children.title: Bounded Search-Tree Reduction Calculus
children.top_down_role: Parameter-decreasing search, safe local simplification, and analyses indexed by the parameter rather than primarily by total input size.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Elementary positive techniques; measure and conquer

knowledge_statements.title: Include–Exclude Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary bounded-search-tree scheme for a pivot with exhaustive inclusion and exclusion cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a partial state \((P,X,k)\) for an exact subset problem, where \(P\) is forced into the solution, \(X\) is forbidden, and \(k\) is the remaining budget or measure. Apply safe reductions; reject if feasibility or the budget is violated, and output \(P\) if it is a complete feasible solution. Otherwise choose an undecided pivot \(v\). Recurse on an include child that adds \(v\) to \(P\) and on an exclude child that adds \(v\) to \(X\), applying all required state updates in each child. Correctness requires the feasible completions of the parent to be exactly the union of the feasible completions represented by the two children.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an undecided object and recurse on exhaustive cases that force it into or out of the solution, applying reductions and budget checks in each child.
assumptions_latex: Solutions are subsets of a finite ground set.
\(P\cap X=\varnothing\).
Child updates preserve exactly the completions consistent with their respective decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parent state is feasible if and only if at least one of its include and exclude children is feasible.

knowledge_statements.title: Obstruction-Driven Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching on an explicit local witness that prevents the current state from being feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a reduced instance-state pair \((x,k)\), find an obstruction \(O\) whose presence certifies that the current state is not terminally feasible. Construct a finite action set \(B(O)=\{a_1,\ldots,a_r\}\) such that every feasible solution realizes at least one action in \(B(O)\). For each \(a_i\), apply the action to obtain \((x_i,k-\delta_i)\), exhaust safe reductions, and recurse. Reject children with negative measure, and accept when no obstruction remains and feasibility is verified. Correctness requires \(B(O)\) to be exhaustive, while termination requires \(\delta_i>0\) for every recursive child.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a forbidden local structure and branch over a finite exhaustive set of actions by which any solution must eliminate it.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb Z\) is a well-founded integer measure on nonrejected states.
A detectable obstruction characterizes nonterminal reduced states.
Every feasible solution realizes an action in \(B(O)\).
Each recursive branch has \(\delta_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state \((x,k)\) is feasible if and only if some reduced child \((x_i,k-\delta_i)\) is feasible.

children.title: Degree-Based Branching
children.top_down_role: Branch selection driven by vertex degree or analogous local frequency measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Based Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical maximum-degree branching rule for parameterized Vertex Cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Vertex Cover instance \((G,k)\), apply safe reductions and reject if \(k<0\); accept if \(E(G)=\varnothing\). Otherwise choose a vertex \(v\) of maximum degree \(d\). In the first branch, place \(v\) in the cover, producing \((G-v,k-1)\). In the second branch, exclude \(v\); every neighbor of \(v\) must then enter the cover, producing \((G-N[v],k-d)\). Return a cover reconstructed from a successful branch, or report failure if both branches fail. The parameter decreases are \((1,d)\), yielding \(T(k,n)\leq T(k-1,n)+T(k-d,n)+n^{O(1)}\), where \(n\) is the input size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Vertex Cover, branch on a maximum-degree vertex: either select it or select all its neighbors, decreasing the budget by one or its degree.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple graph.
\(k\in\mathbb Z\) is the remaining cover budget.
\(d=\deg_G(v)\) for the selected vertex \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The branching vector is \((1,d)\), and \(T(k,n)\leq T(k-1,n)+T(k-d,n)+n^{O(1)}\).

notation.meaning: encoding length of the current input instance

children.title: Neighborhood-Pattern Branching
children.top_down_role: Branch selection driven by open, closed, shared, or nested neighborhood structure.

assumptions_latex: The instance is a parameterized minimization state \((I,k)\) with a finite set of admissible local decisions.
Every feasible completion resolves each currently selected local obstruction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned search tree is exhaustive, and a root-to-leaf path yields a feasible solution of cost at most \(k\) exactly when one exists.

notation.meaning: branching alternatives determined by pattern P

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exhaustive branching on all locally admissible resolutions is standard bounded-search-tree methodology
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract branching rule parameterized by a finite rooted-neighborhood pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a state \((I,k)\), select a pivot \(v\), compute the rooted pattern \(P=I[N_r[v]]\), and construct a finite family \(\mathcal B(P)=\{(D_i,\delta_i):i\in[q]\}\). Each \(D_i\) is a locally consistent decision set, \(\delta_i\geq 1\) is its charged parameter decrease, and every feasible completion contains or induces at least one \(D_i\).
