Recursively solve the transformed states \((I\mid D_i,k-\delta_i)\), rejecting branches with negative parameter and accepting when a terminal feasibility test succeeds. Output the first accepting branch, or reject if all branches reject.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify a pivot’s bounded neighborhood, enumerate all locally exhaustive decisions for that pattern, decrease the parameter by each decision’s charge, and recursively search every resulting state.
knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Pattern Branching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the branching leaf, but correctness depends on a problem-specific definition of local consistency, transformation, charging, terminal feasibility, and proof that the listed decisions cover every feasible completion. No inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Degree–Neighborhood Interaction
children.top_down_role: Combined local criteria used to distinguish branching regimes.

assumptions_latex: A branch at vertex \(v\) has parameter decreases determined by both \(d(v)\) and overlaps among neighborhoods of its neighbors.
All branch decreases are positive integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Among equal-degree pivots, neighborhood overlap can change the branching number and therefore the exponential running-time bound.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: branching-vector analysis and neighborhood-overlap refinements are standard in parameterized exact algorithms
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-and-conquer interpretation of coupled degree and neighborhood information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a pivot \(v\), let \(\mathbf b(v)=(b_1(v),\ldots,b_q(v))\) be the decreases obtained after exhaustive reduction in its branches. The local recurrence is \(T(k)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{q}T(k-b_i(v))\), and its branching number is the unique \(\rho>1\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^{q}\rho^{-b_i(v)}=1\). Consequently, degree alone determines the bound only when it determines the entire vector. Shared neighbors, forced follow-up decisions, and neighborhood containment may increase some \(b_i(v)\), so two vertices of equal degree can have different branching numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degree fixes a branching bound only when it fixes every branch decrease; neighborhood overlaps and forced follow-up reductions can make equal-degree pivots have different branching numbers.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree–Neighborhood Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the interaction leaf. A source or precise instantiation must support how neighborhood structure changes the decreases; additionally, the asserted unique root greater than one requires at least two branches, which is not stated.

children.title: Local-Structure Failure Cases
children.top_down_role: Instances where degree or neighborhood information yields persistently weak branching.

assumptions_latex: The rule inspects only the rooted radius-\(r\) neighborhood of its pivot, for fixed \(r\geq 1\).
The optimization problem is unweighted Vertex Cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded local isomorphism does not determine the global optimum or the correct residual budget.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cycle vertex-cover numbers and bounded-radius indistinguishability are elementary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete locality obstruction for vertex-cover branching rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Root arbitrary vertices in \(C_{2r+2}\) and \(C_{2r+3}\). Their rooted radius-\(r\) induced neighborhoods are isomorphic paths, so any deterministic rule whose decision depends only on that neighborhood makes the same local choice in both instances. Nevertheless, \(\tau(C_{2r+2})=r+1\) whereas \(\tau(C_{2r+3})=r+2\). Thus identical bounded local structure can conceal a different optimum, and local-pattern reasoning without a globally valid exhaustiveness or safeness argument cannot certify the residual parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even and odd cycles can have identical bounded neighborhoods around a pivot but different minimum vertex-cover sizes, so local structure alone cannot certify a branch or reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Structure Failure Cases

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and cycle calculations are appropriate, but the record supplies no inspectable citation for the claimed limitation on deterministic local branching or reduction rules.

assumptions_latex: The current instance decomposes as \(I=I_L\cup I_R\) with interface \(S\), and no constraint directly joins \(I_L\setminus S\) to \(I_R\setminus S\).
All feasible interface assignments on \(S\) can be enumerated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enumerating all feasible interface assignments and solving the two conditioned sides is exhaustive.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic separator conditioning for finite-domain combinatorial problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute a separator \(S\) and the components of \(I-S\). For every \(\sigma\in\Sigma(S)\), charge its cost \(c(\sigma)\), propagate the decisions fixed by \(\sigma\), and recursively solve each resulting component with the induced boundary condition. Reject \(\sigma\) if propagation is inconsistent or the sum of required component budgets exceeds \(k-c(\sigma)\). Accept if some \(\sigma\) yields compatible component solutions of total cost at most \(k\); otherwise reject. Exhaustiveness follows from restricting any global feasible solution to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch over every feasible state of a separator, propagate it into the separated components, solve those conditioned components independently, and combine compatible solutions within the budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Separator-Guided Branching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits separator-guided branching, but independence, compatible boundary assignments, cost accounting, and component-budget combination depend on a formally specified problem and gluing model. No supporting source is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P=\{Q_1,\ldots,Q_p\}\) is a family of pairwise disjoint obstructions.
Every feasible solution must spend at least one unit on each \(Q_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(p>k\) the state is infeasible; otherwise branching on one unresolved \(Q_i\) is exhaustive.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Packing lower bounds coupled with obstruction-resolution branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Construct a packing \(\mathcal P=\{Q_1,
\ldots,Q_p\}\). If \(p>k\), reject. Otherwise choose an unresolved \(Q_i\) and enumerate a finite family \(R(Q_i)=\{D_1,\ldots,D_q\}\) such that every feasible solution resolves \(Q_i\) through at least one \(D_j\). For each \(D_j\), apply it, decrease \(k\) by its cost, update the packing, and recurse. Accept the first successful branch. The maintained packing supplies a residual lower bound, while coverage of \(R(Q_i)\) supplies branch exhaustiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use disjoint obstructions as an additive lower bound; reject when their number exceeds the budget, or branch exhaustively over ways to resolve one packed obstruction.
knowledge_statements.title: Packing-Guided Branching

assumptions_latex: \(R\) is computable from a bounded local configuration of a parameterized instance \((I,k)\).
A polynomial-time lifting map is supplied for solutions of the reduced instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Applying \(R\) preserves the yes/no answer and permits reconstruction of an original solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeness definition for bounded-radius preprocessing rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local rule \(R\) is safe if, whenever its bounded local applicability predicate holds and \(R(I,k)=(I',k')\), one has \((I,k)\in\mathrm{YES}\) if and only if \((I',k')\in\mathrm{YES}\). For optimization reconstruction, the rule additionally provides a polynomial-time map \(L_R\) sending every reduced solution \(S'\) of cost at most \(k'\) to an original solution \(L_R(S')\) of cost at most \(k\). Exhaustive application stops when no local applicability predicate holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local reduction is safe when it preserves the decision answer in both directions and supplies an efficient map lifting every reduced solution to an original solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Safe Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits local safe reductions, and the decision-equivalence and lifting requirements are coherent. An authoritative reduction-framework source with a specific locator is still required.

children.title: Dominance Reductions
children.top_down_role: Elimination based on one choice being no better than an alternative.

assumptions_latex: A search state has a finite alternative set \(A\), with residual objective contribution \(c(a)+F(a)\) for \(a\in A\).
Two alternatives \(a,b\in A\) satisfy \(c(a)\leq c(b)\) and \(F(a)\leq F(b)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Alternative \(b\) may be deleted without changing the minimum state value.

notation.meaning: minimum feasible continuation cost after a

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: componentwise cost-and-continuation dominance is an elementary minimization rule
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract minimization-state dominance, independent of a particular graph problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the state value by \(V=\min_{x\in A}\{c(x)+F(x)\}\), where \(F(x)=+\infty\) denotes an infeasible continuation. If \(c(a)\leq c(b)\) and \(F(a)\leq F(b)\), then \(c(a)+F(a)\leq c(b)+F(b)\). Hence \(V=\min_{x\in A\setminus\{b\}}\{c(x)+F(x)\}\), and deleting \(b\) is safe. An implementable dominance reduction must certify the continuation inequality without first solving the residual optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete an alternative when another has no larger immediate cost and no larger optimal continuation cost; the dominated alternative cannot uniquely improve the minimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind is plausible for dominance reductions, but the continuation-cost inequality is generally as hard to establish as the residual optimization problem. A source or concrete efficiently checkable dominance certificate is needed.

children.title: Subsumption Reductions
children.top_down_role: Elimination based on containment among constraints, sets, clauses, or local structures.

assumptions_latex: Each constraint \(C\) denotes a set \(F(C)\) of assignments satisfying it.
Constraints \(C_1,C_2\) have the same variable scope and satisfy \(F(C_1)\subseteq F(C_2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removing \(C_2\) preserves the feasible set and is therefore safe.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: removal of a logically implied constraint is an elementary equivalence-preserving reduction
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-level subsumption on a common scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the feasible assignments of a constraint system \(\mathcal C\) be \(F(\mathcal C)=\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal C}F(C)\). If \(C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C\) and \(F(C_1)\subseteq F(C_2)\), then \(C_1\) logically implies \(C_2\). Therefore \(F(\mathcal C)=F(\mathcal C\setminus\{C_2\})\), so deletion of \(C_2\) preserves feasibility and every objective value attached solely to assignments. For unequal scopes, the containment must instead be checked after projection to a common assignment space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint may be removed when another constraint implies it; with unequal scopes, implication must be tested after placing both on a common assignment space.
knowledge_statements.title: Subsumption Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits subsumption reductions and the implication direction is correct on a common assignment space. A cited constraint framework is needed to formalize intersections and projections when other constraints have different scopes.

children.title: Dominance–Subsumption Interaction
children.top_down_role: Reduction systems combining comparative quality with structural containment.

assumptions_latex: Dominance deletes alternatives, whereas subsumption deletes constraints or descriptions.
Each individual deletion is safe in the state where it is applied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any finite interleaving preserves the original optimum, although the resulting irreducible state may depend on rule order.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: composition of equivalence-preserving reductions preserves equivalence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional safeness without a confluence claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every applicable dominance or subsumption step \(I_j\to_R I_{j+1}\) satisfies \(\operatorname{opt}(I_j)=\operatorname{opt}(I_{j+1})+\Delta_j\), with a known offset \(\Delta_j\), and has a compatible lifting map. Then any finite interleaving satisfies \(\operatorname{opt}(I_0)=\operatorname{opt}(I_t)+\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\Delta_j\), and composing the lifting maps reconstructs an optimum solution. This compositional property does not imply confluence: one rule may destroy the applicability certificate of another, producing distinct irreducible states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safe dominance and subsumption steps remain safe under arbitrary finite interleaving, but different rule orders can yield different irreducible instances unless confluence is separately established.
knowledge_statements.title: Dominance–Subsumption Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the interaction leaf, and the finite composition claim is coherent under the stated offset and lifting assumptions. No inspectable source supports this reduction-composition framework or the order-sensitivity statement.

children.title: Tie-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where equality, weights, multiplicity, or reconstruction obligations prevent elimination.

assumptions_latex: A reduction selects one alternative using only a scalar score \(s\).
Distinct alternatives \(a,b\) may satisfy \(s(a)=s(b)\) while having different feasible-continuation sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Score equality alone cannot justify deleting either tied alternative.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equal scalar scores do not imply semantic equivalence or set containment
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of score-based dominance under tied local comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let alternatives \(a,b\) have equal local score \(s(a)=s(b)\), but suppose there exist continuations \(x\in E(a)\setminus E(b)\) and \(y\in E(b)\setminus E(a)\). Then neither continuation set contains the other, so neither dominance nor subsumption follows from the tie. Deleting \(a\) can remove the only completion represented by \(x\), while deleting \(b\) can remove the only completion represented by \(y\). A safe tie-breaking reduction therefore requires an additional exchange map, equivalence certificate, or deterministic retention of both alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal local scores do not establish dominance when tied alternatives admit incomparable continuations; safe tie breaking needs an exchange or equivalence certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Sensitivity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and incomparable continuation sets correctly prevent a dominance inference from score equality alone. The named boundary and its reduction interpretation lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Folding Reductions
children.top_down_role: Local contractions that encode several tightly coupled choices.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph and \(v\) has exactly two nonadjacent neighbors \(u,w\).
The problem is unweighted Vertex Cover parameterized by budget \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has a vertex cover of size at most \(k\) if and only if the folded graph has one of size at most \(k-1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: degree-two folding for Vertex Cover is a standard kernelization rule
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical degree-two folding rule for unweighted Vertex Cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Delete \(u,v,w\), introduce a vertex \(x\), and join \(x\) to every vertex in \((N_G(u)\cup N_G(w))\setminus\{v\}\), obtaining \(G'\). Replace \(k\) by \(k'=k-1\). Given a cover \(S'\) of \(G'\), lift it by replacing \(x\in S'\) with \(u,w\); if \(x\notin S'\), add \(v\) instead. The lifted set has size \(|S'|+1\), and \(G\) has a cover of size at most \(k\) exactly when \(G'\) has one of size at most \(k-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a degree-two vertex with nonadjacent neighbors, fold the three vertices into one, reduce the budget by one, and reconstruct by choosing either both neighbors or the center.
knowledge_statements.title: Folding Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits folding reductions, and the stated degree-two Vertex Cover fold and lifting rule are standard and internally consistent. However, no source reference or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Replacement Reductions
children.top_down_role: Exchange of a subinstance for a smaller representative with preserved solution behavior.

assumptions_latex: A subinstance \(H\) interacts with the remainder only through a finite boundary \(B\).
A gadget \(H'\) has the same boundary and a known integer offset \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(H\) by \(H'\) preserves the global optimum up to \(\Delta\) exactly when their boundary signatures differ uniformly by \(\Delta\).

notation.meaning: minimum internal cost under boundary condition sigma

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality of finite-boundary cost signatures up to an offset is the standard replacement criterion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-boundary signature criterion for exact gadget replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\sigma\in\Sigma_B\), define \(f_H(\sigma)\) as the minimum cost of a feasible internal solution of \(H\) consistent with \(\sigma\), using \(+\infty\) for infeasibility. The replacement \(H\mapsto H'\) with parameter adjustment \(k'=k-\Delta\) is safe precisely when \(f_H(\sigma)=f_{H'}(\sigma)+\Delta\) for every boundary condition that can be induced by an exterior instance. A lifting table mapping optimum realizations of each finite signature entry reconstructs a solution before replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundaried subinstance can be replaced by a gadget when both have identical minimum-cost behavior for every realizable boundary condition, up to one fixed cost offset.
knowledge_statements.title: Replacement Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind is suitable for a finite-boundary replacement criterion, but necessity and sufficiency depend on the exact boundary semantics, realizable exterior contexts, objective decomposition, and lifting model. These require a supporting source and formal problem-specific gluing framework.

children.title: Replacement-Gadget Design
children.top_down_role: Structural choices governing representative interfaces and reconstruction data.

knowledge_statements.title: Replacement-Gadget Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signature-based replacement for finite-boundary minimization instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a boundaried instance with interface \(B\), and let \(Q(B)\) be the finite set of admissible boundary states. Define \(\sigma_H(q)\) as the minimum internal objective contribution of a feasible partial solution of \(H\) inducing \(q\), with value \(+\infty\) when none exists. A boundaried gadget \(G\) is a replacement for \(H\) with offset \(\delta\) when \(\sigma_H(q)=\sigma_G(q)+\delta\) for every \(q\in Q(B)\). Consequently, for every compatible context \(C\), gluing along \(B\) satisfies \(\operatorname{OPT}(C\oplus H)=\operatorname{OPT}(C\oplus G)+\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gadget safely replaces a boundaried subinstance when all boundary-state costs agree up to one constant offset, thereby preserving every compatible context’s optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(B)\) is finite and records all interactions between the subinstance and its context.
The objective decomposes into context and internal contributions under gluing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(C\oplus H)=\operatorname{OPT}(C\oplus G)+\delta\) for every compatible \(C\).

notation.meaning: context C glued to H along their common interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is internally plausible, but no cited source supports the boundary-state signature framework or the claimed preservation for every compatible context.

children.title: Nonreplaceable Interface Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Configurations whose external interactions resist bounded local replacement.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonreplaceable Interface Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of replacement relative to a prescribed gadget class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an interface \(B\), its state set \(Q(B)\), and an allowed gadget class \(\mathcal G_B\). A boundaried instance \(H\) is nonreplaceable within \(\mathcal G_B\) if no \(G\in\mathcal G_B\) and \(\delta\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(\sigma_H(q)=\sigma_G(q)+\delta\) for every \(q\in Q(B)\). Equivalently, each candidate \(G\) has two realizable states \(q_1,q_2\) for which \(\sigma_H(q_1)-\sigma_G(q_1)\ne\sigma_H(q_2)-\sigma_G(q_2)\). Compatible contexts selecting these states then prevent any context-independent objective offset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interface is nonreplaceable by a gadget class when every candidate produces state-dependent cost discrepancies, so no single offset preserves all contexts.
assumptions_latex: Boundary states in \(Q(B)\) can be realized by compatible contexts.
Replacement is required to preserve every compatible context up to one additive offset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) admits no context-independent replacement from \(\mathcal G_B\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the stated equivalence uses differences of signature values without ensuring they are finite and requires a sourced formal model of realizable boundary states and the allowed gadget class.

children.title: Reduction-Safeness Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence that preprocessing preserves the relevant instance outcome or optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Safeness Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-preserving certificate for one parameterized reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized decision problem with predicate \(P(I,k)\), consider a reduction \(R(I,k)=(I',k')\). A reduction-safeness certificate is a finite object \(\pi_R\) accepted by a sound checker only if it establishes both implications \(P(I,k)\Rightarrow P(I',k')\) and \(P(I',k')\Rightarrow P(I,k)\), together with the claimed parameter relation \(k'=k-d\). Acceptance therefore certifies \(P(I,k)\Longleftrightarrow P(I',k')\). The certificate may encode local case exhaustion, exchange mappings, or formally checkable identities, but its checker must validate every side condition used by the rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A safeness certificate checkably establishes both directions of decision equivalence and the claimed parameter change for a reduction.
assumptions_latex: The certificate checker is sound for the reduction-rule proof system.
\(R\) and the predicate \(P\) have explicit finite encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(I,k)\Longleftrightarrow P(I',k')\) and \(k'=k-d\).

notation.meaning: decision predicate for instance I and parameter k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the leaf, but no source or defined proof system establishes what finite certificate and sound checker support the two implications and parameter relation.

children.title: Solution-Lifting Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence supporting recovery of original-instance solutions from reduced-instance solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Lifting Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive recovery certificate for an optimization reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a minimization reduction map \(I\) to \(I'\) with certified offset \(\delta\), so that \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I')+\delta\). A solution-lifting certificate specifies an effectively evaluable map \(L\) and checkable local data such that every feasible solution \(S'\in\mathcal F(I')\) yields \(L(S')\in\mathcal F(I)\) with \(c_I(L(S'))=c_{I'}(S')+\delta\). Hence applying \(L\) to an optimal reduced solution produces an optimal solution of the original instance. The certificate checker verifies feasibility preservation, the objective identity, and all applicability conditions of the reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifting certificate provides a checked map that reconstructs an original feasible solution with the certified objective offset, preserving optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I')+\delta\) has been safely established.
The lifting map \(L\) is effectively evaluable on encoded reduced solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S'\in\operatorname{argmin}\mathcal F(I')\Rightarrow L(S')\in\operatorname{argmin}\mathcal F(I)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role is appropriate, but the optimization-reduction framework is uncited, and the conclusion's argmin notation omits the objective being minimized.

children.title: Certificate Composition
children.top_down_role: Composition of certification data across sequences of reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential composition of safeness and lifting certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose certified reductions map \(I_0\) to \(I_1\) and \(I_1\) to \(I_2\), with objective offsets \(\delta_1,\delta_2\) and lifting maps \(L_1:\mathcal F(I_1)\to\mathcal F(I_0)\), \(L_2:\mathcal F(I_2)\to\mathcal F(I_1)\). Their composed certificate records both component certificates, offset \(\delta_1+\delta_2\), and lift \(L_1\circ L_2\). A checker accepting both components certifies \(\operatorname{OPT}(I_0)=\operatorname{OPT}(I_2)+\delta_1+\delta_2\) and, for every feasible \(S_2\), the identity \(c_{I_0}(L_1(L_2(S_2)))=c_{I_2}(S_2)+\delta_1+\delta_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential reduction certificates compose by adding offsets and applying lifting maps in reverse reduction order.
assumptions_latex: Each component safeness and lifting certificate is accepted by a sound checker.
The output instance of the first reduction is the input instance of the second.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{1:2}=L_1\circ L_2\) and \(\delta_{1:2}=\delta_1+\delta_2\) certify the composite reduction.

notation.meaning: successive instances in the reduction sequence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The composition statement is mathematically plausible and fits the container, but no source supports the assumed component certificate semantics or their additive-offset composition.

children.title: Irreversible-Reduction Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where discarded information prevents valid recovery or verification.

knowledge_statements.title: Irreversible-Reduction Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-loss boundary for reconstructing explicit solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A safe decision reduction \(R\) crosses an irreversible boundary when it preserves the truth value but its retained output contains insufficient information to reconstruct a required original solution. Concretely, if distinct original instances \(I_1,I_2\) satisfy \(R(I_1)=R(I_2)=J\), while their admissible output sets \(\mathcal O(I_1)\) and \(\mathcal O(I_2)\) are disjoint, then no deterministic map depending only on \(J\) can return a valid output for both originals. Reversibility therefore requires retained annotations distinguishing the lost cases or a lifting certificate recorded when the reduction is applied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision-safe reduction is irreversible when different originals collapse to one reduced state but require incompatible outputs, unless distinguishing annotations are retained.
assumptions_latex: Reconstruction receives only the reduced instance and retained annotations.
\(\mathcal O(I_1)\cap\mathcal O(I_2)=\varnothing\) for two originals having the same retained reduction output.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No reconstruction map depending only on the common reduced output is valid for both \(I_1\) and \(I_2\).

notation.meaning: valid explicit outputs for instance I
common reduced instance and retained annotation

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction–Branching Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search-tree accounting when reductions are exhausted between branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu\) be a nonnegative instance measure. At every search node, exhaust sound deterministic reductions before selecting a branching rule, and apply reductions again to every child. If the resulting children have measure decreases \(d_1,\ldots,d_r>0\), then the subtree size obeys \(T(\mu)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}T(\mu-d_i)+p(\mu)\), where \(p\) bounds local reduction and branching work. Thus branching decreases must be measured after child reductions; reductions may improve the recurrence, eliminate branches, or change which branching vector applies, but may not be counted twice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exhaust reductions at branching, and measure each child’s decrease afterward; the resulting decreases determine the valid search-tree recurrence.
assumptions_latex: All applied reductions are sound and terminate.
Every surviving branch decreases \(\mu\) by a positive amount.
Local node processing is bounded by \(p(\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\mu)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}T(\mu-d_i)+p(\mu)\) using post-reduction decreases.

notation.meaning: post-reduction measure decrease in child i
worst-case work from measure at most μ

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the topic and the recurrence is plausible, but no source supports the post-reduction accounting convention or its stated no-double-counting requirement.

children.title: Branching-Vector Analysis
children.top_down_role: Classification of recursive cases by their parameter or measure decreases.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Vector Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recurrence representation of one bounded-search branching rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a branching rule applied at measure \(\mu\) creates \(r\) exhaustive children whose measures are at most \(\mu-d_1,\ldots,\mu-d_r\), where every \(d_i>0\). Its branching vector is \(\mathbf d=(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\), and it represents the recurrence \(T(\mu)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}T(\mu-d_i)+p(\mu)\). The entries must include all measure changes forced before the next branching point. Permuting entries does not change the vector’s recurrence, whereas omitting a feasible child or overstating any decrease invalidates the representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching vector lists the positive measure decreases of all exhaustive children and directly represents the corresponding search-tree recurrence.
assumptions_latex: The children exhaust all solutions represented by the parent node.
Each child has measure at most \(\mu-d_i\) with \(d_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbf d=(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\) represents \(T(\mu)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}T(\mu-d_i)+p(\mu)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and mathematical formulation fit the leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative source with an inspectable locator for the branching-vector convention.

children.title: Branching-Number Analysis
children.top_down_role: Comparison of the exponential growth rates induced by branching cases.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Number Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential bound induced by a fixed branching vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a branching vector \(\mathbf d=(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\) with \(d_i>0\) and \(r\geq2\), its branching number \(\alpha(\mathbf d)>1\) is the unique positive root of \(\sum_{i=1}^{r}\alpha^{-d_i}=1\). If every recursive node uses this vector, leaves have constant cost, and node overhead is polynomial, then the recurrence \(T(\mu)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}T(\mu-d_i)+\mu^{O(1)}\) yields \(T(\mu)=O(\alpha(\mathbf d)^{\mu}\mu^{O(1)})\). For one child, the recursion is nonbranching and is analyzed separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The branching number is the characteristic root of a branching vector and determines its exponential running-time base, up to polynomial factors.
assumptions_latex: \(d_i>0\) for every branch and \(r\geq2\).
Nonrecursive work and leaf processing are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\mu)=O(\alpha(\mathbf d)^{\mu}\mu^{O(1)})\), where \(\sum_i\alpha(\mathbf d)^{-d_i}=1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind is appropriate and the characteristic-root claim is standard for positive fixed vectors, but no supporting citation is supplied.

children.title: Vector Dominance
children.top_down_role: Ordering and pruning of branching cases through componentwise or growth-rate comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Vector Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise comparison of equal-arity branching vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbf a=(a_1,
\ldots,a_r)\) and \(\mathbf b=(b_1,\ldots,b_r)\) be positive branching vectors of equal arity, with their entries paired so that \(a_i\geq b_i\) for every \(i\). Then \(\mathbf a\) dominates \(\mathbf b\). For every \(x>1\), one has \(\sum_i x^{-a_i}\leq\sum_i x^{-b_i}\); consequently their characteristic roots satisfy \(\alpha(\mathbf a)\leq\alpha(\mathbf b)\). Hence a recurrence using \(\mathbf a\) is no worse in exponential base than the corresponding recurrence using \(\mathbf b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every decrease in one equal-arity branching vector is at least the paired decrease in another, its branching number is no larger.
assumptions_latex: Both vectors have the same number of positive entries.
Entries are paired so that \(a_i\geq b_i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(\mathbf a)\leq\alpha(\mathbf b)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits and the equal-arity componentwise implication is plausible, but the selected dominance convention and root comparison lack an authoritative citation.

children.title: Mixed-Vector Regimes
children.top_down_role: Analyses in which distinct branching vectors apply across structural instance classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Vector Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform bound for search trees using several branching vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal V\) be a finite set of positive branching vectors, and suppose every recursive node uses some \(\mathbf d\in\mathcal V\). Define \(\alpha_* = \max_{\mathbf d\in\mathcal V}\alpha(\mathbf d)\). Since \(\sum_i\alpha_*^{-d_i}\leq1\) for each permitted vector, induction on the measure gives a uniform search-tree bound \(T(\mu)=O(\alpha_*^{\mu}\mu^{O(1)})\) when local work is polynomial. This maximum-root estimate remains valid when the selected vector depends on the current reduced instance; correlations between successive regimes may permit a smaller bound but are not used here.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When nodes may use several branching vectors, the largest individual branching number gives a valid uniform exponential bound without exploiting regime correlations.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal V\) is finite and every entry of every vector is positive.
Every recursive node uses a vector in \(\mathcal V\).
Local work is polynomial in the encoded instance size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\mu)=O(\alpha_*^{\mu}\mu^{O(1)})\), where \(\alpha_*=\max_{\mathbf d\in\mathcal V}\alpha(\mathbf d)\).

notation.meaning: finite family of permitted branching vectors
largest branching number in the family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits, but the family is not restricted to genuinely branching vectors for which the cited branching number was defined, and polynomial work in encoding size is not related to the displayed polynomial factor in the measure. A source is needed to fix the precise hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Instance Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear measure-and-conquer potential over instance features.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance \(I\) have nonnegative feature counts \(n_1(I),\ldots,n_m(I)\), and choose nonnegative real weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_m\). The associated weighted instance measure is \(\mu_w(I)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_j n_j(I)\), optionally plus a fixed parameter term. For a transition from \(I\) to \(I'\), its measured decrease is \(\Delta_w(I,I')=\mu_w(I)-\mu_w(I')\). A measure is admissible for bounded-search analysis when it is bounded below, every recursive transition has strictly positive decrease, and its value is polynomially bounded in the input encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted instance measure is a nonnegative linear potential over feature counts whose strictly positive branch decreases support search-tree analysis.
assumptions_latex: Each feature count \(n_j(I)\) is finite and nonnegative.
Each weight satisfies \(w_j\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_w(I)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_jn_j(I)\) and \(\Delta_w(I,I')=\mu_w(I)-\mu_w(I')\).

notation.meaning: count of feature type j in instance I
nonnegative weight of feature type j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, but no measure-and-conquer source is cited, and the optional parameter term is mentioned without being introduced or included in the displayed definition.

children.title: Piecewise Instance Measures
children.top_down_role: Measures whose weights or forms differ across explicit structural regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Instance Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a regime-indexed measure for measure-and-conquer analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be an instance with feature vector \(x(I)\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^d\). Let \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) partition the attainable feature space, and choose \(w^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^d\) and \(b_j\in\mathbb{R}\) for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). The piecewise instance measure is
\[
\mu(I)=\langle w^{(j)},x(I)\rangle+b_j\quad\text{when }x(I)\in R_j.
\]
It is valid for the intended branching analysis only if \(\mu(I)\ge 0\) for every nonterminal instance and every reduction or branch \(I\to I'\) has an explicitly bounded change \(\mu(I)-\mu(I')\), including transitions between regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise measure assigns an affine weighted feature sum in each regime. Its use in branching analysis requires nonnegativity and control of both within-regime and cross-regime changes.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) partition all attainable feature vectors.
\(w^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^d\) and \(b_j\in\mathbb{R}\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu(I)=\langle w^{(j)},x(I)\rangle+b_j\) for the unique \(j\) satisfying \(x(I)\in R_j\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative feature vector of instance I

children.title: Adaptive Instance Measures
children.top_down_role: Measures selected or adjusted according to the current instance regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Instance Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the validity requirement for state-dependent measure selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let an analysis state \(s(I)\in S\) select a measure \(\mu_{s(I)}\). For every algorithmic transition \(I\to I'\), define
\[
\Delta(I,I')=\mu_{s(I)}(I)-\mu_{s(I')}(I').
\]
Suppose the selected measures are nonnegative on nonterminal instances. If every branching state \(I\) with children \(I_1,\ldots,I_r\) satisfies
\[
\sum_{i=1}^r\alpha^{-\Delta(I,I_i)}\le 1
\]
for one common \(\alpha>1\), then the usual branching-vector induction uses the adaptive decreases. Each decrease must use the child's selected measure; evaluating both endpoints with the parent's measure can omit the cost of adaptation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive measure may depend on the current state, but each branch decrease must compare the parent's selected measure with the child's newly selected measure.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu_{s(I)}(I)\ge 0\) for every nonterminal instance \(I\).
One \(\alpha>1\) is common to all reachable branching states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^r\alpha^{-[\mu_{s(I)}(I)-\mu_{s(I_i)}(I_i)]}\le 1\) at every branch yields a search-tree bound proportional to \(\alpha^{\mu_{s(I_0)}(I_0)}\), subject to the stated terminal normalization.

notation.meaning: measure state selected for instance I
adaptive measure decrease across a transition

children.title: Measure-Regime Transitions
children.top_down_role: Interfaces where analysis passes between measure pieces or adaptive choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Measure-Regime Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the cross-regime decrease condition needed by piecewise measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(x(I)\in R_p\), \(x(I')\in R_q\), and an algorithmic rule transforms \(I\) into \(I'\). With affine regime measures \(\mu_j(x)=\langle w^{(j)},x\rangle+b_j\), the rule has certified decrease at least \(\delta\) across this regime transition precisely when
\[
\langle w^{(p)},x(I)\rangle+b_p-\bigl(\langle w^{(q)},x(I')\rangle+b_q\bigr)\ge\delta
\]
for every feasible parent-child pair generated by the rule. This cross-regime decrease, rather than a decrease computed using only \(w^{(p)}\), enters the branching vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime-changing rule has the claimed decrease when the parent-regime measure minus the child-regime measure meets that decrease for every feasible transition.
assumptions_latex: \(x(I)\in R_p\) and \(x(I')\in R_q\).
\(I\to I'\) is generated by the analyzed rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_p(x(I))-\mu_q(x(I'))\ge\delta\) for every feasible transition generated by the rule.

children.title: Transition-Cost Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where switching measures invalidates or weakens global search-tree bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Transition-Cost Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when regime switching invalidates a claimed measure decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a transition \(I\to I'\) from regime \(p\) to regime \(q\), define the parent-measure decrease \(D_p=\mu_p(I)-\mu_p(I')\) and switching cost \(C_{p\to q}(I')=\mu_q(I')-\mu_p(I')\). Then
\[
\mu_p(I)-\mu_q(I')=D_p-C_{p\to q}(I').
\]
Consequently, a claimed decrease \(\delta\) is valid exactly when \(C_{p\to q}(I')\le D_p-\delta\). If this boundary is violated for any reachable child, the within-regime calculation \(D_p\ge\delta\) does not certify that transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regime switching consumes part of the apparent decrease; a branch fails certification when its switching cost exceeds the available decrease slack.
assumptions_latex: \(I\to I'\) changes the active measure from \(\mu_p\) to \(\mu_q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_p(I)-\mu_q(I')\ge\delta\iff C_{p\to q}(I')\le D_p-\delta\).

notation.meaning: decrease evaluated entirely with the parent-regime measure
cost of changing measures at the child

knowledge_statements.title: Amortized Branching Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential-based accounting for nonuniform progress across consecutive branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m(I)\ge 0\) be a base size, let \(\Phi(I)\) be a potential, and define \(\mu(I)=m(I)+\Phi(I)\). Assume \(\mu(I)\ge L\) for every reachable instance. For each branching instance \(I\) with children \(I_1,\ldots,I_r\), set \(d_i=\mu(I)-\mu(I_i)\). If one constant \(\alpha>1\) satisfies
\[
\sum_{i=1}^r\alpha^{-d_i}\le 1
\]
at every branching instance, deterministic reductions do not increase \(\mu\), and each terminal instance contributes at most one leaf, then the number of leaves below \(I_0\) is at most \(\alpha^{\mu(I_0)-L}\). Potential increases may offset local progress only insofar as the combined decreases satisfy these inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A potential redistributes progress among steps. With a common lower bound and valid local inequalities in the combined measure, it yields a global exponential leaf bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu(I)=m(I)+\Phi(I)\ge L\) for every reachable instance.
Every deterministic reduction is nonincreasing in \(\mu\).
One \(\alpha>1\) satisfies every branching inequality.
Each terminal instance contributes at most one leaf.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\#\operatorname{leaves}(I_0)\le\alpha^{\mu(I_0)-L}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Memoized Search Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact branching with caching by canonical residual state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an instance \(I\), a canonicalization map \(c\), reduction rules, and an exact branching rule, initialize an empty table \(M\). To solve state \(J\), exhaustively reduce it to \(J'\), compute \(z=c(J')\), and return \(M[z]\) if present. If \(J'\) is terminal, store and return its exact value. Otherwise generate children \(J_1,dots,J_r\), recursively obtain their exact values, combine them according to the optimization recurrence, store the result under \(z\), and return it. Canonicalization must ensure \(c(J)=c(K)\) only when the residual subproblems have identical objective values and compatible reconstruction data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical residual subproblems are solved once, cached, and reused; correctness requires cache equivalence to preserve objective values and reconstruction.
assumptions_latex: Reductions and branching preserve the exact optimum recurrence.
\(c(J)=c(K)\) implies equivalent residual optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each reachable canonical state is expanded at most once, and the returned value equals the optimum of \(I\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role and memoization statement fit the topic, and the equivalence requirement is sufficiently qualified. No citation or inspectable locator supports the nontrivial correctness and expansion claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Vertex-Cover Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard edge-endpoint branching for parameterized Vertex Cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and an integer \(k\). If \(k<0\), return NO. If \(E=\varnothing\), return YES. Otherwise choose an edge \(uv\in E\). Since every vertex cover contains \(u\) or \(v\), recursively solve
\[
(G-u,k-1)\quad\text{and}\quad(G-v,k-1).
\]
Return YES if either call returns YES, adding the corresponding deleted endpoint during reconstruction; otherwise return NO. The recurrence is \(T(k)\le 2T(k-1)+\operatorname{poly}(|V|+|E|)\), and the search tree has at most \(2^k\) leaves for \(k\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reject a negative budget; otherwise, if edges remain, branch on an edge by placing one endpoint or the other in the cover and decreasing the budget by one.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple graph.
\(k\in\mathbb{Z}\) is the remaining vertex-cover budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(k\ge 0\), the algorithm decides whether \(G\) has a vertex cover of size at most \(k\) in \(O(2^k\operatorname{poly}(|V|+|E|))\) time.

notation.meaning: graph obtained by deleting v and all incident edges

children.title: Low-Degree Vertex Reductions
children.top_down_role: Vertex Cover simplifications triggered by isolated, pendant, or other bounded-degree configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Degree Vertex Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe degree-zero and degree-one reductions for unweighted Vertex Cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \((G,k)\), repeatedly apply the following rules. If \(v\) has degree zero, delete \(v\) without changing \(k\). If \(v\) has degree one with unique neighbor \(u\), delete \(u\) and its incident edges and replace \(k\) by \(k-1\), recording \(u\) for reconstruction. The degree-one rule is safe because any cover containing \(v\) can replace \(v\) by \(u\) without increasing its size. Stop when neither rule applies or when \(k<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete isolated vertices, and for each leaf select its unique neighbor and reduce the cover budget by one.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph.
The objective is minimum-cardinality vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced instance is equivalent to \((G,k)\), with recorded vertices added during reconstruction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The degree-zero and degree-one rules are correctly stated for unweighted Vertex Cover and the algorithm content kind fits, but no supporting citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Vertex-Folding Reductions
children.top_down_role: Vertex Cover contractions encoding local mutually constrained choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Folding Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree-two folding for unweighted Vertex Cover with nonadjacent neighbors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v\) have exactly two nonadjacent neighbors \(u,w\). Construct \(G'\) by deleting \(u,v,w\), adding a new vertex \(x\), and joining \(x\) to every vertex in \((N_G(u)\cup N_G(w))\setminus\{u,v,w\}\). Then
\[
	au(G)=	au(G')+1.
\]
Reduce \((G,k)\) to \((G',k-1)\). From a cover \(C'\) of \(G'\), reconstruct \(C=(C'\setminus\{x\})\cup\{u,w\}\) if \(x\in C'\), and \(C=C'\cup\{v\}\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degree-two vertex with nonadjacent neighbors can be folded into one vertex, lowering the cover budget and optimum by one.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph.
\(N_G(v)=\{u,w\}\) and \(uw\notin E(G)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau(G)=	au(G')+1\), so \((G,k)\) is YES exactly when \((G',k-1)\) is YES.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The degree-two folding construction, optimum shift, and reconstruction cases are internally consistent, but the record lacks an inspectable source for the reduction theorem.

children.title: Degree-Triggered Folding
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where degree information enables a folding replacement.

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Triggered Folding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the local degree conditions selecting reduction or folding rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For unweighted Vertex Cover, inspect a vertex \(v\) of minimum degree. If \(d_G(v)=0\), delete \(v\). If \(d_G(v)=1\), select its unique neighbor. If \(d_G(v)=2\) with \(N_G(v)=\{u,w\}\), then: when \(uw\notin E(G)\), apply vertex folding; when \(uw\in E(G)\), select both \(u,w\), delete them, and decrease the budget by two. The adjacent-neighbor rule is safe because the triangle on \(u,v,w\) requires two vertices, and a minimum cover can contain \(u,w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum degree determines whether to delete, select a neighbor, fold a path, or select both neighbors of a triangle vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph.
The objective is minimum-cardinality vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each listed degree-triggered transformation preserves the existence of a vertex cover within the adjusted budget.

notation.meaning: open neighborhood of the inspected vertex

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind fits the trigger leaf, and the listed unweighted degree cases are mathematically consistent. No citation supports the reduction conditions and safety claims.

children.title: Weighted Folding Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by weights, annotations, reconstruction obligations, or nonstandard objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Folding Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dominance boundary for safely forcing neighbors in weighted Vertex Cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a finite graph with positive vertex weights \(c:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}\), and let \(N_G(v)=\{u,w\}\). If
\[
c(v)\ge c(u)+c(w),
\]
then some minimum-weight vertex cover contains both \(u\) and \(w\). Indeed, any vertex cover containing \(v\) but not both neighbors can replace \(v\) by \(u,w\) without increasing its weight; covers already containing both neighbors require no change. Thus forcing \(u,w\) is safe under this dominance condition. The condition cannot simply be omitted: on the path \(u-v-w\) with \(c(u)=c(v)=c(w)=1\), forcing \(u,w\) costs two, whereas the unique minimum cover \(\{v\}\) costs one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forcing both neighbors is safe when their combined weight does not exceed the center's weight; a unit-weight three-vertex path shows that the same rule can fail without dominance.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph and \(c:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(c(v)\ge c(u)+c(w)\), some minimum-weight vertex cover contains \(u,w\); without this dominance condition, forcing them can be suboptimal.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Cover Above Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Vertex Cover variant parameterized above the standard LP lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), define
\[
\tau^*(G)=\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}x_v: x_u+x_v\ge 1\text{ for every }uv\in E,\ 0\le x_v\le 1\text{ for every }v\in V\right\}.
\]
Given an integral budget \(k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\), Vertex Cover Above LP asks whether \(G\) has a vertex cover of size at most \(k\), using \(\ell=k-\tau^*(G)\) as the above-guarantee parameter. Equivalently, the threshold is \(\tau^*(G)+\ell=k\). Since \(\tau^*(G)\) is half-integral, \(\ell\in\tfrac12\mathbb{Z}\); instances with \(k<\tau^*(G)\) are infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex Cover Above LP parameterizes an integral cover-size budget by its excess over the standard fractional vertex-cover optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite graph.
\(k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) is the requested cover-size bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell=k-\tau^*(G)\in\tfrac12\mathbb{Z}\) measures the budget above the LP guarantee \(\tau^*(G)\le\tau(G)\).

notation.meaning: excess of the integral budget above the LP lower bound

assumptions_latex: Each recursive branch strictly decreases a nonnegative measure \(\mu\).
The same branching vector \((d_1,\ldots,d_r)\) occurs along arbitrarily long root-to-leaf paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The valid exponential base is determined by \(\sum_{i=1}^{r}\rho^{-d_i}=1\), not by an average decrement; if some persistent branch has \(d_i=0\), this recurrence gives no finite search-tree bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching-vector boundary for measure-based search-tree analyses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a recursive algorithm on measure \(\mu\geq 0\) repeatedly creates \(r\geq 2\) children whose measures are at most \(\mu-d_1,\ldots,\mu-d_r\), where \(d_i\geq 0\). When this vector persists, its leaf-count recurrence is \(T(\mu)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}T(\mu-d_i)\). If every \(d_i>0\), the corresponding bound is \(T(\mu)=O(\rho^{\mu})\), where \(\rho>1\) is the unique solution of \(\sum_{i=1}^{r}\rho^{-d_i}=1\). Replacing the vector by its average decrease can underestimate \(\rho\). If some persistent branch has \(d_i=0\), the recurrence alone supplies no finite exponential bound and may permit nontermination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent asymmetric branches must be analyzed by their full branching vector. An average decrease can be unsound, and a recurring zero-decrease branch destroys the usual finite search-tree bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistently Unbalanced Branching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No inspectable source supports the branching-factor claim. The strict-decrease assumption conflicts with the zero-decrement boundary, and the exponential bound also needs explicit base-case and recurrence-domain conditions.

assumptions_latex: The analysis uses a measure \(\mu:S\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\) on recursive states.
Recursive calls and exhaustive reductions are charged through decreases in \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reachable zero-decrease recursive cycle invalidates induction on \(\mu\); a valid bounded-tree analysis requires another well-founded rank that strictly decreases on the cycle.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of measure-based induction under zero-progress transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the reachable state set and let \(\mu:S\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\). Measure stagnation occurs when a nonterminal recursive transition \(s\to t\) satisfies \(\mu(t)=\mu(s)\). A single such transition may be harmless if another well-founded quantity decreases. However, if there is a reachable directed cycle \(s_0\to s_1\to\cdots\to s_q=s_0\) with \(\mu(s_{j+1})=\mu(s_j)\) for every \(j\), then induction on \(\mu\) cannot establish termination or a finite-depth search tree. Any valid recurrence analysis must either eliminate the cycle or refine the rank so that every recursive cycle contains a strict decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measure that remains constant around a reachable recursive cycle cannot prove termination or finite depth. The algorithm needs a stricter, well-founded secondary rank or a cycle-eliminating rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Measure Stagnation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon fits the container, but no source is cited. The proposed refined-rank condition must specify a well-founded order and sufficient monotonicity on recursive transitions, not merely a strict decrease somewhere on a cycle.

assumptions_latex: Each reduction preserves the answer of the represented instance.
Reduction sequences terminate, so irreducible normal forms exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonconfluence occurs when one state has two reachable irreducible forms that are not equivalent under the chosen state identity; correctness may survive, but uniqueness-based counting does not.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonunique normal forms in exhaustive search-tree reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Rightarrow\) be a terminating, answer-preserving reduction relation on states. Reduction nonconfluence is witnessed by states \(s,u,v\) such that \(s\Rightarrow^{*}u\), \(s\Rightarrow^{*}v\), both \(u\) and \(v\) are irreducible, and \(u\not\equiv v\) under the state equivalence used by the algorithm. This does not by itself invalidate answer preservation. It does invalidate any analysis assuming that exhaustive reduction produces a unique canonical residual state. Confluence modulo \(\equiv\) requires that whenever \(s\Rightarrow^{*}u\) and \(s\Rightarrow^{*}v\), there exist \(u',v'\) with \(u\Rightarrow^{*}u'\), \(v\Rightarrow^{*}v'\), and \(u'\equiv v'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Answer-preserving reductions are nonconfluent when different rule orders yield inequivalent irreducible states. Correctness can remain intact, but canonical-state and unique-normal-form analyses then fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Nonconfluence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record appropriately describes a failure boundary, but its formulation of confluence modulo equivalence and the consequences for canonical residual states require an authoritative rewriting-system source.

children.title: Symmetric Branch Explosion
children.top_down_role: Redundant branches induced by automorphisms or interchangeable local choices.

assumptions_latex: A group \(G\) acts on recursive states and preserves feasibility and objective values.
At each of \(d\) levels, the algorithm explicitly explores \(m\geq 2\) branches from one symmetry orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unquotiented tree can contain \(m^d\) equivalent branch histories although the orbit quotient contains only one history per level.

notation.meaning: Number of symmetric branches per level

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential search-tree growth caused solely by unresolved symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on search states, preserving terminal answers and recursive transition structure. Suppose that at each of \(d\) consecutive levels a state produces \(m\geq 2\) children lying in one \(G\)-orbit, and that the same symmetry persists below corresponding children. A tree search that neither breaks the symmetry nor identifies orbit-equivalent states may explore \(m^d\) equivalent branch histories. In the quotient transition system, those histories represent only one orbit history at each level. Thus a bound obtained by counting syntactic branches can be exponentially larger than the number of semantically distinct states, even though every individual branching rule is correct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every level generates an orbit of equivalent children, ordinary tree search can explore exponentially many symmetric histories although the quotient has only one representative history.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Branch Explosion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Children forming one orbit at each level does not alone imply that all m^d complete histories form one orbit. A source or stronger compatibility hypothesis for the persistent group action is required.

children.title: Duplicate-Subproblem Explosion
children.top_down_role: Repeated generation of equivalent residual instances through different search histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Duplicate-Subproblem Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lattice recurrence separating tree calls from distinct states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(0\leq i,j\leq d\), define a subproblem \(S_{i,j}\) that is terminal when \(i=0\) or \(j=0\), and otherwise recursively calls \(S_{i-1,j}\) and \(S_{i,j-1}\). Starting at \(S_{d,d}\), an unmemoized recursion contains \(\binom{2d}{d}\) root-to-boundary interleavings up to polynomial factors, and therefore makes \(2^{\Omega(d)}\) calls. Nevertheless, only \((d+1)^2\) distinct indexed states exist. Memoizing by \((i,j)\) evaluates each state at most once. This family demonstrates duplicate-subproblem explosion independently of any symmetry group or incorrect branching rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-counter recurrence makes exponentially many unmemoized calls through different interleavings, even though only quadratically many distinct counter pairs occur. Memoization removes this duplication.
assumptions_latex: Recursive subproblems are identified by states in a directed acyclic transition graph.
The implementation performs tree recursion without memoizing previously solved states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number of recursive calls can be exponential in depth while the number of distinct reachable states is polynomial.

notation.meaning: A state indexed by two remaining counters

children.title: Canonical-State Quotients
children.top_down_role: State representations that identify equivalent branches or residual subproblems.

assumptions_latex: The equivalence relation preserves terminal answers.
Equivalent states have matching successor classes under every applicable recursive action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Searching the quotient graph evaluates at most one canonical representative of each reachable equivalence class and returns the same answer as searching the original state graph.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient representation for answer-preserving state deduplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a recursive state space and let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation such that equivalent terminal states have equal answers. Require transition compatibility: if \(s\sim t\) and \(s\) has a successor \(s'\) under an applicable action, then \(t\) has a corresponding successor \(t'\) with \(s'\sim t'\), and conversely. The canonical-state quotient has vertices \(S/{\sim}\) and an edge \([s]\to[s']\) whenever some representatives have that transition. If \(\kappa(s)\in[s]\) is computable, search may store only \(\kappa(s)\). It then evaluates at most one representative per reachable class while preserving the original root answer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An answer- and transition-compatible equivalence turns the state graph into a quotient. Searching one computable representative per reachable class preserves the answer and removes equivalent duplicates.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical-State Quotients

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but terminal-answer equality and successor correspondence alone do not fully specify preservation of the recursive answer aggregation. Termination or fixed-point semantics and action-value compatibility need authoritative support.

children.title: Canonicalization-Cost Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where detecting equivalence costs more than the redundancy it removes.

assumptions_latex: Unquotiented search makes \(M\) state expansions of cost at most \(B\) each.
Canonicalization leaves \(N\leq M\) distinct classes and costs at most \(C\) per generated state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Canonicalization guarantees an asymptotic improvement only when its total identification cost is dominated by the eliminated repeated work; the comparison is \(M B\) versus \(M C+N B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost threshold for profitable canonical-state deduplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose raw search performs \(M\) state expansions, each costing at most \(B\). Suppose canonicalization is applied to every generated state, costs at most \(C\) per application, and reduces expansion to \(N\leq M\) distinct equivalence classes. Ignoring common polynomial bookkeeping, raw time is \(O(MB)\), whereas quotient-search time is \(O(MC+NB)\). Hence canonicalization yields an asymptotic time improvement only if \(MC+NB=o(MB)\). In particular, when \(C=\Omega(B)\) and canonicalization is performed on all \(M\) generated states, deduplication alone need not improve the asymptotic bound, although it may still reduce memory or constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotient search costs the canonicalization of every generated state plus one expansion per class. It improves asymptotic time only when saved duplicate work dominates identification cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonicalization-Cost Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cost-boundary role fits, but big-O upper bounds alone do not establish that MC+NB=o(MB) is necessary for actual asymptotic improvement. The record needs an explicit cost model or matching lower bounds.

children.title: Parameterized Kernelization Framework
children.top_down_role: Instance compression models, upper-bound techniques, structural meta-kernelization, solution reconstruction, extended preprocessing models, and preprocessing lower bounds.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^{*}\times\mathbb{N}\) is a decidable parameterized problem.
The preprocessing algorithm runs in time polynomial in \(|x|+k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a kernel of size \(f(k)\); it is a polynomial kernel when \(f\) is polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard many-one definition of a problem kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized decision problem \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^{*}\times\mathbb{N}\), a kernelization is an algorithm that maps every instance \((x,k)\) in time polynomial in \(|x|+k\) to an instance \((x',k')\) of the same problem \(Q\) such that \((x,k)\in Q\) if and only if \((x',k')\in Q\), and \(|x'|+k'\leq f(k)\) for some computable function \(f\) independent of \(|x|\). The output \((x',k')\) is a problem kernel. If \(f(k)\leq k^{O(1)}\), the kernelization is a polynomial kernelization and the output is a polynomial kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem kernel is a polynomial-time equivalent instance of the same parameterized problem whose total encoding size is bounded solely by a computable function of the original parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Problem Kernels

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a standard same-problem kernelization definition and the content kind fits, but no authoritative kernelization citation with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Generalized Kernel Models
children.top_down_role: Reduced instances represented in a parameter-compatible target problem.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\) and \(Q'\) are decidable parameterized problems.
The transformation runs in time polynomial in the source encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformation is a generalized kernelization from \(Q\) into \(Q'\), with size \(f(k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernelization whose output belongs to another parameterized problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^{*}\times\mathbb{N}\) and \(Q'\subseteq\Gamma^{*}\times\mathbb{N}\) be parameterized decision problems. A generalized kernelization from \(Q\) to \(Q'\) is a polynomial-time algorithm mapping each \((x,k)\) to \((y,\ell)\) such that \((x,k)\in Q\) if and only if \((y,\ell)\in Q'\), and \(|y|+\ell\leq f(k)\) for a computable function \(f\). Its output is a generalized kernel. It is polynomial when \(f(k)\leq k^{O(1)}\). Unlike an ordinary problem kernel, the reduced instance need not belong to the source problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized kernel maps an instance to a size-bounded equivalent instance of a possibly different parameterized problem. Polynomial generalized kernels have polynomial parameter-dependent size.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Kernel Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generalized-kernel definition matches the container and is internally coherent, but it lacks an inspectable authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Parameterized Compression Models
children.top_down_role: Polynomial-size encodings into possibly different decision or optimization languages.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^{*}\times\mathbb{N}\) is a parameterized decision problem.
\(L\subseteq\Gamma^{*}\) is a decidable, unparameterized target language.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output string is a compression of size \(f(k)\), polynomial when \(f(k)\leq k^{O(1)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision compression into an unparameterized target language.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^{*}\times\mathbb{N}\) be a parameterized decision problem and let \(L\subseteq\Gamma^{*}\) be a decidable language. A parameterized compression of \(Q\) into \(L\) is a polynomial-time algorithm mapping each \((x,k)\) to a string \(y\in\Gamma^{*}\) such that \((x,k)\in Q\) if and only if \(y\in L\), and \(|y|\leq f(k)\) for some computable function \(f\). The compression is polynomial if \(f(k)\leq k^{O(1)}\). No requirement places \(y\) in the encoding language of \(Q\), and the target carries no distinguished parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized compression produces a short string in any decidable target language, preserving the yes-or-no answer. Its length depends only on the source parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Compression Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The decision-compression definition fits the terminal container, but no authoritative parameterized-compression source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Target-Language Flexibility
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences of preserving or changing the target problem.

assumptions_latex: The source problem is a parameterized decision problem \(Q\).
The selected target language or problem is decidable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Changing the target does not weaken decision equivalence, but the resulting object is a problem kernel only when the target is \(Q\) itself.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by restrictions placed on the reduced instance's language.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) map \((x,k)\) to an output whose size is bounded by a function of \(k\), preserving membership. Requiring \(K(x,k)\) to encode an instance of \(Q\) gives an ordinary problem kernel. Allowing an instance of another parameterized problem gives a generalized kernel. Allowing an arbitrary string \(y\) in a decidable language \(L\), with \((x,k)\in Q\) if and only if \(y\in L\), gives a compression. Thus target-language flexibility preserves the decision-equivalence requirement while weakening closure of the output under the source problem; it does not by itself provide solution lifting for search or optimization versions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary kernels, generalized kernels, and compressions differ by how freely preprocessing may choose the target language. All preserve decisions, but target flexibility alone does not recover solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Target-Language Flexibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly targets language flexibility, but the distinctions among problem kernels, generalized kernels, and compressions require an authoritative taxonomy citation with a precise locator.

children.title: Decoding-Complexity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by interpretation, recovery, or solution transfer from compressed outputs.

assumptions_latex: A preprocessing map produces an encoding \(y\) with \(|y|\leq f(k)\).
The intended task may require either deciding membership or recovering a source solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: FPT decision follows from any computable target decider, but exact solution recovery additionally requires a bounded-time lifting procedure.

notation.meaning: Running time of the target decider

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between decision decoding and recoverable exact solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose polynomial-time preprocessing maps \((x,k)\) to \(y\) with \(|y|\leq f(k)\), and membership of \(y\) in the target language is decidable in time \(g(|y|)\). Then the source decision problem is solvable in time \((|x|+k)^{O(1)}+g(f(k))\), which is fixed-parameter tractable when \(f\) and \(g\) are computable. This implication concerns decisions only. For a search or optimization problem, an equivalent target decision does not ensure recovery of a source witness or optimizer. Such recovery requires an explicit lifting algorithm with parameter-bounded overhead; without it, the preprocessing object is not an exact solution kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computably decidable short target yields an FPT decision algorithm. Recovering an original witness or optimizer is stronger and requires an explicit, parameter-bounded lifting procedure.
knowledge_statements.title: Decoding-Complexity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The decision-time calculation is plausible, but the asserted boundary for exact solution kernels and the required lifting overhead depend on the adopted search/optimization kernelization model. A precise authoritative source is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Bikernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact many-one bikernelization between parameterized decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) be parameterized decision problems. A bikernelization from \(P\) to \(Q\) is a polynomial-time algorithm that maps every \((x,k)\) to \((y,k')\) such that \((x,k)\in P\iff(y,k')\in Q\), \(|y|\le f(k)\), and \(k'\le g(k)\), for computable functions \(f,g\). It is a polynomial bikernelization when both bounds are polynomial in \(k\). Unlike an ordinary kernel, the reduced instance may belong to a different problem \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bikernel maps an instance of one parameterized problem to an equivalent, parameter-bounded instance of another problem in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: \(P,Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\).
\(f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,k)\in P\iff(y,k')\in Q\), with \(|y|\le f(k)\) and \(k'\le g(k)\).

notation.meaning: Source and target parameterized decision problems.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically plausible and fits the Bikernels container, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports the exact size and parameter bounds.

children.title: Strict Kernel Models
children.top_down_role: Kernel models imposing explicit control on the transformed parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Kernel Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernelizations that do not increase the parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized decision problem \(P\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\), a strict kernelization is a polynomial-time mapping \(K(x,k)=(x',k')\) satisfying \((x,k)\in P\iff(x',k')\in P\), \(|x'|\le f(k)\), and \(k'\le k\). The function \(f\) is the kernel-size bound; the model is polynomial when \(f\) is polynomial. Thus strictness constrains parameter evolution in addition to the usual requirement that the total reduced encoding depend only on the original parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict kernel is an equivalent same-problem reduction whose encoding is parameter-bounded and whose new parameter never exceeds the old one.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\).
