\(K\) is computable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,k)\in P\iff(x',k')\in P\), \(|x'|\le f(k)\), and \(k'\le k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed nonincreasing-parameter definition fits the container, but “strict kernelization” varies across the literature and requires an authoritative definition with a precise locator.

children.title: Size-Sensitive Kernel Models
children.top_down_role: Kernel models tracking refined output-size or encoding-size measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Size-Sensitive Kernel Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized compressions whose guarantee explicitly tracks input size as well as parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A size-sensitive compression for \(P\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) is a polynomial-time mapping \((x,k)\mapsto(y,k')\) preserving the required decision predicate and satisfying \(|y|\le h(|x|,k)\) and \(k'\le g(|x|,k)\). It is an ordinary kernel only if there exist computable \(f,q\) independent of \(|x|\) such that \(|y|\le f(k)\) and \(k'\le q(k)\) on every input. Consequently, a bound retaining unbounded dependence on \(|x|\) describes preprocessing but does not by itself establish kernelization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Size-sensitive compression tracks both input length and parameter; it is a kernel only when both output bounds can discard input-length dependence.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\).
The mapping preserves the chosen decision predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Kernelization requires bounds \(|y|\le f(k)\) and \(k'\le q(k)\) independent of \(|x|\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between input-size-sensitive preprocessing and parameter-only kernel bounds is sound, but the named model is not standardized and its intended taxonomic sense lacks evidence.

children.title: Parameter-Blowup Regimes
children.top_down_role: Comparisons based on how preprocessing changes the designated parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Blowup Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by the reduced parameter’s dependence on the original parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an exact polynomial-time compression \((x,k)\mapsto(y,k')\), its parameter-blowup regime is determined by a uniform bound \(k'\le g(k)\). The regime is nonincreasing when \(g(k)=k\), additive when \(g(k)=k+O(1)\), linear when \(g(k)=O(k)\), polynomial when \(g(k)=k^{O(1)}\), and unrestricted parameter-dependent when only computability of \(g\) is required. If no bound depending solely on \(k\) exists, the mapping fails the parameter-bound requirement of standard kernelization, irrespective of the size of \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter blowup is classified by a uniform function bounding the output parameter; no parameter-only bound means the mapping is not a standard kernelization.
assumptions_latex: The compression is exact and runs in polynomial time.
The bound is uniform over all inputs with parameter \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Standard kernelization requires existence of a computable \(g\) with \(k'\le g(k)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A parameter-only bound is standard, but the additive, linear, polynomial, and unrestricted regimes overlap and are not presented as an exclusive hierarchy. A source is needed to establish the intended classification and terminology.

children.title: Encoding-Overhead Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where annotations or representation overhead dominate the structural kernel size.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Overhead Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between structural compression and a kernel-size guarantee on the complete encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a preprocessing map output an object encoded as \(y\), including headers, weights, labels, parameters, and auxiliary data. A kernel-size claim \(|y|\le f(k)\) is valid only for the complete bit encoding. Bounding merely a structural count \(m(y)\le p(k)\) is insufficient when individual entries require unboundedly many bits. For example, one retained integer weight \(W\) has encoding length \(\Theta(\log W)\); if \(W\) is unrestricted by \(k\), then an output with one weighted item can have unbounded length for fixed \(k\), and hence is not a kernel of size depending only on \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded number of retained objects is not a kernel-size bound when labels, weights, or metadata may require unbounded encoding length.
assumptions_latex: Kernel size is measured in bits under a fixed reasonable encoding.
Numeric weights are encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An unrestricted \(W\) yields \(|y|=\Omega(\log W)\), so no bound \(|y|\le f(k)\) follows from a bounded object count alone.

notation.meaning: Number of structural objects in the output.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complete-encoding boundary and binary-weight example are mathematically sound and fit a failure-boundary container, but no formal kernel-encoding source is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Lossy Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation-preserving preprocessing for parameterized optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be a parameterized optimization problem and \(\alpha\ge 1\). An \(\alpha\)-approximate lossy kernelization consists of polynomial-time algorithms \(R,L\). Reduction computes \(R(I,k)=(I',k')\) with \(|I'|+k'\le f(k)\). For every feasible solution \(s'\) of \(I'\) having approximation ratio at most \(\beta\), lifting returns a feasible solution \(s=L(I,k,I',k',s')\) for \(I\) whose approximation ratio is at most \(\alpha\beta\). A polynomial-size approximate kernelization scheme provides such a kernel for every \(\alpha=1+\varepsilon\), with size polynomial in \(k\) for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lossy kernel compresses an optimization instance and lifts approximate reduced solutions while worsening their approximation ratio by at most a controlled factor. A polynomial-size approximate kernelization scheme supplies such kernels for every fixed loss factor 1+ε.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) has a specified minimization or maximization approximation ratio.
\(R\) and \(L\) run in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ratio}_I(s)\le\alpha\operatorname{ratio}_{I'}(s')\) and \(|I'|+k'\le f(k)\).

children.title: Crown Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Kernel reductions based on matched crown-like partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Crown Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical crown structure used in Vertex Cover kernelization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A crown decomposition of a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) is a partition \((C,H,R)\) of \(V\) such that \(C\) is independent, there are no edges between \(C\) and \(R\), and the bipartite graph induced by edges between \(H\) and \(C\) contains a matching saturating \(H\). For Vertex Cover, these conditions imply that some minimum vertex cover contains all vertices of \(H\) and no vertices of \(C\); consequently, deleting \(C\cup H\) and decreasing the budget by \(|H|\) is safe.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A crown partitions a graph into an independent crown, its separating head, and a remainder, with a matching saturating the head.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
\((C,H,R)\) partitions \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is independent, \(E(C,R)=\varnothing\), and a matching from \(H\) into \(C\) saturates \(H\).

notation.meaning: Crown, head, and remainder vertex sets.
Edges with one endpoint in each indicated set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The crown definition and Vertex Cover consequence are standard and locally appropriate, but the record combines a definition with a nontrivial safety claim without any cited theorem or page locator.

children.title: Expansion-Based Reductions
children.top_down_role: Kernel reductions supported by expansion properties in auxiliary incidence structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Expansion-Based Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional safe reduction extracted from a bipartite expansion and an exchange lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an instance \((I,k)\), construct its problem-specific bipartite incidence graph \(B=(A\uplus D,E)). Find nonempty \(X\subseteq A\) and \(Y\subseteq D\) together with \(q\) distinct edges from every \(x\in X\) to \(Y\), all having distinct endpoints in \(Y\), such that \(N_B(Y)\subseteq X\). If the problem's exchange lemma states that every feasible solution of budget \(k\) can be replaced without increased cost by one selecting \(X\) and excluding \(Y\), delete the structures represented by \(X\cup Y\), set \(k'=k-c(X)\), and output the residual instance. Otherwise, apply no reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a closed bipartite expansion and reduce it only when a problem-specific exchange lemma forces an equally good normalized solution.
assumptions_latex: The incidence graph is constructible in polynomial time.
A valid problem-specific exchange lemma supplies the cost \(c(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced instance with \(k'=k-c(X)\) is equivalent to \((I,k)\) under the exchange lemma.

notation.meaning: Budget charged for selecting the forced side.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed algorithm is only a problem-dependent template: the residual construction, feasibility relation, and exchange lemma are unspecified, so equivalence cannot be checked. The displayed incidence graph also has an unmatched closing parenthesis. A precise sourced specialization is required.

children.title: Crown–Expansion Generalizations
children.top_down_role: Structural extensions relating classical crowns to broader expansion certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Crown–Expansion Generalizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard bipartite \(q\)-expansion lemma generalizing matching-based crowns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\ge1\) and let \(B=(A\uplus D,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph in which every vertex of \(D\) has a neighbor. If \(|D|>q|A|\), then there exist nonempty sets \(X\subseteq A\) and \(Y\subseteq D\) such that \(N_B(Y)\subseteq X\) and there is a set of edges assigning to every \(x\in X\) exactly \(q\) distinct neighbors in \(Y\), with all \(q|X|\) assigned vertices distinct. Such \(X,Y\) and the assigned edges can be found in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If one bipartite side is more than q times larger and has no isolated vertices, a nonempty closed q-expansion exists and is polynomial-time findable.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in\mathbb N\) and \(q\ge1\).
Every vertex of \(D\) has positive degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist nonempty \(X\subseteq A\), \(Y\subseteq D\) with \(N_B(Y)\subseteq X\) and a \(q\)-expansion of \(X\) into \(Y\).

notation.meaning: Assignment of q distinct, globally disjoint neighbors to each left vertex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated strict-cardinality version of the q-expansion lemma is mathematically plausible and the theorem kind fits the container, but its hypotheses, conclusion, and polynomial-time claim require an exact authoritative locator.

children.title: Expansion-Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sparse or imbalanced incidence regimes lacking sufficient expansion for reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Expansion-Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of degree and cardinality hypotheses for guaranteed q-expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(q\ge 1\). If isolated vertices on the expanded side are permitted, let \(A=\{a\}\) and let \(D\) contain arbitrarily many isolated vertices. Then \(|D|>q|A|\) may hold, but no nonempty \(q\)-expansion exists. Positive degree alone is also insufficient: let \(|A|=2\), let \(|D|=2q-1\), and join every vertex of \(D\) to both vertices of \(A\). Every vertex of \(D\) has positive degree. A closed expansion with a singleton \(X\subseteq A\) is impossible because every nonempty \(Y\subseteq D\) has both vertices of \(A\) as neighbors, while \(X=A\) would require \(2q\) distinct vertices of \(Y\), more than \(|D|\). Thus neither the size inequality without the degree condition nor the degree condition without sufficient cardinality guarantees a \(q\)-expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily many isolated right vertices can satisfy the size inequality without yielding an expansion. Conversely, a complete bipartite graph with two left vertices and 2q−1 right vertices has positive right-side degree but no closed q-expansion.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in\mathbb N\) and \(q\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removing either the no-isolated-vertex condition or the sufficient-cardinality condition destroys the general \(q\)-expansion guarantee.

notation.meaning: The two sides of the bipartite graph.
Required number of distinct neighbors per expanded vertex.

children.title: Sunflower-Based Kernels
children.top_down_role: Kernel arguments using large families with a common core.

knowledge_statements.title: Sunflower-Based Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical exact kernelization rule for parameterized uniform Hitting Set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \((U,\mathcal F,k)\) of \(d\)-Hitting Set with fixed \(d\) and \(\mathcal F\subseteq\binom Ud\), repeatedly find a sunflower of \(k+2\) sets with core \(C\) and delete one petal-set. Any hitting set of size at most \(k\) hitting the remaining \(k+1\) petals must meet \(C\), because their parts outside \(C\) are pairwise disjoint; it therefore also hits the deleted set. When no such sunflower remains, the sunflower lemma gives \(|\mathcal F|\le d!(k+1)^d\). Delete elements outside \(\bigcup\mathcal F\) and output the resulting equivalent instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly delete one set from every sunflower with k+2 petals; the remaining d-Hitting Set instance has polynomially many sets and is equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(d\ge1\) is fixed.
\(\mathcal F\) is a finite family of \(d\)-element subsets of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is equivalent and satisfies \(|\mathcal F|\le d!(k+1)^d\) and \(|U|\le d\,d!(k+1)^d\).

notation.meaning: Universe and family of sets to be hit.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction rule and stated bounds are consistent with the classical fixed-d Hitting Set sunflower kernel, and algorithm is the correct content kind, but neither the sunflower bound nor the kernel rule has an inspectable citation.

children.title: Set-System Reduction Methods
children.top_down_role: Kernel arguments using incidence, intersection, rank, or bounded-frequency structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-System Reduction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment reduction for parameterized Hitting Set instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite Hitting Set instance \((U,\mathcal F,k)\), repeatedly choose distinct \(A,B\in\mathcal F\) with \(A\subseteq B\) and delete \(B\). Also delete every element of \(U\setminus\bigcup\mathcal F\). Stop when \(\mathcal F\) is an antichain under inclusion, and output \((\bigcup\mathcal F,\mathcal F,k)\). The rule is safe because every set \(S\subseteq U\) that intersects \(A\) also intersects \(B\); hence hitting the reduced family is equivalent to hitting the original family, with the same budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Hitting Set, delete every set containing another retained set and remove unused universe elements; feasibility and the parameter remain unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^U\) are finite.
Feasibility means intersecting every member of \(\mathcal F\) with at most \(k\) elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output family is an inclusion antichain and has a hitting set of size at most \(k\) exactly when the input family does.

notation.meaning: Containment triggering deletion of the redundant superset.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The containment reduction is mathematically correct, its plain and LaTeX statements agree, and algorithm fits the container. Promotion even to sourced candidate-review knowledge requires a specific reference and locator.

children.title: Core–Petal Compression
children.top_down_role: Compression choices based on shared cores and replaceable peripheral sets.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is a finite set family over \(U\).
\(S_1,\ldots,S_r\) is a sunflower with \(r\ge k+2\).
\(k\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal F,k)\) and \((\mathcal F\setminus\{S_r\},k)\) are equivalent Hitting Set instances.

notation.meaning: petal-exclusive part of the ith set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe sunflower reduction for parameterized bounded-rank Hitting Set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\), let \(k\in\mathbb N\), and let \(S_1,\ldots,S_r\in\mathcal F\) form a sunflower with core \(C\), so that \(S_i\cap S_j=C\) for all distinct \(i,j\). If \(r\ge k+2\), the reduction rule deletes \(S_r\) and leaves \(k\) unchanged. The resulting Hitting Set instance \((\mathcal F\setminus\{S_r\},k)\) is equivalent to \((\mathcal F,k)\). Apply the rule repeatedly while such a sunflower exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Hitting Set parameterized by k, a sunflower with at least k+2 petals permits deletion of any one member without changing whether a hitting set of size at most k exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Core–Petal Compression

children.title: Unbounded-Intersection Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Set systems whose intersection patterns defeat bounded representative selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Intersection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of uniform sunflower forcing when set rank is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\ge4\), let \(U_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\mathcal F_n=\{U_n\setminus\{i\}:i\in U_n\}\). Then \(|\mathcal F_n|=n\), while every member has size \(n-1\). No three distinct members form a sunflower: for distinct \(i,j\), their intersection is \(U_n\setminus\{i,j\}\), which depends on the selected pair. Thus arbitrarily large set families of unbounded rank can avoid even a three-petal sunflower. Consequently, cardinality alone cannot support a rank-independent sunflower compression threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily large unbounded-rank families may contain no three-petal sunflower, so sunflower kernel bounds require a rank or comparable intersection restriction.
assumptions_latex: Set sizes are not bounded by a fixed constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_n\) has no sunflower with three petals despite \(|\mathcal F_n|=n\to\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction and conclusion are correct, and failure_boundary is the appropriate role for this leaf. However, the record has no source reference or locator supporting the boundary example.

knowledge_statements.title: Packing–Covering Kernel Arguments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal bounded-set packing yields either rejection or a small covering modulator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) satisfy \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and greedily construct an inclusion-maximal pairwise-disjoint subfamily \(\mathcal P\). For the problem of hitting every member of \(\mathcal F\) with at most \(k\) elements, if \(|\mathcal P|>k\), reject. Otherwise set \(Z=\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal P}S\). Maximality implies that every member of \(\mathcal F\) intersects \(Z\), and \(|Z|\le dk\). Hence subsequent kernel rules may classify or replace sets by their interaction with the bounded covering modulator \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal disjoint packing either exceeds k and rejects the instance, or its union is a cover of size at most dk.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is finite and every member has size at most \(d\).
The desired hitting set has size at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(|\mathcal P|>k\), or \(Z\) intersects every set in \(\mathcal F\) and satisfies \(|Z|\le dk\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The packing-covering dichotomy is correctly stated for finite set families of rank at most d, and principle fits the topic container. An authoritative kernelization source with a specific locator is still required.

knowledge_statements.title: Representative-Set Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroid representative families as lossless compression of partial solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid and let \(\mathcal A\) be a family of independent sets, each of size \(p\). A subfamily \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\subseteq\mathcal A\) is \(q\)-representative for \(\mathcal A\) if, for every \(Y\subseteq E\) with \(|Y|\le q\), whenever some \(A\in\mathcal A\) satisfies \(A\cap Y=\varnothing\) and \(A\cup Y\in\mathcal I\), some \(\widehat A\in\widehat{\mathcal A}\) satisfies the same conditions. A representative-set kernel replaces \(\mathcal A\) by such a bounded subfamily whenever every future extension uses at most \(q\) elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A q-representative subfamily preserves every partial solution that can be extended by at most q matroid elements.
assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.
Every member of \(\mathcal A\) is independent and has size \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\) preserves feasibility against every extension set of cardinality at most \(q\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of q-representativity is mathematically standard and internally consistent; definition is acceptable as the foundational content of this topic. The further interpretation as a kernel replacement requires a representative-families source and a precise locator.

children.title: Linear-Algebraic Kernel Techniques
children.top_down_role: Compression through rank, dependence, basis selection, or matrix representations.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite subset of \(\mathbb F^r\).
Each permitted feasibility test is a linear functional over \(\mathbb F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists v\in V:\ell(v)\ne0\) if and only if \(\exists b\in B:\ell(b)\ne0\), with \(|B|\le r\).

notation.meaning: basis selected from the encoding vectors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis extraction preserves all linear nonvanishing tests used by a reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\subseteq\mathbb F^r\), and choose \(B\subseteq V\) that is a basis of \(\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F}(V)\). For every linear functional \(\ell:\mathbb F^r\to\mathbb F\), there exists \(v\in V\) with \(\ell(v)\ne0\) if and only if there exists \(b\in B\) with \(\ell(b)\ne0\). Therefore, when feasibility queries depend only on whether some encoded object has a nonzero value under a permitted linear functional, retaining basis objects is a lossless compression to at most \(r\) objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing encoded objects by a vector-space basis preserves every query asking whether some object has a nonzero linear evaluation.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Algebraic Kernel Techniques

children.title: Polynomial-Representation Kernels
children.top_down_role: Compression through bounded-degree polynomial encodings or algebraic identities.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Representation Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial span bases compress objects while preserving pointwise nonvanishing witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathbb F[x_1,\ldots,x_s]\) be a finite family of polynomials of total degree at most \(d\), and choose \(\widehat{\mathcal P}\subseteq\mathcal P\) forming a basis of \(\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F}(\mathcal P)\). For every \(a\in\mathbb F^s\), some \(p\in\mathcal P\) satisfies \(p(a)\ne0\) if and only if some \(\widehat p\in\widehat{\mathcal P}\) satisfies \(\widehat p(a)\ne0\). Moreover, \(|\widehat{\mathcal P}|\le\binom{s+d}{d}\). Thus pointwise nonvanishing queries admit compression by retaining polynomials corresponding to a coefficient-vector basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coefficient-space basis of bounded-degree polynomials preserves all pointwise nonvanishing witnesses and has size at most the monomial dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is finite over the field \(\mathbb F\).
Every polynomial has total degree at most \(d\) in \(s\) variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\widehat{\mathcal P}|\le\binom{s+d}{d}\) and all pointwise nonvanishing queries are preserved.

notation.meaning: span basis retained by the kernel

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coefficient-space dimension bound and preservation of pointwise nonvanishing are correct, and representation fits the leaf. A source must substantiate the use of this representation as a kernel technique rather than merely as a linear-algebra fact.

children.title: Rank-Based Compression
children.top_down_role: Kernel size control derived from bounded-dimensional spans.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Based Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis selection compresses a represented linear matroid without changing independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a matrix \(A\in\mathbb F^{r\times m}\), compute by Gaussian elimination a maximal set \(B\) of linearly independent columns. Initialize \(B=\varnothing\), scan the columns, and insert a column exactly when it increases the current rank. Output the submatrix \(A_B\) together with coordinates expressing every discarded column in \(\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F}(B)\). Then \(|B|=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A)\le r\), the column span is unchanged, and any later computation depending only on this span may use \(A_B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian elimination retains a column basis and dependency coordinates, reducing a matrix to its rank while preserving its column span.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite matrix over a field \(\mathbb F\).
Subsequent queries depend only on the represented column span.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F}(A_B)=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F}(A)\) and \(|B|=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The basis-selection algorithm correctly preserves the column span, and algorithm fits the terminal container. The restriction to later computations depending only on that span is essential; a rank-based kernelization source with a specific locator is required before accepting the record.

children.title: Field-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of compression behavior on coefficient domains or representation fields.

knowledge_statements.title: Field-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix rank and resulting algebraic reductions can change with the coefficient field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}\). Its determinant is \(-2\). Hence \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A)=3\) over every field of characteristic different from \(2\), whereas \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A)=2\) over every field of characteristic \(2\). Thus a basis, dependency relation, or rank bound computed over one field need not remain valid over another. An algebraic kernel must therefore specify the field and justify that its encoding represents the intended combinatorial predicates over that field.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same matrix has rank three outside characteristic two and rank two in characteristic two, so algebraic kernels are field-specific.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb F\) is a field.
Rank is computed using arithmetic in \(\mathbb F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rank of \(A\) depends on \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb F)\), invalidating field-independent rank compression claims.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The determinant and characteristic-dependent ranks are correct, and failure_boundary exactly fits the leaf. The record nevertheless lacks the required inspectable source for the field-sensitivity boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Protrusion Replacement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replace a bounded-treewidth boundaried subgraph by an equivalent constant-size representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) contain a subgraph \(X\) whose boundary \(\partial X\) has size at most \(t\) and whose treewidth is at most \(r\). Regard \(X\) as a labeled boundaried graph. Find a constant-size representative \(R\) and integer shift \(\Delta\) such that, for every compatibly labeled context \(H\) and integer \(k\), \((X\oplus H,k)\) is a yes-instance exactly when \((R\oplus H,k+\Delta)\) is. Replace the interior of \(X\) by that of \(R\), update the parameter to \(k+\Delta\), and repeat until no oversized protrusion remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oversized bounded-treewidth region with small boundary is replaced by a constant-size context-equivalent representative, with a computable parameter shift.
assumptions_latex: \(|\partial X|\le t\) and \(\operatorname{tw}(X)\le r\).
A compatible representative \(R\) and shift \(\Delta\) are computable.
Gluing identifies equally labeled boundary vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(X\) by \(R\) preserves the answer after changing the parameter from \(k\) to \(k+\Delta\).

notation.meaning: labeled attachment boundary of the protrusion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits protrusion replacement, but existence and computability of the representative and parameter shift depend on the parameterized problem and its boundaried-graph equivalence. Those substantive conditions require an authoritative source with a specific theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Index Replacement Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite contextual equivalence classes are the state-space condition enabling replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a parameterized graph problem \(\Pi\) and boundary size \(t\). For compatible \(t\)-boundaried graphs \(G_1,G_2\), define \(G_1\equiv_{\Pi,t}G_2\) when there exists \(\Delta\in\mathbb Z\) such that, for every compatible context \(H\) and integer \(k\), \((G_1\oplus H,k)\in\Pi\) if and only if \((G_2\oplus H,k+\Delta)\in\Pi\). The framework has finite integer index when \(\equiv_{\Pi,t}\) has finitely many equivalence classes for every fixed \(t\). Choosing one minimum-size representative from each class then bounds every replacement gadget solely as a function of \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite integer index means fixed-boundary boundaried graphs have finitely many context behaviors up to an additive parameter shift.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is a parameterized graph problem.
Boundary labels and the gluing operation are fixed.
Parameter shifts are integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite index yields a finite representative table for every fixed boundary size \(t\).

notation.meaning: context equivalence with an additive parameter shift

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The contextual equivalence and finite-integer-index condition are coherently stated, and condition is the correct role for this framework leaf. A specific source locator for the formal finite-integer-index definition is missing.

knowledge_statements.title: Bidimensional Kernelization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional linear-kernel principle combining bidimensional structure with finite-state replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be a minimization problem on an excluded-minor graph class. Assume its optimum is minor-monotone and is at least \(c r^2\) on the \(r\times r\) grid for some \(c>0\). Then every instance \((G,k)\) with optimum at most \(k\) excludes grids larger than order \(\sqrt{k}\), yielding the corresponding sublinear treewidth bound through the class's grid-minor theorem. If polynomial preprocessing additionally produces \(O(k)\) bounded-boundary protrusions and \(\Pi\) has finite integer index on them, replacing each protrusion by a constant-size representative produces an equivalent kernel with \(O(k)\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bidimensional growth bounds treewidth on yes-instances; a linear protrusion decomposition plus finite-index replacement then yields a linear vertex kernel.
assumptions_latex: The graph class excludes a fixed minor and admits the required grid-minor bound.
The optimum is minor-monotone and grows quadratically on grids.
A linear protrusion decomposition and finite-index representatives are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under these hypotheses, \(\Pi\) admits a polynomial-time kernel with \(O(k)\) vertices.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Principle is the appropriate role, but the asserted linear-kernel meta-principle combines quantitative grid-minor, decomposition, replacement, and computability hypotheses whose exact formulations are source-sensitive. The supplied inventory contains no relevant theorem locator, so the mathematical scope cannot yet be accepted.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Graph Kernelization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear kernel counting from a small modulator and bounded sparse neighborhood types.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose preprocessing an instance \((G,k)\) produces a modulator \(X\) with \(|X|\le ak\). Assume every component of \(G-X\) is replaced by an equivalent boundaried graph of at most \(s\) vertices, each component has at most \(b\) neighbors in \(X\), and sparsity guarantees at most \(c|X|\) relevant boundary-neighborhood types. If at most \(q\) representatives are retained per type, the reduced graph has at most \(|X|+sqc|X|\le a(1+sqc)k\) vertices. Therefore these computable structural and replacement conditions give a linear vertex kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear modulator, linearly many sparse neighborhood types, and constant-size representatives imply a kernel with linearly many vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(|X|\le ak\) for constants \(a,b,c,s,q\).
Reduced components have at most \(s\) vertices and at most \(b\) neighbors in \(X\).
There are at most \(c|X|\) relevant types and at most \(q\) representatives per type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|V(G')|\le a(1+sqc)k\) for the reduced graph \(G'\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed counting bound follows from the stated constants, and principle fits the topic. The existence of equivalent component replacements, the definition of relevant types, and the sparsity bound are problem-specific substantive assumptions requiring a source with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Based Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-degree reduction for unweighted Vertex Cover parameterized by solution size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), repeatedly choose a vertex \(v\) with \(\deg_G(v)>k\), delete \(v\), and replace \(k\) by \(k-1\); record \(v\) as forced. Reject if the parameter becomes negative. After exhaustion, delete isolated vertices. If the remaining graph has more than \(k^2\) edges, reject; otherwise output it with the current parameter. Every vertex cover of size at most the pre-reduction parameter contains each forced vertex, and the reduced yes-instance has at most \(2k^2\) nonisolated vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Force every vertex of degree above k, reject when the bounded-degree remainder has over k² edges, and otherwise obtain an equivalent kernel with at most 2k² vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, simple, and unweighted.
The parameter asks whether \(G\) has a vertex cover of size at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule preserves the answer and produces either rejection or a kernel with at most \(k^2\) edges and \(2k^2\) nonisolated vertices.

notation.meaning: degree of vertex v in G

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The high-degree rule and quadratic edge/vertex bounds are mathematically standard and fit the algorithm container, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports them.

knowledge_statements.title: Crown-Based Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crown reduction for unweighted Vertex Cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) contain disjoint sets \(C,H\subseteq V\) such that \(C\) is independent, \(N_G(C)=H\), and a matching saturates \(H\) into \(C\). Replace \((G,k)\) by \((G-(C\cup H),k-|H|)\) and record \(H\) as selected. If \(k<|H|\), reject. The original instance has a vertex cover of size at most \(k\) exactly when the reduced graph has one of size at most \(k-|H|\); a reduced solution lifts by adjoining \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A crown permits deleting its independent crown and head, decreasing the budget by the head size; any reduced cover lifts by adding the head.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph.
\(C\) is independent, \(N_G(C)=H\), and a matching saturates \(H\) into \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((G,k)\) and \((G-(C\cup H),k-|H|)\) are equivalent Vertex Cover instances.

notation.meaning: head equal to the neighborhood of the crown
open neighborhood of C in G

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The crown hypotheses and reduction are consistent with the Vertex Cover crown rule and fit the algorithm container, but the record supplies no source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Nemhauser–Trotter Kernel Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Half-integral LP decomposition underlying linear-size Vertex Cover kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), consider the relaxation \(\min\sum_{v\in V}x_v\) subject to \(x_u+x_v\geq1\) for every \(uv\in E\) and \(x_v\geq0\). There exists an optimal half-integral solution \(x\). With \(V_i=\{v:x_v=i\}\) for \(i\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\), some minimum vertex cover contains \(V_1\), excludes \(V_0\), and uses a minimum vertex cover of \(G[V_{1/2}]\). Thus parameter \(k'=k-|V_1|\) suffices on the residual graph; after exhaustive decomposition, every yes-instance satisfies \(|V_{1/2}|\leq2k'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal half-integral LP solution fixes value-one vertices in and value-zero vertices out, leaving an equivalent residual instance of at most twice its remaining budget.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph.
The target is an unweighted minimum vertex cover or its size-k decision form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual instance \((G[V_{1/2}],k-|V_1|)\) is equivalent, and an exhaustively reduced yes-instance has at most \(2(k-|V_1|)\) vertices.

notation.meaning: residual parameter after selecting value-one vertices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the Nemhauser–Trotter container, but the precise persistency, residual equivalence, and linear-size consequence require an authoritative theorem citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Equivalence Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable certificates for equivalence between an instance and its kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized decision problem \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb{N}\), an instance-equivalence certificate for \((I,k)\) and \((I',k')\) is a finite string \(c\) accepted by a deterministic verifier \(V\) exactly only if \((I,k)\in Q\iff(I',k')\in Q\). The certificate system is sound when acceptance implies this equivalence and complete for a reduction \(R\) when every output \((I',k')=R(I,k)\) has an accepted certificate. Verification time is polynomial in the combined encoded lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate lets a polynomial-time verifier confirm that an original parameterized instance and its kernel have the same yes-or-no answer.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a parameterized decision problem with fixed instance encoding.
\(V\) is deterministic and receives both instances and the certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance soundly certifies \((I,k)\in Q\iff(I',k')\in Q\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the container, but this is a proposed formal model rather than a standard kernelization definition, and no source establishes its verifier, soundness, completeness, or complexity conventions.

children.title: Solution Lifting
children.top_down_role: Transfer of reduced-instance solutions into corresponding source-instance solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery map from a solved kernel to the original optimization instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a reduction map an optimization instance \(I\) to a kernel \(I'\) and recovery data \(h\). A solution-lifting algorithm receives \((I,I',h,y')\), where \(y'\) is feasible for \(I'\), and outputs \(y=L(I,I',h,y')\) feasible for \(I\). For exact preservation it must satisfy \(f_I(y)=f_{I'}(y')+\Delta(h)\); consequently an optimal kernel solution lifts to an optimal original solution. The running time must be polynomial in the encoded input, history, and output lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solution lifting combines a kernel solution with recorded recovery data to produce an original feasible solution while preserving the objective up to a known offset.
assumptions_latex: \(I'\) and recovery data \(h\) are produced from \(I\) by a sound reduction.
\(y'\) is feasible for \(I'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(I,I',h,y')\) is feasible for \(I\) and has objective value \(f_{I'}(y')+\Delta(h)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Feasibility and an objective identity for lifted kernel solutions alone do not ensure that an optimal kernel solution is globally optimal for the original instance; a reverse-coverage or optimal-value correspondence condition is also needed. A source is required to fix the intended lifting model.

children.title: Witness Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of complete witnesses using retained preprocessing information.

knowledge_statements.title: Witness Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward reconstruction through a sequence of kernelization rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(I_0\to I_1\to\cdots\to I_t\) is a reduction sequence, and each step stores data \(h_i\) with a polynomial-time local recovery map \(L_i\) sending every valid witness for \(I_{i+1}\) to a valid witness for \(I_i\). Given a witness \(y_t\) for \(I_t\), compute \(y_i=L_i(h_i,y_{i+1})\) for \(i=t-1,t-2,\ldots,0\), and output \(y_0\). If every local map preserves the required objective relation, their composition reconstructs a valid correspondingly valued witness for \(I_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process reduction records in reverse order, applying each local recovery map to reconstruct a valid witness for the original instance.
assumptions_latex: Every reduction step has a sound local recovery map.
The terminal witness \(y_t\) is valid for \(I_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reverse composition \(L_0\circ L_1\circ\cdots\circ L_{t-1}\) produces a valid witness for \(I_0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Reverse composition of sound local recovery maps is mathematically coherent and fits the algorithm container, but no source or locator supports the stated compositional recovery framework.

children.title: Reduction-History Encoding
children.top_down_role: Metadata retained to support compositional recovery after multiple reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-History Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composable encoding of information needed to reverse kernel reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((I_0,k_0)\to(I_1,k_1)\to\cdots\to(I_t,k_t)\) be a finite reduction sequence. Its reduction history is the ordered encoding \(H=((r_0,h_0),\ldots,(r_{t-1},h_{t-1}))\), where \(r_i\) identifies the rule taking \((I_i,k_i)\) to \((I_{i+1},k_{i+1})\), and \(h_i\) contains the rule-specific data required by its recovery map. The history is recovery-sufficient when, for every \(i\in\{0,\ldots,t-1\}\), a predecessor witness can be computed from \((r_i,h_i)\), the adjacent instances, and a successor witness. It is polynomially bounded when \(|H|\leq p(|\operatorname{enc}(I_0,k_0)|)\) for some fixed polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduction history is an ordered list of rule identifiers and local recovery data that suffices to reverse every reduction; it is polynomially bounded when its encoded length is polynomial in the initial parameterized instance length.
assumptions_latex: The sequence \((I_0,k_0)\to\cdots\to(I_t,k_t)\) is finite.
Every reduction rule has a specified recovery interface, and all instance, witness, and history encodings are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A recovery-sufficient history permits reverse witness reconstruction, and polynomial boundedness means \(|H|\leq p(|\operatorname{enc}(I_0,k_0)|)\) for a fixed polynomial \(p\).

notation.meaning: local recovery data for reduction i
fixed encoding of the initial parameterized instance

children.title: Ambiguous-Recovery Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where reduced solutions lack enough information for valid source recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambiguous-Recovery Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of recovery when equivalent kernels omit solution correspondence data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Decision equivalence alone does not determine a solution-lifting map. If two original instances \(I_1,I_2\) reduce to the same kernel \(I'\) but require different predecessors for some kernel witness \(y'\), then no deterministic recovery function depending only on \((I',y')\) can correctly reconstruct witnesses for both originals. Recovery is well-defined only after supplying the original instance, a distinguishing reduction history, or a canonical rule whose inverse image is uniquely specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A kernel’s yes-or-no equivalence is insufficient for witness recovery when identical kernel witnesses can require different original solutions without distinguishing history.
assumptions_latex: The reduction retains only \(I'\) and discards the original instance and recovery history.
Some kernel witness has incompatible required preimages for two originals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No recovery function of \((I',y')\) alone is sound for both original instances.

notation.meaning: a witness for the reduced instance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The information-loss phenomenon fits a failure-boundary container, but “different predecessors” needs a formal incompatibility condition or concrete counterexample, supported by a source.

children.title: Weight Preservation
children.top_down_role: Retention or controlled transformation of weighted solution contributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact preservation of encoded weights under annotated kernelization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a reduction map a weighted minimization instance \(I=(X,w,\mathcal F)\) to \(I'=(X',w',\mathcal F')\), with lifting map \(L:\mathcal F'\to\mathcal F\) and fixed offset \(\Delta\). It is weight-preserving when every \(S'\in\mathcal F'\) satisfies \(\sum_{x\in L(S')}w(x)=\sum_{x\in S'}w'(x)+\Delta\), and for every \(S\in\mathcal F\) there exists \(S'\in\mathcal F'\) satisfying \(\sum_{x\in S}w(x)=\sum_{x\in S'}w'(x)+\Delta\). For an at-most threshold \(B\), set \(B'=B-\Delta\); then \(I\) has a feasible solution of weight at most \(B\) if and only if \(I'\) has one of weight at most \(B'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted reduction preserves weights when lifting adds a fixed offset and every original feasible weight is represented in the kernel; subtracting that offset from the threshold preserves the decision answer.
assumptions_latex: \(I=(X,w,\mathcal F)\) and \(I'=(X',w',\mathcal F')\) are weighted minimization instances.
Weights, thresholds, and \(\Delta\) have exact finite encodings.
The lifting map \(L\) is defined on every member of \(\mathcal F'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With \(B'=B-\Delta\), a solution in \(\mathcal F\) has weight at most \(B\) if and only if a solution in \(\mathcal F'\) has weight at most \(B'\).

children.title: Annotation Preservation
children.top_down_role: Retention of auxiliary labels, constraints, or recovery metadata.

knowledge_statements.title: Annotation Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Commuting condition for annotations under reduction and lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let feasible solutions of \(I\) and \(I'\) carry annotations in sets \(A\) and \(A'\), with maps \(a_I:\mathcal{F}(I)\to A\), \(a_{I'}:\mathcal{F}(I')\to A'\), and an annotation decoder \(D_h:A'\to A\) determined by recovery data \(h\). A lifting map \(L_h\) preserves annotations exactly when \(a_I(L_h(S'))=D_h(a_{I'}(S'))\) for every \(S'\in\mathcal{F}(I')\). Lossless preservation additionally requires the relevant decoder to be injective on attainable kernel annotations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Annotations are preserved when annotating a lifted solution equals decoding the annotation of its kernel solution; injectivity prevents relevant annotation loss.
assumptions_latex: Annotation and lifting maps are defined on all feasible solutions.
Recovery data \(h\) determines the decoder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact preservation is the commuting identity \(a_I\circ L_h=D_h\circ a_{I'}\) on \(\mathcal{F}(I')\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The commuting identity is coherent and fits a condition container, but injectivity of the decoder only prevents collisions among attainable kernel annotations; it does not by itself guarantee coverage of relevant original annotations. The intended losslessness model requires a source and sharper scope.

children.title: Objective-Value Preservation
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between reduced-instance and source-instance objective values.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Value Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine objective correspondence between kernel and original solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization instances \(I\) and \(I'\), a reduction with lifting map \(L\), scale \(\alpha>0\), and offset \(\beta\) preserves objective values affinely when every feasible kernel solution \(y'\) satisfies \(f_I(L(y'))=\alpha f_{I'}(y')+\beta\), and every relevant original solution has a kernel representative satisfying the same identity. Then \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I')+\beta\), and any optimal solution of \(I'\) lifts to an optimal solution of \(I\). Exact additive preservation is the case \(\alpha=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine objective correspondence transfers optimal values and ensures that every optimal kernel solution lifts to an optimal original solution.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\) are exactly represented.
Lifting is feasible and the correspondence covers all objective-relevant original solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I')+\beta\), and kernel optimality is preserved by lifting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine correspondence is mathematically plausible and fits a property container, but “every relevant original solution” is not a defined quantified domain. An authoritative source is needed to determine the exact coverage hypothesis.

children.title: Encoding-Growth Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where weights or annotations prevent a genuinely small encoded kernel.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Growth Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-length boundary separating combinatorial shrinkage from genuine kernel size reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a reduced annotated instance contain \(m\) objects with integer annotations \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). Under binary encoding its size is at least \(\sum_{i=1}^m(\lfloor\log_2(|a_i|+1)\rfloor+1)\) bits. Hence bounding \(m\) by a polynomial in parameter \(k\) does not yield a polynomial kernel if annotation magnitudes have superpolynomial bit length in \(k\). A polynomial kernel requires the total encoding length, including recovery data, weights, offsets, and multiplicities, to be bounded by \(k^{O(1)}\), not merely the number of retained objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Few retained objects do not form a polynomial kernel when their annotations or recovery data require superpolynomially many bits in the parameter.
assumptions_latex: Annotations are integers represented in binary.
Kernel size is measured by total encoded bit length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polynomial object-count bound is insufficient unless all annotations and recovery data together use \(k^{O(1)}\) bits.

notation.meaning: integer annotation of retained object i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between object count and total encoded bit length is correct in the standard kernelization model and fits a failure-boundary container, but no source or specific locator is supplied for that model or the encoding claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Turing Kernelization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-based kernelization for parameterized decision problems, allowing adaptive access to multiple small instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) be a parameterized decision problem. A Turing kernelization of size \(f\) is a deterministic algorithm that, on input \((x,k)\), decides whether \((x,k)\in Q\) in time polynomial in \(|x|+k\), given oracle access to \(Q\), while every oracle query \((y,\ell)\) satisfies \(|y|+\ell\le f(k)\). Queries may be adaptive and their number is bounded by a polynomial in \(|x|+k\). It is a polynomial Turing kernelization when \(f\) is polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Turing kernel decides an instance using polynomially many, possibly adaptive oracle queries whose individual sizes depend only polynomially on the parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) is a parameterized decision problem.
Oracle calls are charged unit cost when measuring the kernelization algorithm's running time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every queried instance has encoding size and parameter bounded by \(f(k)\), and the original membership question is decided correctly.

notation.meaning: Parameterized decision problem and oracle language.
Maximum permitted query size as a function of the input parameter.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the customary bounded-query formulation of Turing kernelization.
A targeted parameterized-complexity source is required; supplied locators concern network optimization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but no cited source fixes the query-size, query-count, oracle-cost, or adaptivity conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Preprocessing Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate kernelization scheme for maximization problems, with explicit solution lifting and multiplicative loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be a parameterized maximization problem. An approximate preprocessing scheme consists, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), of polynomial-time algorithms that map an instance \((I,k)\) to an instance \((I',k')\) of encoding length at most \(g(k,\varepsilon)\), and lift every feasible solution \(s'\) for \(I'\) to a feasible solution \(s\) for \(I\). For every \(c\ge1\), if \(\operatorname{val}_{I'}(s')\ge \operatorname{OPT}(I')/c\), then \(\operatorname{val}_{I}(s)\ge \operatorname{OPT}(I)/(c(1+\varepsilon))\). It is a polynomial-size scheme when \(g(k,\varepsilon)\) is polynomial in \(k\) for each fixed \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each accuracy tolerance, preprocessing produces a parameter-bounded instance and lifts any reduced-instance approximation while losing at most an additional factor of one plus the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is a parameterized maximization problem with polynomially recognizable feasible solutions.
\(\varepsilon>0\) and the approximation factor satisfies \(c\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced encoding has length at most \(g(k,\varepsilon)\), and solution lifting multiplies the approximation factor by at most \(1+\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Optimal objective value of instance I.
Approximation factor achieved on the reduced instance.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The statement specializes approximate kernelization to the common multiplicative maximization convention.
A source is needed to confirm whether this node intends PSAKS, approximate kernels, or a broader preprocessing notion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The leaf may denote PSAKS, approximate kernelization, or a broader approximate preprocessing model. A source is required to validate the stated lifting guarantee and size dependence on epsilon.

children.title: Streaming Kernels
children.top_down_role: Kernelization under pass, memory, and arrival-order constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Streaming Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact kernelization under bounded-pass streaming access to the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\). A streaming kernelization with pass bound \(p\), memory bound \(m\), and size bound \(g\) reads the encoding of \((x,k)\) sequentially for at most \(p(k)\) passes, uses at most \(m(k)\log(|x|+2)\) bits of working memory, and outputs \((x',k')\) such that \((x,k)\in Q\) if and only if \((x',k')\in Q\), with \(|x'|+k'\le g(k)\). A polynomial streaming kernel has polynomially bounded \(p\), \(m\), and \(g\); a one-pass kernel has \(p(k)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A streaming kernel makes parameter-bounded passes over sequential input, uses parameter-bounded memory up to logarithmic indexing overhead, and outputs an equivalent parameter-bounded instance.
assumptions_latex: The input encoding is presented as a sequential stream.
\(Q\) is a parameterized decision problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is equivalent to the input and has total encoding size at most \(g(k)\).

notation.meaning: Parameterized memory bound excluding logarithmic indexing overhead.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The definition combines exact kernel equivalence with standard streaming resource bounds.
Streaming-kernel conventions vary on memory, pass, and output models; a targeted source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but streaming-kernel conventions differ regarding passes, memory, output access, and whether bounds may depend polynomially on the parameter.

children.title: Distributed Kernels
children.top_down_role: Kernelization with input or state partitioned across communicating processors.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact kernelization when an instance is partitioned among communicating processors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an encoding of \((x,k)\) for a parameterized problem \(Q\) be partitioned as \(x=x_1\uplus\cdots\uplus x_r\) among \(r\) processors. A distributed kernelization is a communication protocol after which a designated processor, or all processors jointly, outputs \((x',k')\) satisfying \((x,k)\in Q\) if and only if \((x',k')\in Q\), and \(|x'|+k'\le g(k)\). Its resource bounds specify the communication topology, number of rounds, total communicated bits, local computation, and local memory. It is polynomial-size when \(g\) is polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Processors holding separate input parts communicate under a stated model and produce a small instance equivalent to the combined parameterized input.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) is a parameterized decision problem.
The input partition and communication model are fixed as part of the algorithmic specification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The protocol outputs an equivalent instance of size at most \(g(k)\) under its stated round and communication bounds.

notation.meaning: Distributed partition of the input encoding.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Exact equivalence and parameter-bounded output are the kernel requirements; communication resources describe the distributed model.
The literature uses multiple distributed models, so the intended topology and output convention require a source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No authoritative locator supports this generalized distributed-kernel definition or fixes its topology, partition, output-placement, round, and communication conventions.

children.title: Parallel Kernels
children.top_down_role: Kernelization exploiting concurrent computation under work and depth constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact kernelization measured by parallel depth, work, and output size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\). A parallel kernelization is a uniform family of parallel algorithms that maps each input \((x,k)\) to \((x',k')\) such that \((x,k)\in Q\) if and only if \((x',k')\in Q\), and \(|x'|+k'\le g(k)\). The family has depth \(D(|x|,k)\) and work \(W(|x|,k)\), measured in a specified parallel computation model. A polylogarithmic-depth polynomial-work kernel satisfies \(D(n,k)\le h(k)(\log n)^{O(1)}\), \(W(n,k)\le h(k)n^{O(1)}\), and polynomially bounded \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parallel kernel computes an equivalent parameter-bounded instance while exposing explicit bounds on parallel depth, total work, and kernel size.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a parameterized decision problem.
The parallel machine model and uniformity convention are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output preserves membership in \(Q\), has size bounded by \(g(k)\), and is computed within the stated depth and work.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The definition applies exact kernel equivalence under conventional parameterized parallel resource bounds.
A source must fix the intended PRAM, circuit, or parameterized complexity model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits the leaf conceptually, but the claimed parameterized depth/work formulation depends on an unspecified PRAM, circuit, or uniform parallel model.

children.title: Communication Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Limits caused by data movement, synchronization, or global coordination.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-relative lower-bound predicate for communication required by distributed exact kernelization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a distributed input model for a parameterized problem \(Q\). A communication bottleneck of magnitude \(B(n,k,r)\) holds if every randomized protocol that, on every partitioned input of length \(n\) and parameter \(k\) across \(r\) processors, outputs with probability at least \(2/3\) an equivalent kernel of a prescribed size uses \(\Omega(B(n,k,r))\) communicated bits in the worst case. Consequently, no protocol in that model can simultaneously attain the prescribed kernel size and communication \(o(B(n,k,r))\); changing the topology, round bound, error probability, or output placement changes the claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A communication bottleneck is a model-specific lower bound showing that producing a kernel of the prescribed size necessarily transmits many bits.
assumptions_latex: The communication topology, input partition, round regime, and output location are fixed.
Protocols must succeed on every input with probability at least \(2/3\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Worst-case communication is \(\Omega(B(n,k,r))\) for every protocol meeting the prescribed exact-kernel guarantee.

notation.meaning: Claimed lower bound on communicated bits.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Communication lower bounds are meaningful only after fixing the distributed model and success criterion.
No problem-specific lower bound or intended communication model is supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a template for a lower bound rather than a supported complexity bound. No problem, kernel-size target, communication model, or source establishes any particular function B.

children.title: Composition Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Mappings that combine multiple source instances into one bounded-parameter instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Composition Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General Boolean composition used to derive polynomial-kernel lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\), let \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\), and let \(F:\{0,1\}^t\to\{0,1\}\). An \(F\)-composition from \(L\) into \(Q\) is a polynomial-time algorithm that receives instances \(x_1,\ldots,x_t\) satisfying the framework's common-class or promise condition and outputs \((y,k)\) such that \((y,k)\in Q\) if and only if \(F(\mathbf1_{x_1\in L},\ldots,\mathbf1_{x_t\in L})=1\). The composition is polynomially parameter bounded when \(k\le p(\max_i|x_i|+\log t)\) for a fixed polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composition combines many source instances into one parameterized instance whose answer is a specified Boolean function of the source answers, with controlled parameter growth.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a classical language and \(Q\) is a parameterized decision problem.
The inputs satisfy any common-class or promise restriction required by the framework.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output truth value equals \(F\) applied to the input truth values, and its parameter is polynomially bounded in the largest input and \(\log t\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This abstracts AND-, OR-, and related polynomial-parameter composition notions.
A targeted kernel-lower-bound source is required to fix the intended composition variant.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Boolean F-composition abstraction is plausible, but it is broader than standard named composition variants and lacks a source defining the applicable promise and parameter bound.

children.title: OR-Composition Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Compositions preserving whether at least one source instance is positive.

knowledge_statements.title: OR-Composition Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-parameter composition whose output is positive exactly when some input is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) and \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\). An OR-composition is a polynomial-time algorithm that, on instances \(x_1,\ldots,x_t\) satisfying the framework's common-class condition, produces \((y,k)\) such that \((y,k)\in Q\) if and only if \(x_i\in L\) for at least one \(i\in\{1,\ldots,t\}\). There must be a fixed polynomial \(p\) for which \(k\le p(\max_i|x_i|+\log t)\). If all inputs are required to share one polynomial-equivalence class, this is the OR-cross-composition form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An OR-composition encodes many inputs into one parameterized instance that is positive exactly when at least one input is positive, while controlling the output parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a classical language and \(Q\) is a parameterized decision problem.
Input instances satisfy the composition framework's common-class restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((y,k)\in Q\iff\bigvee_{i=1}^{t}(x_i\in L)\), with \(k\le p(\max_i|x_i|+\log t)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: OR-composition is the disjunctive specialization of Boolean composition.
The distinction among OR-composition, weak composition, and OR-cross-composition needs an authoritative source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement blends generic OR-composition and OR-cross-composition conventions. A source must determine the intended common-class condition and exact parameter bound.

children.title: Parameter-Control Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Structural devices keeping the composed parameter bounded by source size.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Control Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-parameter bound preventing a composition from encoding its input count directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a composition receiving \(t\) strings \(x_1,\ldots,x_t\) and producing a parameterized instance \((y,k')\), polynomial parameter control is the condition that a fixed polynomial \(p\), independent of \(t\) and the particular inputs, satisfies \(k'\le p(n+\log t)\), where \(n=\max_i|x_i|\). Thus dependence on the number of instances is permitted only through \(\log t\); a bound polynomial in \(t\) alone does not satisfy this condition. Stronger frameworks may require \(k'\le p(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter control requires the composed parameter to be polynomial in the largest input length plus the logarithm of the number of inputs.
assumptions_latex: The composition algorithm runs in time polynomial in the total input length.
The polynomial \(p\) is fixed independently of the input family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output parameter obeys \(k'\le p(\max_i|x_i|+\log t)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The displayed bound is the standard parameter-growth requirement in cross-composition frameworks.
No supplied source addresses kernel lower-bound compositions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is standard for cross-composition-style frameworks, but no citation establishes that this exact leaf uses the bound polynomial in max input length plus log t rather than a stronger variant.

children.title: Composition-Promise Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Restrictions on source equivalence classes, input counts, or target encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Composition-Promise Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of a composition guarantee restricted to promised inputs or one equivalence class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a composition algorithm is specified only for tuples \((x_1,\ldots,x_t)\) belonging to a promise domain \(D_t\), such as tuples whose members lie in one equivalence class. Its correctness and parameter bound are required only on \(D_t\): for every tuple in \(D_t\), the output represents the prescribed Boolean combination and has the stated parameter bound. For tuples outside \(D_t\), neither correctness nor parameter control follows. Consequently, applying the associated kernel lower-bound theorem requires a polynomial-time method for recognizing, partitioning into, or otherwise enforcing the promised classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A promised composition supports lower-bound reasoning only on admissible input tuples; mixing classes or violating the promise voids its correctness and parameter guarantees.
assumptions_latex: The composition is defined relative to promise sets \(D_t\subseteq(\Sigma^*)^t\).
Correctness and parameter control have been established only for tuples in \(D_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside \(D_t\), the composition guarantee is unavailable; any lower-bound application must enforce membership in \(D_t\).

notation.meaning: Promise domain for tuples of t source instances.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: A promise-restricted reduction guarantees behavior only on its declared domain.
The node title is nonstandard; a source is needed to determine whether it specifically concerns polynomial equivalence relations or another promise.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The promise-domain boundary is plausible, but the title is nonstandard and the asserted need to recognize, partition, or otherwise enforce classes depends on the particular lower-bound theorem.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard OR-cross-composition from a classical language into a parameterized problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial equivalence relation \(\mathcal R\) on \(\Sigma^*\) is decidable in polynomial time and partitions every finite set into at most polynomially many classes in its maximum string length. A language \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) OR-cross-composes into a parameterized problem \(Q\) if a polynomial-time algorithm, given \(t\) strings \(x_1,\ldots,x_t\) from one \(\mathcal R\)-class, outputs \((y,k)\) such that \((y,k)\in Q\) exactly when some \(x_i\in L\), and \(k\le p(\max_i|x_i|+\log t)\) for a fixed polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: OR-cross-composition combines equivalent-class inputs into one parameterized instance that is positive iff some input is positive, with polynomially controlled parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) is a classical language and \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) is parameterized.
All source instances belong to one class of a polynomial equivalence relation \(\mathcal R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((y,k)\in Q\iff\bigvee_{i=1}^{t}(x_i\in L)\), and \(k\le p(\max_i|x_i|+\log t)\).

notation.meaning: Polynomial equivalence relation controlling admissible input families.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard OR-cross-composition definition used in polynomial-kernel lower bounds.
An authoritative locator for the formal definition is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is recognizably the standard OR-cross-composition definition and its content kind fits, but it has no authoritative source with a specific definition or theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Parameter Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-preserving many-one transformation between parameterized decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q,Q'\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) be parameterized decision problems. A polynomial-parameter transformation from \(Q\) to \(Q'\) is a polynomial-time mapping that sends every \((x,k)\) to \((x',k')\) such that \((x,k)\in Q\) if and only if \((x',k')\in Q'\), and \(k'\le p(k)\) for some fixed polynomial \(p\). No bound depending only on \(k\) is required for \(|x'|\), beyond the polynomial-time output-length bound. Such transformations transfer polynomial kernels or compressions backward when the target preprocessing guarantee has the corresponding form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-parameter transformation preserves yes-instances and maps the new parameter to a polynomial in the original parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) and \(Q'\) are parameterized decision problems.
The mapping is computable in time polynomial in the complete input encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership is preserved and the output parameter satisfies \(k'\le p(k)\) for a fixed polynomial \(p\).

notation.meaning: Polynomial bound on the transformed parameter.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The definition is the standard polynomial-parameter many-one transformation used to transfer kernel bounds.
An authoritative parameterized-complexity source is required; supplied transformation locator concerns network optimization instead.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The core transformation definition is standard and fits the leaf, but neither it nor the additional backward-transfer claim has an authoritative parameterized-complexity citation.

children.title: Distillation Barriers
children.top_down_role: Limits on condensing many equivalent inputs into one small representative.

knowledge_statements.title: Distillation Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical OR-distillation lower-bound form for NP-hard languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) be NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions. An OR-distillation for \(L\) is a polynomial-time algorithm that, given \(x_1,\ldots,x_t\) of maximum length \(n\), outputs \(y\) of size polynomial in \(n\) such that \(y\) is a yes-instance of a fixed language exactly when \(x_i\in L\) for some \(i\). If such an OR-distillation exists, then \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\). Consequently, unless \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\), no NP-hard language admits an OR-distillation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NP-hard language cannot combine arbitrarily many equal-size instances into one polynomial-size OR-equivalent instance unless NP is contained in coNP/poly.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
The distillation output size is bounded by a polynomial in the maximum input length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\) has an OR-distillation \(\Longrightarrow \mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\).

notation.meaning: number of input instances being distilled

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the Distillation Barriers leaf, but no citation supports the precise OR-distillation definition, its allowance of a fixed target language, or the stated NP-to-coNP/poly consequence.

children.title: Compression Barriers
children.top_down_role: Limits on polynomial-size encodings into same-problem or arbitrary target languages.

knowledge_statements.title: Compression Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional polynomial-compression barrier obtained from OR-cross-composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be NP-hard and let \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) be a parameterized problem. Suppose \(L\) OR-cross-composes into \(Q\): from equivalent instances \(x_1,\ldots,x_t\), one can construct \((y,k)\) in polynomial time such that \((y,k)\in Q\) exactly when some \(x_i\in L\), while \(k\) is polynomially bounded in \(\max_i|x_i|+\log t\). If \(Q\) has a polynomial compression into any decidable language, then \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An OR-cross-composition from an NP-hard language rules out polynomial compression of the target parameterized problem unless NP is contained in coNP/poly.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is NP-hard.
\(L\) OR-cross-composes into \(Q\).
\(Q\) has a polynomial compression.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\).
