intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits Compression Barriers, but the source-free statement omits the formal polynomial-equivalence-relation condition and needs authoritative support for the stronger conclusion concerning compression into any decidable language.

children.title: Target-Language Barrier Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer of lower-bound consequences across kernel and compression models.

knowledge_statements.title: Target-Language Barrier Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of compression consequences along polynomial-parameter transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\). Suppose a polynomial-time transformation maps every \((x,k)\) to \((x',k')\) with \((x,k)\in P\) if and only if \((x',k')\in Q\), and with \(k'\le p(k)\) for a polynomial \(p\). If \(Q\) has a compression of bit size at most \(q(k')\) into a language \(R\), then composing the two maps gives a compression of \(P\) into \(R\) of size at most \(q(p(k))\). Thus any valid compression lower bound for \(P\) transfers to \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-parameter transformation followed by a compression is a compression; therefore a source problem’s compression barrier transfers to the target problem.
assumptions_latex: The reduction preserves yes-instances and no-instances.
\(k'\le p(k)\) for a polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{comp}_Q(k')\le q(k')\Longrightarrow \operatorname{comp}_P(k)\le q(p(k))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transfer property matches the leaf and the composition calculation is plausible, but no source defines the required transformation and compression models or confirms that the claimed lower bound transfers with the same target-language and encoding assumptions.

children.title: Complexity-Assumption Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of preprocessing barriers on designated complexity collapses or separations.

knowledge_statements.title: Complexity-Assumption Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of standard distillation and compression lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conclusion of the form “\(Q\) has no polynomial compression unless \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\)” is conditional: it excludes the compression only under \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\). If that separation assumption is removed, the implication supplied by a distillation or cross-composition argument remains valid, but it no longer yields nonexistence of a compression. Moreover, such an argument does not by itself exclude superpolynomial compression, approximation, randomized compression, or compression on restricted instance classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard composition barriers exclude polynomial compression only under a complexity separation and do not automatically cover larger, approximate, randomized, or restricted compressions.
assumptions_latex: The available lower-bound argument proves only \(\text{compression}\Rightarrow\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\), nonexistence of the compression does not follow.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate and the logical caveat is plausible, but citations are required for the exact deterministic barrier and for the exclusions concerning approximate, randomized, superpolynomial, and restricted-instance variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparsification Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic constraint-count and encoding-length formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized problem \(Q\), a sparsification lower bound \(s(k)\) asserts that no polynomial-time equivalence-preserving map can transform every instance \((x,k)\) into an encoded instance \(y\) having fewer than \(s(k)\) bits, or fewer than \(s(k)\) explicitly represented constraints under the stated encoding, unless a specified complexity-class collapse occurs. Bit and constraint bounds are interchangeable only when every retained constraint has encoding length polynomially bounded in \(k\); otherwise the two resources must be bounded separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparsification lower bound forbids equivalent polynomial-time reductions below a stated bit or constraint count, conditionally on a complexity separation and a fixed encoding.
assumptions_latex: The parameter and output encoding are fixed.
The sparsification preserves yes/no equivalence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|y|<s(k)\) is impossible under the stated complexity assumption and encoding model.

notation.meaning: claimed lower bound on sparsified size

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This generic template does not identify a concrete problem, lower-bound function, complexity assumption, or theorem. A problem-specific sourced result is needed before the asserted complexity bound is reliable.

children.title: Iterative Compression
children.top_down_role: Solution-improvement frameworks that pass through bounded excess solutions and isolate a smaller compression problem.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Reed, Smith, and Vetta, Finding Odd Cycle Transversals
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Reed, Smith, and Vetta, Finding Odd Cycle Transversals

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Solution Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic iterative-compression scheme for hereditary feasibility systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\), let \(I_i\) be the instance induced by \(\{v_1,\ldots,v_i\}\), and seek a feasible solution of size at most \(k\). Initialize with a feasible solution \(S_0\) for \(I_0\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), form \(T_i=S_{i-1}\cup\{v_i\}\), which has size at most \(k+1\), and invoke a compression subroutine on \((I_i,T_i,k)\). If it returns a feasible \(S_i\) with \(|S_i|\le k\), continue; otherwise report no solution. Output \(S_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add elements one at a time, enlarge the previous solution by the new element, then compress the resulting size-k-plus-one solution back to size k.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility is preserved when restricting an instance to an earlier prefix.
The compression subroutine is correct for a supplied feasible solution of size at most \(k+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs a feasible \(S_n\) with \(|S_n|\le k\), or correctly reports that none exists.

notation.meaning: instance on the first i elements
compressed solution for the i-th prefix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the scheme is not valid for an arbitrary hereditary feasibility system: adding the new element must preserve feasibility of the supplied temporary solution, as occurs in suitable deletion formulations, and compression failure must certify that no size-k solution exists. A specialized sourced formulation is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint Compression Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjoint variant of a generic deletion-set compression problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an instance, let \(W\) be a known feasible deletion set for \(I\), and let \(k\in\mathbb N\). The disjoint compression problem asks whether there exists a feasible deletion set \(S\) satisfying \(|S|\le k\) and \(S\cap W=\varnothing\); if so, it outputs such an \(S\). In iterative compression, the unrestricted compression step can be decomposed by guessing \(S\cap W\), committing that intersection, and solving the corresponding residual disjoint instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given an existing solution W, disjoint compression seeks a new size-at-most-k solution using no element of W.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) is a feasible deletion set for \(I\).
Feasibility of a proposed deletion set is decidable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists S:\ |S|\le k,\ S\cap W=\varnothing,\text{ and }S\text{ is feasible for }I\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits a disjoint deletion-set compression leaf, but no source supports the stated convention or the additional claim that unrestricted compression decomposes by guessing the intersection and solving a residual disjoint instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioned Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compression with prescribed intersection choices across a partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an instance, let \(W\) be a known feasible solution, and let \(W=W_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}W_r\) be a partition. Given admissible families \(\mathcal A_j\subseteq 2^{W_j}\), the partitioned compression problem asks for a feasible solution \(S\) with \(|S|\le k\) and \(S\cap W_j\in\mathcal A_j\) for every \(j\). Fixing each intersection exactly, forbidding it, or bounding its cardinality yields common special cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partitioned compression seeks a smaller feasible solution whose intersection with every block of the old solution satisfies a prescribed local rule.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) is a known feasible solution.
\(W_1,\ldots,W_r\) are pairwise disjoint and cover \(W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists S:\ |S|\le k,\ S\text{ feasible},\ \forall j,\ S\cap W_j\in\mathcal A_j\).

notation.meaning: j-th block of the known solution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical construction is coherent and definition-like, but “partitioned compression” and the admissible-family formulation are not established as canonical without a specific source and locator.

children.title: Annotated Compression
children.top_down_role: Compression variants carrying auxiliary labels, restrictions, or distinguished elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Annotated Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compression constrained by mandatory and forbidden annotations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an instance with ground set \(V\), let \(W\) be a known feasible solution, and let \(A^+,A^-\subseteq V\) be disjoint annotation sets. Annotated compression asks for a feasible solution \(S\subseteq V\) such that \(|S|\le k\), \(A^+\subseteq S\), and \(S\cap A^-=\varnothing\). Additional restrictions involving \(W\), such as \(S\cap W=\varnothing\), may be imposed to obtain an annotated disjoint-compression instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Annotated compression requires the new bounded solution to include every mandatory element and exclude every forbidden element.
assumptions_latex: \(A^+\cap A^-=\varnothing\).
\(W\) is a known feasible solution for the compression instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists S\subseteq V:\ S\text{ feasible},\ |S|\le k,\ A^+\subseteq S,\ S\cap A^-=\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the leaf, but mandatory-versus-forbidden annotation conventions vary by problem. No cited source establishes this formulation or the annotated disjoint-compression extension.

children.title: Weighted Compression
children.top_down_role: Compression variants with weighted choices or weighted objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compression under an additive nonnegative weight budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) have ground set \(V\), let \(W\subseteq V\) be a known feasible solution, let \(w:V\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\), and let \(B\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). Weighted compression asks for a feasible solution \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \(w(S)=\sum_{v\in S}w(v)\le B\). A cardinality bound may additionally be required. The instance encoding includes the binary representations of all weights and of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted compression replaces or supplements the cardinality target with a bound on the total nonnegative weight of the new feasible solution.
assumptions_latex: Weights and the budget are nonnegative rational numbers encoded in binary.
\(W\) is a known feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists S\subseteq V:\ S\text{ feasible and }w(S)\le B\).

notation.meaning: sum of weights of elements in S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and fits Weighted Compression, but a source is needed to establish the compression model, whether weight replaces or supplements cardinality, and the binary rational encoding convention.

children.title: Annotation–Weight Interaction
children.top_down_role: Compression subproblems in which labels constrain the interpretation of weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Annotation–Weight Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget reduction induced by mandatory annotated elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider annotated weighted compression with disjoint sets \(A^+,A^-\subseteq V\), nonnegative additive weight \(w\), and budget \(B\). Every admissible solution has the form \(S=A^+\mathbin{\dot\cup}T\), where \(T\subseteq V\setminus(A^+\cup A^-)\). Hence feasibility requires \(w(A^+)\le B\), and the residual choice must satisfy \(w(T)\le B-w(A^+)\). Forbidden elements contribute no selectable weight. This reduction is exact provided feasibility can be conditioned on inclusion of \(A^+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mandatory annotations consume weight budget immediately; after fixing them, only unannotated, nonforbidden elements may use the residual budget.
assumptions_latex: \(A^+\cap A^-=\varnothing\).
\(w(v)\ge0\) for every \(v\in V\).
Feasibility can be conditioned on including \(A^+\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(S)\le B\Longleftrightarrow w(T)\le B-w(A^+)\) for \(S=A^+\mathbin{\dot\cup}T\).

notation.meaning: residual selectable part of the solution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The budget identity is mathematically correct for the stated disjoint decomposition, but no source specifies the associated conditioned feasibility transformation or supports presenting it as an exact compression property.

children.title: Encoding-Size Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits caused by large numeric values or extensive auxiliary metadata.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Size Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity boundary for annotated and weighted instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a weighted annotated instance on \(V\), the input length includes the encodings of \(I\), \(A^+\), \(A^-\), all weights, and the budget. If integers are binary encoded and \(M=\max(\{B\}\cup\{w(v):v\in V\})\), explicit weight data may require \(\Theta(|V|\log(M+1))\) bits. Thus a bound polynomial only in the number of elements does not imply a polynomial-bit compression when \(\log(M+1)\) is unbounded by the parameter; unary and binary encodings therefore define different compression regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small number of retained elements need not mean a small encoding: binary weights can contribute element-count times their bit length.
assumptions_latex: Weights and the budget are nonnegative integers represented explicitly in binary.
The parameter need not bound the largest weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O(|V|)\) retained objects does not imply \(\operatorname{poly}(k)\) output bits unless \(\log(M+1)\le\operatorname{poly}(k)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but the claimed Theta encoding size depends on an explicit fixed-width or worst-case encoding convention; ordinary variable-length binary encodings only give the stated upper bound without further conditions. A precise sourced encoding model is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Feedback Vertex Set Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of undirected feedback vertex set compression to disjoint compression instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), an integer \(k\), and a feedback vertex set \(Z\subseteq V\) with \(|Z|\le k+1\), enumerate every \(Y\subseteq Z\) with \(|Y|\le k\). Interpret \(Y\) as the guessed intersection of a new solution with \(Z\). Discard the branch unless \(G[Z\setminus Y]\) is a forest. In each remaining branch, solve the disjoint compression instance seeking \(S'\subseteq V\setminus Z\) such that \(|S'|\le k-|Y|\) and \(G-(Y\cup S')\) is a forest. Output \(Y\cup S'\) from any successful branch; report failure if every branch fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Guess the old-solution vertices retained in the new deletion set, then solve the resulting disjoint feedback vertex set instance.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(G-Z\) is a forest and \(|Z|\le k+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure outputs a feedback vertex set of size at most \(k\) exactly when one exists.

notation.meaning: given feedback vertex set of size at most k+1
guessed intersection of the new solution with Z

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard iterative-compression reduction by guessing the intersection with the old solution
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is sound, complete, and appropriate for the Feedback Vertex Set Compression container, but no citation with an inspectable locator supports the reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Odd Cycle Transversal Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of undirected odd cycle transversal compression to disjoint compression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), an integer \(k\), and an odd cycle transversal \(Z\subseteq V\) with \(|Z|\le k+1\), enumerate every \(Y\subseteq Z\) with \(|Y|\le k\). Discard the branch if \(G[Z\setminus Y]\) is not bipartite. Otherwise seek \(S'\subseteq V\setminus Z\) with \(|S'|\le k-|Y|\) such that \(G-(Y\cup S')\) is bipartite. This is a disjoint odd cycle transversal instance because \(S'\cap Z=\varnothing\). Output \(Y\cup S'\) for a successful branch, and report failure if none succeeds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Guess the overlap with the old transversal and solve a disjoint odd cycle transversal problem in each feasible branch.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(G-Z\) is bipartite and \(|Z|\le k+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A successful branch yields an odd cycle transversal of size at most \(k\), and every such transversal appears in one branch.

notation.meaning: guessed overlap with a compressed solution

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard disjoint-compression decomposition for odd cycle transversal
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The disjoint-compression decomposition is mathematically consistent and fits the container, but the record supplies no source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Feedback Vertex Set Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection-guessing reduction for directed feedback vertex set compression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite digraph \(D=(V,A)\), an integer \(k\), and a directed feedback vertex set \(Z\subseteq V\) with \(|Z|\le k+1\), enumerate every \(Y\subseteq Z\) satisfying \(|Y|\le k\). Discard a branch when \(D[Z\setminus Y]\) contains a directed cycle. In every remaining branch, seek \(S'\subseteq V\setminus Z\) with \(|S'|\le k-|Y|\) such that \(D-(Y\cup S')\) is acyclic. Output \(Y\cup S'\) if a disjoint subproblem succeeds; if all subproblems fail, report that no directed feedback vertex set of size at most \(k\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Guess the compressed solution’s overlap with the old set and solve the corresponding disjoint directed feedback vertex set instances.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite directed graph.
\(D-Z\) is acyclic and \(|Z|\le k+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduction is complete and sound for directed feedback vertex sets of size at most \(k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct intersection-guessing formulation of disjoint iterative compression
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The directed intersection-guessing reduction is sound and complete, and algorithm is the correct knowledge kind, but authoritative source support is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Modification Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic vertex-deletion compression for a hereditary target graph class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a hereditary graph class. Given a graph \(G=(V,E)\), an integer \(k\), and \(Z\subseteq V\) with \(|Z|\le k+1\) and \(G-Z\in\mathcal C\), enumerate \(Y\subseteq Z\) with \(|Y|\le k\). Reject a branch unless \(G[Z\setminus Y]\in\mathcal C\). For each remaining branch, solve the disjoint modification problem for \(S'\subseteq V\setminus Z\), requiring \(|S'|\le k-|Y|\) and \(G-(Y\cup S')\in\mathcal C\). Return \(Y\cup S'\) from a successful branch, or report failure when all branches fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hereditary vertex-deletion compression problem reduces to branches that guess overlap with the old solution and solve disjoint modification.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is closed under taking induced subgraphs.
Only vertex deletions are allowed.
\(G-Z\in\mathcal C\) and \(|Z|\le k+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The branching reduction finds a size-at-most-\(k\) deletion set exactly when one exists.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic overlap decomposition for hereditary vertex-deletion problems
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For hereditary vertex-deletion targets, the stated branching reduction is sound and complete and fits the generic compression container. It nevertheless lacks a cited source and inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Extension Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary imposed by the ability to extend the solution maintained by a specified iterative-compression scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider instances \(I_1,\ldots,I_n\) built by successive extensions and a minimization parameter \(k\). Suppose a specified iterative-compression scheme maintains a feasible solution \(Z_i\) for \(I_i\) and requires, after each extension, a feasible solution \(Z_{i+1}\) for \(I_{i+1}\) with \(|Z_{i+1}|\le k+c\), where \(c\) is independent of \(n\). The standard maintained-solution transition requires a fixed-parameter procedure that constructs such a \(Z_{i+1}\) from every solution \(Z_i\) that can arise under the scheme. If an extension and a reachable maintained solution admit no such parameter-bounded transition, the scheme cannot generate its next promised compression instance. This does not exclude a different invariant or a different compression scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A specified iterative-compression scheme reaches a boundary when one of its reachable maintained solutions cannot be extended to the next promised larger solution with parameter-bounded overhead.
assumptions_latex: \(I_1,\ldots,I_n\) is a specified extension sequence.
The scheme requires a feasible supplied solution of size at most \(k+c\) at each compression step.
\(c\) is independent of the input length \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of the bounded transition for a reachable maintained solution prevents the specified standard iterative-compression invariant from continuing.

notation.meaning: feasible solution maintained by the specified scheme
extension overhead independent of input length

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the next compression call requires construction of its promised larger solution from each maintained state reachable under the specified scheme

children.title: Nonmonotone Compression Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Problems where extending or shrinking a solution does not preserve feasibility predictably.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Compression Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for a specified compression transition that initializes its next promise solely by bounded augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F(I)\subseteq 2^{U(I)}\) be the feasible solutions of an instance \(I\), and fix an augmentation-based transition for extensions \(I\preceq I'\). For each reachable maintained solution \(S\in\mathcal F(I)\), let \(\mathcal A_k(I,I',S)\) be the family of bounded augmentations that the transition is allowed to use. A nonmonotone boundary for this transition occurs if some extension and reachable \(S\) satisfy \(S\cup A\notin\mathcal F(I')\) for every \(A\in\mathcal A_k(I,I',S)\). The transition then cannot initialize the promised compression instance by augmentation alone. Nonmonotonicity by itself does not rule out compression using a different transition or repair rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An augmentation-based transition fails when none of its allowed parameter-bounded augmentations preserves feasibility for a reachable maintained solution; nonmonotonicity alone does not exclude other compression schemes.
assumptions_latex: Feasible solutions are subsets of an instance-dependent universe \(U(I)\).
The specified transition initializes the next promise using an augmentation from \(\mathcal A_k(I,I',S)\).
The solution \(S\) is reachable under the specified scheme.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every allowed bounded augmentation destroys feasibility, the specified augmentation-only compression initialization fails.

notation.meaning: I' is an extension of I
bounded augmentations allowed by the specified transition

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: an augmentation-only transition cannot continue when none of its allowed augmentations yields its required feasible promise

children.title: Nonhereditary Compression Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Problems whose feasible structure is not preserved under induced subinstances or incremental restriction.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonhereditary Compression Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction failure for deletion problems whose target class is not hereditary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a graph class used as the target of vertex deletion. If \(\mathcal C\) is not hereditary, there exist a graph \(G\in\mathcal C\) and an induced subgraph \(H\) of \(G\) with \(H\notin\mathcal C\). Consequently, feasibility of a deletion set on a processed graph need not remain valid after restricting to an induced intermediate instance, and the condition \(G-Z\in\mathcal C\) alone does not justify hereditary restriction arguments inside disjoint compression. Iterative compression may still be possible, but any algorithm relying on induced-subgraph closure requires an additional invariant or a problem-specific repair rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the target class is nonhereditary, restricting a feasible residual graph can invalidate feasibility and defeat closure-based compression arguments.
assumptions_latex: The modification operation is vertex deletion.
Intermediate instances are related by induced-subgraph restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonheredity blocks generic compression arguments that require target-class closure under induced subgraphs.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct consequence of the definition of a hereditary graph class
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim correctly limits the obstruction to generic arguments requiring induced-subgraph closure and does not overstate nonheredity as ruling out all compression. Its terminology and application to iterative compression still require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Extension-Instability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Incremental stages where prior solutions cease to provide useful compression witnesses.

knowledge_statements.title: Extension-Instability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regimes where small input extensions force unbounded changes in maintained solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an extension relation \(I\preceq I'\), define the extension distance of a feasible solution \(S\in\mathcal F(I)\) by \(d(S,I')=\min\{|S\triangle S'|:S'\in\mathcal F(I')\}\), with value \(+\infty\) if \(I'\) is infeasible. An extension-instability regime occurs when, for some fixed parameter value \(k\), one-element extensions admit feasible \(S\) with \(|S|\le k\) but \(d(S,I')\) is unbounded as the input grows. Compression methods whose transition enumerates or locally repairs only \(f(k)\) changes cannot maintain their invariant in this regime, although unrelated global compression algorithms are not excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension instability occurs when adding one input element can force more than any parameter-bounded number of changes to a solution.
assumptions_latex: Solutions are subsets of a common universe under each extension.
The transition method searches only parameter-bounded edits of the maintained solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unbounded extension distance rules out bounded-local-repair implementations of iterative compression.

notation.meaning: minimum edit distance from S to a solution of I'

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes stability through parameter-bounded symmetric-difference repair
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The extension-distance definition and the conditional limitation on bounded-local-repair transitions are internally coherent, but the named regime and its connection to iterative compression have no cited source.

children.title: Repairability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on restoring feasibility through bounded modifications of an existing solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Repairability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for compression algorithms based on bounded local repair of the supplied solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a compression instance \((I,k,Z)\), let \(r(I,k,Z)=\min\{|Z\triangle S|:S\in\mathcal F(I),\ |S|\le k\}\), taking \(r=+\infty\) when no compressed solution exists. A bounded-repair compression method assumes that every positive instance in its promised class satisfies \(r(I,k,Z)\le f(k)\) for some computable function \(f\). If positive promised instances have unbounded repair distance at fixed \(k\), then enumerating, branching over, or dynamically programming only \(f(k)\) edits around \(Z\) is incomplete. This boundary concerns local-repair methods and does not by itself establish hardness of the unrestricted compression problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local-repair compression is incomplete when a smaller solution can be arbitrarily far from the supplied larger solution at fixed parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is the feasible solution supplied with the compression instance.
The algorithm explores only parameter-bounded modifications of \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unbounded \(r(I,k,Z)\) at fixed \(k\) is a failure boundary for bounded-repair compression.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local-search completeness requires the search radius to contain some compressed solution
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The repair-distance formulation correctly identifies a boundary only for methods restricted to a parameter-bounded neighborhood of the supplied solution. A source with a specific locator is needed for this terminology and framework.

knowledge_statements.title: Compression-Subproblem Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional limitation when the promised compression problem is parameterized-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be a parameterized minimization problem and let \(Q_{\mathrm{comp}}\) be its compression problem: the input is \((I,k,Z)\), where \(Z\) is feasible for \(I\), \(|Z|\le k+c\), and \(c\) is a fixed nonnegative constant; the question is whether \(I\) has a feasible solution of size at most \(k\). If \(Q_{\mathrm{comp}}\) is \(\mathrm{W[1]}\)-hard under parameterized reductions with parameter \(k\), then it has no algorithm with running time \(f(k)|I|^{O(1)}\) unless \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W[1]}\). Hence an iterative-compression design that invokes this subproblem cannot establish fixed-parameter tractability without exploiting additional promise structure or using a different parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A W[1]-hard compression subproblem prevents the stated iterative-compression pipeline from yielding an FPT algorithm unless FPT equals W[1], absent additional promise structure or a different parameter.
assumptions_latex: The hardness reduction is a parameterized reduction whose output parameter is bounded by a computable function of the input parameter.
The compression call must handle the promised instance class on which hardness is established.
\(c\) is a fixed nonnegative constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unless \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W[1]}\), the compression subproblem has no \(f(k)|I|^{O(1)}\)-time algorithm.

notation.meaning: supplied feasible solution of size at most k+c

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the stated running-time exclusion is the defining conditional consequence of W[1]-hardness under parameterized reductions

children.title: Implicit-Witness FPT Method Family
children.top_down_role: Witness isolation, random separation, algebraic cancellation, and representative structures used to avoid direct combinatorial enumeration.

knowledge_statements.title: Colorful Substructure Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized color-coding template for detecting a size-k witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a witness consist of \(k\) distinct elements of a universe \(U\). Independently assign each element a color from \([k]\) uniformly at random, and invoke a problem-specific procedure that decides whether a witness using every color exactly once exists. Any fixed size-\(k\) witness is colorful with probability \(k!/k^k\ge e^{-k}\). Repeat the coloring and colorful decision procedure \(t\) times, outputting a recovered witness upon success and reporting failure otherwise. If a witness exists, the failure probability is at most \((1-k!/k^k)^t\le \exp(-t k!/k^k)\); if the colorful procedure is sound, no nonexistent witness is returned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomly color the universe with k colors and search for a witness using each color once; repetition amplifies success probability.
assumptions_latex: Every sought witness contains exactly \(k\) distinct universe elements.
The colorful-search subroutine is sound and complete for a fixed coloring.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Choosing \(t\ge (k^k/k!)\ln(1/\delta)\) gives one-sided failure probability at most \(\delta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary color-coding success probability and independent repetition bound
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The color-coding probability, independent-repetition bound, and one-sided-error conclusion are correct and fit an algorithm container, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Colorful Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset dynamic programming over an exact finite-state representation of colorful partial witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a coloring \(h:U\to[k]\) and an exact finite-state representation of partial witnesses. For every state \(x\) and color subset \(C\subseteq[k]\), maintain a Boolean entry \(D[x,C]\) meaning that some valid partial witness represented by \(x\) uses exactly the colors in \(C\), each once. For each valid one-element partial witness consisting of \(u\in U\) and represented by state \(x\), initialize \(D[x,\{h(u)\}]=\mathrm{true}\). For every valid transition from state \(x\) to state \(y\) that appends an element \(u\in U\), set \(D[y,C\cup\{h(u)\}]=\mathrm{true}\) whenever \(D[x,C]\) is true and \(h(u)\notin C\). Accept exactly when a designated terminal state \(y\) satisfies \(D[y,[k]]=\mathrm{true}\), and recover a represented witness using predecessor pointers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Index exact partial-witness states by their used color subsets and allow a transition only when its appended universe element introduces a new color.
assumptions_latex: The witness problem has an exact finite-state representation: initial states represent precisely the valid one-element partial witnesses, valid transitions represent precisely valid element extensions, and designated terminal states represent precisely complete witnesses.
Every complete witness contains exactly \(k\) elements.
The coloring is a map \(h:U\to[k]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The table accepts exactly the colorful complete witnesses represented by the specified exact state system.

notation.meaning: existence of a valid partial witness in state x using exactly colors C
the complete set of k colors

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subset-state dynamic programming tracks exactly the colors used when the underlying state representation and transitions are exact

assumptions_latex: The universe is \(U=[n]\), and every sought witness has exactly \(k\) elements.
A colorful-witness routine is correct whenever its input coloring is injective on a witness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enumerating the family deterministically replaces random colorings while preserving witness detection.

notation.meaning: A coloring from the universe to k colors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic color-coding through a perfect-hash family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a family of functions \(h:U\to[k]\) such that, for every \(S\subseteq U\) with \(|S|=k\), some \(h\in\mathcal H\) is injective on \(S\). Enumerate every \(h\in\mathcal H\), invoke the colorful-witness routine under coloring \(h\), and return the first witness found; return failure if every invocation fails. If a witness \(S\) exists, the defining property supplies an invocation in which \(S\) is colorful, so the algorithm finds a witness. Its running time is \(O(|\mathcal H|T(n,k))\), apart from family construction, when one colorful invocation costs \(T(n,k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate a perfect-hash family and run the colorful search for each coloring; some coloring is injective on every possible k-element witness.
knowledge_statements.title: Perfect-Hash Derandomization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits this terminal container, and the perfect-hash enumeration claim is mathematically coherent. However, no source or inspectable locator is supplied for the perfect-hash definition, correctness claim, or running-time accounting.

assumptions_latex: The universe is \(U=[n]\), and a relevant set has size at most \(a\).
At most \(b\) colors are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enumerating a suitable splitter guarantees a coloring that sufficiently separates every relevant set.

notation.meaning: The number of colors used on a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derandomization by enumerating balanced separating colorings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \((n,a,b)\)-splitter is a family \(\mathcal S\) of functions \(h:[n]\to[b]\) such that, for every \(X\subseteq[n]\) with \(|X|=a\), some \(h\in\mathcal S\) satisfies \(|h(X)|=\min\{a,b\}\). To derandomize a procedure whose success for a relevant set \(X\) follows from this separation property, enumerate \(h\in\mathcal S\), execute the procedure with \(h\), and accept if any execution accepts. Completeness follows from the splitter property, while soundness is inherited from each deterministic execution. If one execution costs \(T(n,a,b)\), enumeration costs \(O(|\mathcal S|T(n,a,b))\), excluding construction of \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A splitter family contains a coloring that maximally separates every relevant set, so exhaustive enumeration derandomizes any routine relying on that event.
knowledge_statements.title: Splitter-Based Derandomization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the container, but the displayed condition |h(X)|=min{a,b} is not the usual balanced-splitting definition when b<a; it requires surjectivity rather than balanced color-class sizes. A cited parameter convention and corrected definition are required before the mathematical statement can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Success-Probability Amplification
children.top_down_role: Reliability improvement through controlled aggregation of randomized trials.

assumptions_latex: Each trial has one-sided error and succeeds with probability at least \(p>0\) on every yes-instance.
The trials use mutually independent random bits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(r\) trials, the failure probability is at most \((1-p)^r\le e^{-pr}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided amplification by independent repetitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run the randomized decision or search procedure independently \(r\) times and accept, or return a witness, if any trial succeeds. On a yes-instance, independence gives failure probability at most \((1-p)^r\), hence \((1-p)^r\le e^{-pr}\). Therefore \(r=\lceil p^{-1}\ln(1/\delta)\rceil\) trials suffice to make failure probability at most \(\delta\in(0,1)\). If one trial costs \(T\) time and \(R\) random bits, the amplified procedure costs \(O(rT)\) time and uses \(rR\) random bits. One-sided soundness is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeating an independent one-sided procedure about p^{-1} log(1/delta) times reduces its failure probability to at most delta.
knowledge_statements.title: Success-Probability Amplification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role appropriately distinguishes this leaf from the operational Independent Repetition leaf. The probability, time, and random-bit bounds are coherent, but the record supplies no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Independent Repetition
children.top_down_role: Repeated trials using independent random choices.

assumptions_latex: A base one-sided randomized algorithm succeeds with probability at least \(p\).
Fresh independent randomness is used in every invocation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The repeated algorithm succeeds if any invocation succeeds and fails with probability at most \((1-p)^r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational repetition rule for one-sided randomized algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given input \(x\) and repetition count \(r\ge1\), independently sample random tapes \(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_r\) and compute \(A(x;\rho_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,r\). Stop and output the first certified witness returned by an invocation; if no invocation succeeds, output failure. When a witness exists and each invocation succeeds with probability at least \(p\), mutual independence implies that all invocations fail with probability at most \((1-p)^r\). When the base algorithm has no false positive, the repeated algorithm also has no false positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run the base algorithm on fresh independent random tapes and return the first certified witness; all runs fail with probability at most (1-p)^r.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Repetition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the exact leaf, and the one-sided independent-repetition procedure is stated consistently. No citation or inspectable locator supports the amplification claim.

children.title: Limited-Independence Repetition
children.top_down_role: Repetition regimes using restricted randomness or structured sample spaces.

assumptions_latex: The success indicators are \(X_1,\ldots,X_r\in\{0,1\}\), where \(r\ge 1\).
For every \(i\in[r]\), \(\Pr[X_i=1]\ge p\), where \(p\in(0,1]\).
The indicators are \(t\)-wise independent for an integer \(t\) satisfying \(1\le t\le r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The probability that all \(r\) trials fail is at most \((1-p)^t\); this elementary argument therefore amplifies only through the available independence order.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic all-failure bound under limited independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_r\in\{0,1\}\) be \(t\)-wise independent success indicators with \(\Pr[X_i=1]\ge p\) for every \(i\in[r]\). For any fixed set \(I\subseteq[r]\) with \(|I|=t\), the event \(\{X_1=\cdots=X_r=0\}\) is contained in \(\{X_i=0\text{ for every }i\in I\}\). Consequently, \[\Pr[X_1=\cdots=X_r=0]\le\prod_{i\in I}\Pr[X_i=0]\le(1-p)^t.\] Thus \(t\ge\lceil p^{-1}\ln(1/\delta)\rceil\) suffices to bound the failure probability by \(\delta\in(0,1)\), even when \(r>t\). Increasing \(r\) alone gives no stronger bound from this argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With only t-wise independence, the elementary all-failure guarantee is (1-p)^t; extra repetitions alone do not reproduce full-independence amplification.
knowledge_statements.title: Limited-Independence Repetition

children.title: Randomness-Budget Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs among reliability, trial count, random bits, and running time.

assumptions_latex: One trial uses \(R\) random bits and succeeds with probability at least \(p\).
Independent repetition is used to target failure probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard amplified algorithm uses \(rR\) random bits for \(r=\lceil p^{-1}\ln(1/\delta)\rceil\); reducing randomness requires structured dependence or deterministic enumeration.

notation.meaning: Random bits consumed by one trial

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-bit cost of repetition and its basic alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Full independent amplification to failure at most \(\delta\) uses \(r=\lceil p^{-1}\ln(1/\delta)\rceil\) trials and hence \(rR\) random bits. Replacing full independence by \(t\)-wise independence can reduce the seed length when an explicit generator is available, but the elementary guarantee becomes only \((1-p)^t\). Replacing randomness by enumeration of a family \(\mathcal F\) uses no runtime random bits but multiplies deterministic running time by \(|\mathcal F|\). Thus random-bit savings must be accounted for together with the weaker probability bound, seed-generation cost, or enumeration overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent amplification spends R bits per trial; limited independence shortens seeds but weakens guarantees, while deterministic families exchange random bits for enumeration time.
knowledge_statements.title: Randomness-Budget Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the tradeoff leaf. The independent-randomness accounting is precise, but the limited-independence seed-length claim depends on an unspecified explicit generator and computational model, and no source or locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: A desired witness set \(W\) and a forbidden interface \(B\) are disjoint subsets of a universe \(U\).
Every element of \(U\) is colored red or blue independently and uniformly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coloring separates \(W\) from \(B\) with probability exactly \(2^{-(|W|+|B|)}\).

notation.meaning: Elements required to receive the selected color
Elements required to receive the opposite color

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-color separation of a witness from its forbidden interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Independently color every element of \(U\) red or blue with probability \(1/2\) each. Invoke a deterministic recovery routine that is complete whenever every element of \(W\) is red and every element of \(B\) is blue, and accept only a verifiable witness returned by that routine. Because \(W\cap B=\varnothing\), the favorable coloring event has probability \[\Pr[W\text{ red and }B\text{ blue}]=2^{-(|W|+|B|)}.\] Repeating the experiment supplies a fixed-parameter algorithm whenever \(|W|+|B|\) is bounded by a function of the parameter and recovery is fixed-parameter tractable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomly two-color the universe so the witness and its forbidden boundary receive opposite colors; the favorable event has probability 2^{-(|W|+|B|)}.
knowledge_statements.title: Random Separation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits Random Separation, and the favorable coloring probability is correct for fixed disjoint sets. The FPT conclusion depends on a problem-specific recovery routine and repetition regime, and no supporting source or locator is provided.

assumptions_latex: The universe is \(U=[n]\).
Every favorable separation prescribes colors on at most \(k\) elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enumerating an \((n,k)\)-universal set deterministically realizes every favorable local coloring.

notation.meaning: A subset on which colors are prescribed

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic realization of every binary pattern on small subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\mathcal U\subseteq\{0,1\}^{[n]}\) is \((n,k)\)-universal if, for every \(S\subseteq[n]\) with \(|S|=k\), the restrictions satisfy \(\{u|_S:u\in\mathcal U\}=\{0,1\}^S\). Enumerate all \(u\in\mathcal U\) and invoke the deterministic recovery routine for each induced coloring. If a randomized-separation argument succeeds whenever a specified binary pattern occurs on a set of at most \(k\) relevant elements, extend that set to size \(k\); universality supplies an enumerated coloring realizing the pattern. The resulting running time is \(O(|\mathcal U|T(n,k))\), excluding construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate a universal family containing every binary coloring of every k-element subset; one member realizes the favorable random-separation pattern.
knowledge_statements.title: Universal-Set Derandomization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits this derandomization leaf, and extending a prescribed set of size at most k to size k is valid when n is at least k. The universal-set definition, construction assumptions, and enumeration bound lack a cited source and inspectable locator.

assumptions_latex: The family \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is fixed independently of the random weights.
The integer \(N\ge1\), and the weights \(w(1),\ldots,w(n)\) are independent and uniform on \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With probability at least \(1-n/N\), exactly one member of \(\mathcal F\) has minimum total weight.

notation.meaning: Total weight of a feasible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-set isolation lemma with uniform integer weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{[n]}\), let \(N\ge1\), and choose \(w(1),\ldots,w(n)\) independently and uniformly from \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\). For each \(F\in\mathcal F\), define \(w(F)=\sum_{i\in F}w(i)\). Then \[\Pr\!\left[\text{there is a unique }F^*\in\mathcal F\text{ minimizing }w(F)\right]\ge 1-\frac{n}{N}.\] Consequently, for \(\delta\in(0,1)\), choosing \(N\ge n/\delta\) isolates a unique minimum-weight feasible set with probability at least \(1-\delta\). An algorithm may exploit this uniqueness through a problem-specific algebraic, counting, or decision oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent uniform integer weights from {1,...,N} give a nonempty set family a unique minimum-weight member with probability at least 1-n/N.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolation-Lemma Methods

assumptions_latex: A contraction trajectory has a fixed finite length \(m\ge0\) and produces instances \(I_0,I_1,\ldots,I_m\).
At each step \(i\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\), conditional on preservation at all earlier steps, the sampled contraction preserves at least one fixed target witness with probability at least \(q_i\in[0,1]\).
A deterministic base routine applies to \(I_m\), and every recursive output can be lifted and verified in \(I_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One trajectory preserves the fixed target witness with probability at least \(\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}q_i\), and verification provides one-sided soundness.

notation.meaning: Conditional witness-preservation lower bound at step i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract interface between witness preservation and randomized contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from \(I_0\), for each \(i\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\), sample a contractible object, form the smaller instance \(I_{i+1}\), and continue until a deterministic base routine applies to \(I_m\). Lift its output through the contractions and accept only if the lifted object is a valid witness for \(I_0\). Suppose that, conditional on preservation through steps \(0,\ldots,i-1\), step \(i\) preserves at least one fixed target witness with probability at least \(q_i\). Then one contraction trajectory preserves that witness with probability at least \(\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}q_i\). Verification gives one-sided soundness, and independent trajectories can amplify the success probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Across m contraction steps, conditional witness-preservation bounds q_i give trajectory success at least their product; lifting and final verification prevent false positives.
knowledge_statements.title: Randomized-Contraction Interface

assumptions_latex: The polynomial \(P\in\mathbb F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is nonzero and has total degree at most \(d\).
The set \(S\subseteq\mathbb F\) is finite and nonempty.
The coordinates \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) are sampled independently and uniformly from \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The probability of the false identity outcome \(P(a)=0\) is at most \(d/|S|\).

notation.meaning: Finite sampling set in the field

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schwartz-Zippel form of randomized polynomial identity testing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb F\) be a field, let \(S\subseteq\mathbb F\) be finite and nonempty, and let \(P\in\mathbb F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be a nonzero polynomial of total degree at most \(d\). If \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) is sampled uniformly from \(S^n\), then \[\Pr[P(a)=0]\le\frac{d}{|S|}.\] Hence evaluating an implicitly represented polynomial at a random point is a one-sided identity test: a nonzero value certifies \(P\ne0\), while a zero value can occur for a nonzero polynomial with probability at most \(d/|S|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero polynomial of total degree at most d vanishes at a uniformly sampled point from S^n with probability at most d/|S|.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Identity Methods

children.title: Multilinear Monomial Detection
children.top_down_role: Algebraic detection of multilinear terms encoding feasible combinatorial objects.

assumptions_latex: The polynomial \(P\in\mathbb F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is homogeneous of degree \(k\).
Arithmetic is exact over the field \(\mathbb F\).
The ideal is \(J=(x_1^2,\ldots,x_n^2)\), and \(R=\mathbb F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A degree-\(k\) multilinear monomial has nonzero coefficient in \(P\) if and only if the residue class \([P]_J\) is nonzero.

notation.meaning: Ideal generated by all variable squares
Residue class of P in the quotient
Coefficient of the squarefree monomial indexed by S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Squarefree-quotient characterization for homogeneous degree-k polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\in\mathbb F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be homogeneous of degree \(k\), and let \(J=(x_1^2,\ldots,x_n^2)\). In the quotient \(R=\mathbb F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J\), every monomial containing a repeated variable vanishes, while every multilinear monomial \(x_S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\) remains a distinct basis element. Therefore \[[P]_J=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq[n]\\|S|=k}}([x_S]P)x_S,\] and \([P]_J\ne0\) if and only if \(P\) contains a multilinear monomial of degree \(k\) with nonzero coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduce a homogeneous degree-k polynomial modulo all variable squares; the residue is nonzero exactly when a degree-k multilinear monomial has nonzero coefficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Multilinear Monomial Detection

children.title: Algebraic Sieving
children.top_down_role: Cancellation-based sieves for retaining algebraically encoded solutions.

assumptions_latex: The input is an arithmetic circuit for a polynomial \(P\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and a target degree \(k\).

A substitution algebra \(A\) is chosen so that every non-multilinear monomial of degree \(k\) maps to \(0\), while each target multilinear monomial has a nonzero image with positive detection probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero evaluated image certifies the existence of a degree-\(k\) multilinear monomial in \(P\); repeated independent evaluations reduce one-sided false negatives.

notation.meaning: input polynomial represented by an arithmetic circuit
substitution algebra used by the sieve

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic one-sided algebraic sieve for multilinear witness detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose independent random substitution elements \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A\) and evaluate the degree-\(k\) homogeneous component \(P_k(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\). The algebra must satisfy \(a_i^2=0\), so every degree-\(k\) monomial containing a repeated variable vanishes. Output YES when \(P_k(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\neq 0\), and otherwise repeat for a prescribed number \(r\) of independent trials before outputting NO. Under the stated separation property, YES is always correct, whereas NO may be false only when all surviving target contributions cancel in every trial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate the circuit in a nilpotent algebra that kills repeated variables. A nonzero value detects a multilinear witness; repetition controls one-sided cancellation error.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Sieving

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and terminal placement are appropriate, and the mathematical description is plausible under the stated separation assumption. However, no inspectable source is supplied for the required substitution algebra, survival probability, cancellation control, or one-sided-error guarantee; these details vary across algebraic sieves and cannot be validated from standard-field rationale alone.

children.title: Characteristic-Sensitive Sieves
children.top_down_role: Sieve behavior governed by the characteristic of the underlying field.

assumptions_latex: The sieve evaluates a polynomial over a field \(F\) of characteristic \(p\geq 0\).
Its annihilation and separation identities may use signs, integer multiplicities, or binomial coefficients interpreted in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sieve is valid only if every required nonzero scalar remains nonzero in \(F\) and every intended cancellation identity holds modulo \(p\).

notation.meaning: integer coefficient or multiplicity used by the sieve

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Field-characteristic compatibility condition for algebraic sieves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer coefficient \(c\) whose invertibility or nonvanishing is used in the detection argument, require \(c\cdot 1_F\neq 0\); equivalently, if \(p>0\), require \(p\nmid c\). Every identity intended to annihilate forbidden monomials must hold after reduction in \(F\), and every target monomial must retain a substitution with nonzero coefficient. Thus a characteristic-sensitive sieve is applicable precisely when its annihilation identities and target-separation inequalities remain valid in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sieve is sound in a field only when reduction modulo its characteristic preserves both forbidden-term cancellation and a nonzero contribution from every detectable target.
knowledge_statements.title: Characteristic-Sensitive Sieves

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the characteristic-sensitive terminal. The stated compatibility principle is plausible, but no source identifies the class of sieves for which checking scalar nonvanishing, annihilation identities, and target separation is sufficient. A characteristic-specific theorem, proposition, or algorithm locator is required.

children.title: False-Cancellation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Encoding regimes where cancellation can also remove desired witnesses.

assumptions_latex: Sieve evaluation aggregates distinct target witnesses into one field element.
The encoding does not attach algebraically independent tags to distinguish those witnesses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A zero evaluation need not imply absence of a target witness; opposite or characteristic-induced coefficients can cancel.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete cancellation mechanism causing false negatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose two distinct target witnesses evaluate to the same basis element \(u=v\neq 0\). If their coefficients are \(1\) and \(-1\), then their combined image is \(u-v=0\) although both witnesses exist. In characteristic \(2\), two equal contributions similarly satisfy \(u+u=0\). Consequently, zero testing is not a valid absence certificate unless the construction proves that surviving target contributions cannot cancel, or random witness tags make such cancellation occur only with a bounded probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct valid witnesses may map to equal and opposite values, making the sieve return zero. Separation or randomized tagging is therefore essential.
knowledge_statements.title: False-Cancellation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is correct, and the cancellation examples are algebraically sound. No inspectable citation supports the claimed boundary or the randomized-tagging remedy and its bounded-probability interpretation.

children.title: Determinant Methods
children.top_down_role: Determinantal encodings used in exact or parameterized computation.

assumptions_latex: The matrix \(M=(m_{ij})\) is square of order \(n\) over a commutative field \(F\).
Each selected permutation term is intended to encode one combinatorial object.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The determinant represents a signed sum of encoded objects and is computable in polynomial time, but a zero value may result from sign cancellation.

notation.meaning: symmetric group on the matrix indices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leibniz determinant expansion as a signed combinatorial encoding.

source_refs.locator: 0.1 Linear Algebra and Linear Programming p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The determinant expansion is \[\det M=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^{n}m_{i,\pi(i)}.\] If nonzero products are placed in bijection with feasible encoded objects, then \(\det M\) is their signed generating sum. Evaluating \(\det M\) by Gaussian elimination uses polynomially many field operations. Nonvanishing certifies that at least one encoded object exists, while vanishing is conclusive only when the encoding rules out cancellation among distinct permutation terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A determinant compactly sums permutation-encoded objects with signs and is polynomial-time evaluable. Nonzero certifies existence, but zero may reflect cancellation.
knowledge_statements.title: Determinant Methods

source_witnesses.locator: 0.1 Linear Algebra and Linear Programming p. 1

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits Determinant Methods, and the displayed Leibniz expansion is standard. The cited locator is only a general linear-algebra section and does not specifically support the combinatorial encoding, polynomial field-operation evaluation claim, or cancellation boundary. A determinant theorem or explicit algebraic-combinatorial encoding locator is needed.

children.title: Pfaffian Methods
children.top_down_role: Pfaffian encodings associated with skew-symmetric structures.

assumptions_latex: The matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\) is skew-symmetric of even order \(2m\) over a commutative field.
Perfect matchings of the index set provide the intended combinatorial terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Pfaffian is a signed perfect-matching sum satisfying \(\det A=\operatorname{Pf}(A)^2\).

notation.meaning: set of perfect matchings of the index set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pfaffian expansion for even-order skew-symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a skew-symmetric matrix \(A\) of order \(2m\), define \[\operatorname{Pf}(A)=\sum_{M\in\mathcal M_{2m}}\varepsilon(M)\prod_{\{i,j\}\in M,\ i<j}a_{ij}.\] Each term corresponds to a perfect matching of \(\{1,\ldots,2m\}\), and \(\operatorname{Pf}(A)^2=\det A\). Hence a graph or constraint system encoded by zero and nonzero entries of \(A\) yields a compact signed sum over its permitted perfect matchings; nonvanishing certifies that at least one such matching exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Pfaffian is a signed generating sum over perfect matchings of a skew-symmetric matrix and squares to its determinant.
knowledge_statements.title: Pfaffian Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits Pfaffian Methods, but no source is supplied. Moreover, over characteristic two, 'skew-symmetric' alone can be ambiguous because it need not enforce a zero diagonal; the Pfaffian identity should be sourced with the precise alternating-matrix hypothesis or the field characteristic should be restricted appropriately.

children.title: Matching Encodings
children.top_down_role: Interfaces from determinant or Pfaffian constructions to matching-type problems.

assumptions_latex: The graph \(G=(V,E)\) has \(V=\{1,\ldots,2m\}\).
Each edge \(\{i,j\}\) receives an indeterminate \(x_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Pfaffian monomials of the Tutte matrix are in bijection with perfect matchings of \(G\), and distinct matchings produce distinct monomials.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symbolic Tutte-matrix encoding of perfect matchings.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.5. Edmonds' Matching Algorithm p. 259

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T(G)\) by \(T_{ij}=x_{ij}\) when \(i<j\) and \(\{i,j\}\in E\), by \(T_{ij}=-x_{ji}\) when \(i>j\) and \(\{i,j\}\in E\), and by \(T_{ij}=0\) otherwise. Then \[\operatorname{Pf}(T(G))=\sum_{M}\varepsilon(M)\prod_{\{i,j\}\in M}x_{ij},\] where the sum ranges over perfect matchings \(M\) of \(G\). Thus \(G\) has a perfect matching if and only if \(\operatorname{Pf}(T(G))\) is not the zero polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Tutte matrix turns every perfect matching into a distinct Pfaffian monomial, so symbolic nonvanishing is equivalent to perfect-matching existence.
knowledge_statements.title: Matching Encodings

source_witnesses.locator: Section 10.5. Edmonds' Matching Algorithm p. 259

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role and symbolic Tutte-matrix statement are mathematically standard. The cited Edmonds-algorithm section is not a specific locator for the Tutte matrix, its Pfaffian expansion, distinct matching monomials, or the symbolic nonvanishing equivalence. A source explicitly covering this encoding is required.

children.title: Sign-Cancellation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits caused by incompatible signs or uncontrolled algebraic cancellation.

assumptions_latex: A determinant or Pfaffian encoding is evaluated after identifying some indeterminates or assigning field values.
At least two feasible objects can then contribute the same monomial or scalar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vanishing of the evaluated expression is not an absence certificate unless cancellation is excluded or controlled probabilistically.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cancellation boundary for specialized determinantal and Pfaffian encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If two feasible objects \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) have opposite expansion signs and specialize to the same nonzero weight \(w\), their total contribution is \(w-w=0\). More generally, in characteristic \(p>0\), any multiplicity divisible by \(p\) vanishes. Therefore the implication from symbolic nonvanishing to existence survives specialization, but the converse can fail. Reliable zero testing requires distinct indeterminates, a sign-coherent encoding, or random evaluation together with a polynomial-identity error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Specialization can merge oppositely signed terms, so a determinant or Pfaffian may vanish despite feasible objects. Symbolic separation or randomized identity testing is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Cancellation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the terminal, and the cancellation mechanism is plausible. No source supports the boundary or the polynomial-identity-testing remedy. The phrase that the implication from symbolic nonvanishing to existence 'survives specialization' is also imprecise: the reliable specialized implication is that a nonzero evaluated value certifies symbolic nonvanishing and hence existence, whereas an existing object may still yield a zero specialization.

assumptions_latex: The input is an arithmetic circuit for \(P\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), with \(F\) of characteristic \(2\), and a target degree \(k\).
The group algebra is \(F[\mathbb Z_2^k]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The substitution annihilates every non-multilinear monomial, while suitable random vectors and scalar tags allow one-sided detection of a degree-\(k\) multilinear monomial.

notation.meaning: elementary abelian group used for substitution
identity basis element of the group algebra
random group vectors assigned to variables

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characteristic-two group-algebra sieve for multilinear detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose independent vectors \(v_i\in G\) and scalar tags \(y_i\) from a finite extension field, and substitute \(x_i\mapsto y_i(e_0+e_{v_i})\). Because the characteristic is \(2\), \((e_0+e_v)^2=0\), so every monomial repeating a variable vanishes. Evaluate the degree-\(k\) component of the circuit in \(F[G]\); output YES if any group-algebra coefficient is nonzero, and repeat independently before outputting NO. Linear independence of the vectors assigned to a multilinear monomial makes its image nonzero, while random tags bound cancellation probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In characteristic two, group-algebra substitutions square to zero and eliminate repeated variables; random vectors and tags preserve target multilinear terms with bounded error.
knowledge_statements.title: Group-Algebra Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits Group-Algebra Methods, but no source is supplied for this specific characteristic-two sieve. If the tags lie in an extension field K, evaluation naturally occurs in K[Z_2^k], not F[Z_2^k] unless K=F. The vector-independence probability, tag distribution, cancellation bound, and number of repetitions also require a precise theorem or algorithm citation.

assumptions_latex: The universe is a finite set \(U\), and \(\mathcal A\subseteq\binom{U}{p}\).
Extensions are tested in the uniform matroid of rank \(p+q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A subfamily \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\) is representative exactly when it preserves extendability by every set of at most \(q\) new elements.

notation.meaning: family of partial solutions of size p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted representative families in a uniform matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subfamily \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\subseteq\mathcal A\) is \(q\)-representative for \(\mathcal A\) if, for every \(Y\subseteq U\) with \(|Y|\leq q\), whenever some \(X\in\mathcal A\) satisfies \(X\cap Y=\varnothing\) and \(|X\cup Y|\leq p+q\), there exists \(\widehat X\in\widehat{\mathcal A}\) satisfying \(\widehat X\cap Y=\varnothing\) and \(|\widehat X\cup Y|\leq p+q\). Since every set of size at most \(p+q\) is independent in the uniform matroid, this is precisely preservation of all feasible extensions of size at most \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform-matroid representative subfamily preserves whether every set of at most q new elements can extend some stored p-element partial solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Matroid Representative Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role is appropriate and the unweighted uniform-matroid formulation is precise; the rank inequality is redundant under the stated p-set and extension-size assumptions but not incorrect. No inspectable source is supplied for the representative-family definition.

assumptions_latex: The matroid \(M=(U,\mathcal I)\) is represented by a matrix over a field \(F\).
The family \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal I\) consists of independent sets of a fixed size \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A \(q\)-representative subfamily preserves every independent extension by at most \(q\) elements.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted representative families for a represented linear matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subfamily \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\subseteq\mathcal A\) is \(q\)-representative for \(\mathcal A\) in \(M\) if, for every \(Y\subseteq U\) with \(|Y|\leq q\), the existence of \(X\in\mathcal A\) such that \(X\cap Y=\varnothing\) and \(X\cup Y\in\mathcal I\) implies the existence of \(\widehat X\in\widehat{\mathcal A}\) such that \(\widehat X\cap Y=\varnothing\) and \(\widehat X\cup Y\in\mathcal I\). Thus replacing \(\mathcal A\) by \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\) preserves all independent extensions of size at most \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-matroid representative family retains a partial solution for every small set that can independently extend an original partial solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Matroid Representative Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits Linear-Matroid Representative Families, and the quantified extension-preservation predicate is mathematically coherent. No source with a definition, theorem, section, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Representative-Family Products
children.top_down_role: Composition of representative families across compatible partial structures.

assumptions_latex: The families \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) consist of independent subsets of a matroid \(M=(U,\mathcal I)\).
Only disjoint unions that remain independent are feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representative-family product is the family of feasible disjoint unions; it may subsequently be replaced by a representative subfamily for future extensions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product operation on partial-solution families under matroid feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the matroid-compatible product by \[\mathcal A\star_M\mathcal B=\{A\cup B:A\in\mathcal A,\ B\in\mathcal B,\ A\cap B=\varnothing,\ A\cup B\in\mathcal I\}.\] In a uniform matroid, the final independence condition reduces to the applicable rank bound. The operation composes two partial solutions while enforcing compatibility. For a future extension budget \(q\), an interface may replace \(\mathcal A\star_M\mathcal B\) by any \(q\)-representative subfamily of that product without changing which extensions of size at most \(q\) remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The product joins disjoint partial solutions whose union stays independent; representative compression may then preserve all future extensions within the chosen budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Representative-Family Products

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits Representative-Family Products, and the feasible disjoint-union operation is stated consistently. No source supports either this product notation or the assertion that subsequent q-representative compression preserves the specified extension interface.

children.title: Representative-Family Truncation
children.top_down_role: Size or rank restriction within representative-family computations.

assumptions_latex: The family \(\mathcal A\) consists of independent partial solutions in a matroid \(M\).
A subfamily \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\subseteq\mathcal A\) has been computed for a future extension budget \(q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(\mathcal A\) by \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\) is a valid truncation precisely when \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\) is \(q\)-representative for \(\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compression step that preserves extensions up to a fixed budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \((M,\mathcal A,q)\), compute a subfamily \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\subseteq\mathcal A\) satisfying the \(q\)-representative predicate and replace the stored state \(\mathcal A\) by \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\). Subsequent dynamic-programming operations may query only extensions \(Y\) with \(|Y|\leq q\). For every such \(Y\), feasibility of \(X\cup Y\) for some \(X\in\mathcal A\) is then equivalent to feasibility of \(\widehat X\cup Y\) for some \(\widehat X\in\widehat{\mathcal A}\). Output \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\); no claim is made for larger extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truncation replaces a partial-solution family by a q-representative subfamily, preserving exactly the future extension queries whose size is at most q.
knowledge_statements.title: Representative-Family Truncation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The preservation predicate describes the intended truncation interface, but the record says to compute a representative subfamily without specifying any computation method, applicability conditions, or complexity. Thus the algorithm content kind is not yet justified; the statement currently functions as a condition or operation specification. A source is required before deciding whether this leaf should contain a concrete truncation algorithm or a preservation condition.

children.title: Representative-Family Extension
children.top_down_role: Preservation of future extension possibilities for partial solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Representative-Family Extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension of representative set families by one fixed matroid element.
