knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid, let \(e\in E\), and let \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\subseteq\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal I\). Suppose \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\) is \(q\)-representative for \(\mathcal A\): every set \(Y\subseteq E\) with \(|Y|\le q\) extendible by a member of \(\mathcal A\) is extendible by a member of \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\). Define \(\operatorname{Ext}_e(\mathcal F)=\{X\cup\{e\}:X\in\mathcal F,\ e\notin X,\ X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\}\). Then \(\operatorname{Ext}_e(\widehat{\mathcal A})\) is \((q-1)\)-representative for \(\operatorname{Ext}_e(\mathcal A)\) when \(q\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extending every feasible representative set by the same matroid element preserves representativity while reducing the remaining extension budget by one.
assumptions_latex: M=(E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid}
q\ge 1
\widehat{\mathcal A}\subseteq\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal I\text{ and }\widehat{\mathcal A}\text{ is }q\text{-representative for }\mathcal A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Ext}_e(\widehat{\mathcal A})\text{ is }(q-1)\text{-representative for }\operatorname{Ext}_e(\mathcal A)

notation.meaning: feasible extension by the fixed element e
maximum size of a tested continuation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard lifting argument for matroid representative families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The extension property fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible under the standard disjoint-extension definition of q-representativity, but no inspectable citation is supplied and that definition is only implicit.

children.title: Interface Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting safe composition across product, truncation, or extension interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Interface Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility criterion for operations consuming compressed representative families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For matroids \(M,M'\), an operation \(\Phi\) on families is \((q,q')\)-compatible with representativity if, for every \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\subseteq\mathcal A\), the implication \[\widehat{\mathcal A}\text{ is }q\text{-representative for }\mathcal A\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Phi(\widehat{\mathcal A})\text{ is }q'\text{-representative for }\Phi(\mathcal A)\] holds, with representativity interpreted in \(M\) before the operation and in \(M'\) afterward. A dynamic-programming transition may soundly consume a compressed family precisely when its operation satisfies this implication for the continuation budgets used by the adjacent states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operation is interface-compatible when replacing its input by a representative subfamily yields a representative output at the next state’s continuation budget.
assumptions_latex: \Phi\text{ maps feasible families in }M\text{ to feasible families in }M'
q,q'\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\text{-representativity of the input implies }q'\text{-representativity of the output}

notation.meaning: family transformation induced by a state transition

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: compositional interface condition for representative-family dynamic programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the interface-compatibility leaf, but the terminology is synthetic and the claim that the implication is precisely necessary for sound consumption requires a cited formal framework.

children.title: Path Applications
children.top_down_role: Representative-family uses in path construction or path selection problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Path Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative-family dynamic programming for simple paths of prescribed length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), vertices \(s,t\in V\), and \(k\ge 1\), return no immediately if \(k+1>|V|\). Otherwise let \(U_{k+1,V}\) be the uniform matroid of rank \(k+1\) on \(V\). Initialize \(\mathcal P_{1,s}=\{\{s\}\}\) and \(\mathcal P_{1,v}=\varnothing\) for \(v
e s\). For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and \(v\in V\), form \[\mathcal C_{i+1,v}= igcup_{u:\{u,v\}\in E}\{X\cup\{v\}:X\in\mathcal P_{i,u},\ v
otin X\},\] and choose \(\mathcal P_{i+1,v}\subseteq\mathcal C_{i+1,v}\) that is \((k-i)\)-representative for \(\mathcal C_{i+1,v}\) in \(U_{k+1,V}\). Output yes exactly when \(\mathcal P_{k+1,t}
e\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every path length and endpoint, combine all one-edge extensions and then retain a representative subfamily; the final target table is nonempty exactly when a simple s-to-t path with k edges exists.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
s,t\in V
k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P_{k+1,t}\ne\varnothing\iff G\text{ has a simple }s\text{-}t\text{ path with }k\text{ edges}

notation.meaning: all uncompressed vertex sets of partial paths on i vertices ending at v
representative subfamily of partial-path vertex sets ending at v
uniform matroid of rank k+1 on V

children.title: Packing Applications
children.top_down_role: Representative-family uses for selecting mutually compatible objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Packing Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compression of partial packings whose future feasibility is governed by disjointness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S\subseteq 2^U\) consist of sets of size \(r\), and seek \(k\) pairwise disjoint members. At level \(i\), encode a partial packing by its used set \(X\subseteq U\), where \(|X|=ir\). If \(\widehat{\mathcal A}_i\) is \((k-i)r\)-representative for the family \(\mathcal A_i\) of used sets in the uniform matroid of rank \(kr\), then every collection of at most \(k-i\) further members of \(\mathcal S\) that completes some state in \(\mathcal A_i\) also completes a state in \(\widehat{\mathcal A}_i\). Thus compression preserves existence of a size-\(k\) packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed-size set packing, representative used-element sets preserve every disjoint collection capable of completing a partial packing.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal S\subseteq\binom{U}{r}
0\le i\le k
\widehat{\mathcal A}_i\text{ is }(k-i)r\text{-representative for }\mathcal A_i\text{ in }U_{kr,U}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal A_i\text{ has a completion to a }k\text{-packing iff }\widehat{\mathcal A}_i\text{ does}

notation.meaning: used-element sets of partial packings with i members
uniform matroid of rank kr on U

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform-matroid representative families encode disjoint completion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle matches packing applications and is correct under the standard disjoint-extension interpretation, but no authoritative packing or representative-family source with a locator is supplied.

children.title: Connectivity Applications
children.top_down_role: Representative-family uses in connected-substructure problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphic-matroid compression for partial forests awaiting connectivity completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be connected and let \(M(G)\) be its graphic matroid of rank \(|V|-1\). For a family \(\mathcal A\) of independent edge sets of common size \(p\), let \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\) be \((|V|-1-p)\)-representative for \(\mathcal A\) in \(M(G)\). Then an edge set \(Y\) can extend some \(X\in\mathcal A\) to a spanning tree if and only if it can extend some \(\widehat X\in\widehat{\mathcal A}\) to a spanning tree. Hence a connectivity dynamic program may discard \(\mathcal A\setminus\widehat{\mathcal A}\) without losing spanning-tree completions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A representative family of partial forests preserves whether future edges can complete one of them to a spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is finite and connected}
\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal I(M(G))\text{ and every }X\in\mathcal A\text{ has size }p
\widehat{\mathcal A}\text{ is }(|V|-1-p)\text{-representative for }\mathcal A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal A\text{ and }\widehat{\mathcal A}\text{ admit exactly the same spanning-tree completions}

notation.meaning: number of edges in a partial forest

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: graphic-matroid representativity preserves forest extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graphic-matroid principle fits connectivity applications, but the fixed-completion claim relies on the standard disjoint-extension definition and has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Cross-Regime State Design
children.top_down_role: State representations shared across path, packing, or connectivity applications.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Regime State Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State criterion combining discrete boundary signatures with representative families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let partial solutions be partitioned by a finite boundary signature \(\sigma\in\Sigma\), and let \(q(\sigma)\) bound the size of every admissible continuation for that signature. A compressed state system is cross-regime sound if, for each \(\sigma\), it retains a subfamily \(\widehat{\mathcal A}_\sigma\subseteq\mathcal A_\sigma\) that is \(q(\sigma)\)-representative in the matroid governing extensions, and every transition maps signature-compatible continuations to continuations tested by that representativity relation. Under these conditions, replacing every \(\mathcal A_\sigma\) by \(\widehat{\mathcal A}_\sigma\) preserves the existence of a globally feasible completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hybrid states are sound when signatures capture boundary behavior and representative families preserve all bounded matroidal continuations within each signature.
assumptions_latex: \Sigma\text{ is a finite signature set}
q:\Sigma\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
\widehat{\mathcal A}_\sigma\text{ is }q(\sigma)\text{-representative for every }\sigma
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a feasible completion before compression}\iff\exists\text{ one after compression}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind fits the state-design leaf, but signature compatibility and the correspondence between global completions and matroid continuations are not formalized sufficiently to validate the global equivalence without a source.

children.title: Width-Based Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: Construction and normalization of decompositions, state representations, transitions by decomposition type, state-space compression, and width-sensitive limitations.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Treewidth and dynamic programming; other width metrics

knowledge_statements.title: Given-Decomposition Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up dynamic programming when a bounded-width tree decomposition is supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph \(G\), a rooted nice tree decomposition \((T,\beta)\) of width \(w\), and a finite-state specification with state set \(S_B\) for each bag \(B\), compute tables bottom-up. Initialize leaf tables; apply the specified introduce and forget maps at unary nodes; combine compatible child states at join nodes; and discard states violating local constraints. If each table has at most \(f(w)\) states and every transition costs \(g(w)\) per generated state tuple, the algorithm returns the root optimum or feasibility value in time \(O(|T|g(w)f(w)^2)\) and space \(O(|T|f(w))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a supplied nice decomposition, finite boundary states are propagated from leaves to root using introduce, forget, and join transitions.
assumptions_latex: (T,\beta)\text{ is a rooted nice tree decomposition of }G\text{ of width }w
\text{the state specification is complete and transition-correct}
|S_B|\le f(w)\text{ for every bag }B
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{the root table equals the specified global feasibility or optimum value}

notation.meaning: maximum number of states per bag
transition cost per generated state tuple

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bottom-up algorithm fits the leaf, but its correctness is conditional on an unspecified transition-correct state system, and the stated time bound requires a source fixing the generated-tuple and transition-cost model.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Treewidth Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recognition through exhaustive elimination-order search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(k\ge0\), enumerate all permutations \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of \(V\). For each \(\pi\), eliminate vertices in order, first completing the current neighborhood of \(v_i\) into a clique, and record \(w(\pi)=\max_i |N_i(v_i)|\), where \(N_i(v_i)\) is the neighborhood immediately before elimination. Accept exactly when some \(\pi\) has \(w(\pi)\le k\). From such an ordering, output the standard bags \(\{v_i\}\cup N_i(v_i)\), connected according to their earliest later vertices; otherwise certify \(\operatorname{tw}(G)>k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerating elimination orders recognizes treewidth exactly because the minimum induced elimination width equals graph treewidth.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{accept}\iff\operatorname{tw}(G)\le k

notation.meaning: current neighbors of the vertex eliminated at step i
induced width of elimination ordering pi

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: treewidth equals minimum induced elimination width

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Exact elimination-order enumeration has the correct algorithmic role and acceptance criterion, but no authoritative treewidth citation is supplied, and the bag-connection construction needs a sourced convention covering components and empty later neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Treewidth Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Guarantee required of a parameterized treewidth-approximation interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\alpha\ge1\). An \(\alpha\)-approximate treewidth construction algorithm receives a graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\ge0\) and returns either a tree decomposition of \(G\) having width at most \(\alpha k\), or the answer \(\operatorname{tw}(G)>k\). The second answer must be correct; when \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\le k\), the algorithm must return the decomposition. Thus either output is permitted only in the gap regime \(k<\operatorname{tw}(G)\le\alpha k\). A parameterized construction additionally runs in time \(f(k)|V(G)|^{O(1)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A treewidth approximation either constructs width at most αk or correctly certifies that width k is impossible, with ambiguity only in the approximation gap.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
\alpha\ge1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{tw}(G)\le k\Longrightarrow\text{a decomposition of width at most }\alpha k\text{ is returned}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: As a definition of the required approximation interface, the content kind is defensible and the gap guarantee is coherent. No cited source supports this convention or any concrete construction guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Nice-Decomposition Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization into introduce, forget, join, and leaf nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a tree decomposition \((T,\beta)\) of a graph \(G\) with width \(w\), root \(T\), make it binary by duplicating bags, and subdivide every parent-child edge by a sequence that changes one vertex at a time. Insert introduce nodes when a vertex enters a bag, forget nodes when it leaves, and join nodes with two children carrying the same bag; append empty leaf and root paths if required. The resulting rooted nice decomposition represents \(G\), has width at most \(w\), and can be constructed with a number of nodes polynomial in \(|V(G)|+|T|\) and \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any supplied tree decomposition can be normalized into a rooted nice decomposition without increasing its width.
assumptions_latex: (T,\beta)\text{ is a finite tree decomposition of }G
\max_{t\in V(T)}|\beta(t)|-1=w
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{the output is a nice tree decomposition of }G\text{ with width at most }w

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalization algorithm fits the leaf and states the standard width-preservation property, but the precise nice-node convention and construction-size bound lack a cited source and explicit bound.

children.title: Rooted Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Decomposition representations equipped with a distinguished root.

knowledge_statements.title: Rooted Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree decompositions equipped with an orientation toward a designated root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rooted tree decomposition of a graph \(G=(V,E)\) is a triple \((T,\beta,r)\), where \(T\) is a tree, \(r\in V(T)\) is its root, and \(\beta:V(T)\to2^V\) satisfies: every vertex of \(G\) occurs in some bag; every edge \(uv\in E\) has both endpoints in some bag; and, for each \(v\in V\), the nodes \(\{t:v\in\beta(t)\}\) induce a connected subtree. Rooting gives every nonroot node a parent and defines the subgraph below each node for bottom-up dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rooted tree decomposition is an ordinary tree decomposition with one decomposition node designated as the root.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (T,\beta,r)\text{ is rooted while preserving all tree-decomposition axioms}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rooted-decomposition definition fits the leaf and correctly retains the ordinary decomposition axioms, but no citation is supplied and the claimed subgraph below a node requires an explicit convention.

children.title: Labeled Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Decomposition representations carrying labels on structural objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Labeled Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree decompositions enriched by finite labels used in state transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) and let \(\Lambda\) be a finite alphabet. A \(\Lambda\)-labeled tree decomposition is a tree decomposition \((T,\beta)\) together with a labeling map \(\lambda\) whose declared domain is either decomposition nodes, bag incidences, or graph elements appearing in bags. The label of an object must agree across all bags containing that object whenever labels encode persistent graph data. The width remains \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|\beta(t)|-1\); labels enrich the dynamic-programming state but do not alter vertex or edge coverage or the connected-occurrence axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A labeled decomposition adds finite persistent annotations to an ordinary tree decomposition without changing its bags, axioms, or width.
assumptions_latex: (T,\beta)\text{ is a tree decomposition of }G
\Lambda\text{ is a finite label alphabet}
\lambda\text{ has a fixed declared labeling domain}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (T,\beta,\lambda)\text{ retains the underlying decomposition width and axioms}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition does not select one labeling domain and makes consistency conditional on label semantics. A taxonomy-specific source is needed before choosing among node, incidence, and persistent graph-element labeling conventions.

children.title: Annotated Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Decomposition representations enriched with auxiliary problem data.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite graph and \((T,\beta)\) is a tree decomposition of \(G\).
For each \(t\in V(T)\), the annotation set \(A_t\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D^A=(T,\beta,(a_t)_{t\in V(T)})\) is an annotated tree decomposition precisely when \((T,\beta)\) is a tree decomposition and \(a_t\in A_t\) for every \(t\in V(T)\).

notation.meaning: bag map of the underlying tree decomposition
admissible annotation set at decomposition node t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic formalization of an annotated tree decomposition; annotation semantics depend on the target dynamic program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic node-local annotations; no problem-specific annotation alphabet is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph. An annotated tree decomposition of \(G\) is a triple \(\mathcal D^A=(T,\beta,(a_t)_{t\in V(T)})\), where \((T,\beta)\) is a tree decomposition of \(G\), each node \(t\) has a prescribed finite annotation set \(A_t\), and \(a_t\in A_t\). The annotation may encode node type, local graph data, or algorithmic metadata, but it does not alter the vertex-covering, edge-covering, or connected-occurrence axioms imposed on \((T,\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An annotated decomposition is a tree decomposition whose nodes additionally carry values from prescribed finite annotation sets; these values do not change the underlying decomposition axioms.
knowledge_statements.title: Annotated Decompositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Annotated Decompositions leaf and is internally coherent, but it has no inspectable citation. The finiteness and node-local nature of the annotation sets are modeling choices rather than universal properties of annotated tree decompositions, so source support matching this formulation is required.

children.title: Enrichment Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility among rooting, labeling, or annotation conventions.

assumptions_latex: \((T,\beta)\) is a tree decomposition and each node \(t\) carries an enrichment \(a_t\).
Each oriented tree edge \(tu\) has adhesion \(S_{tu}=\beta(t)\cap\beta(u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The enrichment is compatible exactly when every adjacent pair satisfies \(a_t|_{S_{tu}}=a_u|_{S_{tu}}\), or the specified interface relation \(R_{tu}(a_t,a_u)\) when equality is not the intended consistency rule.

notation.meaning: bag intersection across decomposition edge tu
restriction of node t's enrichment to the adhesion
prescribed compatibility relation across edge tu

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: interface agreement is the standard compatibility predicate for enriched decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers equality-based labels and problem-specific relational interfaces on adhesions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An enrichment \((a_t)_{t\in V(T)}\) is compatible if, for every edge \(tu\in E(T)\), its two endpoint annotations induce consistent data on the adhesion \(S_{tu}=\beta(t)\cap\beta(u)\). For restriction-based annotations this predicate is \(a_t|_{S_{tu}}=a_u|_{S_{tu}}\). More generally, given a specified interface relation \(R_{tu}\subseteq A_t\times A_u\), compatibility means \((a_t,a_u)\in R_{tu}\) for every \(tu\in E(T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enrichments are compatible when adjacent decomposition nodes agree, or satisfy a prescribed relation, on the information shared by their intersecting bags.
knowledge_statements.title: Enrichment Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Enrichment Compatibility and distinguishes restriction agreement from a prescribed relational interface. No citation supports the general relation-based formulation or establishes which enrichments admit restrictions to adhesions, so the exact mathematical scope remains source-dependent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum Independent Set via Treewidth Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact maximum-independent-set computation from a supplied tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a tree decomposition of a graph $G=(V,E)$ with decomposition-node set $V'$ and treewidth $t$, a maximum independent set of $G$ can be found by dynamic programming in time $O\!\left(2^{O(t)}|V'|\right)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a tree decomposition of width t with node set V', dynamic programming finds a maximum independent set in time exponential in t and linear in the number of decomposition nodes.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a graph}
(T,(X_i)_{i\in V'})\text{ is a supplied tree decomposition of width }t
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{MIS}(G)\text{ can be computed in }O\!\left(2^{O(t)}|V'|\right)\text{ time}

source_evidence.locator: Further uses of rounding data and dynamic programming / 10.2. The maximum independent set problem in planar graphs / Theorem 10.12

source_refs.locator: Further uses of rounding data and dynamic programming / 10.2. The maximum independent set problem in planar graphs / Theorem 10.12

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Independent Set via Treewidth Dynamic Programming

source_witnesses.locator: Further uses of rounding data and dynamic programming / 10.2. The maximum independent set problem in planar graphs / Theorem 10.12

directory_assessment.rationale: The runtime guarantee belongs primarily under treewidth dynamic programming, with a legitimate cross-index from the Independent Set problem route.

children.title: Local Assignment States
children.top_down_role: States recording assignments restricted to the current decomposition region.

assumptions_latex: \((T,\beta)\) is a rooted tree decomposition of a finite constraint instance with finite value domain \(D\).
\(V_t\) is the set of variables introduced in the subtree rooted at \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local assignment family at \(t\) is \(\mathcal L_t=\{x:V_t\to D:x\text{ satisfies every constraint whose scope lies in }V_t\}\).

notation.meaning: variables processed in the subtree rooted at t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subtree assignments are the standard semantic objects underlying treewidth dynamic programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain constraint formulation; graph problems arise by encoding vertex or edge decisions as variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rooted tree decomposition \((T,\beta)\), let \(V_t\) be the variables occurring in bags of the subtree rooted at \(t\). A local assignment state before boundary compression is a map \(x:V_t\to D\) satisfying every constraint whose entire scope is contained in \(V_t\). Thus \(\mathcal L_t=\{x:V_t\to D:x\text{ satisfies all constraints internal to }V_t\}\); constraints meeting variables outside \(V_t\) are deferred to the interface state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local assignment state assigns finite-domain values to all variables processed below a decomposition node and satisfies every constraint already internal to that subtree.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Assignment States

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Local Assignment States and consistently specifies a finite-domain constraint formulation. It lacks an inspectable source establishing the intended subtree variable set and the treatment of constraints whose scopes are not wholly processed.

children.title: Boundary States
children.top_down_role: States recording interaction through the active decomposition boundary.

assumptions_latex: \(V_t\) is the processed variable set and \(B_t=V_t\cap(V\setminus V_t)^+\) is its interface to unprocessed constraints.
\(D\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assignment boundary-state space is \(\Sigma_t=\{x|_{B_t}:x\in\mathcal L_t\}\subseteq D^{B_t}\).

notation.meaning: restriction of assignment x to the boundary

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: realizable restrictions define assignment boundary states
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment-valued boundary states, prior to any quotienting or additional connectivity metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At node \(t\), let \(B_t\subseteq V_t\) contain exactly the processed variables that occur together in some constraint with an unprocessed variable; for a tree decomposition one may use the current bag as a valid boundary superset. The boundary states induced by local assignments are \(\Sigma_t=\{x|_{B_t}:x\in\mathcal L_t\}\subseteq D^{B_t}\). A member \(\sigma\in\Sigma_t\) records only values visible to constraints outside the processed region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary state is a realizable assignment on the processed variables that can still interact with the unprocessed part of the instance.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary States

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Boundary States, and the realizable-restriction formula is coherent. The notation used to characterize the interface in the assumptions is not standardized or defined in the record, while the statement uses a different explicit characterization; a source is needed to fix the intended boundary convention.

children.title: Assignment-to-Boundary Projection
children.top_down_role: Interfaces connecting local information to its boundary-visible summary.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal L_t\) is the family of feasible local assignments on \(V_t\).
\(B_t\subseteq V_t\) is the chosen boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assignment-to-boundary projection is the surjection \(p_t:\mathcal L_t\to\Sigma_t\) defined by \(p_t(x)=x|_{B_t}\), where \(\Sigma_t=p_t(\mathcal L_t)\).

notation.meaning: projection from local assignments to boundary states

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: restriction is the canonical projection from assignments to an interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical restriction map for assignment-valued interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every node \(t\), define \(p_t:\mathcal L_t\to D^{B_t}\) by \(p_t(x)=x|_{B_t}\). Its image \(\Sigma_t=p_t(\mathcal L_t)\) is the realizable boundary-state space, so the codomain restriction \(p_t:\mathcal L_t\to\Sigma_t\) is surjective. Two local assignments have the same projection exactly when they agree on every boundary variable: \(p_t(x)=p_t(y)\iff (\forall v\in B_t)\,x(v)=y(v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a local assignment means restricting it to boundary variables; every realizable boundary state is obtained this way, and equal projections mean boundary agreement.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment-to-Boundary Projection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits Assignment-to-Boundary Projection, and surjectivity follows from defining the boundary-state space as the image. No inspectable citation is supplied for this interface representation in the stated treewidth dynamic-programming context.

children.title: Boundary Sufficiency
children.top_down_role: Limits on which local distinctions may safely be omitted from boundary states.

assumptions_latex: Every constraint crossing from \(V_t\) to its complement meets \(V_t\) only in \(B_t\).
The objective decomposes into contributions of constraint scopes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(p_t(x)=p_t(y)\), then every outside assignment \(z\) is compatible with \(x\) exactly when it is compatible with \(y\); their completed objective values differ only by the stored internal aggregate.

notation.meaning: assignment on variables outside the processed region

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: separator agreement makes subtree assignments interchangeable to the exterior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separator sufficiency for finite-scope constraints with a separately stored internal objective aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,y\in\mathcal L_t\) satisfy \(p_t(x)=p_t(y)\). If every constraint containing both a variable in \(V_t\) and a variable outside \(V_t\) intersects \(V_t\) only through \(B_t\), then for every outside assignment \(z\), the union \(x\cup z\) satisfies all crossing constraints if and only if \(y\cup z\) does. For a scope-decomposable objective, exterior contributions are consequently identical; only the stored aggregate of internal contributions may distinguish \(x\) from \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assignments agreeing on a valid boundary are indistinguishable to the unprocessed instance, apart from an internal objective value that the state must store separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Sufficiency

children.title: Partition-State Explosion

If a state also chooses an active subset \(S\subseteq B\), the total number is \(\sum_{i=0}^{b}\binom bi\mathrm B_i=\mathrm B_{b+1}\), which has the same asymptotic form.

children.title: Counting States
children.top_down_role: States carrying multiplicity information for partial solutions.

assumptions_latex: \((K,\oplus,\otimes,0_K,1_K)\) is a commutative semiring.
Each partial solution projects to a finite interface-state set \(\Sigma_t\).

Equivalently, \(C_t(\sigma)=\sum_{x:p_t(x)=\sigma}1\) in the semiring \((\mathbb N,+,\cdot,0,1)\). Mutually exclusive constructions contributing to the same state are added, while independent compatible choices at a join are multiplied, with any required agreement on the shared interface enforced before multiplication.

children.title: Weighted States

assumptions_latex: \((K,\oplus,\otimes,0_K,1_K)\) is a commutative semiring.

children.title: Optimization States
children.top_down_role: States retaining objective-relevant summaries of partial solutions.

assumptions_latex: For every \(\sigma\in\Sigma_B\), the set \(F_B(\sigma)\) is finite.
The objective decomposes consistently across decomposition transitions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a decomposition bag, let \(\Sigma_B\) be its finite interface-state set, and, for each \(\sigma\in\Sigma_B\), let \(F_B(\sigma)\) be the finite set of partial solutions inducing \(\sigma\). Given a minimization objective \(w:\bigcup_{\sigma\in\Sigma_B}F_B(\sigma)\to\mathbb R\), define \[D_B(\sigma)=\min_{S\in F_B(\sigma)}w(S),\] with \(D_B(\sigma)=+\infty\) when \(F_B(\sigma)=\varnothing\). Partial solutions inducing the same interface may be represented by their least objective value when every future extension depends only on the interface and combines with the accumulated value additively.

children.title: Objective-Semiring Regimes

assumptions_latex: The transition recurrence uses only finite aggregation over alternatives and compositional multiplication.
Every local contribution has a value in \(K\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform semiring interpretation of feasibility, counting, weighting, and optimization tables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((K,\oplus,\otimes,0_K,1_K)\) be a commutative semiring. A decomposition table assigns \(D_B:\Sigma_B\to K\), aggregates alternative partial solutions with \(\oplus\), and composes independent contributions with \(\otimes\). Standard regimes include \((\{0,1\},\lor,\land,0,1)\) for feasibility, \((\mathbb N,+,\cdot,0,1)\) for counting, and \((\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\},\min,+,+\infty,0)\) for minimization. Polynomial or formal-power-series semirings over a coefficient semiring encode weighted generating functions. A recurrence expressed solely through semiring aggregation, semiring multiplication, and local constants can be interpreted in any selected regime for which those constants and the state semantics are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility, counting, weighted enumeration, and minimization can share a table architecture when its recurrence is expressed using the operations of the selected semiring.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Semiring Regimes

children.title: Introduce Interfaces
children.top_down_role: State transitions associated with introducing a decomposition element.

knowledge_statements.title: Introduce Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic introduce-vertex transition on a nice tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an introduce node with child bag \(B\) and parent bag \(B'=B\cup\{v\}\), initialize \(D_{B'}(\sigma')=0_K\) for every \(\sigma'\in\Sigma_{B'}\). For each child state \(\sigma\in\Sigma_B\) and each admissible local status \(a\) of \(v\), construct \(\sigma'=\operatorname{intro}_v(\sigma,a)\). If all constraints whose complete scope becomes visible are satisfied, update \[D_{B'}(\sigma')\leftarrow D_{B'}(\sigma')\oplus\bigl(D_B(\sigma)\otimes c_v(\sigma,a)\bigr).\] Output the resulting parent table after all admissible pairs have been processed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extend every child interface by each admissible status of the introduced vertex and aggregate its local contribution.
assumptions_latex: \(B'=B\cup\{v\}\) is an introduce node.
\(c_v(\sigma,a)\in K\) accounts for contributions charged at this node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output table represents exactly the partial solutions compatible with each state in \(\Sigma_{B'}\).

notation.meaning: local status assigned to the introduced vertex

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a forget node with child bag \(B'=B\cup\{v\}\) and parent bag \(B\), initialize \(D_B(\tau)=0_K\) for every \(\tau\in\Sigma_B\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic join transition for two subtrees sharing the same bag.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a join node whose two children and parent have bag \(B\), initialize \(D_B(\tau)=0_K\) for every \(\tau\in\Sigma_B\). For every compatible pair \((\sigma_1,\sigma_2)\in\Sigma_B^2\), form \(\tau=\operatorname{join}(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)\) and update \[D_B(\tau)\leftarrow D_B(\tau)\oplus\Bigl(D_1(\sigma_1)\otimes D_2(\sigma_2)\otimes q_B(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)\Bigr).\] Here \(q_B(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)\in K\) is a problem-specific factor that compensates contributions represented in both child tables. children.title: Interface Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility requirements across the three transition-interface families.

knowledge_statements.title: Interface Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate ensuring that a table state summarizes all future-relevant boundary information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bag \(B\), let \(P\) be a partial solution below \(B\) and let \(\sigma\in\Sigma_B\). The consistency predicate \(C_B(P,\sigma)\) holds exactly when: the restriction of \(P\) to \(B\) equals the assignment encoded by \(\sigma\); every boundary relation induced by \(P\) equals the relation recorded by \(\sigma\); and every constraint fully contained below \(B\) is satisfied. Moreover, any unresolved obligation of \(P\) must have all of its possible future interaction represented in \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state is consistent when it exactly records boundary assignments, relations, and every obligation that can interact with future vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a partial solution in the subgraph below bag \(B\).
\(\sigma\) belongs to the declared state space \(\Sigma_B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(C_B(P,\sigma)\) and \(C_B(P',\sigma)\), then every common outside extension accepts or rejects \(P\) and \(P'\) identically.
review_flags: The exact boundary relations and obligations depend on the optimization problem; no problem-specific source was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the listed assignment, relation, and obligation clauses are problem-dependent and do not formally imply extension equivalence without a defined extension model. No source is supplied from which those missing semantics can be recovered reliably.

assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is a fixed graph property.
Each boundary label occurs at most once in a boundaried graph, and gluing is applied to operands with the same boundary-label set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\equiv_{\Pi,t}\) has finite index, its equivalence classes form a finite abstract state space for distinguishing \(t\)-boundaried graphs by extensions with respect to \(\Pi\).
review_flags: No supplied locator supports canonical equivalence of boundaried graphs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical extension equivalence for fixed-label boundaried graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a graph property \(\Pi\) and an integer \(t\ge 0\). For two \(t\)-boundaried graphs \(G_1,G_2\) with the same injective boundary labels, define \(G_1\equiv_{\Pi,t}G_2\) if and only if, for every \(t\)-boundaried graph \(H\) with the same boundary-label set, \[G_1\oplus H\in\Pi\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_2\oplus H\in\Pi,\] where gluing \(\oplus\) identifies boundary vertices carrying equal labels. The property has finite-state equivalence at boundary size \(t\) when \(\equiv_{\Pi,t}\) has finitely many equivalence classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two equally labeled boundaried graphs are equivalent when every compatible graph glued to their boundaries yields the same property decision; the equivalence is finite-state when it has finitely many classes.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-State Equivalence

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a nonempty finite bag.
Weights are real, combine additively, and are minimized.
For partitions \(p,q\in\Pi(B)\), completion is represented by \(p\vee q=\{B\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rank-based reduction returns a representative subfamily of size at most \(2^{|B|-1}\) and preserves the minimum completion weight for every query partition.

notation.meaning: set of partitions of the bag

review_flags: The rank bound and representative-family guarantee require a directly relevant rank-based dynamic-programming source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative-set compression of weighted connectivity partitions over a bag.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty finite bag \(B\), let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\Pi(B)\times\mathbb R\) be a weighted family of boundary-connectivity partitions. Define the completion matrix \(M\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), with rows and columns indexed by \(\Pi(B)\), by \[M[p,q]=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\vee q=\{B\},\] where \(\{B\}\) denotes the one-block partition. Process the distinct partitions represented in \(\mathcal A\) in nondecreasing order of their least associated weight, retaining a partition exactly when its row increases the span of the previously retained rows. Denote the retained weighted family by \(\operatorname{reduce}(\mathcal A)\). The reduction is representative when, for every \(q\in\Pi(B)\), it preserves the minimum weight among pairs \((p,w)\in\mathcal A\) satisfying \(p\vee q=\{B\}\). Apply this reduction after ordinary decomposition transitions before continuing the dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compress weighted connectivity partitions by scanning them in nondecreasing weight and retaining only rows that increase the completion-matrix span, while preserving the best completion for every future partition query.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Based Dynamic Programming

children.title: Consistent-Cut Encodings
children.top_down_role: Cut-based encodings used to distinguish connectivity-compatible candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Consistent-Cut Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut encoding of the connected components of a selected subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G[X]\) be a selected nonempty subgraph and fix a root \(r\in X\). A rooted consistent cut is an ordered bipartition \((X_L,X_R)\) of \(X\) such that \(r\in X_L\) and no selected edge has one endpoint in \(X_L\) and the other in \(X_R\). Equivalently, every connected component of \(G[X]\) lies wholly on one side, while the root component is forced to the left side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rooted consistent cut assigns whole connected components to two sides while fixing the root component on the left.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\).
\(r\in X\) is distinguished.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistent cuts encode independent side choices for all components except the component containing \(r\).
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses consistent-cut encodings.

The notation also leaves unresolved whether the selected object is the induced graph on X or an edge-selected subgraph, which affects what 'selected edge' means.

children.title: Parity Counting
children.top_down_role: Parity-based cancellation of disconnected or otherwise invalid candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Parity Counting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity test for connectivity using rooted consistent cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G[X]\) be nonempty, let \(r\in X\), and suppose \(G[X]\) has \(c\) connected components. Each component other than the root component may independently be assigned to either side of a rooted consistent cut. Consequently, the number of rooted consistent cuts equals \[2^{c-1}.\] Over \(\mathbb F_2\), this count is \(1\) precisely when \(c=1\), and it is \(0\) whenever \(c\ge 2\). Thus parity distinguishes connected selected subgraphs from disconnected ones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected subgraph has an odd number of rooted consistent cuts exactly when it is connected.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\).
A root \(r\in X\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\#	ext{ rooted consistent cuts of }G[X]\equiv 1\pmod 2\) if and only if \(G[X]\) is connected.

notation.meaning: number of connected components of the selected subgraph

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the consistent-cut parity identity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind correctly captures the parity identity, and the hypotheses and conclusion are internally consistent. However, there is no source reference or inspectable locator supporting the consistent-cut count, so the candidate cannot be accepted under the evidence contract.

children.title: Isolation Interface
children.top_down_role: Use of isolation to support recovery of a unique relevant candidate.

knowledge_statements.title: Isolation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random isolation converts parity detection into a one-sided existence test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be a ground set of size \(m\), let \(\varnothing
eq\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\), and choose weights \(w(u)\) independently and uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\). With probability at least \(1-m/N\), the function \(w(F)=\sum_{u\in F}w(u)\) has a unique minimum over \(\mathcal F\). If a parity dynamic program counts feasible connected objects separately by total weight, then on this event the minimum occupied weight has odd parity, thereby certifying existence; an empty family always produces zero parity at every weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random weights isolate a unique minimum with high probability, allowing parity counting to detect existence without false positives.
assumptions_latex: \(|U|=m\) and \(\mathcal F\neq\varnothing\).
Weights are independent and uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parity test has no false positive and succeeds on a nonempty family with probability at least \(1-m/N\).
review_flags: The Isolation Lemma and its parity-algorithm interface require a directly relevant source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the isolation-interface leaf, and the stated isolation probability is mathematically plausible. A directly relevant source is required for both the Isolation Lemma bound and the additional claim connecting a uniquely isolated feasible object to the parity table.

children.title: Parity-Cancellation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where the required cancellation or isolation behavior is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Parity-Cancellation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which consistent-cut parity ceases to identify a feasible connected object.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cancellation argument requires a nonempty selected subgraph and a fixed root component. Without fixing a root side, a subgraph with \(c\ge 1\) components has \(2^c\) consistent cuts, so even connected subgraphs contribute zero modulo \(2\). With a fixed root, disconnected subgraphs cancel because they contribute \(2^{c-1}\), but multiple connected solutions in the same counted class may still cancel each other. Hence existence cannot be inferred from raw parity unless the counted class contains a unique target solution, typically supplied by isolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parity fails without a fixed root or uniqueness: connected solutions can then occur an even number of times and cancel.
assumptions_latex: Counting is performed modulo \(2\).
Solutions are grouped into the same dynamic-programming count class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rooting removes cut-symmetry cancellation, while isolation or another uniqueness mechanism prevents cancellation among distinct connected solutions.

notation.meaning: number of unrooted ordered consistent cuts

review_flags: No supplied locator directly documents the parity-cancellation failure conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind exactly fits this terminal container, and the rooting and uniqueness failure modes are stated consistently with the preceding parity records. No citation or inspectable locator supports these cancellation boundaries, so evidence is insufficient for acceptance.

knowledge_statements.title: Representative Partition Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted representative families for connectivity states on a decomposition bag.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite boundary, let \(\Pi(U)\) be its partitions, and let \(\mathcal A\subseteq \Pi(U)\times\mathbb R\) be a weighted family. For \(q\in\Pi(U)\), define \(\operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal A}(q)=\min\{w:(p,w)\in\mathcal A,\ p\vee q=\{U\}\}\), with minimum \(+\infty\) over the empty set. A subfamily \(\mathcal A'\subseteq\mathcal A\) represents \(\mathcal A\) when \[\operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal A'}(q)=\operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal A}(q)\qquad\text{for every }q\in\Pi(U).\] Thus replacing a dynamic-programming table by \(\mathcal A'\) preserves every future connectivity completion query on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A representative subfamily preserves the minimum weight of every partial connectivity state under every possible future boundary completion.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite.
Weights are minimized in \(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal A'}(q)=\operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal A}(q)\) for all \(q\in\Pi(U)\).

notation.meaning: set of partitions of the boundary U
join of partitions p and q

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the representative-partition leaf and is internally coherent, but no cited source supports the precise join convention, optimization direction, or completion interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset-Transform Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fast subset convolution for accelerating decomposition-table join operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a ring and let \(f,g:2^{[k]}\to R\). Define their subset convolution by \[h(S)=\sum_{A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B=S}f(A)g(B).\] For each rank \(r\), form \(f_r(S)=f(S)\) if \(|S|=r\) and \(0\) otherwise, and similarly \(g_r\). Compute the ranked zeta transforms \(F_r(X)=\sum_{S\subseteq X}f_r(S)\) and \(G_r(X)=\sum_{S\subseteq X}g_r(S)\). Set \(H_r(X)=\sum_{i=0}^{r}F_i(X)G_{r-i}(X)\), apply ranked Möbius inversion, and output \(h(S)=H_{|S|}^{-1}(S)\). The computation uses \(O(k^2 2^k)\) ring operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ranked zeta transforms turn disjoint-union convolution into pointwise rank convolution, followed by Möbius inversion, using singly exponential time.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) take values in a ring \(R\).
The ground set has size \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All values of \(h=f*_{\mathrm{sub}}g\) are computed using \(O(k^2 2^k)\) ring operations.

notation.meaning: disjoint union of A and B
Möbius inverse of the transformed rank-r function

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits subset-transform acceleration, but the ranked inversion step and O(k^2 2^k) ring-operation bound require an inspectable authoritative locator. The notation H_r^{-1} is also nonstandard enough to require source confirmation.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Set MSO Property Meta-Theorems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Courcelle-type model checking for fixed MSO1 sentences on bounded-treewidth graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every monadic second-order sentence \(\varphi\) over graphs whose second-order variables range over vertex sets, and every integer \(k\ge 0\), there exist a computable function \(f\) and an algorithm such that, given a graph \(G\) with \(n\) vertices and a tree decomposition of width at most \(k\), the algorithm decides whether \(G\models\varphi\) in time \(f(k,|\varphi|)n\). In particular, when \(k\) and \(\varphi\) are fixed, the property defined by \(\varphi\) is decidable in linear time on the supplied decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every fixed vertex-set MSO property is decidable in linear time on graphs of bounded treewidth when a suitable decomposition is supplied.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi\) is an MSO1 sentence.
A width-at-most-\(k\) tree decomposition of \(G\) is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\models\varphi\) is decidable in time \(f(k,|\varphi|)n\) for a computable \(f\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem and content kind fit the MSO1 meta-theorem leaf, but the stated parameterized linear-time bound has no citation or locator supporting its exact signature and supplied-decomposition convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Set MSO Property Meta-Theorems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Courcelle-type model checking for fixed MSO2 sentences on bounded-treewidth graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every monadic second-order sentence \(\varphi\) over the incidence representation of graphs, allowing quantification over vertex sets and edge sets, and every \(k\ge 0\), there exist a computable function \(f\) and an algorithm such that, given an \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\) and a tree decomposition of width at most \(k\), the algorithm decides whether \(G\models\varphi\) in time \(f(k,|\varphi|)n\). Hence every fixed MSO2-definable graph property is linear-time decidable on bounded-treewidth graphs with a supplied decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every fixed MSO property permitting edge-set quantification is decidable in linear time on bounded-treewidth graphs with a supplied decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi\) is an MSO2 sentence interpreted through graph incidence.
A width-at-most-\(k\) tree decomposition of \(G\) is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\models\varphi\) is decidable in time \(f(k,|\varphi|)n\) for a computable \(f\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the MSO2 leaf, but the exact incidence representation, allowed edge-set quantification, and linear-time bound need a specific authoritative theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.title: MSO Optimization Meta-Theorems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-objective optimization over assignments satisfying a fixed MSO formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an MSO formula \(\varphi(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\), a treewidth bound \(k\), and integer coefficients \(a_1,\ldots,a_p\). There is a computable function \(f\) such that, given an \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\) of treewidth at most \(k\) with a corresponding tree decomposition, one can find vertex sets \(X_1,
\ldots,X_p\) satisfying \(G\models\varphi(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\) and minimizing \(\sum_{i=1}^{p}a_i|X_i|\), or report infeasibility, in time \(f(k,|\varphi|,p)n\). The analogous maximization problem follows by negating the coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed MSO-definable feasible family with a fixed linear cardinality objective can be optimized in linear time on bounded-treewidth graphs.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi\), \(p\), the coefficients, and the treewidth bound are fixed.
A qualifying tree decomposition is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal satisfying tuple is found, or infeasibility reported, in \(f(k,|\varphi|,p)n\) time.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the optimization meta-theorem leaf, but no source establishes this exact free-variable, integer-cardinality-objective, witness-producing formulation and running-time dependence.

children.title: Counting Meta-Theorems
children.top_down_role: Meta-theorem routes for counting logically specified structures on bounded-width inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Counting Meta-Theorems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counting satisfying assignments to free set variables in fixed MSO formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an MSO formula \(\varphi(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\) and an integer \(k\ge 0\). There exist a computable function \(f\) and an algorithm which, given an \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\) with a tree decomposition of width at most \(k\), computes \[N_\varphi(G)=\left|\{(X_1,\ldots,X_p):G\models\varphi(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\}\right|\] in \(f(k,|\varphi|)n\) arithmetic operations on integers. Bit complexity additionally depends on the sizes of intermediate counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed MSO formula, satisfying assignments to its free set variables can be counted by linear-many integer arithmetic operations on bounded-treewidth graphs.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi\) and \(k\) are fixed.
A width-at-most-\(k\) tree decomposition is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\varphi(G)\) is computable using \(f(k,|\varphi|)n\) integer arithmetic operations.

notation.meaning: number of satisfying tuples of set assignments

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement fits the counting meta-theorem leaf and distinguishes arithmetic from bit complexity, but both the counting formulation and its linear arithmetic-operation bound require a specific source locator.

children.title: Weighted Evaluation Meta-Theorems
children.top_down_role: Meta-theorem routes for aggregating weights over logically specified structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Evaluation Meta-Theorems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semiring-weighted evaluation of assignments defined by a fixed MSO formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(k\), an MSO formula \(\varphi(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\), and a commutative semiring \(S\). Assign each membership choice \((i,v,b)\), where \(b\in\{0,1\}\), a weight \(w_{i,v,b}\in S\). For a graph \(G\), define \[Z_\varphi(G)=\sum_{G\models\varphi(\mathbf X)}\prod_{i=1}^{p}\prod_{v\in V(G)}w_{i,v,\mathbf1[v\in X_i]}.\] Given \(G\), the weights, and a width-at-most-\(k\) tree decomposition, \(Z_\varphi(G)\) is computable using \(f(k,|\varphi|)n\) semiring operations, provided semiring operations are available as oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed MSO-defined weighted partition function is evaluable with linear-many semiring operations on a supplied bounded-width tree decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a commutative semiring with effective addition and multiplication.
\(k\) and \(\varphi\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z_\varphi(G)\) is computable using \(f(k,|\varphi|)n\) operations in \(S\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits weighted evaluation, but the unrestricted commutative-semiring oracle formulation and per-membership weight model are materially stronger and more specific than ordinary counting; an exact supporting theorem is required.

children.title: Algebraic Evaluation Meta-Theorems
children.top_down_role: Evaluation regimes using algebraic aggregation beyond ordinary counting.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Evaluation Meta-Theorems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state algebraic evaluation over decomposition terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a width bound \(k\), a finite set \(Q\) of decomposition states, a commutative semiring \(S\), and for every decomposition constructor \(\sigma\) an \(S\)-multilinear transition map \(T_\sigma\) between the corresponding free semimodules \(S^Q\). For any well-formed width-\(k\) decomposition term \(t\), recursively assign leaves their prescribed vectors and internal nodes the value obtained from \(T_\sigma\). If \(F\subseteq Q\) is the accepting set, then the evaluation is \[\operatorname{val}(t)=\sum_{q\in F}v_t(q).\] A bottom-up traversal computes this value using \(O(|t|C)\) semiring operations, where \(C\) bounds one transition evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-state semiring transitions on decomposition terms yield a bottom-up algebraic evaluator whose work is linear in the term size.
assumptions_latex: The state set and constructor signature are finite.
Every transition is effectively evaluable over \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(t)=\sum_{q\in F}v_t(q)\) is computable in \(O(|t|C)\) semiring operations.

notation.meaning: state-value vector computed for term t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-state algebraic evaluator is plausible, but it is presented as a representation/construction rather than an algebraic evaluation meta-theorem matching the terminal title. A source is needed to determine the intended theorem scope and correct mathematical role.

children.title: Evaluation-Uniformity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Uniformity or effectiveness limitations affecting meta-theorem evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-Uniformity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of uniform evaluation when formulas or coefficient operations are unrestricted inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The fixed-formula evaluation bounds do not imply a uniform polynomial bound independent of the formula. Even on width-one structures, MSO model checking with \(\varphi\) supplied as part of the input has parameter dependence on \(|\varphi|\) that cannot generally be bounded by any fixed-height tower of exponentials under standard complexity assumptions. Moreover, a bound stated in semiring operations is not a bit-complexity bound: if coefficients have unbounded encodings or semiring operations lack effective polynomial-time implementations, intermediate values and individual operations may require superpolynomial time. Thus formula dependence and coefficient cost must remain explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear decomposition size does not give uniform elementary formula dependence or polynomial bit complexity for unrestricted coefficient domains.
assumptions_latex: The formula is allowed to vary with the input.
Complexity is measured uniformly rather than with the formula compiled in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No formula-independent elementary evaluation guarantee or coefficient-independent bit bound follows from fixed-formula meta-theorems.

notation.meaning: encoding length of the input formula

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the fixed-height-tower lower-bound claim is sensitive to the structure class, logic, parameterization, and complexity assumption. Those details cannot be validated without an exact lower-bound citation.

children.title: Decomposition Automata
children.top_down_role: Automaton representations operating over encoded decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Automata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic bottom-up automata over bounded-width graph decomposition terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite ranked signature \(\Sigma_k\) whose terms encode graphs of width at most \(k\). A deterministic bottom-up decomposition automaton is a tuple \(\mathcal A=(Q,(\delta_\sigma)_{\sigma\in\Sigma_k},F)\), where \(Q\) is finite, \(F\subseteq Q\), and each rank-\(r\) constructor \(\sigma\) has a transition \(\delta_\sigma:Q^r\to Q\). For a term \(t=\sigma(t_1,\ldots,t_r)\), define recursively \(q_t=\delta_\sigma(q_{t_1},\ldots,q_{t_r})\). The automaton accepts \(t\) exactly when \(q_t\in F\); it recognizes the graphs represented by accepted well-formed terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition automaton assigns finite states bottom-up to bounded-width graph-construction terms and accepts according to the root state.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma_k\) is a finite ranked decomposition signature.
Only well-formed terms representing graphs are interpreted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\) is accepted if and only if its recursively computed root state satisfies \(q_t\in F\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit decomposition automata, but recognizability depends on the precise bounded-width term signature and graph interpretation, neither of which has cited support.

children.title: Recognizable Graph Properties
children.top_down_role: Graph-property classes recognizable through finite decomposition states.

knowledge_statements.title: Recognizable Graph Properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state recognizability relative to a fixed bounded-width decomposition algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a width bound \(k\), a finite decomposition signature \(\Sigma_k\), and an interpretation \(\operatorname{val}\) mapping every well-formed term to a graph. A graph property \(\mathcal P\) is \(\Sigma_k\)-recognizable if there exists a finite deterministic bottom-up automaton \(\mathcal A\) such that, for every well-formed term \(t\), \[\mathcal A\text{ accepts }t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{val}(t)\in\mathcal P.\] Consequently, acceptance must be invariant under distinct well-formed terms representing the same graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-width graph property is recognizable when one finite tree automaton accepts exactly all decomposition terms representing graphs with that property.
assumptions_latex: The width bound and decomposition signature are fixed.
The automaton is finite and deterministic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is recognizable exactly when acceptance agrees with membership for every well-formed representing term.

notation.meaning: graph represented by decomposition term t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits recognizable graph properties, but the chosen term-based convention, including invariance across all representations of the same graph, requires an inspectable source tied to the decomposition algebra.

children.title: Automaton-to-Dynamic-Programming Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer from decomposition automata to width-based dynamic programs.

knowledge_statements.title: Automaton-to-Dynamic-Programming Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct compilation of a finite decomposition automaton into table dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a well-formed decomposition term \(t\) and a deterministic automaton \(\mathcal A=(Q,(\delta_\sigma),F)\). Traverse \(t\) in postorder. At a leaf labeled \(\sigma\), store \(q_x=\delta_\sigma()\). At an internal node \(x=\sigma(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\), store \(q_x=\delta_\sigma(q_{x_1},\ldots,q_{x_r})\). Output yes exactly when the root state belongs to \(F\). With constant-time transition lookup, the algorithm uses \(O(|t|)\) time and \(O(h)\) working states under depth-first evaluation, where \(h\) is the height of \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluating automaton transitions bottom-up is a dynamic program deciding acceptance in linear time in the decomposition term size.
assumptions_latex: The automaton and ranked signature are fixed.
Transitions support constant-time lookup.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance is decided in \(O(|t|)\) time using \(O(h)\) working states under depth-first evaluation.

notation.meaning: number of nodes in the decomposition term
automaton state stored at term node x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the automaton-to-dynamic-programming transfer leaf, but the O(|t|) time and O(h) working-state bounds depend on fixed arity, traversal storage, input access, and transition lookup conventions that need a specific locator.

children.title: Finite-Recognizability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Property regimes not captured by the selected finite-state representation.

assumptions_latex: A finite graph signature with a fixed boundary size \(k\) is used.
Graph composition identifies equally labeled boundary vertices.
The property \(P\) is invariant under graph isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite recognizability is exactly the finiteness of the stated contextual equivalence; failure of finite index prevents any finite-state decomposition automaton from deciding \(P\).

notation.meaning: Set of finite graphs with boundary labels from \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\).

review_flags: exact finite-congruence formulation needs authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contextual finite-state recognizability for fixed-boundary graph composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(G,H\in\mathcal G_k\), define \(G\equiv_{P,k}H\) precisely when, for every \(F\in\mathcal G_k\), \(P(G\oplus F)\) holds if and only if \(P(H\oplus F)\) holds. A deterministic finite-state bottom-up automaton over a fixed finite decomposition algebra can recognize \(P\) only if \(\equiv_{P,k}\) has finite index on the graphs generated by that algebra. Conversely, when this congruence has finite index and every algebraic operation respects its classes, the equivalence classes form states of a recognizing automaton. Thus infinitely many pairwise context-distinguishable boundaried graphs are a certificate that no such finite-state decomposition algorithm exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph property admits finite-state decomposition processing exactly when fixed-boundary graphs have finitely many context behaviors; infinitely many distinguishable behaviors rule it out.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Recognizability Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the container, but the exact automaton–finite-index correspondence depends on the chosen finite decomposition algebra and requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: A graph \(G\) and a nice path decomposition of width at most \(k\) are supplied.
The target problem has finitely many boundary states for each fixed \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns the exact optimum or decision value in time \(O(n\,s(k)^c)\) and space \(O(s(k))\), where \(c\) bounds transition arity.

notation.meaning: Number of valid states on a bag of size at most \(k+1\).

review_flags: generic finite-state path-decomposition schema needs authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exact dynamic programming on a supplied nice path decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(T_0\) with the unique empty-boundary state and its neutral value. Scan the nice path decomposition from left to right. At an introduce-vertex or introduce-edge step, extend every compatible state and add the local objective contribution; at a forget-vertex step, project each state to the smaller bag and combine equal projections by the problem's optimization operator. Reject incompatible states after every transition. After the final empty bag, output the accepting entry of \(T_m\), or report infeasibility if none exists. If each transition examines at most \(s(k)^c\) state tuples for a constant \(c\), the running time is \(O(n\,s(k)^c)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan a nice path decomposition, updating finite boundary-state tables at introduce and forget steps; the final accepting entry is the exact answer.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but finite boundary states alone do not specify correct transitions, objective aggregation, or the claimed time and space bounds. A source and problem-independent theorem with explicit hypotheses are required.

assumptions_latex: A graph \(G\) and a branch decomposition of width at most \(k\) are supplied.
Partial solutions are equivalent whenever all extensions across the middle set give the same result.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root table gives the exact result, with running time \(O(n\,s(k)^c)\) when each merge examines at most \(s(k)^c\) compatible tuples.

notation.meaning: Maximum number of retained states on a middle set of size at most \(k\).

review_flags: generic branch-decomposition DP schema needs authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up exact dynamic programming on a supplied branch decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Root the branch-decomposition tree by subdividing an edge. For each oriented decomposition edge \(e\), construct a table indexed by equivalence classes of partial solutions inside its edge set, recording their interaction with \(M_e\) and the best objective value in each class. At a leaf, enumerate the states induced by its single graph edge. At an internal node, combine two child states when their assignments agree on shared middle vertices, remove information not exposed through the parent middle set, and retain the optimum representative of every resulting class. At the root, select the best accepting state. If at most \(s(k)\) states occur per table and merge arity is bounded by \(c\), the time is \(O(n\,s(k)^c)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Store partial-solution behavior on each branch-decomposition middle set, merge compatible child tables, and read the exact result at the root.
knowledge_statements.title: Branchwidth Algorithms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but extension equivalence, merge compatibility, and reduction correctness are stated only schematically. The exactness and complexity claims need a branch-decomposition DP theorem with a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: A graph \(G\) is supplied by a clique-width expression using at most \(k\) labels.
The property is specified by a fixed monadic second-order sentence using vertex-set quantification only.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed \(k\) and fixed \(\varphi\), bottom-up evaluation decides whether \(G\models\varphi\) in time linear in the expression size, with a parameter-dependent constant.

notation.meaning: Fixed monadic second-order sentence over vertices and vertex sets.
A supplied clique-width expression evaluating to \(G\).

review_flags: MSO1 clique-width meta-theorem needs authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state evaluation of fixed vertex-set logic on a supplied clique-width expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct the finite set of logical types determined by \(k\) and the quantifier rank of \(\varphi\). Evaluate the parse tree of \(t\) bottom-up: assign the appropriate type to every labeled-vertex leaf, and apply the precomputed type transition for disjoint union, relabeling, or complete edge insertion between two labels. At the root, output true exactly when the resulting type satisfies \(\varphi\). Because the type set and all transition tables depend only on \(k\) and \(\varphi\), each expression node is processed in constant parameter-dependent time; hence the running time is \(O(f(k,\varphi)\,|t|)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and supplied-expression scope fit clique-width algorithms, and the claim resembles the standard MSO1 meta-theorem, but no authoritative citation or locator supports the logical-type construction and linear expression-size bound.

assumptions_latex: A graph \(G=(V,E)\) and a rank decomposition of width at most \(k\) are supplied.
The target problem admits finite representative families across cuts of rank at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bottom-up merging yields the exact answer in \(O(n\,s(k)^c)\) time whenever at most \(s(k)\) representatives are retained per cut.

notation.meaning: Binary rank of the adjacency matrix between \(X\) and \(V\setminus X\).
Maximum number of retained representatives for a cut of rank at most \(k\).
