knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative-state dynamic programming over a supplied rank decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Root the rank decomposition. For each oriented edge inducing \(X\subseteq V\), group partial solutions on \(G[X]\) by their extension behavior through the cut matrix between \(X\) and \(V\setminus X\), whose rank is \(\rho_G(X)\le k\). Retain an optimum representative for each behavior. At an internal node, enumerate compatible pairs of child representatives, combine their objective values and local interactions, then reduce the resulting family to representatives for the parent cut. At the root, output the optimum accepting representative. If reductions preserve all possible extensions and leave at most \(s(k)\) states, while a merge examines at most \(s(k)^c\) pairs or tuples, the algorithm runs in \(O(n\,s(k)^c)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compress partial solutions by their behavior across low-rank cuts, merge representatives along the rank decomposition, and return the exact root optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Width Algorithms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but bounded cut-rank alone does not guarantee finite representative families of the asserted size for an arbitrary problem. A problem class and sourced preservation theorem are needed.

children.title: Cutwidth Algorithms
children.top_down_role: Exact or parameterized algorithms organized around cutwidth.

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\).
All vertex subsets may be represented as bit masks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence computes the minimum cutwidth exactly in \(O(n2^n)\) time and \(O(2^n)\) space.

notation.meaning: Number of edges with exactly one endpoint in \(S\).
Minimum maximum prefix cut among orderings whose first vertex set is \(S\).

review_flags: subset recurrence for exact cutwidth needs authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact subset dynamic programming for minimum cutwidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(D(\varnothing)=0\). For every nonempty \(S\subseteq V\), compute
\[
D(S)=\min_{v\in S}\max\bigl\{D(S\setminus\{v\}),\delta(S)\bigr\}.
\]
Store a minimizing vertex with each entry. Output \(D(V)\), and recover an optimal ordering by repeatedly removing the stored last vertex. The recurrence is valid because an ordering of \(S\) ending in \(v\) has all earlier prefix cuts represented by \(D(S\setminus\{v\})\), while its final prefix cut has size \(\delta(S)\). Evaluating all \(n2^{n-1}\) transitions takes \(O(n2^n)\) time and the table uses \(O(2^n)\) space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset recurrence chooses the last vertex of each prefix and minimizes the largest encountered edge cut, yielding exact cutwidth in exponential time.
knowledge_statements.title: Cutwidth Algorithms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subset recurrence and algorithm role fit exact cutwidth, but the record has no supporting citation and includes proof-style justification, which is prohibited in this knowledge layer.

children.title: Layout-Width Algorithms
children.top_down_role: Algorithms organized around width measures induced by vertex layouts.

assumptions_latex: A finite vertex set \(V\) and a nonnegative prefix-cost function \(w:2^V\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) are given.
The width of an ordering is the maximum cost of its prefixes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence returns an ordering minimizing maximum prefix cost in \(O(n2^n)\) evaluations of \(w\).

notation.meaning: Minimum attainable maximum prefix cost for an ordering of \(S\).

review_flags: generic prefix-cost recurrence needs authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exact algorithm for set-dependent linear-layout width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(D(\varnothing)=0\). For each nonempty \(S\subseteq V\), set
\[
D(S)=\min_{v\in S}\max\bigl\{D(S\setminus\{v\}),w(S)\bigr\}.
\]
For every \(S\), record a vertex attaining the minimum. Return \(D(V)\) and reconstruct an optimal ordering by following these choices backward. This algorithm applies whenever the contribution of a layout position depends only on its prefix set: appending \(v\) to an optimal ordering of \(S\setminus\{v\}\) introduces precisely the additional prefix cost \(w(S)\). There are \(2^n\) states and at most \(n\) transitions per state, so the running time is \(O(n2^n)\), excluding the cost of evaluating \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any width determined solely by prefix sets, subset dynamic programming selects each prefix's last vertex and minimizes the maximum prefix cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Layout-Width Algorithms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic prefix-cost algorithm fits the container, but it lacks a source, contains proof-style justification, and must state the total runtime in terms of the cost of evaluating w rather than only the number of evaluations.

children.title: Linear-Layout Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations of linear vertex orders used by layout-width algorithms.

The chosen dynamic program depends on each prefix only through a finite boundary summary.

review_flags: encoding sufficiency criterion needs authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prefix-cut encoding for finite-state processing of linear layouts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(0\le i\le n\), let \(L_i=\{v_1,[... ELLIPSIZATION ...]\ldots,v_i\}\) and
\[
\partial L_i=\{xy\in E:x\in L_i,\ y\notin L_i\}.
\]
Encode position \(i\) by \(\sigma_i=(i,\lambda_i,\eta_i)\), where \(\lambda_i\) records the active boundary objects needed by the problem and \(\eta_i\) records their finite labels, connectivity data, or objective counters. The encoding is sufficient if any two prefixes with equal \(\sigma_i\) admit exactly the same feasible continuations with equal incremental objective effects. Under this condition, appending \(v_{i+1}\) induces a well-defined transition from \(\sigma_i\) to \(\sigma_{i+1}\), so the ordering is represented by a finite-state path of prefix encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent an ordering by finite summaries of successive prefix cuts; equal summaries must have identical feasible continuations and objective effects.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Layout Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits, but including the unbounded position i in sigma_i prevents the displayed encoding from forming a fixed finite state space as written. The components lambda_i and eta_i are also only informally specified, so a sourced, precise encoding criterion is required.

children.title: Width-Measure Transfer
children.top_down_role: Algorithmic transfer across related cut-based layout measures.

assumptions_latex: Two layout widths \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are defined on the same finite graphs.
Every ordering \(\pi\) satisfies \(\mu(G,\pi)\le f(\nu(G,\pi))\) for a nondecreasing computable function \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any supplied ordering of \(\nu\)-width at most \(k\) is also a valid \(\mu\)-width certificate of value at most \(f(k)\), allowing \(\mu\)-parameterized processing with parameter \(f(k)\).

notation.meaning: Two width values of graph \(G\) under ordering \(\pi\).

review_flags: generic transfer statement needs measure-specific instantiation and source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter transfer induced by a pointwise comparison of linear-layout widths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\pi\) be an ordering of \(V(G)\), and suppose \(\mu(G,\pi)\le f(\nu(G,\pi))\) for every \(G\) and \(\pi\), where \(f\) is nondecreasing and computable. Taking minima over orderings gives
\[
\mu(G)\le f(\nu(G)).
\]
Moreover, if an algorithm for a problem runs in \(T(n,r)\) time when supplied an ordering of \(\mu\)-width at most \(r\), then the same algorithm, supplied an ordering of \(\nu\)-width at most \(k\), runs in \(T(n,f(k))\) time. This transfers an algorithmic guarantee only when the comparison applies to the supplied ordering or an appropriate ordering can also be constructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise bound between two layout widths transfers decomposition certificates and parameterized running times through the comparison function.
knowledge_statements.title: Width-Measure Transfer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits width-measure transfer, and the pointwise inequality supports the stated parameter substitution. However, no cited width measures or authoritative locator establish a substantive transfer result for this container.

assumptions_latex: A width-based dynamic program uses a boundary of size \(k\).
Its table explicitly distinguishes every assignment of \(q\) labels to boundary elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The explicit table has at least \(q^k\) entries before any additional structural information is represented, so polynomial dependence on \(k\) is impossible for this representation when \(q\ge2\).

notation.meaning: Number of distinguishable local labels per boundary element.

review_flags: counting lower bound needs a source tied to width-based DP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary counting boundary for explicit labeled-state tables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The number of functions from a \(k\)-element boundary to a \(q\)-element label set is
\[
q^k.
\]
If two distinct assignments can lead to different feasibility or objective values under some continuation, correctness requires the dynamic program to retain them as distinct states. Consequently its table contains at least \(q^k\) states and requires \(\Omega(q^k)\) time merely to enumerate them in an explicit-state model. If each state additionally stores a relation, partition, ordering, or pairing on the boundary, the state count can grow as \(2^{\Theta(k^2)}\), \(k!\), or a Bell-number factor. Compression can avoid this bound only by identifying assignments that are extension-equivalent or by using an implicit representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicitly labeling every boundary element already creates exponentially many states; relations, orders, or partitions can increase the table much further.
knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Explosion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits state-space explosion, but the lower bound is representation-specific and the additional asymptotic examples require precise hypotheses and authoritative sources.

assumptions_latex: A boundary contains \(k\) distinguishable vertices.
A connectivity dynamic program explicitly stores the partition induced by partial connected components.
Every stored partition is extension-distinguishable in the considered instance family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The table requires at least \(B_k=2^{\Theta(k\log k)}\) connectivity states in the explicit-partition model.

notation.meaning: Number of set partitions of a \(k\)-element set.

review_flags: extension-distinguishable partition premise needs authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bell-number growth of explicit connectivity partitions on a boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A partial solution induces an equivalence relation on the boundary: two boundary vertices are equivalent exactly when they already lie in the same partial connected component. There are exactly \(B_k\) such equivalence relations. If, for each pair of distinct partitions, some continuation accepts one induced connectivity pattern and rejects the other, no correct explicit-state dynamic program may merge their states. It must therefore retain at least
\[
B_k=2^{\Theta(k\log k)}
\]
states in the worst case. Thus connectivity partitions yield superexponential dependence on boundary size, even before auxiliary degree, parity, or objective information is included; reducing this dependence requires representative-set, rank-based, or problem-specific equivalence compression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit boundary connectivity uses one state per set partition, producing Bell-number growth when distinct partitions have distinguishable continuations.
knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity-Partition Explosion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role and Bell-number count fit the container, but the crucial extension-distinguishability premise is instance-family dependent and unsourced. The statement also contains proof-style argumentation.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Discovery Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: End-to-end boundary separating decomposition discovery from conditional dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An algorithm whose input contract includes a width-\(k\) decomposition provides only a conditional running-time guarantee. To solve from the graph alone, prepend a procedure that either returns a decomposition of width at most \(g(k)\) or correctly reports that the promised width bound fails. The resulting time is
\[
T_{\mathrm{dec}}(n,k)+T_{\mathrm{DP}}(n,g(k)).
\]
Hence a fast table computation does not imply a fast end-to-end algorithm when \(T_{\mathrm{dec}}\) dominates, when only a large-width approximation \(g(k)\) is available, or when recognition and construction are not covered by the parameterized guarantee. A supplied decomposition removes this bottleneck but strengthens the input model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic-programming bounds are conditional on obtaining a suitable decomposition; discovery time, approximation loss, or failure to construct one may dominate the full algorithm.
assumptions_latex: An exact solver needs a width decomposition of value bounded by a parameter \(k\).
The downstream dynamic program runs in \(T_{\mathrm{DP}}(n,k)\) time once such a decomposition is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The end-to-end running time is the sum of decomposition discovery and dynamic programming, and failure to obtain the promised decomposition invalidates the downstream guarantee.

notation.meaning: Time to find or certify absence of the required width decomposition.
Time for dynamic programming on the supplied decomposition.

review_flags: decomposition-discovery boundary needs width-specific authoritative sources

children.title: Meta-Theorem Nonuniformity
children.top_down_role: Dependence on property-specific constructions not supplied uniformly.

knowledge_statements.title: Meta-Theorem Nonuniformity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical limitation of fixed-formula width-based meta-theorems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be a class of formulas and suppose that, for every fixed \(\varphi\in\Phi\), some algorithm \(A_\varphi\) decides \(G\models\varphi\) on graphs of width at most \(k\) in time \(f_\varphi(k)|V(G)|^{O(1)}\). This pointwise assertion alone does not yield a uniform synthesis algorithm: it neither supplies a computable map \(\varphi\mapsto A_\varphi\) nor guarantees a computable common bound \(f(k,|\varphi|)\). Consequently, algorithm construction, preprocessing cost, and parameter dependence cannot be inferred from the fixed-formula statement without an additional effective-uniformity theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Existence of an algorithm for every fixed formula does not by itself provide an effective compiler or a uniform computable running-time bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is a specified formula class.
\(A_\varphi\) is asserted only separately for each fixed \(\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{A_\varphi:\varphi\in\Phi\}\) need not determine a computable uniform synthesis procedure.

notation.meaning: algorithm associated with the fixed formula

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and the pointwise-versus-effective-uniform distinction is mathematically coherent. However, no citation or inspectable locator supports the intended uniformity model or the stated consequences, so the record requires an authoritative parameterized model-checking or computability source.

children.title: Hidden Constant Growth
children.top_down_role: Large implicit constants arising in meta-theorem algorithm bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Constant Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative limitation of asymptotic meta-theorem bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A running-time guarantee of the form \(T(G,\varphi,k)\leq f(k,|\varphi|)|V(G)|^c\), with unspecified computable \(f\) and constant \(c\), controls polynomial growth only in the graph size. It gives no numerical upper bound on preprocessing, state-space size, or the multiplicative constant for fixed \(k\) and \(\varphi\). Thus two implementations satisfying the same asymptotic meta-theorem may differ by arbitrarily large parameter-dependent factors, and fixed-parameter tractability alone does not imply practical efficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unspecified parameter function can hide enormous preprocessing and state-space costs even when dependence on graph size is polynomial.
assumptions_latex: \(T(G,\varphi,k)\leq f(k,|\varphi|)|V(G)|^c\).
\(f\) is not accompanied by an explicit numerical bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed bound does not imply a practical bound uniform in \(k\) and \(|\varphi|\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and statement match the hidden-constant boundary. The asymptotic observation is plausible, but the record supplies no source for the quantitative interpretation or practical-efficiency conclusion; the local inventory contains no relevant parameterized-algorithms locator.

children.title: Formula-Size Dependence
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of algorithmic constants to the size of the logical specification.

knowledge_statements.title: Formula-Size Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formula size is part of the parameter in uniform logical model checking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a uniform width-based model-checking algorithm, the appropriate bound has the form \(T(G,\varphi,k)\leq f(k,|\varphi|)|V(G)|^c\), where the exponent \(c\) is independent of \(G\), \(k\), and \(\varphi\). Fixing \(\varphi\) permits the factor depending on \(|\varphi|\) to be absorbed into a constant, but allowing formulas as input restores that dependence. Therefore a fixed-formula linear-time assertion does not imply a bound of the form \(g(k)|V(G)|^c\) for formulas of unbounded size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the formula is input, its length must enter the parameter dependence; fixed-formula bounds cannot hide it uniformly.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has width at most \(k\).
\(\varphi\) is supplied as part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform model checking requires a bound depending on both \(k\) and \(|\varphi|\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role is appropriate, and the distinction between fixed-formula and uniform formula-input bounds is precise. No relevant citation or locator is supplied, however, so the claimed uniform dependence on formula length remains unsupported.

children.title: Practical Applicability Limits
children.top_down_role: Implementation regimes where abstract tractability does not yield usable performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Practical Applicability Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational boundary of width-based logical meta-theorems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a meta-theorem guarantees time \(f(k,|\varphi|)|V(G)|^c\) for model checking on graphs of width at most \(k\). This guarantee alone does not ensure applicability when a width decomposition is unavailable, when computing one is costly, or when the generated dynamic program has more states than available resources permit. Practical use therefore additionally requires an obtainable decomposition, an explicit and moderate parameter function, and a formula representation whose compilation cost is controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The meta-theorem is operationally useful only when decompositions, compilation, and parameter-dependent state spaces are also manageable.
assumptions_latex: \(T(G,\varphi,k)\leq f(k,|\varphi|)|V(G)|^c\) is only an asymptotic guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-parameter tractability does not alone imply feasible implementation on the intended instances.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the exact leaf. The listed operational requirements are reasonable but depend on the decomposition model, compiler, and implementation regime; no source identifies the intended framework or supports these criteria.

children.title: Sparse-Graph Structural Decomposition Methods
children.top_down_role: Structural FPT methods based on cuts, separators, recursive decomposition, graph minors, sparsity, and irrelevant objects; separated from routine tree-decomposition dynamic programming.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Local treewidth and structural graph techniques

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Designing FPT Algorithms for Cut Problems Using Randomized Contractions
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Designing FPT Algorithms for Cut Problems Using Randomized Contractions

knowledge_statements.title: Important Separators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard directed vertex-separator definition and domination order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a directed graph and let \(X,Y\subseteq V(G)\) be disjoint. An \(X\)-to-\(Y\) separator is a set \(S\subseteq V(G)\setminus(X\cup Y)\) such that \(G-S\) has no directed path from \(X\) to \(Y\). Write \(R_X(S)\) for the vertices reachable from \(X\) in \(G-S\). A separator \(S\) is important if it is inclusion-minimal and there is no \(X\)-to-\(Y\) separator \(S'\) satisfying \(|S'|\leq |S|\) and \(R_X(S)\subsetneq R_X(S')\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An important separator is minimal and is not dominated by an equally small separator that leaves more vertices reachable from the source side.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite directed graph.
\(X,Y\subseteq V(G)\) are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is important exactly when it is minimal and undominated under reachability expansion without size increase.

notation.meaning: vertices reachable from the source set after deleting the separator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent and the definition kind fits the leaf. Separator conventions differ concerning terminal deletion and directed reachability, and no authoritative source with a definition-level locator is supplied to confirm this exact convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Shadow Removal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic shadow-removal reduction for directed separation problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a directed graph \(G\), terminals \(X,Y\), and a separator budget \(k\), define the shadow of an \(X\)-to-\(Y\) separator \(S\) as the vertices unreachable from \(X\) in \(G-S\), together with vertices from which \(Y\) is unreachable in \(G-S\). A shadow-removal procedure constructs candidate sets \(Z\subseteq V(G)\setminus(X\cup Y)\). Its correctness condition is that every feasible separator \(S\) of size at most \(k\) is represented by some candidate with \(S\cap Z=\varnothing\) and with the relevant shadow contained in \(Z\). Deleting \(Z\) then reduces that candidate to a shadowless separator instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Guess a set containing a solution's shadow but avoiding the separator, delete it, and solve the resulting shadowless instance.
assumptions_latex: Candidate generation satisfies the stated coverage condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At least one generated instance preserves each feasible separator while removing its relevant shadow.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An algorithmic reduction is suitable for this leaf, but shadow definitions and coverage guarantees are problem-specific. The record gives no source establishing that the union of the stated forward and reverse shadows, candidate coverage condition, and deletion step form a valid shadow-removal algorithm in the intended framework.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Contractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-preserving contraction scheme underlying randomized decomposition methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a multigraph with terminals that must remain distinct, and let \(F\subseteq E(G)\) be an unknown target cut with \(|F|\leq k\). Independently mark every eligible edge protected with probability \(p\), never contracting terminal-forbidden edges, and contract every unprotected eligible edge. Output the resulting quotient instance. The target cut survives whenever every edge of \(F\) is protected; this event has probability at least \(p^k\) when \(0<p\leq1\). Conditional on survival, contraction preserves the two sides of \(F\) and may compress irrelevant connected regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomly protect candidate cut edges and contract the others; a cut of size at most k survives with probability at least p to the k.
assumptions_latex: Edges whose contraction would identify forbidden terminals are ineligible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[F\text{ survives}]\geq p^k\), and survival preserves the cut in the quotient graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary cut-survival calculation is coherent, and algorithm is an appropriate kind. Nevertheless, the generic independent edge-protection scheme may not represent the named randomized-contractions framework, and no source or locator supports the contraction rules or preservation claim in that framework.

assumptions_latex: \(|A\cap B|\) is bounded by a function of \(k\).
Replacement equivalence is preserved under compatible gluing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recursive replacement preserves the original decision value, including any specified parameter shift.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-equivalence recursion for separator-based parameterized algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph instance \(G\) with parameter \(k\), find a separation \((A,B)\) whose boundary \(D=A\cap B\) has size bounded by a function of \(k\). Recursively solve or classify the boundaried subinstance \(G[A]\) with boundary \(D\) under every admissible interaction on \(D\), and replace it by a smaller representative having the same interaction table. Repeat until no reducible separation remains, solve the resulting highly connected core, and combine the stored boundary tables. Correctness requires replacement equivalence: gluing either boundaried graph to any compatible context must preserve the answer, with any recorded parameter shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursively summarize one side of a small separation by an equivalent boundaried representative, then solve and recombine the reduced core.
knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Understanding
Minor-Bidimensional Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-based definition of minor bidimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) be a nonnegative graph parameter. It is minor-bidimensional if two conditions hold: whenever \(H\) is a minor of \(G\), one has \(p(H)\leq p(G)\); and there is a constant \(c>0\) such that, for every sufficiently large \(r\), the \(r\)-by-\(r\) grid \(Q_r\) satisfies \(p(Q_r)\geq c r^2\). A parameterized problem with threshold question \(p(G)\leq k\) or \(p(G)\geq k\), as appropriate, is called minor-bidimensional when its underlying parameter has these properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter is minor-bidimensional when minors cannot increase it and its value grows quadratically on square grids.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a nonnegative parameter on finite graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is minor-monotone and \(p(Q_r)=\Omega(r^2)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, and the two stated conditions match the usual shape of minor bidimensionality. No definition-level source is supplied to confirm the exact grid-growth and threshold-problem convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Contraction-Bidimensional Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-based definition using contractions and grid-like witness graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a graph class \(\mathcal C\) and a designated family of grid-like graphs \((\Gamma_r)_{r\geq1}\subseteq\mathcal C\). A nonnegative graph parameter \(p\) is contraction-bidimensional on \(\mathcal C\) if \(p(H)\leq p(G)\) whenever \(H\) is obtained from \(G\in\mathcal C\) by edge contractions, and if there exists \(c>0\) such that \(p(\Gamma_r)\geq c r^2\) for every sufficiently large \(r\). The witness family is chosen to remain appropriate for the class, commonly using triangulated grids rather than ordinary grids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contraction-bidimensional parameter cannot increase under edge contraction and grows quadratically on an appropriate grid-like family.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a fixed graph class.
\((\Gamma_r)_{r\geq1}\) is the designated witness family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is contraction-monotone and \(p(\Gamma_r)=\Omega(r^2)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role is appropriate, but contraction bidimensionality requires a precisely specified class and witness family. Treating an arbitrary designated grid-like family as sufficient may be broader than standard definitions, and no source fixes the intended triangulated-grid convention.

assumptions_latex: \(G\in\mathcal C\), and every yes-instance satisfies \(\operatorname{tw}(G)=O(\sqrt{k})\).
Width-\(w\) instances are solvable in time \(2^{O(w)}|V(G)|^{O(1)}\).
A width decomposition with \(w=O(\operatorname{tw}(G))\), or a valid rejection certificate, can be obtained within the claimed running time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is solvable in \(2^{O(\sqrt{k})}|V(G)|^{O(1)}\) time.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard treewidth route to square-root parameter dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a fixed proper minor-closed graph class, and let \(p\) be a bidimensional parameter for which every yes-instance \((G,k)\) satisfies \(\operatorname{tw}(G)=O(\sqrt{k})\). If a width decomposition of width \(w=O(\operatorname{tw}(G))\) can be found within the claimed bound and the problem is solvable on that decomposition in time \(2^{O(w)}|V(G)|^{O(1)}\), then substituting \(w=O(\sqrt{k})\) yields running time \(2^{O(\sqrt{k})}|V(G)|^{O(1)}\). Rejection may occur earlier when the structural test certifies that the treewidth exceeds the yes-instance bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square-root treewidth bound plus single-exponential treewidth dynamic programming yields a subexponential parameterized algorithm.
knowledge_statements.title: Subexponential Bidimensional Algorithms
Bidimensional Kernelization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional linear-kernel interface via protrusion decomposition and replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be a parameterized problem on a fixed sparse graph class. Suppose every yes-instance \((G,k)\) admits, in polynomial time, a decomposition into a core of \(O(k)\) vertices and protrusions whose boundaries and treewidth are bounded by constants, with total boundary incidence \(O(k)\). Suppose further that \(\Pi\) has finitely many equivalence classes of constant-boundary protrusions under gluing, and that equivalent protrusions can be replaced while preserving the answer with a computable parameter shift. Replacing every oversized protrusion by a constant-size representative produces an equivalent instance \((G',k')\) with \(|V(G')|=O(k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bidimensional structure supplies few bounded-width protrusions; finite-state replacement of large protrusions then gives a linear-vertex kernel.
assumptions_latex: A polynomial-time \(O(k)\)-size protrusion decomposition exists.
Constant-boundary protrusions have finite replaceable equivalence classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a polynomial-time equivalent reduction with \(|V(G')|=O(k)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conclusion is a linear kernel-size bound, so complexity_bound is defensible for this interface leaf, although the statement also has a conditional-theorem role. The protrusion decomposition, finite-equivalence, replacement, and parameter-shift assumptions are highly problem-specific and have no supporting source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Local Treewidth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard radius-ball definition for a graph class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a graph \(G\), vertex \(v\), and integer \(r\ge 0\), let \(N_r^G[v]\) contain the vertices at distance at most \(r\) from \(v\). A graph class \(\mathcal C\) has bounded local treewidth if there exists a function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that
\[
\operatorname{tw}\bigl(G[N_r^G[v]]\bigr)\le f(r)
\]
for every \(G\in\mathcal C\), every \(v\in V(G)\), and every \(r\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A class has bounded local treewidth when every radius-r neighborhood has treewidth bounded solely as a function of r.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{tw}(G[N_r^G[v]])\le f(r)\).

notation.meaning: Closed radius-r neighborhood of v in G.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf and are mathematically standard, but the record supplies no citation or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Layered Treewidth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition using a layering and a compatible tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A layering of \(G\) is an ordered partition \((L_0,\ldots,L_m)\) of \(V(G)\) such that every edge has endpoints in the same layer or in consecutive layers. The layered treewidth of \(G\) is the least integer \(k\) for which some layering and some tree decomposition \((T,\{B_x\}_{x\in V(T)})\) satisfy
\[
|B_x\cap L_i|\le k
\]
for every decomposition node \(x\) and every layer index \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Layered treewidth bounds how many vertices from any one layer may occur in any bag of a suitable tree decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ltw}(G)=\min_{(L_i),(T,B)}\max_{x,i}|B_x\cap L_i|\).

notation.meaning: Bag at node x of a tree decomposition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is consistent with the standard notion of layered treewidth and fits the container, but no supporting source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Expansion Graph Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition through densities of shallow minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An \(r\)-shallow minor of \(G\) is obtained from a subgraph of \(G\) by contracting pairwise vertex-disjoint connected subgraphs of radius at most \(r\). Define
\[
\nabla_r(G)=\max_H\frac{|E(H)|}{|V(H)|},
\]
where the maximum ranges over nonempty \(r\)-shallow minors \(H\) of \(G\). A graph class \(\mathcal C\) has bounded expansion if a function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R_{ge0}\) exists such that \(\nabla_r(G)\le f(r)\) for every \(r\ge0\) and \(G\in\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A class has bounded expansion when the density of every fixed-depth shallow minor is uniformly bounded throughout the class.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall r\ge0\;\sup_{G\in\mathcal C}\nabla_r(G)<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Maximum edge-to-vertex ratio among nonempty r-shallow minors of G.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A source is required to fix the shallow-minor radius convention. Also, \(\mathbb R_{ge0}\) is malformed notation and should be \(\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nowhere-Dense Graph Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by exclusion of depth-bounded clique minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph class \(\mathcal C\) is nowhere dense if, for every integer \(r\ge0\), there exists an integer \(N(r)\) such that the complete graph \(K_{N(r)}\) is not an \(r\)-shallow minor of any graph \(G\in\mathcal C\). Equivalently, at each fixed depth \(r\), the orders of complete \(r\)-shallow minors occurring in members of \(\mathcal C\) are uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A class is nowhere dense when, at every fixed shallow-minor depth, sufficiently large cliques are excluded uniformly.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a class of finite simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall r\ge0\;\exists N(r)\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:\ K_{N(r)}\not\preccurlyeq_r G\).

notation.meaning: H is an r-shallow minor of G.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shallow-clique-minor definition is standard and appropriate for this leaf, but it has no citation or locator supporting the selected convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Irrelevant-Vertex Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-problem form of iterative irrelevant-vertex reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Pi\) be a parameterized graph decision problem. A vertex \(v\in V(G)\) is irrelevant for an instance \((G,k)\) when
\[
(G,k)\in\Pi\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(G-v,k)\in\Pi.
\]
The irrelevant-vertex method repeatedly either decides the current instance or finds and deletes such a vertex. If this process reaches a graph in a tractable base class and every reported vertex satisfies the displayed equivalence, solving the final reduced instance returns the answer for the original instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete vertices whose removal preserves the answer until the remaining instance belongs to a directly solvable base class.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is invariant under graph isomorphism.
Every deletion step supplies a valid irrelevance guarantee for the current instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((G_0,k)\in\Pi\Longleftrightarrow(G_s,k)\in\Pi\).

notation.meaning: Graph obtained by deleting v and its incident edges.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and answer-preserving deletion principle fit the leaf, but the generic method and its tractable-base termination conditions require authoritative support.

children.title: Wall Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Wall structures used to expose large, regular graph regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Wall Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundaried representation of a wall for decomposition algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A wall interface is a tuple \((W,\beta,A)\), where \(W\) is a subdivision of an elementary wall, \(\beta=(b_1,\ldots,b_t)\) is an ordered list of distinct perimeter vertices, and \(A\subseteq V(W)\) is an optional set of attachment vertices. In an ambient graph \(G\), the interface represents an occurrence of \(W\subseteq G\) whose interaction with \(G-V(W)\) is confined to \(\{b_1,\ldots,b_t\}\cup A\). The ordering records the perimeter incidence needed for gluing or replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A wall interface records a wall, its ordered perimeter boundary, and all vertices through which the surrounding graph may attach.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) is a finite wall subdivision contained in an ambient graph \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_G(V(W))\setminus V(W)\subseteq N_G(\{b_1,\ldots,b_t\}\cup A)\).

notation.meaning: Ordered boundary vertices on the wall perimeter.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed wall-interface tuple is not a standard source-independent convention. Moreover, the conclusion does not correctly express that external attachments occur only through the designated vertices, so a source-backed formulation is needed.

children.title: Grid-Minor Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Grid-minor structures used in irrelevant-object arguments.

knowledge_statements.title: Grid-Minor Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit branch-set representation of a grid minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(q\)-grid-minor interface in \(G\) consists of pairwise vertex-disjoint connected branch sets \(\{X_{i,j}:1\le i,j\le q\}\) and, for every horizontally or vertically adjacent pair of grid indices, a chosen edge of \(G\) joining the corresponding branch sets. Contracting every \(X_{i,j}\) and deleting all unchosen vertices and edges yields the \(q\times q\) grid. Designated boundary branch sets may additionally be ordered to expose the minor to gluing operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A grid-minor interface explicitly lists disjoint connected branch sets and adjacency edges realizing a square grid minor.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph.
The branch sets are nonempty, connected, and pairwise disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_q\preccurlyeq G\).

notation.meaning: The q by q square grid graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The branch-set representation is broadly standard, but the interface convention and instruction to delete all unchosen edges are underspecified; internal edges needed to keep branch sets connected are not addressed.

children.title: Wall-to-Grid Transfer
children.top_down_role: Structural transfer between wall witnesses and grid-minor witnesses.

knowledge_statements.title: Wall-to-Grid Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative linear-order transfer from walls to grid minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a universal constant \(c>0\) such that every wall of order \(h\) contains the square grid \(Q_{\lfloor ch\rfloor}\) as a minor. Moreover, when the wall is supplied by its subdivision paths and incidence structure, branch sets for this grid minor can be obtained by selecting suitable horizontal and vertical wall paths and contracting connected path segments. Thus a sufficiently large explicit wall supplies an explicit grid-minor interface of linearly related order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit wall of order h contains, and can constructively expose, a square grid minor whose order is linear in h.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a positive integer.
The wall model is explicitly represented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\lfloor ch\rfloor}\preccurlyeq W\).

notation.meaning: The q by q square grid.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative linear wall-to-grid relation is plausible, but the constant depends on the wall convention and the constructive extraction claim needs a specific theorem or algorithmic locator.

children.title: Extraction Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Algorithmic limits in locating or certifying the required large structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Extraction Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unavoidable output-size cost for explicit grid-minor extraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an extraction algorithm must output an explicit model of a \(q\times q\) grid minor by listing its nonempty branch sets. Because these \(q^2\) branch sets are pairwise disjoint and each requires at least one output identifier, every such algorithm has output size \(\Omega(q^2)\) and therefore running time \(\Omega(q^2)\) in any sequential model charging constant time per emitted identifier. An existential grid-minor guarantee alone consequently does not furnish a subquadratic explicit extraction routine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicitly outputting a q-by-q grid-minor model already requires quadratic output size and hence quadratic sequential time.
assumptions_latex: The output lists every branch set explicitly.
Emitting one vertex or branch-set identifier costs constant time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{extract}}(q)=\Omega(q^2)\).

notation.meaning: Side length of the requested grid minor.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic output lower bound follows only under the stated explicit encoding and sequential cost model. Those conventions and the resulting complexity claim require a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Irrelevant Regions
children.top_down_role: Graph regions whose detailed contents may be discarded for the target problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Irrelevant Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance-relative deletion form of region irrelevance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((G,k)\) be an instance of a parameterized graph decision problem \(\Pi\), and let \(R\subseteq V(G)\) have boundary \(B=N_G(R\setminus B)\setminus(R\setminus B)\) contained in \(R\). The region \((R,B)\) is irrelevant for \((G,k)\) if deleting its interior preserves the decision:
\[
(G,k)\in\Pi\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(G-(R\setminus B),k)\in\Pi.
\]
The boundary is retained so that all incidences between the removed interior and the remainder are represented at the interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A region is irrelevant when deleting its interior while retaining its boundary leaves the instance’s answer unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq V(G)\) and \(B\subseteq R\).
Every neighbor of \(R\setminus B\) outside its interior lies in \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((G,k)\in\Pi\Longleftrightarrow(G-(R\setminus B),k)\in\Pi\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed equation defining \(B\) is circular because \(B\) occurs on both sides and may also include vertices outside \(R\), conflicting with \(B\subseteq R\). A source-backed region and boundary convention is required.

children.title: Local Replacement
children.top_down_role: Substitution of a bounded region by an equivalent local representative.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Replacement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replacement principle for equivalent boundaried regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) be \(t\)-boundaried graphs with equally labeled boundaries, and let \(H\) be any compatible context. If \(R_1\equiv_{\Pi,t}R_2\), then gluing either region into \(H\) preserves membership in the decision problem \(\Pi\):
\[
(H\oplus R_1,k)\in\Pi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(H\oplus R_2,k)\in\Pi.
\]
Consequently, a region may be replaced locally by a smaller equivalent representative without changing the answer, provided gluing introduces no identifications except equally labeled boundary vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any boundaried region may be replaced by an equivalent representative because every compatible surrounding context receives the same answer.
assumptions_latex: Boundary labels are injective and compatible.
\(R_1\equiv_{\Pi,t}R_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((H\oplus R_1,k)\in\Pi\Longleftrightarrow(H\oplus R_2,k)\in\Pi\).

notation.meaning: Graph obtained by identifying equally labeled boundary vertices.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The replacement principle follows from the stated unshifted context equivalence, but the domain of \(k\) and the choice between shifted and unshifted equivalence are not specified or sourced.

children.title: Region Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Equivalence notions supporting safe replacement of local regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Region Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Context equivalence for equally labeled boundaried graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a parameterized graph decision problem \(\Pi\) and an integer \(t\ge0\). For two \(t\)-boundaried graphs \(R_1,R_2\) with the same boundary-label set, define
\[
R_1\equiv_{\Pi,t}R_2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall H\;\forall k:\ (H\oplus R_1,k)\in\Pi\iff(H\oplus R_2,k)\in\Pi,
\]
where \(H\) ranges over all compatible \(t\)-boundaried graphs. This relation is an equivalence relation, and each equivalence class consists precisely of regions interchangeable in every compatible context without changing the parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two equally boundaried regions are equivalent when gluing either into every compatible context yields the same answer for every parameter value.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is a parameterized graph decision problem.
\(R_1\) and \(R_2\) have the same injective boundary labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\equiv_{\Pi,t}R_2\).

notation.meaning: Context equivalence relative to problem Pi.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but \(k\) lacks an explicit domain and the unshifted equivalence convention differs from common parameter-shift formulations. An authoritative source and locator are needed.

children.title: Replacement-Safety Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Contexts where external interactions prevent a safe local substitution.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a boundaried graph with ordered boundary \(B\).
\(R_1\) and \(R_2\) have the same boundary type, and gluing identifies equally labeled boundary vertices.
The optimization problem \(\Pi\) has an additive objective under gluing, up to a region-dependent offset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\) may safely replace \(R_2\) in every compatible context if and only if a constant \(\Delta\in\mathbb{R}\) exists such that \(\operatorname{OPT}_\Pi(H\oplus R_1)=\operatorname{OPT}_\Pi(H\oplus R_2)+\Delta\) for every compatible boundaried context \(H\). Replacement safety fails when no context-independent \(\Delta\) exists; equivalently, there are compatible contexts \(H_1,H_2\) for which the two optimum differences are unequal, including cases where exactly one glued instance is feasible.

notation.meaning: Gluing operation identifying equally labeled boundary vertices.
Optimal objective value, extended by \(+\infty\) for infeasible minimization instances.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contextual equivalence boundary for additive optimization on boundaried graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) be boundaried graphs having the same ordered boundary \(B\), and let \(\Pi\) be an additive minimization problem. Define replacement equivalence by
\[
R_1\equiv_\Pi R_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists\Delta\in\mathbb{R}\ \forall H:\ \operatorname{OPT}_\Pi(H\oplus R_1)=\operatorname{OPT}_\Pi(H\oplus R_2)+\Delta,
\]
where \(H\) ranges over all compatible boundaried contexts and infeasibility has value \(+\infty\). Thus replacement is unsafe precisely if no single offset works for every context; a witness is a pair \(H_1,H_2\) producing distinct finite differences, or one context for which only one gluing is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A region replacement is universally safe exactly when every compatible context preserves feasibility and changes the optimum by one fixed offset; any context-dependent offset or feasibility mismatch witnesses failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Replacement-Safety Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the terminal container, and the contextual-offset formulation is coherent for additive minimization with extended infeasibility values. However, no citation is supplied for the claimed equivalence or its applicability to boundaried-graph replacement, so the problem-specific hypotheses cannot be validated.

assumptions_latex: The method attempts to obtain bounded-width pieces solely from membership in a sparse hereditary graph class.
The input family contains complete graphs of unbounded order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No constant \(w\) can bound the treewidth of all inputs, because \(\operatorname{tw}(K_n)=n-1\). Consequently, a sparse-class decomposition theorem requiring exclusion of a fixed minor cannot be applied uniformly to arbitrary dense graphs without an additional parameter, deletion set, or dense-graph decomposition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of sparse-graph bounded-width reasoning on unrestricted dense inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(n\ge 1\), the complete graph \(K_n\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{tw}(K_n)=n-1
\]
and contains every graph on at most \(n\) vertices as a minor. Hence the family \(\{K_n:n\ge 1\}\) excludes no fixed finite graph as a minor and has unbounded treewidth. Therefore an algorithmic synthesis rule whose structural step assumes a fixed excluded minor, bounded local treewidth, or a constant-width decomposition cannot extend uniformly to unrestricted dense graphs merely by retaining the same parameter; an additional structural restriction or parameter is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete graphs have unbounded treewidth and exclude no fixed minor, so sparse-graph decomposition guarantees do not automatically extend to unrestricted dense inputs.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the container, and the complete-graph obstruction is mathematically standard. No source with a specific locator is cited for the treewidth and minor claims or for the scope of the structural consequences.

assumptions_latex: A directed problem distinguishes arc orientation.
The proposed structural method applies an undirected decomposition only to the underlying graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any replacement or state abstraction based solely on \(U(D)\) is incomplete for orientation-sensitive problems: oppositely oriented digraphs can share \(U(D)\) but have different feasibility. Directed reachability therefore requires orientation-aware interfaces or a genuinely directed width/decomposition theory.

notation.meaning: Underlying undirected graph obtained by forgetting arc directions.
Directed path from s to t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orientation loss as a boundary of undirected structural decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_1\) have vertices \(\{s,v,t\}\) and arcs \(\{(s,v),(v,t)\}\), and let \(D_2\) have the same vertices and arcs \(\{(v,s),(t,v)\}\). Then
\[
U(D_1)=U(D_2)=s-v-t,
\]
but \(s\leadsto_{D_1}t\) while \(s\not\leadsto_{D_2}t\). Thus the underlying undirected graph, its separators, and its undirected width parameters do not determine even directed reachability. Any structural reduction for an orientation-sensitive problem that records only undirected interface data can therefore identify inequivalent directed regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two digraphs can have the same underlying undirected graph but opposite reachability behavior, so undirected decompositions alone cannot support orientation-sensitive replacement or dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed-Structure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role fits the terminal container, and the two explicitly defined digraphs establish that the underlying undirected graph does not determine directed reachability. A source is still required for the broader methodological claim about orientation-aware interfaces or directed decomposition theory.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a fixed pattern graph.
A structural algorithm requires an explicit \(H\)-minor model rather than only deciding that one exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction step must output pairwise disjoint connected branch sets and verify every pattern edge between them. Existence-only structural theorems do not by themselves supply this certificate or its running-time bound.

notation.meaning: Branch set representing vertex v of H.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit certificate required when a decomposition uses a minor model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An explicit \(H\)-minor model in a graph \(G\) is a family \((X_v)_{v\in V(H)}\) of nonempty, pairwise disjoint vertex sets such that each induced subgraph \(G[X_v]\) is connected and
\[
\forall uv\in E(H)\ \exists xy\in E(G):\ x\in X_u\ \land\ y\in X_v.
\]
This family is directly verifiable in polynomial time. A theorem asserting only that \(H\) occurs as a minor does not complete an algorithmic decomposition that needs the branch sets: synthesis additionally requires a constructive procedure with a stated running time for producing either this model or the alternative structural outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A usable minor model must explicitly provide disjoint connected branch sets with the required adjacencies; an existence theorem alone leaves a construction and runtime bottleneck.
knowledge_statements.title: Minor-Model Construction Bottlenecks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role is appropriate, and the branch-set conditions correctly describe an explicit minor model. The direct polynomial-time verifiability claim and the asserted constructive bottleneck have no cited source or inspectable complexity locator.

children.title: Exact Exponential Algorithms
children.top_down_role: Worst-case exact methods indexed primarily by total input size, including exponential-space, polynomial-space, and subexponential structural designs.

assumptions_latex: Each recursive instance is a graph problem instance \(I\).
Reductions preserve the answer, and every branching family is exhaustive.
A nonnegative integer measure \(\mu\) strictly decreases in every child.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns the exact answer. If every branch has decreases \(d_1,\ldots,d_r\), its search-tree size satisfies \(T(m)\le\sum_{i=1}^rT(m-d_i)+m^{O(1)}\), and is \(O^*(\rho^m)\) when \(\rho\ge1\) is the positive root of \(1=\sum_i\rho^{-d_i}\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative progress measure of an instance.
Worst-case running time at measure m.
Branching factor determined by the branching vector.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exact branching scheme specialized to graph instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On a graph instance \(I\), first apply sound polynomial-time reductions to a fixed point. If the reduced instance is terminal, solve it directly. Otherwise select a graph configuration and construct exhaustive children \(I_1,\ldots,I_r\), meaning that an optimal solution of \(I\) is represented in at least one child and child solutions lift correctly. Recursively solve every child and combine their values by the problem's exact optimum operator. For a measure \(\mu\), if \(\mu(I_i)\le\mu(I)-d_i\) with \(d_i>0\), then
\[
T(m)\le \sum_{i=1}^rT(m-d_i)+m^{O(1)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduce the graph, branch exhaustively on a local configuration, solve every smaller child, and combine exactly; the branching vector determines the exponential running time.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Branching Algorithms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the graph-branching container. The exactness conditions and recurrence are plausible, but no authoritative source is supplied for the branching-vector analysis, including the characteristic-root bound stated outside the main statement.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a finite universe and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) is a finite family of available sets.
The task is to decide whether a cover using at most \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) sets exists.
All preprocessing rules preserve feasibility within the residual budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recursion returns a cover of size at most \(k\) exactly when one exists. If the selected element belongs to at most \(r\) available sets, the recursion has at most \(r\) children at that node, and every child decreases the residual budget by one. A minimum-cardinality cover can be obtained by finding the least feasible budget \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact element-centered branching for bounded-frequency set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a residual set-cover instance \((U,\mathcal F,k)\), apply sound reductions. If \(U=\varnothing\), return the empty residual cover; if \(k=0\) and \(U\ne\varnothing\), reject. Otherwise choose \(u\in U\) and create one child for every \(S\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \(u\in S\). In that child, select \(S\), replace \(U\) by \(U\setminus S\), and replace \(k\) by \(k-1\). Accept and lift a cover exactly when at least one child accepts. Every cover of \(U\) contains a set incident with \(u\), so the branches are exhaustive. If \(u\) belongs to at most \(r\) available sets, the node has at most \(r\) children.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an uncovered element and branch over every available set containing it. This decides whether a cover within the residual budget exists; bounded element frequency bounds the branching factor, and the least feasible budget gives a minimum cover.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-System Branching Algorithms

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a propositional CNF formula.
Assignments are simplified by deleting satisfied clauses and falsified literals.
Both truth values are explored for every branching variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure decides satisfiability exactly. Without additional reductions, branching on one variable yields \(T(n)\le2T(n-1)+|F|^{O(1)}=O^*(2^n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic exhaustive DPLL-style branching for CNF satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a CNF formula \(F\), repeatedly apply sound simplifications, including unit propagation. Return satisfiable if no clause remains, and return unsatisfiable if an empty clause occurs. Otherwise choose an unassigned variable \(x\) and recursively evaluate
\[
F[x\leftarrow0]\quad\text{and}\quad F[x\leftarrow1].
\]
Return satisfiable exactly when at least one child is satisfiable, retaining that child's assignment as a witness. The two branches partition all total assignments according to the value of \(x\); hence the procedure is exact. With \(n\) unassigned variables and no stronger measure decrease, \(T(n)\le2T(n-1)+|F|^{O(1)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simplify a CNF formula, branch on both values of an unassigned variable, and accept if either child accepts; exhaustive assignment partitioning gives exactness.
knowledge_statements.title: Satisfiability Branching Algorithms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, the two branches exhaust all assignments, and the stated basic recurrence is consistent with branching on one unassigned variable. No authoritative source with a specific locator is provided for the DPLL-style procedure or complexity bound.

children.title: Exact Branching
children.top_down_role: Exact exponential algorithms driven by exhaustive branching choices.

assumptions_latex: Each recursive instance \(I\) has a finite feasible-solution set \(\mathcal S(I)\).
Every branching family covers all feasible solutions through objective-preserving lifting maps.
A well-founded measure \(\mu\) strictly decreases in every child.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recursive optimization over all children returns \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), and termination follows from strict decrease of the well-founded measure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract correctness condition for exact recursive branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An exact branching rule for an optimization instance \(I\) constructs children \(I_1,\ldots,I_r\) and lifting maps \(L_j:\mathcal S(I_j)\to\mathcal S(I)\) such that
\[
\mathcal S(I)=\bigcup_{j=1}^r L_j\bigl(\mathcal S(I_j)\bigr),
\]
and each lift preserves the objective value, including any explicitly recorded offset. The algorithm solves every child and takes the best lifted solution. If \(\mu(I_j)<\mu(I)\) for every child under a well-founded measure \(\mu\), recursion terminates; the covering equality then implies that the returned value equals \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact branching covers all feasible solutions with objective-preserving child instances; solving every smaller child and taking the best lifted result preserves the optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Branching

children.title: Instance Reduction
children.top_down_role: Sound simplification of exact-algorithm instances before or between branches.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is an optimization or decision instance.
A polynomial-time reduction produces \(I'\) and polynomial-time solution-translation data.
For optimization, the translation preserves feasibility and objective values up to a recorded constant \(c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(I\) by \(I'\) is exact, and an optimum solution or decision witness for \(I\) can be recovered from corresponding data for \(I'\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness condition for preprocessing inside a branching algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimization problem, a reduction from \(I\) to \(I'\) is exact if it is computable in polynomial time, records a constant \(c\), satisfies
\[
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I')+c,
\]
and provides a polynomial-time map that lifts an optimum solution \(S'\in\mathcal S(I')\) to a feasible solution of \(I\) having objective value \(\operatorname{val}(S')+c\). For a decision problem, the corresponding requirements are that \(I\) is a yes-instance if and only if \(I'\) is a yes-instance and that required witnesses can be translated in polynomial time. A reduction may be iterated only while its applicability conditions remain valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance reduction is exact when it preserves the decision answer or optimum up to a recorded offset and permits polynomial-time reconstruction of a corresponding solution or witness.
knowledge_statements.title: Instance Reduction

children.title: Reduction-Enhanced Branching
children.top_down_role: Interaction between simplification strength and branching behavior.

assumptions_latex: Reductions are sound and terminate at a fixed point.
Every subsequent branch is exhaustive and supports solution lifting.
A measure decreases across every fully reduced child transition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The combined procedure is exact, and its recurrence is governed by the measure decreases of fully reduced children rather than raw branching instances.

notation.meaning: Raw child produced by branch j.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interleaving fixed-point reductions with exact branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an instance \(I\), compute the reduction fixed point \(J=R(I)\). If \(J\) is terminal, solve it directly. Otherwise construct exhaustive raw children \(B_1(J),\ldots,B_r(J)\), reduce each child to \(J_i=R(B_i(J))\), recursively solve every \(J_i\), lift solutions through both transformations, and return the best one. If
\[
\mu(J_i)\le\mu(J)-d_i
\]
for positive decreases \(d_i\), then the search recurrence is
\[
T(m)\le\sum_{i=1}^r T(m-d_i)+m^{O(1)}.
\]
Sound reductions and exhaustive branches imply exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduce to a fixed point before and after every exhaustive branch, then analyze the fully reduced children; their measure decreases govern the exact search recurrence.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Enhanced Branching

children.title: Reduction-Stagnation Cases
children.top_down_role: Instance regimes where available reductions provide little structural progress.

assumptions_latex: A finite collection of sound reduction rules is fixed.
Rules are applied until none is applicable.
The remaining instance is nonterminal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonterminal reduced instance lies in the stagnation set \(\mathcal Z\); correctness must then come from a direct solver or a branch rule exhaustive on \(\mathcal Z\), and runtime analysis must use measure decreases valid for those irreducible instances.

notation.meaning: Set of nonterminal instances to which no reduction applies.
Predicate that rule i is applicable to I.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where preprocessing ceases to provide progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For reduction rules \(R_1,\ldots,R_q\) with applicability predicates \(A_1,
\ldots,A_q\), define the stagnation set
\[
\mathcal Z=\left\{I: I\text{ is nonterminal and }\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,q\},\ \neg A_i(I)\right\}.
\]
A reduction-to-fixed-point procedure makes no further progress on any \(I\in\mathcal Z\). Therefore reductions alone do not constitute an exact algorithm unless \(\mathcal Z\) is empty or every member of \(\mathcal Z\) is directly solvable. Otherwise the algorithm must supply an exhaustive branching rule for every instance in \(\mathcal Z\), and its recurrence must be valid under the structural invariants defining \(\mathcal Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduction stagnates on nonterminal instances where no rule applies; completeness then requires a direct solver or exhaustive branch covering every such irreducible case.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Stagnation Cases

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a complete directed graph on \(n=|V|\ge 2\) vertices with arc costs \(c_{uv}\in\mathbb R\).
A root \(r\in V\) is fixed.
The objective is a minimum-cost directed Hamiltonian cycle through all vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum tour cost is \(\min_{v\ne r}\bigl(D[V\setminus\{r\},v]+c_{vr}\bigr)\). The direct dynamic program uses \(O(n2^n)\) states, \(O(n^2 2^n)\) time, and \(O(n2^n)\) space.

notation.meaning: Minimum cost of a root-starting path visiting exactly S and ending at v.
Arc cost from u to v.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical subset dynamic program for asymmetric traveling salesperson.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(r\in V\). For \(S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\) and \(v\in S\), let \(D[S,v]\) be the minimum cost of a path beginning at \(r\), visiting exactly the vertices of \(S\), and ending at \(v\). Initialize \(D[\{v\},v]=c_{rv}\), and for \(|S|>1\) use
\[
D[S,v]=\min_{u\in S\setminus\{v\}}\bigl(D[S\setminus\{v\},u]+c_{uv}\bigr).
\]
Output \(\min_{v\ne r}\bigl(D[V\setminus\{r\},v]+c_{vr}\bigr)\), retaining minimizing predecessors to reconstruct a tour. The direct implementation takes \(O(n^2 2^n)\) time and \(O(n2^n)\) space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Store the cheapest root-starting path for each visited subset and endpoint, extend it by one vertex, and then close the cheapest full path into a directed Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Held–Karp-Style Dynamic Programming
Partition Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost partition of a finite ground set into admissible blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite, let \(\mathcal B\subseteq 2^V\setminus\{\varnothing\}\) be admissible blocks, and let \(c:\mathcal B\to\mathbb R\). Fix an order on \(V\). Initialize \(D(\varnothing)=0\). For every nonempty \(S\subseteq V\), set \[D(S)=\min\{D(S\setminus B)+c(B):B\in\mathcal B,\ B\subseteq S,\ \min S\in B\},\] with the minimum of an empty set equal to \(+\infty\). Store a minimizing block at each finite state. Output \(D(V)\) and recover a partition by repeatedly removing stored blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset recurrence chooses the unique block containing the least remaining element, thereby finding a minimum-cost admissible partition without duplicating block orders.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and totally ordered.
\(\mathcal B\subseteq 2^V\setminus\{\varnothing\}\).
\(c(B)\in\mathbb R\) for every \(B\in\mathcal B\).

children.title: Covering Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Covering Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted set cover solved by dynamic programming over uncovered subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite, \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\), and \(w:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\). Initialize \(D(\varnothing)=0\). For each nonempty \(S\subseteq U\), define \[D(S)=\min\{w(A)+D(S\setminus A):A\in\mathcal F,\ A\cap S\ne\varnothing\},\] taking an empty minimum as \(+\infty\). Evaluate states in nondecreasing cardinality, store a minimizing set, and output \(D(U)\). Following stored choices yields a family whose union contains \(U\); repeated choices may be removed without increasing cost when all weights are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The state records uncovered elements; choosing a set removes everything it covers and yields an optimal weighted cover.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(\mathcal F\) are finite.
\(w(A)\ge 0\) for every \(A\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(U)=\min\{\sum_{A\in\mathcal C}w(A):\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal F,\ \bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}A=U\}\).

children.title: Set-System Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Set-System Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indexed subset dynamic programming for attainable unions of a set family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite, enumerate \(\mathcal F=\{A_1,\ldots,A_m\}\), and let \(w_i\in\mathbb R\) be the weight of \(A_i\). Define \(D_0(\varnothing)=0\) and \(D_0(S)=+\infty\) for every nonempty \(S\subseteq U\). For \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(S\subseteq U\), set \[D_i(S)=\min\left\{D_{i-1}(S),\;w_i+\min\left\{D_{i-1}(R):R\subseteq S,\ R\cup A_i=S\right\}\right\},\] where an empty inner minimum is \(+\infty\). Store minimizing transitions, and output \(D_m(T)\) for a requested target union \(T\subseteq U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Processing sets one at a time computes the minimum weight of a subfamily having each exact target union; the selection transition considers all preceding unions compatible with overlaps.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(\mathcal F\) are finite.
\(w_i\in\mathbb R\) for \(1\le i\le m\).
\(T\subseteq U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_m(T)=\min\{\sum_{i\in I}w_i:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\},\ \bigcup_{i\in I}A_i=T\}\).

notation.meaning: minimum weight using the first i sets with union exactly S
union attained before deciding whether to select the current set

children.title: Coverage-State Encodings

knowledge_statements.title: Coverage-State Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-mask representation of covered and uncovered subsets of a finite universe.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a bijection \(\iota:U\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). Encode \(S\subseteq U\) by \[\mu(S)=\sum_{e\in S}2^{\iota(e)}.\] Then \(\mu(S\cup A)=\mu(S)\mathbin{\mathrm{OR}}\mu(A)\), and the elements of \(U\) not covered by \(S\) are encoded by \(M\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}\mu(S)\), where \(M=2^n-1\). Thus a coverage dynamic program may index states either by covered sets \(S\) or uncovered sets \(U\setminus S\), with a bijective conversion between the two conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subsets become bit masks; bitwise union and complementation implement coverage transitions and interchange covered-state with uncovered-state formulations.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite with \(|U|=n\).
\(\iota:U\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) is bijective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\mapsto\mu(S)\) is a bijection from \(2^U\) to \(\{0,\ldots,2^n-1\}\) preserving union through bitwise OR.

children.title: Set-Family Sparsification

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Family Sparsification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance deletion for unconstrained nonnegative weighted set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider weighted set cover on a finite universe \(U\), with \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) and \(w:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). If distinct \(A,B\in\mathcal F\) satisfy \(A\subseteq B\) and \(w(B)\le w(A)\), then deleting \(A\) preserves the optimum value. Repeatedly applying this deletion terminates with a family in which no member is contained in a distinct member of no greater weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set contained in a no-more-expensive set is dominated and may be deleted from an unconstrained weighted set-cover instance without changing the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) are finite.
\(w:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\).
Feasibility depends only on covering \(U\), with no side constraints on selected sets.
\(A,B\in\mathcal F\), \(A\ne B\), \(A\subseteq B\), and \(w(B)\le w(A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(U,\mathcal F,w)=\operatorname{OPT}(U,\mathcal F\setminus\{A\},w|_{\mathcal F\setminus\{A\}})\).

notation.meaning: A is contained in B and B has no greater weight

children.title: Ordering Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset recurrence for objectives decomposable by appending one item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(g:\{(v,S):S\subseteq V,\ v\in V\setminus S\}\to\mathbb R\), where \(g(v,S)\) is the cost of appending \(v\) after a prefix whose item set is \(S\). Initialize \(D(\varnothing)=0\), and for every nonempty \(S\subseteq V\) set \[D(S)=\min_{v\in S}\bigl(D(S\setminus\{v\})+g(v,S\setminus\{v\})\bigr).\] Evaluate states by increasing cardinality and store a minimizing final item. Output \(D(V)\); recursively removing stored final items reconstructs an optimal linear order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When each appended item has a real cost determined only by the preceding item set, a subset recurrence finds an optimal ordering.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(g:\{(v,S):S\subseteq V,\ v\notin S\}\to\mathbb R\).
The cost of every order \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) is \(\sum_{i=1}^n g(v_i,\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(V)=\min_{\pi\in\operatorname{Sym}(V)}\sum_{i=1}^{|V|}g(\pi_i,\{\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_{i-1}\})\).

notation.meaning: minimum cost of ordering exactly the elements of S

children.title: Permutation Dynamic Programming
