knowledge_statements.title: Permutation Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint-refined subset dynamic programming for sequence-dependent permutation costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and nonempty. For \(v\in V\), let \(a_v\in\mathbb R\); for \(v\in V\) and \(1\le k\le |V|\), let \(p_{v,k}\in\mathbb R\); and for distinct \(u,v\in V\), let \(c_{uv}\in\mathbb R\). The cost of a permutation \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_{|V|})\) is \[a_{\pi_1}+\sum_{k=1}^{|V|}p_{\pi_k,k}+\sum_{k=2}^{|V|}c_{\pi_{k-1},\pi_k}.\] Initialize \(D(\{v\},v)=a_v+p_{v,1}\). For \(|S|\ge2\) and \(v\in S\), set \[D(S,v)=p_{v,|S|}+\min_{u\in S\setminus\{v\}}\bigl(D(S\setminus\{v\},u)+c_{uv}\bigr).\] Evaluate by increasing \(|S|\), store a minimizing predecessor, and output \(\min_{v\in V}D(V,v)\) with its reconstructed permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state consisting of a used subset and its last item minimizes the explicitly defined sum of starting, position, and adjacent-transition costs over all permutations.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and nonempty.
\(a_v\in\mathbb R\) for \(v\in V\).
\(p_{v,k}\in\mathbb R\) for \(v\in V\) and \(1\le k\le |V|\).
\(c_{uv}\in\mathbb R\) for distinct \(u,v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{v\in V}D(V,v)=\min_{\pi\in\operatorname{Sym}(V)}\left(a_{\pi_1}+\sum_{k=1}^{|V|}p_{\pi_k,k}+\sum_{k=2}^{|V|}c_{\pi_{k-1},\pi_k}\right)\).

children.title: Prefix-State Encodings

knowledge_statements.title: Prefix-State Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State representation for permutation prefixes under Markovian incremental costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a permutation prefix \(P=(v_1,\ldots,v_k)\), define its prefix state as \(\sigma(P)=(S,v_k)\), where \(S=\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}\); use \((\varnothing,\bot)\) for the empty prefix. If every feasible extension and its incremental cost depend on \(P\) only through \(\sigma(P)\), then prefixes having the same state are interchangeable for all continuations. Appending \(u\notin S\) updates the state by \[(S,v)\longmapsto(S\cup\{u\},u).\] Consequently only the least-cost representative of each state must be retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permutation prefix can be compressed to its used subset and last item whenever all future decisions depend only on those data.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
Extension feasibility and incremental costs are functions only of \((S,v)\) and the appended item.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma(P)=\sigma(Q)\) implies that \(P\) and \(Q\) have identical feasible continuation sets and continuation costs.

children.title: Order-Symmetry Reduction

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Symmetry Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotienting ordering states by a cost-preserving group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal S,\mathcal E)\) be a finite directed acyclic state graph with edge costs \(c:\mathcal E\to\mathbb R\), terminal set \(T\subseteq\mathcal S\), and terminal costs \(h:T\to\mathbb R\). Let \(D(s)\) be the minimum cost of a directed path from \(s\) to a state \(t\in T\), including \(h(t)\), with \(D(s)=+\infty\) when no such path exists. Suppose a finite group \(G\) acts on \(\mathcal S\), preserves \(\mathcal E\), \(c\), \(T\), and \(h\). Then \[D(g\cdot s)=D(s)\qquad(g\in G,\ s\in\mathcal S).\] Hence a quotient dynamic program may retain one canonical representative \(\operatorname{can}(s)\) per orbit and preserves the value of every state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite acyclic dynamic program, a group action preserving transitions, costs, and terminal data makes the value function constant on state orbits, so one canonical representative per orbit suffices.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal S,\mathcal E)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
\(c:\mathcal E\to\mathbb R\), \(T\subseteq\mathcal S\), and \(h:T\to\mathbb R\).
\(G\) is a finite group acting on \(\mathcal S\).
The action preserves edges, edge costs, terminal states, and terminal costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is constant on each \(G\)-orbit, and the orbit-quotient dynamic program preserves all optimal cost-to-go values.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Covering Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion–exclusion count of ordered set-family covers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite, let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\), and let \(q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). For \(Y\subseteq U\), define \(a(Y)=|\{A\in\mathcal F:A\subseteq Y\}|\), and adopt \(x^0=1\) for every integer \(x\ge0\), including \(0^0=1\). If \(C_q\) denotes the number of ordered tuples \((A_1,\ldots,A_q)\in\mathcal F^q\) satisfying \(A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_q=U\), then \[C_q=\sum_{X\subseteq U}(-1)^{|X|}a(U\setminus X)^q.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The number of ordered q-tuples of family members covering the universe is the stated inclusion–exclusion sum over sets of elements omitted by every tuple member.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioning Applications

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Cover Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite with \(|U|=n\), let \(J\) be a finite index set, and let \((A_j)_{j\in J}\) be a family with \(A_j\subseteq U\) for every \(j\in J\). Let \(E\) be the number of index subsets \(I\subseteq J\) for which the sets \((A_j)_{j\in I}\) are pairwise disjoint and have union \(U\). Then \[E=\sum_{X\subseteq U}(-1)^{|X|}[z^n]\prod_{\substack{j\in J\\A_j\subseteq U\setminus X}}(1+z^{|A_j|}).\]

knowledge_statements.title: Overlap-Correction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order overlap correction for weighted finite set systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each nonempty \(J\subseteq[m]\), define \(W_J\) as the total weight of elements contained in every \(A_j\) with \(j\in J\). Then the total weight of elements belonging to exactly one member of the family is
\[
W_{=1}=\sum_{\varnothing\ne J\subseteq[m]}(-1)^{|J|-1}|J|\,W_J.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating weighted intersection sums, with a factor equal to the number of selected sets, retain exactly the elements covered once.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a finite universe and \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq U\).
\(w:2^U\to R\), where \(R\) is a commutative ring.

knowledge_statements.title: Hamiltonicity Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed Hamiltonian-cycle counting by vertex-set inclusion-exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The number of directed Hamiltonian cycles of \(D\), counted up to cyclic rotation, is
\[
h(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{S\subseteq V}(-1)^{n-|S|}\operatorname{tr}\!\left(A[S]^n\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating sum of traces of induced adjacency-matrix powers counts directed Hamiltonian cycles, with division by the number of vertices removing the choice of starting vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with \(|V|=n\ge 2\).
\(A\in\{0,1\}^{V\times V}\) is the adjacency matrix of \(D\), and \(A[S]\) is its principal submatrix on \(S\subseteq V\).

trace of the nth power of the induced adjacency matrix

All indicated cardinalities are finite.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite counting by exclusion of indexed failure events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_P=\{x:P(x)\}\), and call \(x\in X_P\) valid when \(A_u(x)\) is false for every \(u\in U\). For \(S\subseteq U\), define \(N(S)=|\{x\in X_P:\forall u\in S,\ A_u(x)\}|\). Then
\[
N_{\mathrm{valid}}=\sum_{S\subseteq U}(-1)^{|S|}N(S).
\]
Thus a counting problem admitting efficient evaluation of every \(N(S)\) yields an exact inclusion-exclusion algorithm using \(2^{|U|}\) evaluations and the cost of accumulating their signed sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count objects satisfying all requirements by alternately adding and subtracting counts in which selected requirements are forced to fail.

Enumerate the subsets \(S\subseteq U\) one at a time, evaluate \(g(S)\), add \((-1)^{n-|S|}g(S)\) to a single accumulator, and discard the value before generating the next subset. If evaluating \(g(S)\) takes \(T_g(n)\) time and polynomial workspace, then the complete sum

F=\sum_{S\subseteq U}(-1)^{n-|S|}g(S)

children.title: Zeta Transform Methods
children.top_down_role: Subset-lattice aggregation through zeta-transform computation.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and \(f:2^U\to R\), where \((R,+,\cdot)\) is a semiring.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All values \((\zeta f)(S)\) are computable using \(n2^{n-1}\) semiring additions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fast subset-lattice zeta transform over a semiring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(F_0(S)=f(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq U\), and fix an ordering \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\) of \(U\). For \(i=1,
\ldots,n\), update every subset containing \(u_i\) by
\[
F_i(S)=F_{i-1}(S)+F_{i-1}(S\setminus\{u_i\}),
\]
and leave \(F_i(S)=F_{i-1}(S)\) when \(u_i\notin S\). The output satisfies \(F_n(S)=(\zeta f)(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f(T)\) for all \(S\), using \(n2^{n-1}\) additions and \(O(2^n)\) stored semiring elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fast zeta transform accumulates values along each subset-lattice coordinate, producing every lower-subset sum in order n times two-to-n operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Zeta Transform Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fast zeta-transform recurrence, operation count, storage bound, and semiring assumptions are standard and internally consistent, but no supporting citation is supplied.

children.title: Möbius Transform Methods
children.top_down_role: Subset-lattice inversion through Möbius-transform computation.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and \(g:2^U\to R\), where \(R\) is a commutative ring.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}g(T)\) is computable for all \(S\) in \(O(n2^n)\) ring operations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fast Möbius transform on the Boolean subset lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(F_0(S)=g(S)\) for all \(S\subseteq U\), and order \(U\) as \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), set
\[
F_i(S)=F_{i-1}(S)-F_{i-1}(S\setminus\{u_i\})
\]
when \(u_i\in S\), and otherwise retain \(F_i(S)=F_{i-1}(S)\). Then \(F_n(S)=(\mu g)(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}g(T)\). The algorithm uses \(n2^{n-1}\) subtractions and \(O(2^n)\) ring elements of storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing coordinate-wise addition by subtraction computes all Boolean-lattice Möbius coefficients in order n times two-to-n ring operations.

children.title: Transform Inversion
children.top_down_role: The inversion relationship connecting the two subset transforms.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and \(R\) is a commutative ring.
\(f:2^U\to R\) and \(g(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f(T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}g(T)\) for every \(S\subseteq U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Möbius inversion for lower-subset sums on a Boolean lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(S\subseteq U\), the relations
\[
g(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f(T)
\quad\text{and}\quad
f(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}g(T)
\]
are equivalent. Consequently the zeta and Möbius operators are mutual inverses on functions \(2^U\to R\): \(\mu(\zeta f)=f\) and \(\zeta(\mu g)=g\). The additive inverses in \(R\) are essential to the alternating coefficients in the inverse transform.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the Boolean lattice, lower-subset summation is inverted by an alternating sum indexed by the difference in subset sizes.
knowledge_statements.title: Transform Inversion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inversion duality is correctly stated over a commutative ring and matches the Transform Inversion container. No source or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Semiring Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Algebraic regimes governing which transform or inversion operations remain available.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and \((R,+,\cdot,0,1)\) is a semiring.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The zeta transform is defined over \(R\), whereas ordinary Möbius inversion requires additive inverses.

notation.meaning: subset zeta transform over the semiring addition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic requirements for Boolean-lattice transforms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every function \(f:2^U\to R\), finite semiring addition suffices to define and compute
\[
(\zeta f)(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f(T).
\]
The usual inverse formula \((\mu g)(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}g(T)\) is available when the additive monoid of \(R\) is an abelian group, hence when subtraction is defined. In a general semiring, the forward zeta transform remains valid, but this alternating Möbius inversion need not be expressible or recover \(f\) internally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subset summation needs only semiring addition, but the standard alternating inverse requires additive inverses and therefore a ring-like coefficient domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Semiring Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between semiring-compatible forward zeta transforms and inversion requiring additive inverses is mathematically sound, and condition is the appropriate knowledge kind. It remains unsupported by a cited source.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and \(f,g:2^U\to R\), where \(R\) is a commutative ring.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f*g)(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f(T)g(S\setminus T)\).

notation.meaning: subset convolution of f and g
a component of the ordered bipartition of S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered two-block convolution on the Boolean subset lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The subset convolution of \(f\) and \(g\) is the function \(f*g:2^U\to R\) defined for every \(S\subseteq U\) by
\[
(f*g)(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f(T)g(S\setminus T).
\]
Each term corresponds to an ordered decomposition \(S=T\mathbin{\dot\cup}(S\setminus T)\). The operation is associative and bilinear over \(R\); when multiplication in \(R\) is commutative, it is also commutative. Its identity is the function \(e\) with \(e(\varnothing)=1\) and \(e(S)=0\) for nonempty \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subset convolution combines values over every ordered bipartition of a set and forms an associative convolution algebra with the empty-set delta as identity.
knowledge_statements.title: Subset Convolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and stated algebraic properties of subset convolution are correct under the commutative-ring assumption, and definition fits the exact topic. A source with a specific locator is missing.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioning via Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding weighted ordered set partitions by iterated subset convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(a^{*1}=a\) and \(a^{*(k+1)}=a^{*k}*a\). For every integer \(k\ge 1\) and every \(S\subseteq U\),
\[
a^{*k}(S)=\sum_{S=B_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_k}\prod_{i=1}^{k}a(B_i),
\]
where the sum ranges over ordered \(k\)-tuples of pairwise disjoint subsets with union \(S\). Because \(a(\varnothing)=0\), only tuples with nonempty blocks contribute. In particular, if \(a(B)\) is the indicator that the nonempty set \(B\) is admissible, then \(a^{*k}(U)\) is the number of ordered admissible \(k\)-partitions of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated subset convolution with zero weight on the empty set counts weighted ordered partitions into nonempty admissible blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and \(a:2^U\to R\) assigns a weight to each admissible block.
\(R\) is a commutative ring, \(a(\varnothing)=0\), and ordered block sequences are counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^{*k}(S)=\sum_{S=B_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_k}\prod_{i=1}^{k}a(B_i)\) for every integer \(k\ge 1\) and \(S\subseteq U\).

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph and \(S\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is minimal for separating some pair \(a,b\in V\setminus S\).

notation.meaning: graph obtained by deleting S and its incident edges
open neighborhood of a vertex set C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal vertex separators and their full-component characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq V\) is a minimal separator of \(G\) if there exist distinct vertices \(a,b\in V\setminus S\) lying in different connected components of \(G-S\), while no proper subset of \(S\) separates \(a\) from \(b\). Equivalently, \(S\) is a minimal separator exactly when \(G-S\) has at least two components \(C_1,C_2\) satisfying \(N_G(C_1)=N_G(C_2)=S\). Such components are called full components associated with \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal separator is inclusion-minimal for disconnecting some vertex pair; equivalently, its deletion creates at least two components having exactly that separator as neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Separator Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and full-component characterization of a minimal separator are correct and relevant foundational knowledge for Minimal-Separator Methods. No supporting source or locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph and \(\Omega\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Omega\) is a maximal clique in some minimal triangulation of \(G\).

notation.meaning: a chordal supergraph on V obtained by adding edges to G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential maximal cliques defined through minimal chordal completions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A triangulation of \(G\) is a chordal graph \(H=(V,E\cup F)\). It is minimal when no proper subset \(F'\subsetneq F\) makes \((V,E\cup F')\) chordal. A set \(\Omega\subseteq V\) is a potential maximal clique of \(G\) if there exists a minimal triangulation \(H\) of \(G\) in which \(\Omega\) is a maximal clique. Thus potential maximal cliques enumerate precisely the vertex sets that can occur as maximal bags induced by minimal chordal completions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A potential maximal clique is a vertex set that becomes a maximal clique in at least one inclusion-minimal chordal completion of the graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Potential Maximal Clique Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of a potential maximal clique through a minimal triangulation is correct and fits the topic, but the record has no authoritative citation or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Triangulation-Based Exact Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exact optimization over tree decompositions induced by chordal completions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a graph \(G=(V,E)\) and an objective \(F\) admitting exact dynamic programming on tree decompositions. Enumerate a family \(\mathcal H\) of chordal completions \(H=(V,E\cup D)\) containing at least one completion relevant to an optimal solution. For each \(H\in\mathcal H\), construct a clique tree whose bags are the maximal cliques of \(H\), run the exact bag-state recurrence for \(F\), and obtain value \(z_H\). Return a feasible solution attaining \(\min_{H\in\mathcal H}z_H\) for minimization, or \(\max_{H\in\mathcal H}z_H\) for maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate sufficient chordal completions, solve the problem exactly on each resulting clique tree, and return the best feasible solution found.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
The state recurrence is exact for every enumerated clique tree.
\(\mathcal H\) contains a completion supporting an optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned solution is globally optimal for \(F\) on \(G\).

notation.meaning: a chordal completion of the input graph
the optimum computed on the clique tree of H

review_flags: No supplied locator supports triangulation-based exact algorithms.
Exact completeness conditions for the enumerated completion family require a domain-specific source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but “relevant to an optimal solution” does not specify the problem-dependent condition under which a chordal completion supports an optimum. No citation or locator supports this completeness claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Separator Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exact dynamic programming across vertex separators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(S\subseteq V\) separate components \(C_1,\ldots,C_q\) of \(G-S\), and let \(\Sigma(S)\) be a finite interface-state set. For every component \(C_i\) and state \(\sigma\in\Sigma(S)\), compute \(D_i(\sigma)\), the optimum contribution on \(G[C_i\cup S]\) consistent with \(\sigma\). Combine compatible entries by \[D_S(\sigma)=b_S(\sigma)+\sum_{i=1}^{q}D_i(\sigma),\] with any separator contribution counted exactly once. Recursively apply the construction inside components and return the best feasible root state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Condition on a separator state, solve separated components independently, combine compatible values without double counting, and optimize over root states.
assumptions_latex: All interactions between distinct components of \(G-S\) are determined by the state on \(S\).
The component subproblems and compatibility tests are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimizing the root table yields the exact optimum on \(G\).

notation.meaning: finite states describing the separator interface
component optimum conditional on state sigma

review_flags: No supplied locator supports separator dynamic programming.
Problem-specific state sufficiency and accounting conventions need a source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, and the recurrence is conditionally coherent. A source is required to substantiate the separator-state sufficiency, recursive decomposition, and exact accounting conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Way Meet-in-the-Middle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact two-block combination through complementary signatures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance decompose as \(U=U_L\mathbin{\dot\cup}U_R\). Enumerate all admissible partial solutions \(x_L\) on \(U_L\) and \(x_R\) on \(U_R\), storing signatures \(s_L(x_L)\in\Gamma\) and \(s_R(x_R)\in\Gamma\). Define a compatibility predicate \(K:\Gamma\times\Gamma\to\{0,1\}\) such that \(K(s_L(x_L),s_R(x_R))=1\) exactly when \(x_L\cup x_R\) is globally feasible. Index one list by signature, scan the other for compatible entries, and return the best combined objective value, counting cross-block terms during combination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split the variables into two blocks, enumerate partial solutions, match exactly compatible signatures, and return the best combined solution.
assumptions_latex: Every global solution restricts to enumerated partial solutions on both blocks.
The signature compatibility predicate is necessary and sufficient for global feasibility.
The combined objective is evaluated exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns an optimal global solution.
review_flags: No supplied locator concerns meet-in-the-middle algorithms.
The statement is a generic synthesis template rather than a sourced problem-specific algorithm.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but this is a generic exactness template whose necessary-and-sufficient signature construction is entirely problem dependent. No supporting source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Multiway Instance Splitting
children.top_down_role: Decomposition of an instance into more than two coordinated parts.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiway Instance Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partitioning an exact-search instance into multiple independently enumerable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite ground set \(U\) and an integer \(k\ge 2\), choose a disjoint partition \[U=U_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}U_k.\] For each block \(U_i\), enumerate every locally admissible partial assignment and retain sufficient boundary data to evaluate all constraints involving other blocks. The split is exact when every feasible global assignment has one retained restriction in each block and a tuple of retained restrictions combines to a feasible global assignment exactly when its boundary data satisfy the prescribed multiway compatibility predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition the instance into several blocks while retaining enough boundary information to reconstruct every feasible global solution exactly.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite.
All cross-block constraints admit a finite sufficient boundary description.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible global solutions correspond exactly to compatible tuples of retained block solutions.

notation.meaning: the ground-set portion assigned to block i

review_flags: No supplied locator supports multiway meet-in-the-middle splitting.
A source is needed for standard terminology and concrete admissibility conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is appropriate, but the existence and sufficiency of finite boundary data are substantive assumptions requiring a source and concrete applicability conditions.

children.title: Partial-Solution Lists
children.top_down_role: List representations for partial solutions generated from individual parts.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Solution Lists
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite list representation of blockwise candidates and their interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a block \(U_i\), a partial-solution list is \[L_i=\{(\sigma_i(x),c_i(x),w_i(x)):x\in\mathcal X_i\},\] where \(\mathcal X_i\) is the set of enumerated locally admissible assignments, \(\sigma_i(x)\) is sufficient interface data, \(c_i(x)\) records the contribution used by the global compatibility relation, and \(w_i(x)\) is the local objective contribution. Entries with identical \((\sigma_i,c_i)\) may be reduced to the best objective value whenever future feasibility and objective contributions depend only on \((\sigma_i,c_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent each block candidate by sufficient interface data, combination data, and objective value; safely discard dominated duplicates with identical future behavior.
assumptions_latex: Future compatibility depends only on \((\sigma_i,c_i)\).
The objective ordering used for duplicate reduction is preserved by every continuation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced list preserves at least one representative of every globally relevant partial solution.

notation.meaning: the partial-solution list for block i

review_flags: No supplied locator supports partial-solution list representations.
Safe reduction criteria vary by optimization problem and require sourcing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits. The duplicate-reduction claim is conditional and coherent, but no source supports the future-equivalence and objective-ordering criterion.

children.title: Multi-List Combination
children.top_down_role: Compatibility search across several partial-solution lists.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-List Combination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact joining of multiple partial-solution lists under a compatibility relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given lists \(L_1,\ldots,L_k\) and an exact predicate \(K:L_1\times\cdots\times L_k\to\{0,1\}\), enumerate or indexed-search the tuples \((e_1,\ldots,e_k)\) satisfying \(K(e_1,\ldots,e_k)=1\). For each compatible tuple, reconstruct its global solution and evaluate \[W(e_1,\ldots,e_k)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_i(e_i)+w_{\mathrm{cross}}(e_1,\ldots,e_k).\] Return a feasible tuple minimizing or maximizing \(W\), according to the problem. The indexing scheme may alter running time but must not omit any compatible tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Join one entry from each list, retain exactly compatible tuples, evaluate local and cross-block costs, and return the best tuple.
assumptions_latex: Each globally feasible solution induces a tuple present in \(L_1\times\cdots\times L_k\).
\(K\) is necessary and sufficient for compatibility.
\(W\) equals the global objective of the reconstructed solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned tuple reconstructs an optimal global solution.

children.title: List-Size Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Time or space regimes governed by the number and size of generated lists.

knowledge_statements.title: List-Size Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic time-space bound for split-and-list exact algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose block \(i\) produces and materializes a list of size \(N_i\) in \(O(N_i)\) time and \(O(N_i)\) total space. If the combination procedure runs in time \(J(N_1,\ldots,N_k)\) and additional space \(S_J(N_1,\ldots,N_k)\), then the complete split-and-list algorithm uses \[T=O\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}N_i+J(N_1,\ldots,N_k)\right),\qquad S=O\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}N_i+S_J(N_1,\ldots,N_k)\right).\] Changing the block sizes therefore trades list-generation and storage costs against the join cost; subject to a memory constraint, a chosen split may be optimized against these bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When all lists are materialized, total time is list construction plus joining, and total space is list storage plus the join procedure's additional workspace.
assumptions_latex: Each stored entry occupies \(O(1)\) machine words.
Every list is materialized, and list \(i\) is generated in \(O(N_i)\) time.
\(J\) and \(S_J\) bound the time and additional space of the selected exact join procedure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed expressions bound the total running time and working space under the stated materialization assumptions.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports meet-in-the-middle time-space tradeoffs.
The corrected bound assumes simultaneous materialization of all lists.

children.title: Solution Representations
children.top_down_role: Alternative encodings of partial solutions for split-instance algorithms.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Many-to-one encodings used to expose searchable collisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a finite set of candidate solutions, let \(\mathcal R\) be a finite representation space, and let \(Q\subseteq\mathcal X\times\mathcal R\) be a representation relation. For \(x\in\mathcal X\), define \[Q(x)=\{r\in\mathcal R:(x,r)\in Q\}.\] The representation scheme is complete for a feasible set \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal X\) when \(Q(x)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(x\in\mathcal F\). It is collision-decodable when every accepted collision of compatible representation fragments can be decoded to a candidate in \(\mathcal X\), which is then tested by the original feasibility predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Associate each candidate with one or more finite representations; require every feasible candidate to be represented, and decode and verify every accepted fragment collision.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal R\) are finite.
Every feasible candidate has at least one representation.
The decoder and original feasibility test are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustively searching accepted representation collisions and verifying their decoded candidates is complete whenever every feasible candidate has an accepted collision representation.

notation.meaning: the set of representations assigned to candidate x

children.title: Collision Search
children.top_down_role: Search for compatible or matching encodings across partial-solution collections.

knowledge_statements.title: Collision Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact candidate recovery by matching representation keys.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a finite candidate set with feasibility predicate \(P:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}\) and objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) to be minimized. Generate finite collections \(A\) and \(B\) of representation fragments, associate keys \(h_A:A\to\Gamma\) and \(h_B:B\to\Gamma\), and define a matching relation \(M\subseteq\Gamma\times\Gamma\). Index \(B\) by \(h_B\); for each \(a\in A\), enumerate every \(b\in B\) satisfying \((h_A(a),h_B(b))\in M\). Decode each matching pair to a candidate \(d(a,b)\in\mathcal X\), test \(P(d(a,b))\), and return a feasible decoded candidate of minimum objective value. Process all matching pairs unless a valid optimality certificate permits earlier termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate every matching fragment pair, decode and verify each candidate, and return the feasible decoded candidate with minimum objective value.
assumptions_latex: For every feasible \(x\in\mathcal X\), at least one matching pair \((a,b)\in A\times B\) satisfies \(d(a,b)=x\).
The decoder and feasibility test are exact.
Every matching pair is processed unless an exact optimality certificate permits termination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If a feasible candidate exists, the algorithm returns one minimizing \(f\) over all feasible candidates in \(\mathcal X\); otherwise it reports that none exists.

notation.meaning: the objective function to be minimized

review_flags: No supplied locator supports collision-search algorithms.
The repaired exactness statement still requires a canonical source.

children.title: Representation Multiplicity
children.top_down_role: Regimes where solutions admit multiple useful partial representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Multiplicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of admissible encodings associated with one candidate solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq\mathcal X\times\mathcal R\) be a representation relation between candidates and finite encodings. The representation multiplicity of \(x\in\mathcal X\) is \[m_R(x)=\left|\{r\in\mathcal R:(x,r)\in R\}\right|.\] For a subset \(Y\subseteq\mathcal X\), its minimum and maximum multiplicities are \(m_R^{-}(Y)=\min_{x\in Y}m_R(x)\) and \(m_R^{+}(Y)=\max_{x\in Y}m_R(x)\). A representation scheme is uniform on \(Y\) when these two quantities are equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Representation multiplicity counts how many admissible encodings correspond to a candidate; uniformity means that count is constant over a specified set.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal R\) are finite.
\(Y\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_R(x)\) is a well-defined nonnegative integer for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
review_flags: No supplied locator supports this terminology.
The definition is locally coherent but needs alignment with a canonical representation-technique source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind exactly fits the leaf, and the finite-set formulas are internally coherent. No citation or specific locator establishes that this terminology and its uniformity convention are canonical in representation-based exact algorithms.

children.title: Spurious-Collision Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where encoding collisions do not correspond to valid combined solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Spurious-Collision Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collision equality alone need not imply a valid original solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let fragment pairs be accepted whenever their keys match under \(M\). If there exist \(a\in A\) and \(b\in B\) such that \((h_A(a),h_B(b))\in M\) but the decoded candidate \(d(a,b)\) violates the original feasibility predicate \(P\), then key collision is not a sufficient certificate of feasibility. Any exact collision-search algorithm must therefore verify \(P(d(a,b))\), or strengthen its key and matching relation so that \[(h_A(a),h_B(b))\in M\implies P(d(a,b))=1.\] Omitting both safeguards permits false positive outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching representation keys can produce infeasible candidates; exact search must verify decoded solutions or use a matching relation that guarantees feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The decoder \(d:A\times B\to\mathcal X\) is defined for accepted pairs.
At least one accepted pair decodes to an infeasible candidate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Collision matching without verification or sufficient keys is not an exact decision procedure.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports spurious-collision boundaries.
A canonical example and source are needed for promotion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, and the conditional countercondition is mathematically coherent. A canonical source and inspectable locator are required for this collision-search failure phenomenon.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Radius Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive exact search within a prescribed Hamming ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a Boolean assignment \(a\in\{0,1\}^n\), a radius \(r\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), and a feasibility predicate \(P:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), enumerate every assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfying \(d_H(x,a)\le r\). Test \(P(x)\) for each enumerated assignment and return a feasible one if found; otherwise return \(\mathrm{NONE}\). Direct enumeration examines \[|B_r(a)|=\sum_{i=0}^{r}\binom{n}{i}\] assignments. Sequential generation requires polynomial enumeration overhead in addition to the workspace used to evaluate \(P\) and store an assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate and test every Boolean assignment within Hamming radius r of the center. The search examines the binomial-size Hamming ball and uses polynomial enumeration overhead beyond predicate evaluation.
assumptions_latex: \(P(x)\) is decidable exactly.
The search enumerates every assignment in \(B_r(a)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is feasible, or \(\mathrm{NONE}\) correctly certifies \(B_r(a)\cap P^{-1}(1)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: the radius-r Hamming ball centered at a

review_flags: No supplied locator supports bounded-radius SAT local search.
The space statement now separates enumeration overhead from predicate-evaluation workspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Covering-Code Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic covering of the Boolean cube followed by bounded-radius SAT search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a CNF formula \(F\) on \(n\) variables, a radius \(r\), an \(r\)-covering code \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), and a complete procedure \(\operatorname{SearchBall}(F,a,r)\) for assignments within Hamming distance at most \(r\) from \(a\), inspect the codewords \(a\in C\) in any fixed order. Return the first satisfying assignment produced by \(\operatorname{SearchBall}(F,a,r)\); return UNSAT if every call fails. Since \(\bigcup_{a\in C}B_r(a)=\{0,1\}^n\), the algorithm is complete. Its running time is at most \(O(|C|T(n,r))\), where \(T(n,r)\) bounds one local-search call.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cover the assignment cube by Hamming balls and run an exact bounded-radius SAT search at every center; coverage guarantees completeness.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a CNF formula on \(n\) Boolean variables.
\(C\) is an \(r\)-covering code of \(\{0,1\}^n\).
\(\operatorname{SearchBall}\) is complete within its specified Hamming ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure decides satisfiability in time \(O(|C|T(n,r))\).

notation.meaning: Hamming ball of radius r centered at a
covering code used as the set of search centers
worst-case time for one bounded-radius search

knowledge_statements.title: Satisfiability Transfer Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of exact SAT routines through solution-preserving reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\\) be a decision problem with size measure \(n\). Suppose an instance \(I\) can be transformed in time \(p(n)\) into a CNF formula \(F_I\) having at most \(g(n)\) variables, and suppose \(I\) is a yes-instance if and only if \(F_I\) is satisfiable. If formulas in the image of the transformation are decidable by a SAT algorithm in time \(T(m)\) and space \(S(m)\), then \(P\) is decidable in time \(p(n)+T(g(n))\) and space bounded by the reduction workspace plus \(S(g(n))\). Witness-decoding time must be added when solutions, rather than decisions, are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution-preserving reduction to a controlled-size SAT instance transfers the SAT solver’s time and space bounds to the original problem.
assumptions_latex: \(I\mapsto F_I\) is computable in time \(p(n)\).
\(I\in P\) if and only if \(F_I\) is satisfiable.
\(F_I\) has at most \(g(n)\) variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Problem \(P\) is decidable in time \(p(n)+T(g(n))\), with the corresponding reduction-plus-SAT space bound.

notation.meaning: upper bound on the encoding's variable count
time and space bounds of the SAT procedure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transfer principle fits the leaf, but it has no supporting source and the expression \(P\\\) is malformed. A sourced revision should also specify the reduction workspace and the SAT bound's applicable formula class.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Space Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Memoized subset dynamic programming over all subsets of an \(n\)-element ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be an \(n\)-element set, and suppose each state value \(D(S)\), for \(S\subseteq U\), is computed once from at most \(q(n)\) previously computed states using \(p(n)\) time and \(b(n)\) bits of stored data. Evaluating states in an order compatible with the recurrence computes \(D(U)\) in time \(O(2^n q(n)p(n))\) and space \(O(2^n b(n))\), apart from polynomial-size control data. The bound assumes constant-time addressing of stored states up to the stated word-cost convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Storing every subset state avoids recomputation, giving exponential memory and time proportional to the number of states times transition cost.
assumptions_latex: There is one state \(D(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq U\).
The state-dependency relation admits a compatible evaluation order.
Each state examines at most \(q(n)\) predecessors at cost \(p(n)\) each.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The full memoized computation uses time \(O(2^nq(n)p(n))\) and space \(O(2^nb(n))\).

notation.meaning: dynamic-programming value associated with subset S
maximum number of transitions examined per state
bits stored for one state value

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Space Recomputation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth-first evaluation of an acyclic recurrence without retaining its full state table.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite acyclic state-dependency graph, a terminal state \(t\), base-state values, and a recurrence for every nonbase state, initialize an empty recursion stack and evaluate \(t\) depth first. To evaluate a state, recursively obtain each predecessor value, combine those values according to the recurrence, and discard predecessor values when the current call returns; no global memo table is maintained. Output the resulting value at \(t\). If recursion depth, state descriptions, and local transition storage are polynomial in input size, then workspace is polynomial, although repeated evaluation of shared predecessors can increase running time, potentially exponentially.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate a recurrence depth first and discard intermediate values, exchanging repeated computation for polynomial workspace.
assumptions_latex: The state-dependency graph is finite and acyclic.
Recursion depth and each state description are polynomially bounded.
Each recurrence can be evaluated with polynomial local workspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The terminal value is computed using polynomial workspace, with time enlarged by repeated subproblem evaluation.

notation.meaning: terminal state whose value is requested

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits polynomial-space recomputation and its qualitative space claim is plausible, but no source supports the framework or delineates when the time overhead is exponential.

knowledge_statements.title: Meet-in-the-Middle Space Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced splitting and streamed matching of partial solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance whose solutions decompose into compatible partial solutions on disjoint parts \(U_1\) and \(U_2\), choose \(|U_1|=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) and \(U_2=U\setminus U_1\). Enumerate partial solutions on \(U_1\), storing only a key and the best representative required by the compatibility rule. Enumerate partial solutions on \(U_2\) and query the stored keys for a compatible complement; output the best combined feasible pair, or report failure if none exists. If each side has at most \(c^{n/2}\operatorname{poly}(n)\) partial solutions and lookup is polynomial-time, both time and stored-list space are \(O(c^{n/2}\operatorname{poly}(n))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split the ground set, store summarized partial solutions from one half, and match them against streamed solutions from the other half.
assumptions_latex: Every full solution decomposes across \(U_1\) and \(U_2\).
A key-based test exactly characterizes compatibility.
Dominated representatives sharing a key may be discarded safely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The balanced construction uses \(O(c^{n/2}\operatorname{poly}(n))\) time and stored-list space under the stated enumeration bound.

notation.meaning: the two disjoint parts of the ground set
base of the partial-solution enumeration bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic kind fits the leaf, but exactness and the claimed time-space bound depend on unstated enumeration, key-compression, dominance, and lookup details that require a concrete source.

knowledge_statements.title: Selective Memoization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Caching only a designated subset of states in an acyclic dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an acyclic recurrence with terminal state \(t\), choose a cache set \(M\) of states and initialize an empty table indexed by \(M\). Evaluate \(t\) recursively. When a requested state lies in \(M\), return its stored value if present; otherwise compute it, store it, and return it. When a state does not lie in \(M\), compute it recursively and discard its value after use. Output the value at \(t\). If cached state \(s\) occupies \(b(s)\) bits, cache space is at most \(\sum_{s\in M}b(s)\) plus recursion workspace; running time equals the total cost of all resulting state evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cache strategically chosen states while recomputing the rest, interpolating between full memoization and pure depth-first recomputation.
assumptions_latex: The recurrence dependency graph is finite and acyclic.
The cache set \(M\) is fixed or selected without compromising recurrence correctness.
Stored values are exact and keyed uniquely by state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm is exact and uses cache space at most \(\sum_{s\in M}b(s)\), plus recursion workspace.

notation.meaning: set of states selected for memoization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits selective memoization and the cache-space expression is plausible, but no cited source supports the framework, and the running-time statement is tautological without a cache-dependent bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Size Stratification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimization obtained by partitioning candidate solutions according to cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance have an \(n\)-element universe, and suppose every feasible solution \(X\) has size in \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\). If procedure \(A_k\) correctly decides whether a feasible solution of size exactly \(k\) exists in time \(T(n,k)\) and space \(S(n,k)\), then invoking \(A_k\) for all relevant \(k\) decides feasibility and identifies the minimum or maximum feasible cardinality. The total time is \(O(\sum_{k=0}^{n}T(n,k))\), and sequential execution uses space \(O(\max_{0\le k\le n}S(n,k)+\operatorname{poly}(n))\). Early stopping is valid when sizes are inspected monotonically toward the desired optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run an exact parameterized routine separately for each possible solution size; summing layer costs yields an exact exponential algorithm.
assumptions_latex: Every feasible solution is a subset of an \(n\)-element universe.
\(A_k\) decides existence at exact cardinality \(k\).
Calls are executed sequentially and their workspaces are reusable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimization takes time \(O(\sum_{k=0}^{n}T(n,k))\) and space \(O(\max_k S(n,k)+\operatorname{poly}(n))\).

notation.meaning: decision procedure for solutions of exact size k
running time on the cardinality-k layer
space used on the cardinality-k layer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the transfer leaf, but no source is supplied. Moreover, decision procedures alone identify the optimum cardinality but do not produce an optimizing solution unless witness recovery is assumed.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Local-Search Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer from an extension oracle for an upward-closed subset problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let feasible solutions form an upward-closed family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^U\), where \(|U|=n\). Suppose an extension algorithm, given \(S\subseteq U\) and \(k\ge0\), decides in time \(T(k)\operatorname{poly}(n)\) whether some \(X\subseteq U\setminus S\) with \(|X|\le k\) satisfies \(S\cup X\in\mathcal F\), and returns such an \(X\) when one exists. For any family \(\mathcal C_k\subseteq2^U\) such that every feasible set of size \(k\) contains some \(S\in\mathcal C_k\), invoking the extension algorithm on each \((S,k-|S|)\) finds a size-at-most-\(k\) solution in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\sum_{S\in\mathcal C_k}T(k-|S|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covering family of partial solutions converts a parameterized extension routine for a monotone problem into an exact search bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is upward closed under inclusion.
The extension algorithm is correct for every \((S,k)\).
Every feasible size-\(k\) set contains a member of \(\mathcal C_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated calls find a solution of size at most \(k\) within \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\sum_{S\in\mathcal C_k}T(k-|S|)\) time.

notation.meaning: covering family of partial size-k solutions
parameter dependence of the extension algorithm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role is plausible, but this particular transfer formulation needs validation. It must require every invoked \(S\) to satisfy \(|S|\le k\), and the coverage argument for solutions smaller than \(k\) should be stated explicitly.

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel-Then-Enumerate Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact search after a parameter-preserving reduction to a bounded kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an instance \((I,k)\), apply a kernelization producing \((I',k')\) with \(|I'|\le g(k)\), together with a sound lifting map. Enumerate every candidate solution encoded by a subset of the kernel universe, test each candidate for feasibility in \(q(g(k))\) time, and retain the best feasible candidate. Lift the retained candidate to a solution of \(I\); if none is feasible, return NO. If the kernel universe has at most \(g(k)\) elements, the enumeration takes \(O(2^{g(k)}q(g(k))+p(|I|))\) time and \(O(g(k)+s(|I|))\) working space when candidates are streamed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kernelize the parameterized instance, exhaustively inspect all kernel candidates, and lift the best one to the original instance.
assumptions_latex: Kernelization runs in time \(p(|I|)\) and yields size at most \(g(k)\).
Feasibility and objective values are preserved by reduction and lifting.
Kernel candidates can be streamed and tested in time \(q(g(k))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The design is exact with time \(O(2^{g(k)}q(g(k))+p(|I|))\) and streaming workspace \(O(g(k)+s(|I|))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the leaf, but no source supports the generic construction. The workspace bound omits candidate-testing and best-solution storage unless these are explicitly absorbed into \(s(|I|)\), and subset enumeration requires a specified kernel universe encoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard vertex-deletion formulation for finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a vertex cover is a set \(C\subseteq V\) such that every edge has at least one endpoint in \(C\): \[\forall\{u,v\}\in E,\quad u\in C\ \lor\ v\in C.\] Equivalently, deleting \(C\) leaves an edgeless graph, or \(V\setminus C\) is an independent set. The parameterized decision problem asks, for an integer \(k\ge0\), whether such a set exists with \(|C|\le k\); the optimization problem minimizes \(|C|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex cover meets every edge; equivalently, deleting it leaves no edges. The parameter is commonly the allowed cover size.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(k\) is a nonnegative integer in the decision version.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible decision witness is precisely a set \(C\subseteq V\) with \(|C|\le k\) meeting every edge.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the set-level equivalence between vertex covers, complementary independent sets, and cliques in the complement graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple undirected graph, let $V'\subseteq V$, and let $G^c=(V,E^c)$, where $E^c=\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V,\ u\neq v,\ \{u,v\}\notin E\}$. Then $V'$ is a vertex cover of $G$ if and only if $V\setminus V'$ is an independent set of $G$, if and only if $V\setminus V'$ is a clique of $G^c$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex subset is a vertex cover exactly when its complement is an independent set; equivalently, that complement is a clique in the complement graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Directedness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates symmetric directed encodings from genuinely directed instances, with the directed 2-cycle boundary made explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(k\in\mathbb N\), the graph \(G\) has a simple path of length at least \(k\) if and only if \(\overleftrightarrow G\) has a directed simple path of length at least \(k\). The restriction \(k\ge3\) avoids directed 2-cycles created by a single bidirected edge. These equivalences fail for arbitrary orientations: the acyclic orientation \(D_\triangle\) with arcs \((1,2),(1,3),(2,3)\) has an underlying triangle but no directed cycle.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Steiner Tree decision problem asks whether there is a connected subgraph \(F\subseteq G\) satisfying \(T\subseteq V(F)\) and
\[w(F)=\sum_{e\in E(F)}w(e)\le B.\]
Vertices in \(V(F)\setminus T\) are permitted and are called Steiner vertices. Because weights are nonnegative, any feasible connected subgraph contains a spanning tree of no greater weight, so the selected subgraph may be required to be a tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypergraph Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses blocker duality for finite clutters and explicitly identifies the clutter reduction of an arbitrary finite hypergraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{H}=(V,\mathcal{E})\) be a finite clutter, meaning that no distinct \(E,F\in\mathcal{E}\) satisfy \(E\subsetneq F\). A transversal is a set \(T\subseteq V\) such that \(T\cap E\ne\varnothing\) for every \(E\in\mathcal{E}\). Define
\[b(\mathcal{H})=\bigl(V,\{T:T\text{ is an inclusion-minimal transversal of }\mathcal{H}\}\bigr).\]
Blocker duality states that
\[b(b(\mathcal{H}))=\mathcal{H}.\]
Thus the inclusion-minimal transversals determine a finite clutter uniquely. For an arbitrary finite hypergraph \(\mathcal{K}\), applying the blocker twice yields its clutter reduction, obtained by retaining precisely its inclusion-minimal hyperedges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite clutter, forming the hypergraph of minimal hitting sets twice recovers the original clutter. For an arbitrary finite hypergraph, the double blocker recovers its inclusion-minimal-edge reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{H}=(V,\mathcal{E})\) is a finite hypergraph.

\(b(\mathcal{H})\) is the hypergraph of inclusion-minimal transversals of \(\mathcal{H}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The blocker operation is involutive on finite clutters: \(b(b(\mathcal{H}))=\mathcal{H}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Set-Size Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to unweighted Hitting Set with fixed maximum hyperedge size \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an unweighted Hitting Set instance \((U,\mathcal{F},k)\) with \(|F|\le d\) for every \(F\in\mathcal{F}\). Maintain the family \(\mathcal{F}'\) of sets not yet hit and a remaining budget \(\ell\). Accept if \(\mathcal{F}'=\varnothing\). If \(\mathcal{F}'\ne\varnothing\) and \(\ell=0\), reject. Otherwise choose any \(F\in\mathcal{F}'\) and branch once for each \(u\in F\): select \(u\), delete every residual set containing \(u\), and replace \(\ell\) by \(\ell-1\). Every feasible completion must follow at least one such branch. Each branching node has at most \(d\) children and every root-to-leaf path has at most \(k\) branching steps, so the search tree has at most \(d^k\) leaves and can be implemented in time \(O(d^k\operatorname{poly}(|U|+|\mathcal{F}|))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every set has at most d elements, branch on an element of one unhit set, rejecting before branching if the remaining budget is zero. This decides size-k Hitting Set with at most d^k leaves and polynomial work per branch.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and \(\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^U\) is finite.
\(k\in\mathbb{N}\) is the hitting-set size bound.
There is a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that \(|F|\le d\) for every \(F\in\mathcal{F}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance is decidable using at most \(d^k\) search-tree leaves and time \(O(d^k\operatorname{poly}(|U|+|\mathcal{F}|))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An \(H\)-packing in \(G\) is a family \(\mathcal{Q}=\{G_1,\ldots,G_r\}\) of subgraphs of \(G\) such that each \(G_i\) is isomorphic to \(H\) and

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies hypergraph packing with vertex-disjoint hyperedge matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A hypergraph packing, also called a matching, is a subfamily \(M\subseteq\mathcal{E}\) satisfying
\[e\cap f=\varnothing\quad\text{for all distinct }e,f\in M.\]
The weighted packing problem maximizes \(w(M)=\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\). With unit weights, its optimum is the matching number

The parameterized decision version asks, given \((\mathcal{H},k)\), whether \(\nu(\mathcal{H})\ge k\). Under the identification of hyperedges with subsets of \(V\), this is exactly the corresponding Set Packing instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Packing-Model Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence among finite set packing, hypergraph matching, and conflict-graph independent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite and let \(\mathcal S\subseteq 2^U\). Form the hypergraph \(H=(U,\mathcal S)\) and the conflict graph \(C\) with vertex set \(\mathcal S\), where distinct \(A,B\in\mathcal S\) are adjacent exactly when \(A\cap B\ne\varnothing\). A subfamily \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal S\) is a set packing if and only if it is a matching of \(H\), if and only if \(\mathcal P\) is an independent set of \(C\). Consequently, \[\max\{|\mathcal P|:\mathcal P\text{ is a packing}\}=\nu(H)=\alpha(C).\] The constructions preserve solution cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set packings are exactly hypergraph matchings and independent sets in the associated conflict graph, with solution size preserved.
assumptions_latex: U\text{ and }\mathcal S\text{ are finite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{pack}(U,\mathcal S)=\nu(H)=\alpha(C)

knowledge_statements.title: Traveling Salesperson
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite symmetric traveling-salesperson optimization on a complete graph with extended-real edge costs permitting forbidden edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite vertex set \(V\) with \(|V|\ge 3\), the complete undirected graph \(K_V\), and an edge-cost function \(c:\binom{V}{2}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), a traveling-salesperson tour is a Hamiltonian cycle of \(K_V\). The symmetric traveling-salesperson value is \[\operatorname{TSP}(V,c)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E(C)}c(e):C\text{ is a Hamiltonian cycle of }K_V\right\}.\] A noncomplete input graph is represented by assigning cost \(+\infty\) to each absent edge; the value is \(+\infty\) exactly when no finite-cost Hamiltonian cycle exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric traveling-salesperson problem minimizes the total edge cost of a Hamiltonian cycle; infinite costs can represent forbidden edges.

c:\binom{V}{2}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}

Choosing each of the $n$ cities as the designated start gives $n$ representations of the cyclic traversal.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper vertex coloring and chromatic-number optimization for finite simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph. A proper \(q\)-coloring is a map \(f:V\to\{1,\ldots,q\}\) satisfying \(f(u)\ne f(v)\) for every \(\{u,v\}\in E\). The chromatic number is \[\chi(G)=\min\{q\in\mathbb N: G\text{ admits a proper }q\text{-coloring}\}.\] Equivalently, a proper \(q\)-coloring partitions \(V\) into at most \(q\) independent sets. The parameterized decision form asks, for input \((G,q)\), whether \(\chi(G)\le q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bandwidth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex bandwidth of a finite undirected graph under bijective linear layouts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with \(n=|V|\). A linear layout is a bijection \(\pi:V\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Its bandwidth is \(\max_{\{u,v\}\in E}|\pi(u)-\pi(v)|\), with the maximum over an empty edge set defined as \(0\). The bandwidth of \(G\) is \[\operatorname{bw}(G)=\min_{\pi:V\xrightarrow{\sim}\{1,\ldots,n\}}\max_{\{u,v\}\in E}|\pi(u)-\pi(v)|.\] Thus a threshold instance \((G,b)\) is feasible exactly when some layout places the endpoints of every edge at distance at most \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph bandwidth minimizes the greatest positional separation of adjacent vertices over all bijective linear vertex layouts.

n=|V|
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{bw}(G)=\min_{\pi}\max_{\{u,v\}\in E}|\pi(u)-\pi(v)|

notation.meaning: bijective linear layout of the vertices

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Layout Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic permutation-based optimization framework for finite graph layouts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\), let \(\Pi(V)\) be the set of bijections \(\pi:V\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A linear layout problem is specified by an objective functional \(F_G:\Pi(V)\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and asks for \[\operatorname{OPT}_F(G)=\min_{\pi\in\Pi(V)}F_G(\pi).\] A threshold version additionally receives \(B\) and asks whether some \(\pi\in\Pi(V)\) satisfies \(F_G(\pi)\le B\). Edge-length, cut-load, and vertex-separation objectives arise by choosing different functionals \(F_G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear layout problem optimizes a specified cost functional over all bijective orderings of a graph's vertices.

F_G\text{ is defined on every bijective layout}

knowledge_statements.title: Layout-Cost Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical edge-length and cut-load objectives induced by one vertex ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a layout \(\pi:V\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define edge length \(\ell_\pi(uv)=|\pi(u)-\pi(v)|\) and cut load \(c_\pi(i)=|\{uv\in E:\pi(u)\le i<\pi(v)\text{ or }\pi(v)\le i<\pi(u)\}|\). Standard variants are \[\max_{uv\in E}\ell_\pi(uv),\qquad \sum_{uv\in E}\ell_\pi(uv),\qquad \max_{1\le i<n}c_\pi(i).\] Minimizing these quantities over all layouts yields bandwidth, minimum linear arrangement, and cutwidth, respectively. Moreover, \(\sum_{uv\in E}\ell_\pi(uv)=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}c_\pi(i)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bandwidth-to-Layout Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle reduction from bandwidth optimization to monotone feasibility of edge-bounded bijective layouts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(n=|V|\), and for \(b\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) define \[L(G,b)=\left\{\pi:V\xrightarrow{\sim}\{1,\ldots,n\}:|\pi(u)-\pi(v)|\le b\text{ for every }\{u,v\}\in E\right\}.\] Then \[\operatorname{bw}(G)\le b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L(G,b)\ne\varnothing.\] Moreover, \(L(G,b)\subseteq L(G,b+1)\) whenever \(b<n-1\). Consequently, an oracle deciding whether \(L(G,b)\) is nonempty yields \(\operatorname{bw}(G)\) by binary search over \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), using at most \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) oracle queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bandwidth optimization reduces to monotone feasibility testing for bijective layouts in which every edge has length at most the tested threshold; binary search uses at most the stated logarithmic number of oracle queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-constrained minimum-cut formulation of finite weighted k-way graph partitioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\). Given an integer \(k\ge 2\) and capacities \(L_1,\ldots,L_k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), a feasible partition is an ordered tuple \((V_1,\ldots,V_k)\) of pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \(V\) and which satisfy \(|V_i|\le L_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Its cut cost is \[\operatorname{cut}_w(V_1,\ldots,V_k)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}w(\{u,v\})\,\mathbf 1\!\left[\exists i,j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}:i\ne j,\ u\in V_i,\ v\in V_j\right].\] Capacity-constrained weighted graph partitioning minimizes this cost over all feasible partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity-constrained weighted graph partitioning divides the vertices into ordered capacity-bounded parts while minimizing the total weight of edges whose endpoints lie in different parts.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-weight satisfiability parameterized by the number of true variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi\) be a propositional formula over a finite variable set \(X\), and let \(k\in\{0,\ldots,|X|\}\). The weight of an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) is \(\operatorname{wt}(a)=|\{x\in X:a(x)=1\}|\). The exact-weight satisfiability problem asks whether \[\exists a:X\to\{0,1\}\quad \varphi(a)=1\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{wt}(a)=k.\] Its standard parameter is \(k\). A separately specified at-most-weight variant replaces equality by \(\operatorname{wt}(a)\le k\); these predicates are distinct.

knowledge_statements.title: Backdoor Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong backdoors into a fixed tractable class of formulas or constraint instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a class \(\mathcal C\) of instances closed under applying partial assignments. For an instance \(F\) with variables \(X\), a set \(B\subseteq X\) is a strong \(\mathcal C\)-backdoor if, for every assignment \(\tau:B\to D\), the reduced instance \(F[\tau]\) belongs to \(\mathcal C\). The strong backdoor number is \[\operatorname{bd}_{\mathcal C}(F)=\min\{|B|:B\subseteq X\text{ is a strong }\mathcal C\text{-backdoor}\}.\] If membership and solving in \(\mathcal C\) are tractable, a supplied backdoor permits exhaustive branching over at most \(|D|^{|B|}\) assignments.

\mathcal C\text{ is closed under partial assignments}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{bd}_{\mathcal C}(F)=\min\{|B|:\forall\tau\in D^B,\ F[\tau]\in\mathcal C\}

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Parameters for Constraint Satisfaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal, dual, and incidence graph representations of a finite constraint instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite constraint instance \(I=(X,D,\mathcal C)\), its primal graph has vertex set \(X\) and joins variables occurring together in a constraint. Its dual graph has vertex set \(\mathcal C\) and joins constraints sharing a variable. Its incidence graph is bipartite on \(X\cup\mathcal C\), with an edge \(xC\) exactly when variable \(x\) occurs in constraint \(C\). knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Model Checking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-checking decision problem parameterized by formula size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a logic \(L\) and a finite relational vocabulary. The parameterized model-checking problem \(p\text{-}\mathrm{MC}(L)\) has input a finite structure \(\mathcal A\) and a sentence \(\varphi\in L\), parameter \(|\varphi|\), and asks whether \[\mathcal A\models\varphi.\] For a restricted structure class \(\mathfrak A\), the input additionally satisfies \(\mathcal A\in\mathfrak A\). knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Dimension Integer Programming

\(k\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists X\subseteq E:\ |X|\ge k\ \land\ X\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\).

children.title: Parity–Intersection Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences, separations, and parameter-preserving transfers between the two problem families.

knowledge_statements.title: Parity–Intersection Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why pair-union feasibility is not literally a matroid-intersection family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Common independent sets of two matroids are hereditary: if \(X\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\) and \(Y\subseteq X\), then \(Y\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\). In matroid parity, feasible element sets must be unions of prescribed pairs and need not be hereditary as subsets of \(E\). For the rank-two uniform matroid on \(E=\{a,b\}\) with the sole pair \(\{a,b\}\), the pair-unions are \(\varnothing\) and \(\{a,b\}\), but not \(\{a\}\). Hence an identity-on-elements encoding as common independent sets is impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pair unions are not hereditary, whereas intersections of matroid independence systems are; this blocks a direct identity-on-elements transfer.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are matroids on a common ground set.
Parity-feasible element sets must be unions of complete prescribed pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\text{pair unions independent in }M\}\ne\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\) in general on the unchanged ground set.

notation.meaning: uniform rank-two matroid on two elements
independent-set family of the i-th matroid

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: hereditary closure follows directly from the matroid independence axioms
Boundary excludes only identity-on-elements encodings, not gadget reductions
