children.title: Parameterized Complexity Barrier System
children.top_down_role: Reduction systems, hardness hierarchies, hypothesis-based running-time barriers, counting variants, and structural failure boundaries. Kernel lower bounds remain with preprocessing because their reductions certify a distinct compression barrier.

knowledge_statements.title: FPT Many-One Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard deterministic many-one reduction between parameterized decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For parameterized problems \(P,Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\), an FPT many-one reduction from \(P\) to \(Q\) is a mapping \(R(x,k)=(x',k')\) computable in time \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\) such that \((x,k)\in P\) if and only if \((x',k')\in Q\), and \(k'\le g(k)\) for computable functions \(f,g\). Only one target instance is produced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPT many-one reduction produces one equivalent target instance while bounding runtime and the new parameter solely through the old parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(P,Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\).
\(f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\le_{\mathrm{fpt}}^{\mathrm{m}}Q\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The many-one reduction definition is standard, precise, and correctly classified, but it has no parameterized-complexity source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: FPT Turing Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive oracle reduction with parameter-bounded queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For parameterized problems \(P,Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\), an FPT Turing reduction from \(P\) to \(Q\) is an oracle algorithm that decides every input \((x,k)\) in time \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\), counting each oracle call as one step, and makes only queries \((y,k_y)\) satisfying \(k_y\le g(k)\). The queries may depend on earlier oracle answers, and their total number and written length are bounded by the running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPT Turing reduction may ask adaptive target queries, but its runtime and every query parameter remain controlled by the source parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(P,Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\).
\(f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\le_{\mathrm{fpt}}^{\mathrm{T}}Q\).
review_flags: Oracle-cost convention should be checked against the selected source

children.title: Parameter Mapping
children.top_down_role: Mappings between source parameters and target parameters within parameterized reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter transformation induced by a parameterized reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) map each source instance \((x,k)\) to a target instance \((x',k')\). A parameter mapping for \(R\) is a computable function \(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) satisfying \(k'\le g(k)\) for every input. For an oracle reduction, the condition applies to every generated query parameter \(k_q\). The mapping is independent of \(|x|\), target-instance length, and intermediate oracle answers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter mapping bounds every target parameter by a computable function of the source parameter alone.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a parameterized many-one or oracle reduction.
\(k\) and \(k'\) denote source and target parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall(x,k),\ k'(R(x,k))\le g(k)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar and oracle-query bounds are coherent and definition is an appropriate kind, but the named parameter-mapping concept lacks a supporting reduction source.

children.title: Parameter Blowup Control
children.top_down_role: Admissible parameter growth and the boundaries at which a reduction loses useful parameter dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Blowup Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative admissibility condition for parameter growth under reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reduction has FPT-admissible parameter blowup if there exists a total computable function \(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that every target instance or oracle query produced from a source instance with parameter \(k\) has parameter at most \(g(k)\). Polynomial blowup is the stronger condition \(g(k)\le C(k+1)^c\) for constants \(C,c\ge0\); linear blowup requires \(g(k)\le ak+b\) for constants \(a,b\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter blowup is controlled when target parameters depend only computably on the source parameter; polynomial and linear control are stronger variants.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb N\) is the source parameter.
All produced target parameters are natural numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup k_{\mathrm{target}}\le g(k)\).

notation.meaning: parameter of any produced instance or query

review_flags: Source required for terminology and hierarchy of blowup regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The computable, polynomial, and linear growth conditions are internally consistent and condition fits the leaf, but the terminology and hierarchy require a source locator.

children.title: Multi-Parameter Distortion
children.top_down_role: Interactions among several parameters when a reduction preserves some scales but amplifies others.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Parameter Distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise distortion for reductions between vector-parameterized problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the source and target parameters be vectors \(\kappa(x)\in\mathbb N^r\) and \(\lambda(R(x))\in\mathbb N^s\). A distortion map is a computable function \(G:\mathbb N^r\to\mathbb N^s\) such that \(\lambda_j(R(x))\le G_j(\kappa(x))\) for every target coordinate \(j\in\{1,\ldots,s\}\). For oracle reductions, the inequality must hold for every query. Coordinatewise dependence records which source parameters control each target parameter and prevents hidden dependence on input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distortion map bounds each target parameter coordinate by a computable function of the complete source-parameter vector.
assumptions_latex: \(\kappa:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N^r\) and \(\lambda:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N^s\).
\(R\) is a many-one or oracle reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda(R(x))\le_{\mathrm{cw}}G(\kappa(x))\).
review_flags: Source required for multi-parameter reduction terminology

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinatewise vector bound is mathematically coherent, but distortion map and multi-parameter distortion are not established here as standard reduction terminology and no source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Preserving Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized many-one reductions controlling a designated structural measure and instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q,Q'\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\), let \(\sigma:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) be a structural measure, and let \(\mathcal C,\mathcal C'\subseteq\Sigma^*\). A structure-preserving reduction from \(Q\) to \(Q'\) is an algorithm mapping \((x,k)\) to \((x',k')\) in time \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\) such that \((x,k)\in Q\iff(x',k')\in Q'\), \(k'\le g(k)\), and \(\sigma(x')\le h(k,\sigma(x))\). Relative to the designated classes, it additionally satisfies \(x\in\mathcal C\Rightarrow x'\in\mathcal C'\). Here \(f,g,h\) are computable functions fixed independently of the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structure-preserving FPT reduction preserves answers, bounds parameter growth, and controls a chosen structural measure and target instance class.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) and \(Q'\) are parameterized decision problems.
\(\sigma\), \(\mathcal C\), and \(\mathcal C'\) are fixed before applying the reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\leq_{\mathrm{fpt}}Q'\) with controlled parameter and structural distortion.

notation.meaning: Designated structural measure of instance x.
Designated source and target structural classes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but “structure-preserving reduction” is not governed by one universal convention. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required for the structural-distortion and class-preservation conditions.

children.title: Gap-Preserving Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions organized by preservation of decision or optimization gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap-Preserving Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold-preserving parameterized reductions between maximization gap problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For maximization problems with optima \(\operatorname{OPT}_P\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{P'}\), a gap-preserving FPT reduction maps \((x,k)\) to \((x',k')\) in time \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\), where \(k'\le g(k)\), and supplies thresholds \(a'(k'),b'(k')\) satisfying \[\operatorname{OPT}_P(x)\ge a(k)\Rightarrow\operatorname{OPT}_{P'}(x')\ge a'(k'),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_P(x)\le b(k)\Rightarrow\operatorname{OPT}_{P'}(x')\le b'(k').\]No condition is imposed on instances whose optimum lies strictly between \(b(k)\) and \(a(k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reduction maps YES and NO threshold regions into corresponding target regions while bounding the new parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any algorithm separating the target gap separates the source gap after FPT preprocessing.

notation.meaning: Optimal value of source instance x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the gap-reduction container, but the precise parameterized threshold convention and requirements on the target thresholds vary across sources. No cited evidence supports the selected formulation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The minimization-to-maximization case, together with the parameter-matched composition property and its conditional inapproximability consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \Pi_1 be a minimization problem and \Pi_2 a maximization problem. A gap-preserving reduction \Gamma with parameters f_1,\alpha,f_2,\beta maps every instance x of \Pi_1 in polynomial time to an instance y=\Gamma(x) of \Pi_2 such that
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{\Pi_1}(x)\le f_1(x)\;\Longrightarrow\;\operatorname{OPT}_{\Pi_2}(y)\ge f_2(y),
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{\Pi_1}(x)>\alpha(|x|)f_1(x)\;\Longrightarrow\;\operatorname{OPT}_{\Pi_2}(y)<\beta(|y|)f_2(y),
\]
where \alpha(|x|)\ge 1 and \beta(|y|)\le 1. If \Gamma' is a gap-introducing reduction from SAT to \Pi_1 with matching parameters f_1 and \alpha, then \Gamma\circ\Gamma' is a gap-introducing reduction from SAT to \Pi_2 with parameters f_2 and \beta. Consequently, assuming \mathbf{P}\ne\mathbf{NP}, this composition establishes that \Pi_2 admits no \beta(|y|)-factor approximation algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a minimization problem Pi1 and a maximization problem Pi2, a gap-preserving reduction maps each Pi1 instance x in polynomial time to a Pi2 instance y. The low-optimum case for Pi1 implies the high-optimum case for Pi2, while the alpha-separated high-optimum case for Pi1 implies the beta-separated low-optimum case for Pi2. Here alpha is at least 1 and beta is at most 1. Composing this reduction after a gap-introducing SAT-to-Pi1 reduction with matching parameters yields a gap-introducing SAT-to-Pi2 reduction and, unless P equals NP, the stated beta-factor inapproximability result.
assumptions_latex: \Pi_1\text{ is a minimization problem}
\Pi_2\text{ is a maximization problem}
\Gamma:x\mapsto y\text{ is computable in polynomial time}
\alpha(|x|)\ge 1
\beta(|y|)\le 1
\Gamma'\text{ is a gap-introducing reduction from SAT to }\Pi_1\text{ with parameters }f_1,\alpha
\mathbf{P}\ne\mathbf{NP}\text{ for the inapproximability conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma\circ\Gamma'\text{ is a gap-introducing reduction to }\Pi_2\text{ with parameters }f_2,\beta;\text{ under }\mathbf{P}\ne\mathbf{NP},\text{ it excludes a }\beta(|y|)\text{-factor approximation algorithm for }\Pi_2.

children.title: Counting Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions organized by transfer of parameterized counting complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Counting Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: FPT oracle reductions that reconstruct exact solution counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F,F':\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) be parameterized counting functions. An FPT counting Turing reduction from \(F\) to \(F'\) is an oracle algorithm that, on \((x,k)\), outputs \(F(x,k)\) exactly in time \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\), excluding oracle computation, makes at most \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\) queries \((y_i,\ell_i)\), and satisfies \(\ell_i\le g(k)\) and \(|y_i|\le f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\). A parsimonious reduction is the special case of one query with \(F(x,k)=F'(y,\ell)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A counting reduction computes an exact source count using bounded-parameter oracle queries; parsimonious reductions preserve the count directly.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(F'\) take finite nonnegative-integer values.
\(f\) and \(g\) are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is exactly computable with FPT-bounded access to \(F'\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical role and local scope are suitable, but conventions for parameterized counting Turing and parsimonious reductions require authoritative support. No source establishes the stated runtime, query, and parameter bounds.

children.title: Gap-to-Counting Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Compatibility limits between gap-sensitive reductions and counting-sensitive reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap-to-Counting Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: When counting accuracy suffices, or fails, to distinguish zero from a positive count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N(x,k)\in\mathbb N\) count witnesses, with the associated decision problem accepting exactly when \(N(x,k)>0\). Exact counting decides this gap. An estimate \(\widehat N\) also suffices if either \(|\widehat N-N|<1/2\), because rounding recovers \(N\), or it has a multiplicative guarantee \((1-\varepsilon)N\le\widehat N\le(1+\varepsilon)N\) with \(0\le\varepsilon<1\), including the guarantee at \(N=0\). By contrast, an additive guarantee \(|\widehat N-N|\le\delta\) with \(\delta\ge1/2\) need not distinguish \(N=0\) from \(N=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Counting transfers to existence only when its accuracy distinguishes zero from one; additive error at least one half may not.
assumptions_latex: The source gap is precisely \(N=0\) versus \(N\ge1\).
\(N\) is integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zero-detection, not generic approximate counting alone, is the transfer criterion.

notation.meaning: Number of witnesses for the parameterized instance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, and the zero-versus-positive observations are plausible. A specific source is still required for presenting these approximation guarantees as a named gap-to-counting transfer boundary.

children.title: Weighted Circuit Models
children.top_down_role: Weighted parameterized problem representations based on Boolean circuits.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Circuit Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-weight satisfiability for Boolean circuits, the standard circuit model underlying the W-hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A weighted Boolean circuit instance is a pair \((C,k)\), where \(C\) is a finite acyclic circuit over Boolean inputs \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) with gates from \(\{\neg,\wedge,\vee\}\), and \(k\in\mathbb N\). The instance is accepted when there exists \(\alpha\in\{0,1\}^n\) such that \(C(\alpha)=1\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i=k\). The parameter is \(k\); circuit size, depth, and weft are properties of \(C\), not additional parameters unless explicitly stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted circuit satisfiability asks whether a Boolean circuit accepts an assignment having exactly k true inputs.
assumptions_latex: Circuit gates have finite fan-in, possibly unbounded.
Negations may be normalized to input literals without changing assignment weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance is equivalent to the existence of a satisfying input of Hamming weight exactly \(k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an appropriate definition of exact-weight circuit satisfiability, but no parameterized-complexity source supports the gate basis, weight convention, or normalization assumptions.

children.title: Weighted Formula Models
children.top_down_role: Weighted parameterized problem representations based on Boolean formulas.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Formula Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-weight satisfiability restricted to tree-shaped Boolean computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A weighted Boolean formula instance is a pair \((\varphi,k)\), where \(\varphi\) is a Boolean formula over variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and connectives \(\{\neg,\wedge,\vee\}\), and \(k\in\mathbb N\). Its syntax graph is a rooted tree, so every non-root subformula has exactly one parent occurrence. The instance is accepted if some assignment \(\alpha\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfies \(\varphi\) and has \(\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i=k\). Repeated occurrences of a variable refer to the same input coordinate and are counted only once in the weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted formula satisfiability seeks a satisfying assignment with exactly k true variables in a tree-shaped Boolean expression.
assumptions_latex: Formula connectives have finite fan-in, possibly unbounded.
The parameter is the assignment weight \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance is equivalent to satisfiability by an assignment of Hamming weight exactly \(k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the weighted-formula leaf and consistently counts variables rather than occurrences. An authoritative source with a precise locator is required for the formula model and exact-weight convention.

children.title: Circuit–Formula Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Complexity-preserving translations and expressive separations between the two representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Circuit–Formula Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unfolding circuits into formulas while preserving the computed function and assignment weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every Boolean formula \(\varphi\) is a Boolean circuit computing the same function, with the same size, depth, and satisfying assignment weights. Conversely, a circuit \(C\) of size \(s\) and depth \(d\) can be unfolded by duplicating each shared subcircuit at every use, producing a formula \(\varphi_C\) with \(\varphi_C(\alpha)=C(\alpha)\) for every assignment \(\alpha\). The unfolding preserves depth and weft and has size at most \(1+s+\cdots+s^d\). Thus weighted satisfiability and the weight parameter are preserved, although representation size may grow exponentially when depth is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Formulas are circuits without sharing; unfolding removes sharing while preserving function, weight, depth, and weft, but may enlarge size.
assumptions_latex: Circuit size counts input and gate nodes.
Depth is the maximum number of gates on an input-to-output path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((C,k)\) is satisfiable exactly when \((\varphi_C,k)\) is satisfiable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but the claimed unfolding size bound and preservation of depth and weft require inspectable support. These details depend on the size, depth, and gate conventions adopted.

children.title: Weft Stratification
children.top_down_role: Classification routes based on the placement of large-fanin gates.

knowledge_statements.title: Weft Stratification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit stratification by the number of unbounded-fan-in gates encountered along a path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a constant fan-in bound \(b\ge2\). A gate is large if its fan-in exceeds \(b\), and small otherwise. The weft of a Boolean circuit \(C\) is \[\operatorname{weft}(C)=\max_{P}\bigl|\{v\in P:v\text{ is a large gate}\}\bigr|,\]where \(P\) ranges over directed input-to-output paths. Circuits of weft at most \(t\) form the \(t\)-th weft stratum. Negation gates, having fan-in one, are small and do not increase weft.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Circuit weft is the maximum number of unbounded-fan-in gates on an input-to-output path.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit.
The bound \(b\) is fixed independently of the instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{weft}(C)\le t\) exactly when every input-to-output path contains at most \(t\) large gates.

notation.meaning: Fixed upper bound defining small fan-in.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the leaf and is internally consistent, but the cutoff defining a large gate and the precise path convention must be tied to an authoritative W-hierarchy source.

children.title: Depth Stratification
children.top_down_role: Classification routes based on circuit-depth restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Depth Stratification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit stratification by the maximum gate-path length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The depth of a finite acyclic Boolean circuit \(C\) is \[\operatorname{depth}(C)=\max_P |P\cap G(C)|,\]where \(P\) ranges over directed input-to-output paths and \(G(C)\) is the set of gates, excluding input nodes. The depth-\(d\) stratum consists of circuits satisfying \(\operatorname{depth}(C)\le d\). A circuit family has bounded depth if one constant \(d\), independent of input size and weight parameter, bounds every circuit in the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Circuit depth is the greatest number of gates on an input-to-output path; bounded depth uses one uniform constant.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is finite and acyclic.
Input nodes are assigned depth zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) belongs to the depth-\(d\) stratum if and only if every input-to-output path contains at most \(d\) gates.

notation.meaning: Set of non-input gates of C.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the depth-stratification leaf. A source is needed because circuit depth conventions differ on whether inputs and gates are counted and how path length is measured.

children.title: Joint Weft–Depth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Hierarchy regions determined by simultaneous weft and depth constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Weft–Depth Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit classes indexed simultaneously by maximum weft and maximum depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(t,d\ge0\), define \[\mathcal C_{t,d}=\{C:\operatorname{weft}(C)\le t\text{ and }\operatorname{depth}(C)\le d\}.\]Weighted satisfiability on \(\mathcal C_{t,d}\) asks, with parameter \(k\), whether \(C\in\mathcal C_{t,d}\) accepts an assignment of weight exactly \(k\). For fixed \(t\), the standard bounded-depth regime permits any fixed \(d\); its FPT many-one closure yields the circuit characterization of \(W[t]\). Increasing either index weakens the restriction, so \(\mathcal C_{t,d}\subseteq\mathcal C_{t+1,d}\cap\mathcal C_{t,d+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint regimes bound both large-gate crossings and path length; fixed-weft bounded-depth weighted satisfiability characterizes W-hierarchy levels.
assumptions_latex: The small-gate fan-in convention is fixed.
\(t\) and \(d\) are constants independent of each instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((t,d)\) determines a monotone two-dimensional stratification of weighted circuit satisfiability.

notation.meaning: Circuits of weft at most t and depth at most d.
The t-th class of the W-hierarchy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The joint-regime representation is locally appropriate, and the monotone inclusions follow from the definitions. The substantive characterization of W[t] by FPT closure of bounded-depth, bounded-weft weighted satisfiability requires an authoritative citation and locator.

children.title: W[1]-Complete Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Canonical problem families classified as complete for W[1].

knowledge_statements.title: W[1]-Complete Problem Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical parameterized problems complete for the first nontrivial W-hierarchy level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under FPT many-one reductions, parameterized \(k\)-Clique, parameterized \(k\)-Independent Set, and Short Nondeterministic Turing Machine Acceptance are \(W[1]\)-complete. In the first two problems the parameter is the requested vertex-set size \(k\). In the machine problem, an instance \((M,x,k)\) asks whether nondeterministic machine \(M\) accepts input \(x\) within \(k\) steps, and the parameter is \(k\). Completeness means membership in \(W[1]\) together with an FPT reduction from every problem in \(W[1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clique, Independent Set, and short nondeterministic acceptance are canonical W[1]-complete parameterized problem families.
assumptions_latex: Reductions are FPT many-one reductions.
The machine model is fixed and effectively encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each listed family is both in \(W[1]\) and \(W[1]\)-hard.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind is reasonable for a catalog of complete families, but each W[1]-completeness classification—especially short nondeterministic Turing-machine acceptance and its machine convention—requires authoritative theorem-level support.

children.title: W[1]-Hard Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Problem families carrying W[1]-hardness without requiring a completeness classification.

knowledge_statements.title: W[1]-Hard Problem Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Problem families receiving FPT reductions from every problem in W[1].
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized problem \(Q\) is \(W[1]\)-hard under FPT many-one reductions if, for every \(L\in W[1]\), one has \(L\leq_{\mathrm{fpt}}Q\); membership of \(Q\) in \(W[1]\) is not required. Parameterized Dominating Set and parameterized Set Cover, each parameterized by solution size, are \(W[2]\)-complete and hence \(W[1]\)-hard under the standard inclusion \(W[1]\subseteq W[2]\). More generally, every problem hard for a W-hierarchy class containing \(W[1]\) is \(W[1]\)-hard by transitivity of FPT reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: W[1]-hardness requires reductions from all W[1] problems but not membership; W[2]-complete families provide standard examples.
assumptions_latex: Hardness uses FPT many-one reductions.
The standard hierarchy inclusion \(W[1]\subseteq W[2]\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parameterized Dominating Set and Set Cover are \(W[1]\)-hard.

notation.meaning: There is an FPT many-one reduction from L to Q.
The second level of the W-hierarchy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hardness definition and examples fit the leaf, but the W[2]-completeness of Dominating Set and Set Cover and the hierarchy inclusion used to infer W[1]-hardness require specific authoritative citations.

children.title: W[1] Completeness–Hardness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Membership, reduction, and representation issues separating completeness claims from hardness-only claims.

assumptions_latex: The parameterized problem \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) is W[1]-hard under fpt many-one reductions.
The standard conjecture \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{W[1]}\) holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No algorithm decides every instance \((x,k)\) of \(Q\) in time \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\) for any computable \(f\).

notation.meaning: Class of fixed-parameter tractable parameterized problems.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard conditional consequence of W[1]-hardness under fpt reductions.
No supplied locator directly supports parameterized complexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional algorithmic boundary induced by W[1]-hardness; it does not assert an unconditional time lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized problem \(Q\) is W[1]-complete when \(Q\in\mathrm{W[1]}\) and every problem in \(\mathrm{W[1]}\) fpt-reduces to \(Q\); it is W[1]-hard when only the latter condition is required. If a W[1]-hard problem had an algorithm of running time \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\), closure of \(\mathrm{FPT}\) under fpt reductions would imply \(\mathrm{W[1]}=\mathrm{FPT}\). Hence, assuming \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{W[1]}\), W[1]-hardness is the boundary excluding fixed-parameter tractability, while completeness additionally locates the problem inside \(\mathrm{W[1]}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: W[1]-hardness conditionally excludes fixed-parameter tractability; W[1]-completeness additionally requires membership in W[1].
knowledge_statements.title: W[1] Completeness–Hardness Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional boundary and the distinction between W[1]-hardness and W[1]-completeness are mathematically standard, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. However, no source or inspectable locator supports the reduction convention, closure claim, or conditional consequence.

children.title: W[2]-Complete Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Canonical problem families classified as complete for W[2].

assumptions_latex: Problems are parameterized by the requested solution size \(k\).
Completeness is measured under fpt many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parameterized Dominating Set, Set Cover, and Hitting Set are W[2]-complete in their standard size-parameterized decision forms.

notation.meaning: The parameter bounding the selected vertices or sets.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: These are canonical W[2]-complete covering and domination problems under solution-size parameterization.
No supplied locator directly supports the completeness classifications.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical size-parameterized covering and domination families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \((G,k)\), Dominating Set asks whether \(G\) has a dominating vertex set of size at most \(k\). For \((U,\mathcal S,k)\), Set Cover asks whether at most \(k\) members of \(\mathcal S\) cover \(U\), and Hitting Set asks whether some \(H\subseteq U\) with \(|H|\le k\) intersects every member of \(\mathcal S\). Each parameterized problem belongs to \(\mathrm{W[2]}\), and every problem in \(\mathrm{W[2]}\) admits an fpt many-one reduction to it; consequently, each is W[2]-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dominating Set, Set Cover, and Hitting Set parameterized by solution size are canonical W[2]-complete problems.
knowledge_statements.title: W[2]-Complete Problem Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three size-parameterized formulations are stated consistently, and property is a reasonable kind for this problem-family leaf. Their W[2]-completeness classifications require an authoritative parameterized-complexity citation with a precise locator.

children.title: W[2]-Hard Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Problem families carrying W[2]-hardness without requiring a completeness classification.

assumptions_latex: A parameterized problem \(Q\) receives instances \((x,k)\).
Hardness is measured under fpt many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An fpt reduction from a W[2]-complete problem to \(Q\) certifies that \(Q\) is W[2]-hard, regardless of whether \(Q\in\mathrm{W[2]}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Hardness propagation from a complete source is the standard reduction certificate.
No supplied locator directly supports W[2] reductions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction-based certification for W[2]-hard families, including problems not known to lie in W[2].
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be any W[2]-complete parameterized problem, such as size-parameterized Dominating Set. A mapping \(R:(x,k)\mapsto(x',k')\) certifies W[2]-hardness of \(Q\) when \(R\) is computable in time \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\), satisfies \(k'\le g(k)\) for computable \(f,g\), and obeys \((x,k)\in D\) if and only if \((x',k')\in Q\). By transitivity of fpt reductions, every problem in \(\mathrm{W[2]}\) then fpt-reduces to \(Q\). Membership of \(Q\) in \(\mathrm{W[2]}\) is not part of this certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reducing a W[2]-complete problem to a target certifies W[2]-hardness, without establishing target membership in W[2].
knowledge_statements.title: W[2]-Hard Problem Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction certificate is mathematically coherent, distinguishes hardness from membership, and certificate fits the leaf. No cited source supports the W[2]-complete starting problem, the exact fpt-reduction definition, or hardness propagation.

children.title: W[2] Completeness–Hardness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Membership and reduction issues separating completeness claims from hardness-only claims.

assumptions_latex: The parameterized problem \(Q\) is W[2]-hard under fpt many-one reductions.
The standard conjecture \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{W[2]}\) holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem \(Q\) has no fixed-parameter algorithm; W[2]-completeness further requires \(Q\in\mathrm{W[2]}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The boundary follows from closure of FPT under fpt reductions.
No supplied locator directly supports the W[2] classification boundary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional distinction between W[2]-hardness and W[2]-completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: W[2]-hardness of \(Q\) means that every problem in \(\mathrm{W[2]}\) fpt-reduces to \(Q\), whereas W[2]-completeness means both W[2]-hardness and \(Q\in\mathrm{W[2]}\). If a W[2]-hard \(Q\) were in \(\mathrm{FPT}\), composing its fixed-parameter algorithm with the reductions would give \(\mathrm{W[2]}\subseteq\mathrm{FPT}\); since \(\mathrm{FPT}\subseteq\mathrm{W[2]}\), equality would follow. Thus, under \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{W[2]}\), hardness excludes fixed-parameter tractability, but it does not supply the upper-bound membership needed for completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: W[2]-hardness conditionally rules out FPT, while W[2]-completeness additionally establishes membership in W[2].
knowledge_statements.title: W[2] Completeness–Hardness Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional exclusion of FPT and the additional membership requirement for completeness match this boundary leaf, with an appropriate failure_boundary kind. A precise source is still required for the hierarchy inclusions, reduction closure, and classification convention.

children.title: W[P] Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Problem families classified through W[P]-level parameterized complexity.

assumptions_latex: Boolean circuits have arbitrary depth and are given with a target Hamming weight \(k\).
Reductions are fpt many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weighted Circuit Satisfiability is W[P]-complete and defines the canonical W[P] problem family under fpt reductions.

notation.meaning: Class characterized by weighted satisfiability for unrestricted Boolean circuits.
Hamming weight of a Boolean assignment.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Weighted Circuit Satisfiability is the canonical complete problem defining W[P].
No supplied locator directly supports W[P].
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit characterization of W[P] using the assignment weight as parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Weighted Circuit Satisfiability has input \((C,k)\), where \(C\) is a Boolean circuit with \(n\) inputs, and asks whether there exists \(a\in\{0,1\}^n\) such that \(|a|_1=k\) and \(C(a)=1\). The class \(\mathrm{W[P]}\) consists exactly of parameterized problems admitting fpt many-one reductions to this problem. Consequently, Weighted Circuit Satisfiability is W[P]-complete. Equivalent W[P] problem families arise by encoding the choice of at most \(k\) nondeterministic objects or bits followed by fixed-parameter tractable deterministic verification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: W[P] is characterized by weighted satisfiability of unrestricted Boolean circuits and by bounded nondeterministic choice with tractable verification.
knowledge_statements.title: W[P] Problem Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted unrestricted-circuit characterization is suitable representation content for W[P]. The asserted equivalence with bounded nondeterministic choice depends on a precise machine model and resource bound, neither of which is cited, so the complete mathematical version cannot be validated from the supplied inventory.

children.title: Higher W-Level Families
children.top_down_role: Problem families associated with levels of the W-hierarchy above the standard lower strata.

assumptions_latex: Circuit depth is bounded by a constant independent of input size.
The parameter is the required Hamming weight \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each fixed \(t\ge1\), weighted satisfiability of constant-depth circuits of weft at most \(t\) is complete for \(\mathrm{W[t]}\).

notation.meaning: The t-th level of the W-hierarchy.
Maximum number of large-fan-in gates on an input-output path.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Bounded-depth, bounded-weft weighted circuit satisfiability is the standard representation of W[t].
Exact circuit conventions require an authoritative parameterized-complexity source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard weighted-circuit representation for fixed finite levels above W[2].
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(t\ge1\). A mixed Boolean circuit has weft at most \(t\) when every input-output path contains at most \(t\) gates of unbounded fan-in; its depth is bounded separately by a constant. The weighted satisfiability problem asks, for \((C,k)\), whether \(C\) accepts an input of Hamming weight exactly \(k\). Under the standard circuit convention, the closure of these problems under fpt many-one reductions is \(\mathrm{W[t]}\), and weighted satisfiability for the corresponding circuit family is \(\mathrm{W[t]}\)-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each fixed W[t] level is represented by weighted satisfiability of constant-depth circuits whose weft is at most t.
knowledge_statements.title: Higher W-Level Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is appropriate for this leaf, but the completeness claim depends on the exact circuit basis, treatment of large gates, depth bound, and definition of weft. The phrase "depth is bounded by a constant" also needs a source clarifying the uniform problem family used for completeness.

children.title: Interlevel Placement Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Containment, separation, and classification limits linking W[P] with higher hierarchy levels.

assumptions_latex: All inclusions and reductions use one fixed standard definition of the W-hierarchy.
No unproved collapse or separation conjecture is assumed as a theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership at level \(\mathrm{W[t]}\) gives membership at every higher finite level and in \(\mathrm{W[P]}\), but does not establish strict placement.

notation.meaning: The union of all finite W-levels.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The displayed inclusions and absence of known strict separations are standard features of the W-hierarchy.
No supplied locator directly supports interlevel placement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Known inclusions versus unproved strict separations among upper W-levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard inclusions are \(\mathrm{FPT}\subseteq\mathrm{W[1]}\subseteq\mathrm{W[2]}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathrm{W[*]}\subseteq\mathrm{W[P]}\). Thus, an upper-bound reduction to a \(\mathrm{W[t]}\)-complete problem places a problem at level \(t\) or below, while hardness for \(\mathrm{W[s]}\) with \(s<t\) supplies only a lower placement. A proof of \(\mathrm{W[t]}\)-completeness does not imply exclusion from \(\mathrm{W[t-1]}\) unless the adjacent levels are known to differ. No strict separation between consecutive standard W-levels is presently available unconditionally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: W-level inclusions give upper placements, but completeness at one level does not unconditionally exclude membership in a lower level.
knowledge_statements.title: Interlevel Placement Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly separates established inclusions from unproved strict placement, and failure_boundary fits the container. The inclusion through W[*] into W[P] and the current absence of adjacent-level separations require a precise, authoritative locator.

assumptions_latex: The standard fpt-reduction definitions of \(\mathrm{FPT}\), \(\mathrm{W[t]}\), and \(\mathrm{W[P]}\) are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The known hierarchy consists of inclusions; strictness of its principal adjacent inclusions remains a conjectural boundary.

notation.meaning: The t-th class in the W-hierarchy.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard parameterized-complexity theory provides inclusions but no unconditional principal separations.
No supplied locator directly supports hierarchy separation status.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epistemic boundary between established inclusions and conjectured strictness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Parameterized complexity theory establishes \(\mathrm{FPT}\subseteq\mathrm{W[1]}\subseteq\mathrm{W[2]}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathrm{W[P]}\). The assertions \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{W[1]}\), \(\mathrm{W[1]}\ne\mathrm{W[2]}\), and analogous strict separations are conjectures rather than unconditional theorems. Therefore, W-hardness yields an exclusion from \(\mathrm{FPT}\) only conditionally, and completeness at level \(t\) cannot by itself prove nonmembership in a lower level. Any unconditional statement requiring one of these separations crosses the currently established hierarchy boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The W-hierarchy has established inclusions, but its central strict separations remain unproved and hardness consequences are conditional.
knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchy Separation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement matches the hierarchy-separation topic and appropriately uses failure_boundary. Its claims about the established inclusion chain and present separation status are not supported by any cited parameterized-complexity source.

assumptions_latex: Counting problems output the number of weight-\(k\) accepting assignments.
Reductions are parameterized counting reductions of the selected standard type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(t\ge1\), weighted model counting for bounded-depth, weft-\(t\) circuits is complete for \(\#\mathrm{W[t]}\).

notation.meaning: The t-th counting class corresponding to W[t].
Number of accepting assignments of Hamming weight k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The counting W-hierarchy is canonically defined through weighted model counting for bounded-weft circuits.
The precise reduction convention varies across sources and requires citation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit-based definition; completeness depends on the chosen parameterized counting-reduction convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Boolean circuit \(C\) with \(n\) inputs, define \(\#_k(C)=|\{a\in\{0,1\}^n:|a|_1=k\text{ and }C(a)=1\}|\). Fix \(t\ge1\). The class \(\#\mathrm{W[t]}\) is the closure, under the chosen standard parameterized counting reductions, of the function problem \((C,k)\mapsto\#_k(C)\) restricted to constant-depth circuits of weft at most \(t\). Under that convention, weighted model counting for this circuit family is \(\#\mathrm{W[t]}\)-complete, and the resulting classes form the counting W-hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The class #W[t] is generated by counting weight-k satisfying assignments of constant-depth circuits having weft at most t.
knowledge_statements.title: The Counting W-Hierarchy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is suitable for the counting-hierarchy topic, but the definition and completeness claim are explicitly relative to an unspecified "chosen standard" counting reduction. Different reduction conventions can change the formulation, so an authoritative source and exact locator are necessary before this version can be reviewed reliably.

assumptions_latex: Parameterized counting functions map \(\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) to \(\mathbb N\).
The reduction preserves the exact output value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A parameterized parsimonious reduction transfers exact-counting algorithms and counting hardness from \(G\) to \(F\).

notation.meaning: Source and target parameterized counting functions.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard exact-value-preserving form of a parameterized parsimonious reduction.
No supplied locator directly supports parameterized counting reductions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parsimonious fpt reductions; broader oracle or metric reductions are not included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized parsimonious reduction from \(F:\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) to \(G:\Gamma^*\times\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) is a mapping \(R(x,k)=(y,k')\) computable in time \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\), for some computable \(f\), such that \(k'\le g(k)\) for a computable \(g\) and \(F(x,k)=G(y,k')\) for every \((x,k)\). Consequently, any fpt algorithm for \(G\) yields one for \(F\), and hardness of \(F\) transfers to \(G\) by composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parsimonious fpt reduction preserves the exact count while bounding the target parameter by a function of the source parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Counting Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-value-preserving mapping is a coherent definition of a parameterized parsimonious reduction, and definition fits the topic. No source supports this terminology, its precise time and parameter requirements, or the stated transfer consequences.

assumptions_latex: The counting function \(F(x,k)\) is nonnegative and exactly computable.
Its associated decision problem asks whether at least one witness exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact fixed-parameter counting implies fixed-parameter decision by testing \(F(x,k)>0\); the reverse implication is not generally valid.

notation.meaning: Number of witnesses for instance x at parameter k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Positivity converts exact counting to existence decision, whereas a decision oracle supplies no multiplicity information.
No supplied locator directly supports parameterized decision-counting separations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way algorithmic implication between exact counting and witness existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x,k)\) count the witnesses of a parameterized instance and let \(L_F=\{(x,k):F(x,k)>0\}\). If \(F\) is computable in time \(f(k)|x|^{O(1)}\), then \(L_F\) is decidable within the same asymptotic bound by computing \(F(x,k)\) and testing positivity. Conversely, an algorithm deciding membership in \(L_F\) reveals only whether the count is zero and does not generally determine \(F(x,k)\). Thus decision tractability alone does not imply exact-counting tractability; a separation claim between named classes still requires an appropriate hardness result or complexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact FPT counting yields FPT existence testing, but an existence decision algorithm generally cannot recover the number of witnesses.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision–Counting Separations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positivity reduction from exact counting to existence decision is correct, and the record carefully avoids asserting an unconditional named-class separation. Failure_boundary fits the leaf, but the claimed one-way decision-counting boundary still lacks a cited formal framework and inspectable locator.

assumptions_latex: A parameterized decision problem is \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\).
Hardness is measured by ordinary polynomial-time many-one reductions on a fixed parameter slice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If one fixed slice \(Q_{k_0}\) is NP-hard, then \(Q\) is para-NP-hard and cannot belong to XP unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: The language obtained by fixing the parameter to k.
The class with running time polynomial for every fixed parameter value.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: NP-hardness of a constant parameter slice is the standard sufficient condition for para-NP-hardness and excludes XP conditionally.
No supplied locator directly supports para-NP-hardness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-slice criterion and its conditional exclusion of XP algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized problem \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\), define its \(k\)-th slice by \(Q_k=\{x:(x,k)\in Q\}\). A standard sufficient condition for para-NP-hardness is the existence of a constant \(k_0\) for which \(Q_{k_0}\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions. If \(Q\in\mathrm{XP}\), an algorithm with running time \(|x|^{h(k)}\) would decide the fixed slice \(Q_{k_0}\) in polynomial time. Therefore an NP-hard fixed slice implies \(Q\notin\mathrm{XP}\), and hence \(Q\notin\mathrm{FPT}\), unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: NP-hardness at one constant parameter value establishes para-NP-hardness and conditionally rules out even XP membership.
knowledge_statements.title: Para-NP-Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-slice argument conditionally excluding XP is mathematically coherent, and condition fits the leaf as a sufficient criterion. An authoritative source is needed to establish the adopted definition of para-NP-hardness and to support the fixed-slice criterion; none of the supplied sources addresses parameterized complexity.

children.title: XP Membership Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parameterized problem families whose tractability is confined to XP-type running-time dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: XP Membership Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform deterministic XP for decision problems parameterized by a nonnegative integer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized decision problem \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) belongs to \(\mathrm{XP}\) if there exist a deterministic algorithm, a computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), and a constant \(c\) such that, on every input \((x,k)\), the algorithm decides whether \((x,k)\in Q\) in time at most \((|x|+k+c)^{f(k)}\). Thus the polynomial exponent may depend on the parameter, but one uniform algorithm and one computable running-time bound must handle all parameter values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: XP contains uniformly decidable parameterized problems whose running time is polynomial in input length for every fixed parameter, with parameter-dependent degree.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) is a parameterized decision problem.
The parameter \(k\) is encoded as part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\in\mathrm{XP}\iff Q\) has a uniform running time of the form \((|x|+k+c)^{f(k)}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard uniform definition of the parameterized class XP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the XP leaf, but no authoritative source or inspectable locator supports the chosen uniform runtime formulation.

children.title: Slice-Wise Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity behavior observed after fixing individual parameter values.

knowledge_statements.title: Slice-Wise Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity of the ordinary language obtained by fixing one parameter value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized problem \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\), its \(k\)-th slice is the classical language \(Q_k=\{x\in\Sigma^*:(x,k)\in Q\}\). The problem is slice-wise polynomial-time decidable if, for every fixed \(k\), there exist an algorithm \(A_k\) and constants \(c_k,d_k\) such that \(A_k\) decides \(Q_k\) in time at most \(c_k(|x|+1)^{d_k}\). This definition alone imposes no effective procedure for obtaining \(A_k,c_k,d_k\) from \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each fixed-parameter slice is a classical language; slice-wise polynomiality permits a separate polynomial algorithm and degree for every slice.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\).
\(k\) is fixed when the slice \(Q_k\) is analyzed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is slice-wise polynomial exactly when every \(Q_k\) has some polynomial-time decider.

notation.meaning: Classical language obtained by fixing the parameter to k.
A decider that may depend nonuniformly on the fixed slice.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of slices and nonuniform slice-wise polynomiality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonuniform slice-wise definition is coherent and fits the leaf, but the distinction from uniform XP requires an authoritative parameterized-complexity citation with a specific locator.

children.title: FPT–XP Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural and reduction-based distinctions between fixed-parameter tractability and XP membership.

knowledge_statements.title: FPT–XP Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime-form distinction between uniform fixed-parameter tractability and XP membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\). If a uniform algorithm decides \(Q\) in time \(f(k)(|x|+k+1)^c\), where \(f\) is computable and \(c\) is independent of \(k\), then \(Q\in\mathrm{FPT}\) and hence \(Q\in\mathrm{XP}\). XP additionally permits bounds \((|x|+k+1)^{g(k)}\) with parameter-dependent exponent \(g(k)\). Consequently, an XP algorithm establishes FPT membership only when its input-size exponent can be bounded independently of \(k\), after parameter-only factors are separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FPT is contained in XP. The boundary is whether the input-size exponent is constant or may grow with the parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) are computable.
All stated algorithms are uniform.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{FPT}\subseteq\mathrm{XP}\), with constant versus parameter-dependent input-size exponent distinguishing the two runtime regimes.

notation.meaning: An input-size exponent independent of the parameter.
An exponent allowed to depend on the parameter.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct comparison of the standard FPT and XP runtime definitions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The FPT-versus-XP runtime distinction is mathematically standard and the property kind fits, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonuniform Slice Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Failure modes caused by complexity behavior that varies irregularly across fixed-parameter slices.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniform Slice Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slice-wise triviality does not imply a uniform decider or XP membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\subseteq\mathbb N\) be undecidable and define \(Q\subseteq\{\varepsilon\}^*\times\mathbb N\) by \((\varepsilon,k)\in Q\) exactly when \(k\in H\). For each fixed \(k\), the slice \(Q_k\) is either \(\{\varepsilon\}\) or \(\varnothing\), so it has a constant-time decider. Nevertheless, a uniform decider for \(Q\) would decide \(H\) by running on \((\varepsilon,k)\). Hence \(Q\) is undecidable and is not in \(\mathrm{XP}\), despite every slice being computationally trivial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undecidable set can be encoded across individually trivial slices, showing that nonuniform slice-wise polynomiality does not imply XP membership.
assumptions_latex: \(H\subseteq\mathbb N\) is undecidable.
\(\varepsilon\) denotes the empty word.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_k\in\mathrm{P}\) for every \(k\), while \(Q\notin\mathrm{XP}\).

notation.meaning: An undecidable set of natural numbers.
The slice of Q at parameter k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary undecidability construction separating nonuniform slices from uniform XP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction correctly exhibits a nonuniform-slice pathology and counterexample is the right kind, but it has no cited source or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized-Approximation Hardness Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap reductions transfer parameterized decision hardness to fixed-ratio approximation hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb N\), and let \(\Pi\) be a minimization problem. Suppose an FPT-computable reduction maps \((x,k)\) to an instance \(I\), threshold \(t>0\), and parameter \(k'\le g(k)\), with \((x,k)\in L\Rightarrow\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le t\) and \((x,k)\notin L\Rightarrow\operatorname{OPT}(I)>\rho t\), where \(\rho\ge1\). Any FPT \(\rho\)-approximation for \(\Pi\) would decide \(L\): accept exactly when its returned feasible value is at most \(\rho t\). Thus parameterized hardness of \(L\) excludes such an approximation under the corresponding class-separation assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPT gap reduction converts a fixed-ratio FPT approximation algorithm into an FPT decision algorithm for the source problem.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is a minimization problem and \(\rho\ge1\).
The reduction is FPT-computable and satisfies \(k'\le g(k)\).
The displayed completeness and soundness gap holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An FPT \(\rho\)-approximation for \(\Pi\) implies an FPT algorithm for \(L\).

notation.meaning: Optimal objective value of the reduced minimization instance.
Approximation ratio and reduction gap factor.
Gap threshold produced by the reduction.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard gap-reduction argument for parameterized approximation hardness

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Dependence Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic ETH transfer excluding subexponential dependence on a target parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume ETH: 3-SAT on formulas with \(N\) variables cannot be solved in time \(2^{o(N)}\). Suppose a polynomial-time reduction maps every such formula \(F\) to an equivalent instance \((I,k)\) of a parameterized problem \(Q\), with \(|I|\le N^{O(1)}\) and \(k\le cN\) for a constant \(c\). Then \(Q\) has no algorithm running in time \(2^{o(k)}|I|^{O(1)}\); otherwise composing the algorithm with the reduction would solve 3-SAT in time \(2^{o(N)}N^{O(1)}=2^{o(N)}\), contradicting ETH.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduction assigning parameter at most linear in the SAT variable count transfers ETH into a prohibition on subexponential parameter dependence.
assumptions_latex: ETH holds for 3-SAT parameterized by its number \(N\) of variables.
The reduction is polynomial-time, answer-preserving, and satisfies \(k\le cN\).
The reduced size is polynomial in \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q has no running time \(2^{o(k)}|I|^{O(1)}\) under ETH.

notation.meaning: Number of variables in the source 3-SAT formula.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct conditional lower-bound transfer from ETH through a linear-parameter reduction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional transfer is coherent and complexity_bound fits the leaf, but neither ETH nor the transfer statement has a cited source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Input-Size Exponent Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of the ETH lower bound for Clique to target input-size exponents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the ETH consequence that \(k\)-Clique on an \(n\)-vertex graph admits no algorithm of time \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) for any computable \(f\). Suppose a reduction maps \((G,k)\) to an equivalent instance \((I,k')\) of \(Q\), where \(|I|\le n^c f_0(k)\) and \(a k\le k'\le b k\) for positive constants \(a,b,c\). Then an algorithm for \(Q\) with time \(h(k')|I|^{o(k')}\) would yield an \(f_1(k)n^{o(k)}\)-time algorithm for \(k\)-Clique. Therefore no such algorithm for \(Q\) exists under ETH.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter-preserving reduction from Clique transfers its ETH-based prohibition on input-size exponents sublinear in the parameter.
assumptions_latex: The stated ETH consequence for \(k\)-Clique holds.
The reduction is answer-preserving and has \(k'=\Theta(k)\).
The reduced size is \(f_0(k)n^{O(1)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q has no running time \(h(k')|I|^{o(k')}\) under ETH.

notation.meaning: Number of vertices in the source graph.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard parameter-preserving transfer of the ETH Clique exponent lower bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction calculation is plausible, but the exact ETH consequence for Clique, including its quantification over computable parameter factors, requires an authoritative theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Treewidth-Dependence Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic ETH transfer excluding subexponential dependence on treewidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume ETH. Let \(Q\) be a graph problem for which a polynomial-time reduction transforms every 3-SAT formula with \(N\) variables into an equivalent graph instance \(I\), together with a tree decomposition of width \(w\le cN\), and satisfies \(|I|\le N^{O(1)}\). Then \(Q\) cannot be solved in time \(2^{o(w)}|I|^{O(1)}\), even when the decomposition is supplied. Indeed, such a bound composed with the reduction would be \(2^{o(N)}N^{O(1)}\), violating ETH.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduction producing treewidth linear in SAT size rules out algorithms subexponential in treewidth, even with a decomposition supplied.
assumptions_latex: ETH holds.
The reduction is polynomial-time and answer-preserving.
It outputs a decomposition with \(w\le cN\) and an instance of polynomial size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q has no algorithm of time \(2^{o(w)}|I|^{O(1)}\) under ETH.

notation.meaning: Width of the supplied tree decomposition.
Number of variables in the source formula.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct ETH transfer through a reduction of linear treewidth

children.title: Planar Subexponential Boundaries
children.top_down_role: ETH-based subexponential limitations specific to planar problem instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Planar Subexponential Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional square-root parameter boundary for planar parameterized problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be a parameterized problem on planar graphs. An upper-bound mechanism consisting of a polynomial-time reduction to treewidth \(w=O(\sqrt{k})\) followed by a \(2^{O(w)}|I|^{O(1)}\)-time dynamic program yields time \(2^{O(\sqrt{k})}|I|^{O(1)}\). Conversely, assume ETH and an answer-preserving polynomial reduction from 3-SAT with \(N\) variables to planar instances \((I,k)\) satisfying \(k\le cN^2\) and \(|I|\le N^{O(1)}\). Then a \(2^{o(\sqrt{k})}|I|^{O(1)}\)-time algorithm for \(Q\) would contradict ETH.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Square-root treewidth gives planar subexponential algorithms, while quadratic-parameter SAT reductions can make the square-root exponent conditionally tight.
assumptions_latex: The upper-bound reduction guarantees \(w=O(\sqrt{k})\).
For the lower bound, ETH and the stated quadratic-parameter reduction hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting upper bound is \(2^{O(\sqrt{k})}|I|^{O(1)}\), while the stated reduction excludes \(2^{o(\sqrt{k})}|I|^{O(1)}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conditional composition of square-root treewidth algorithms and quadratic-parameter ETH reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The upper- and lower-bound compositions are conditionally coherent, but the square-root-width mechanism and quadratic-parameter reduction are problem-specific and have no supporting locator.

children.title: Sparse-Graph Subexponential Boundaries
children.top_down_role: ETH-based subexponential limitations across broader sparse-graph classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Graph Subexponential Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional subexponential algorithm schema for structurally sparse graph classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a graph class and \(Q\) a parameterized problem on \(\mathcal C\). Suppose preprocessing either rejects an instance \((G,k)\) or produces, in polynomial time, an equivalent instance \((G',k')\) with \(k'\le g(k)\) and a tree decomposition of width \(w\le c\sqrt{k}\). If \(Q\) is solvable on the decomposition in time \(2^{aw}|G'|^b\), for constants \(a,b,c\), then \(Q\) is solvable on \(\mathcal C\) in time \(2^{O(\sqrt{k})}|G|^{O(1)}\). Without the square-root width guarantee, this conclusion does not follow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse-class subexponential algorithms follow when preprocessing bounds treewidth by a square root of the parameter and dynamic programming is single-exponential in width.
assumptions_latex: Preprocessing is polynomial-time and preserves the answer.
The output satisfies \(w\le c\sqrt{k}\).
Dynamic programming costs \(2^{aw}|G'|^b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q is solvable on \(\mathcal C\) in time \(2^{O(\sqrt{k})}|G|^{O(1)}\).

notation.meaning: Width of the produced tree decomposition.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary composition of a square-root treewidth reduction with width-based dynamic programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The composition schema and complexity_bound kind fit the leaf, but no sparse-graph meta-algorithm source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Planarity-to-Sparsity Transfer
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which planar lower-bound constructions extend to less restrictive sparse settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Planarity-to-Sparsity Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direction of algorithmic and hardness transfer under inclusion of graph classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be the class of planar graphs and let \(\mathcal C\) be a graph class with \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal C\). For the same parameterized problem and parameterization, every algorithm valid on \(\mathcal C\) is valid on \(\mathcal P\) with the same bound. Conversely, any lower bound proved using only instances in \(\mathcal P\) also holds for algorithms claimed on \(\mathcal C\). An upper bound known only for planar instances does not transfer upward to \(\mathcal C\) without an additional reduction or structural theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Algorithms transfer from a larger sparse class to planar graphs; planar-instance hardness transfers to the larger class, but planar algorithms do not automatically transfer upward.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal C\).
The problem and parameter have identical meanings on both classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Upper bounds restrict from \(\mathcal C\) to \(\mathcal P\), whereas planar-instance lower bounds extend from \(\mathcal P\) to \(\mathcal C\).

notation.meaning: A graph class containing all planar graphs.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct restriction and extension logic under graph-class inclusion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The directions of restriction and hardness transfer under class inclusion are correct and principle fits the leaf, but the record has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Density Threshold Failures
children.top_down_role: Points at which increasing graph density invalidates sparse or planar subexponential arguments.

knowledge_statements.title: Density Threshold Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense graphs invalidate square-root treewidth bounds based solely on solution size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(k\ge1\), the complete graph \(K_{k+1}\) has minimum vertex-cover size \(k\), treewidth \(k\), and \(\binom{k+1}{2}\) edges. Hence no universal bound \(\operatorname{tw}(G)=O(\sqrt{k})\) can hold for yes-instances of Vertex Cover on unrestricted graphs when \(k\) is the cover-size parameter. The family identifies the failure mechanism behind planar-style square-root decompositions: allowing quadratic edge density permits treewidth linear, rather than square-root, in the solution parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete graphs have vertex-cover number and treewidth both linear in the parameter, so unrestricted density destroys planar square-root treewidth bounds.
assumptions_latex: The parameter is the requested vertex-cover size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(G=K_{k+1}\), \(\tau(G)=\operatorname{tw}(G)=k\), so \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\notin O(\sqrt{k})\) over this family.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary complete-graph values for vertex-cover number, treewidth, and density

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complete-graph family correctly demonstrates the stated density failure, and failure_boundary is the appropriate kind, but the graph invariants lack an authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Base-of-Exponent Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional exponential-base barrier obtained by composing a SAT reduction with a parameterized exact algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume SETH and let a reduction map every \(k\)-CNF formula with \(n\) variables to an instance \(I\) of problem \(\Pi\), preserving the answer and satisfying \(p(I)\leq \alpha n+O(1)\), in polynomial time. If \(\Pi\) had an algorithm running in \(O^*((b-\varepsilon)^{p(I)})\) time for some \(\varepsilon>0\) with \((b-\varepsilon)^\alpha<2\), composition would solve \(k\)-SAT in \(O^*((2-\delta)^n)\) time for some \(\delta>0\), contradicting SETH. Thus the reduction excludes every such improvement below the critical base \(b=2^{1/\alpha}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under SETH, a reduction with parameter at most α times the SAT variable count forbids problem bases whose α-th power is below 2.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathrm{SETH}\) holds.
The reduction preserves yes/no answers and has polynomial overhead.
\(p(I)\leq \alpha n+O(1)\) for a constant \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No algorithm with running time \(O^*((b-\varepsilon)^{p})\) exists when \((b-\varepsilon)^\alpha<2\).

notation.meaning: Running time with polynomial factors suppressed.
Linear parameter blow-up in the reduction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but no citation supports the transfer claim. The reduction must also cover the clause width selected by SETH's quantifiers; the current fixed-k wording does not make this explicit.

knowledge_statements.title: Width-Parameter Base Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SETH barrier for improving the exponential base of algorithms parameterized by a graph width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume SETH. Suppose a polynomial reduction sends a \(k\)-SAT instance with \(n\) variables to an equivalent graph instance \(I\) having width \(w(I)\leq \alpha n+O(1)\). An algorithm for \(I\) with running time \(O^*((c-\varepsilon)^{w(I)})\) would run after composition in \(O^*(((c-\varepsilon)^\alpha)^n)\) time. Consequently, whenever \((c-\varepsilon)^\alpha<2\), such an algorithm contradicts SETH; the reduction therefore establishes the conditional critical width base \(2^{1/\alpha}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-width SAT reduction converts any sufficiently small width-exponential base into a forbidden sub-2 SAT algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathrm{SETH}\) holds.
The reduction is polynomial and answer-preserving.
\(w(I)\leq \alpha n+O(1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The width dependence cannot be \(O^*((c-\varepsilon)^w)\) when \((c-\varepsilon)^\alpha<2\).

notation.meaning: Specified width parameter of instance I.
Claimed exponential base in the width.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the width measure and a reduction for the SETH-hard clause width are unspecified, and no inspectable source supports the claimed critical base.

knowledge_statements.title: Counting-Hypothesis Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fine-grained barrier for exact counting algorithms under the counting Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\#\mathrm{SETH}\): for every \(\delta>0\), some clause width \(k\) admits no \(O^*((2-\delta)^n)\)-time algorithm for counting satisfying assignments of \(k\)-CNF formulas. Let a parsimonious polynomial reduction produce an instance \(I\) of counting problem \(\#\Pi\) with \(p(I)\leq \alpha n+O(1)\). If \(\#\Pi\) were solvable in \(O^*((b-\varepsilon)^{p(I)})\) time and \((b-\varepsilon)^\alpha<2\), the composition would violate \(\#\mathrm{SETH}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under #SETH, a parsimonious reduction with linear parameter blow-up excludes counting algorithms whose induced SAT-counting base is below 2.
assumptions_latex: \(\#\mathrm{SETH}\) holds.
The reduction is parsimonious and polynomial-time.
\(p(I)\leq \alpha n+O(1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(O^*((b-\varepsilon)^p)\)-time counting algorithm exists when \((b-\varepsilon)^\alpha<2\).

notation.meaning: Exact counting version of the target problem.
Parameter of the target counting instance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits and the transfer is plausible, but the exact #SETH formulation, quantifier alignment, and parsimonious reduction require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Hardness at Bounded Parameter Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic obstruction showing that a parameter cannot yield fixed-parameter tractability when hardness persists at one constant value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be a decision problem with parameter \(p:\mathcal I\to\mathbb N\). If there is a constant \(p_0\) such that the restriction \(\Pi|_{p\leq p_0}\) is NP-hard, then an algorithm with running time \(f(p)\,|I|^{O(1)}\), for any computable \(f\), would solve that NP-hard restriction in polynomial time because \(f(p_0)\) is constant. Hence \(\Pi\) is not fixed-parameter tractable with respect to \(p\) unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a problem remains NP-hard when its parameter is bounded by one constant, that parameter cannot support an FPT algorithm unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: \(p_0\in\mathbb N\) is constant.
\(\Pi|_{p\leq p_0}\) is NP-hard.
\(f\) is computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\Pi\in\mathrm{FPT}\) parameterized by \(p\), then \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: Instances of Π whose parameter is at most p₀.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a correct standard bounded-parameter hardness boundary and its content kind fits, but the record supplies no parameterized-complexity citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Width-Measure Incomparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic incomparability of two graph-width measures over a specified graph class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w_1,w_2:\mathcal G\to\mathbb N\) be width measures on a graph class \(\mathcal G\). They are incomparable on \(\mathcal G\) if there exist graph sequences \((G_n)\) and \((H_n)\) in \(\mathcal G\) such that \(\sup_n w_1(G_n)<\infty\) while \(w_2(G_n)\to\infty\), and \(\sup_n w_2(H_n)<\infty\) while \(w_1(H_n)\to\infty\). Thus neither measure is bounded by any function of the other on \(\mathcal G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two widths are incomparable when each stays bounded on a graph family where the other grows without bound.
assumptions_latex: \(w_1,w_2:\mathcal G\to\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither \(w_1\leq f\circ w_2\) nor \(w_2\leq g\circ w_1\) holds on \(\mathcal G\) for any functions \(f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and matches the title, but no source with a specific locator supports the selected notion of functional incomparability.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Meta-Theorem Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applicability boundary for sparse-graph meta-theorems expressed through unbounded shallow-minor density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G\), let \(\nabla_r(G)\) be the maximum edge-to-vertex ratio among all depth-\(r\) shallow minors of \(G\). A graph class \(\mathcal C\) has bounded expansion only if, for every fixed \(r\geq0\), there exists a finite bound \(f(r)\) with \(\nabla_r(G)\leq f(r)\) for all \(G\in\mathcal C\). If this condition fails, any algorithmic meta-theorem whose hypothesis requires bounded expansion cannot be invoked on all of \(\mathcal C\); separate dense-graph structure or a different parameter is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unbounded shallow-minor density invalidates the bounded-expansion hypothesis, so meta-theorems requiring that hypothesis do not automatically cover the dense class.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a graph class.
The meta-theorem explicitly assumes bounded expansion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\sup_{G\in\mathcal C}\nabla_r(G)=\infty\) for some fixed \(r\), the theorem's bounded-expansion hypothesis fails on \(\mathcal C\).

notation.meaning: Maximum density of a depth-r shallow minor of G.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits and the conclusion is appropriately limited to inapplicability, but the bounded-expansion definition, shallow-minor convention, and meta-theorem boundary lack citations.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed-Width Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic bounded-directed-width hardness criterion preventing an FPT consequence from a proposed directed width measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d:\mathcal D\to\mathbb N\) be a directed-width measure and \(\Pi\) a decision problem on digraphs.
