If a polynomially recognizable class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal D\) satisfies \(d(D)\leq d_0\) for a constant \(d_0\) and \(\Pi|_{\mathcal C}\) is NP-hard, then no algorithm with running time \(f(d(D))\,|D|^{O(1)}\) solves \(\Pi\), unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). This bounded-width hard class is a failure regime for \(d\) as an algorithmically sufficient structural parameter for \(\Pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed width fails for a problem when NP-hardness persists on a recognizable class having constant width.
assumptions_latex: \(d(D)\leq d_0\) for every \(D\in\mathcal C\).
\(\Pi|_{\mathcal C}\) is NP-hard.
Membership in \(\mathcal C\) is polynomially recognizable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An \(f(d)\,|D|^{O(1)}\)-time algorithm for \(\Pi\) implies \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic bounded-width hardness criterion is sound and fits a failure-boundary container, but it is unsupported and does not identify a directed-width measure or hard bounded-width regime.

children.title: Algorithm-Realization Boundary System
children.top_down_role: Cross-method realization issues that affect practical use without forming a second presentation of the algorithms themselves.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Graph Structure and Monadic Second-Order Logic
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Graph Structure and Monadic Second-Order Logic

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Parameter Constants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit expansion of suppressed constants in a parameterized running-time guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound written as \(O^*(c^k)\) asserts the existence of constants \(C>0\), \(q\geq0\), and \(k_0\) such that \(T(I)\leq Cc^{k(I)}|I|^q\) whenever \(k(I)\geq k_0\). For realized performance, the suppressed multiplier \(C|I|^q\), preprocessing cost \(P(I)\), and parameter acquisition cost \(A(I)\) must be restored, giving \(T_{\mathrm{total}}(I)\leq P(I)+A(I)+Cc^{k(I)}|I|^q\). The asymptotic base alone does not order two implementations on finite instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An O-star parameter bound hides polynomial factors, constants, preprocessing, and parameter acquisition; these terms can reverse finite-instance method rankings.
assumptions_latex: \(k(I)\in\mathbb N\).
All displayed costs use the same computation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-instance comparison must use \(P(I)+A(I)+Cc^{k(I)}|I|^q\), not only the base \(c\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity-bound role is suitable, but the stated O-star quantification and the separation of preprocessing and acquisition costs depend on an unstated cost convention and have no supporting source.

children.title: Parameter Estimation Costs
children.top_down_role: Practical cost of obtaining usable parameter estimates before method selection or execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Estimation Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: End-to-end cost of using a computable upper estimate in a monotone parameterized algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an estimator \(E\) return \(\widehat{k}(I)\geq k(I)\) in time \(T_E(I)\), and let algorithm \(A\) have a nondecreasing parameter bound \(F(k,|I|)\). Running \(E\) and then \(A\) with the estimate has total time at most \(T_E(I)+F(\widehat{k}(I),|I|)\). Relative to knowing the exact parameter, the estimation overhead consists of the additive acquisition cost \(T_E(I)\) and the inflation from \(F(k(I),|I|)\) to \(F(\widehat{k}(I),|I|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using an upper parameter estimate costs both estimator time and the larger algorithmic bound caused by overestimating the true parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat{k}(I)\geq k(I)\).
\(F(k,n)\) is nondecreasing in \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{E+A}(I)\leq T_E(I)+F(\widehat{k}(I),|I|)\).

notation.meaning: True parameter and computed upper estimate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits, but an upper estimate yields the displayed solver bound only when the algorithm accepts that bound or otherwise supports monotone substitution. No source or explicit interface assumption establishes this.

children.title: Parameter Certification Costs
children.top_down_role: Practical cost of validating claimed parameter values or supplied structural witnesses.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Certification Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost model for producing and verifying a witness that certifies a usable parameter upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameter certificate for instance \(I\) and bound \(b\) is a string \(W\) accepted by a verifier \(V(I,b,W)\) only if \(k(I)\leq b\). If a constructor produces \((b,W)\) in time \(T_C(I)\), verification takes \(T_V(I,b,W)\), and the parameterized solver uses time \(F(b,|I|)\), then the certified execution costs \(T_C(I)+T_V(I,b,W)+F(b,|I|)\). Soundness of \(V\) makes the bound independently checkable; completeness requires an accepted certificate for every promised bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified parameter bound includes witness construction, verification, and solver costs, while verifier soundness makes the bound independently checkable.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is sound: acceptance implies \(k(I)\leq b\).
The solver is valid for every certified upper bound \(b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{cert}}(I)=T_C(I)+T_V(I,b,W)+F(b,|I|)\).

notation.meaning: Certified upper bound on the parameter.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits, but the certificate model and cost identity are unsupported. Completeness should be quantified over valid claimed bounds or the intended promise relation, which is currently undefined.

children.title: Estimate–Certificate Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Engineering choices between inexpensive estimates and stronger certifiable parameter information.

knowledge_statements.title: Estimate–Certificate Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision rule comparing an uncertified estimate with a verifiable parameter certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an estimation route returns \(\widehat{k}\) at cost \(T_E\), while a certification route returns a verified bound \(b\) at construction-and-verification cost \(T_C+T_V\). For a solver bound \(F\) nondecreasing in its first argument, their end-to-end predicted costs are \(R_E=T_E+F(\widehat{k},n)\) and \(R_C=T_C+T_V+F(b,n)\). Subject to the required assurance level, select certification exactly when \(R_C\leq R_E\); otherwise estimation is cheaper. Certification may dominate despite greater acquisition cost when \(b<\widehat{k}\) sufficiently reduces \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose certification when its construction, verification, and tighter solver bound together cost no more than estimation and its possibly looser bound.
assumptions_latex: \(F(k,n)\) is nondecreasing in \(k\).
Both routes produce solver-valid upper bounds.
The assurance requirement permits the selected route.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Choose the certified route iff \(T_C+T_V+F(b,n)\leq T_E+F(\widehat{k},n)\).

notation.meaning: Estimated end-to-end costs of the two routes.
Solver cost at bound k and input size n.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role fits, but the iff rule is valid only after restricting comparison to assurance-feasible routes and using comparable cost predictions. No source supports this decision model.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Parameter Method Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Portfolio selection using computable end-to-end bounds for methods governed by different parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an instance \(I\) and methods \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\). For each \(i\), acquire a valid parameter bound \(\widehat{k}_i\), its acquisition cost \(Q_i(I)\), and a solver bound \(F_i(\widehat{k}_i,|I|)\). Compute \(R_i=Q_i(I)+F_i(\widehat{k}_i,|I|)\), choose \(i^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\leq i\leq m}R_i\), and run \(A_{i^*}\). Stop when that exact method terminates and return its output. If every bound is valid, the selected execution has predicted cost \(\min_i R_i\), apart from the cost of evaluating the portfolio scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate each method's parameter-acquisition plus solver cost, run a minimum-score exact method, and return its result.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\widehat{k}_i\) is valid for method \(A_i\).
Each \(A_i\) is exact on \(I\).
All \(R_i\) use one computation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected index satisfies \(R_{i^*}=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}\{Q_i(I)+F_i(\widehat{k}_i,|I|)\}\).

notation.meaning: Acquired bound for method i's parameter.
Predicted end-to-end cost of method i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but evaluating every score generally incurs acquisition costs for all methods, so the end-to-end execution cost is not simply min_i R_i unless scores and bounds are already available or score-evaluation costs explicitly include those acquisitions. A source and corrected cost model are required.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Rule Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worklist scheduling for terminating, sound parameterized reduction rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) be reduction rules on instance-parameter pairs. Initialize the current pair as \((J,\kappa)\leftarrow(I,k)\) and place every rule in a worklist \(Q\). Whenever a rule \(R_i\) is removed from \(Q\), apply it if it is applicable, replace \((J,\kappa)\) by the resulting pair, record its solution-lifting data, and enqueue every rule whose applicability could have changed; otherwise discard it until such a change can occur. Stop when \(Q\) is empty. If every successful application strictly decreases a well-founded measure \(\mu(J,\kappa)\), every rule preserves solution equivalence through its recorded lifting map, and the re-enqueue relation covers all possible applicability changes, then the procedure terminates with a solution-equivalent pair to which no \(R_i\) applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process reduction rules from a dependency-complete worklist, recording lifting data and rescheduling every rule whose applicability may change. A strictly decreasing well-founded measure gives termination, and sound lifting rules preserve solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) are sound reduction rules on instance-parameter pairs and provide sufficient solution-lifting data.
Every successful application strictly decreases the well-founded measure \(\mu\).
After an application, every rule whose applicability could have changed is enqueued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure terminates at a pair \((J,\kappa)\) equivalent to \((I,k)\), and no rule \(R_i\) is applicable to \((J,\kappa)\).

children.title: Kernel Expansion Costs
children.top_down_role: Resource growth incurred when translating reduced-instance information back toward the original instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Expansion Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost of reversing kernel reductions through set-valued lifting maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let preprocessing produce a kernel \(K\) and a reduction history of length \(r\). For a kernel solution \(x_r\), let \(L_i(x_i)\) be the candidate predecessor solutions generated when reversing reduction \(i\), and suppose generating and checking one candidate costs at most \(c_i\). If \(|L_i(x_i)|\le b_i\) for every reachable \(x_i\), then exhaustive expansion costs at most \(O\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}c_i\prod_{j=i}^{r}b_j\right)\) time and produces at most \(\prod_{i=1}^{r}b_i\) original-instance candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set-valued reverse reductions can multiply candidates; expansion time is bounded by the cumulative products of their branching factors.
assumptions_latex: The history contains \(r\) reversible reduction records.
Each reachable lifting set satisfies \(|L_i(x)|\le b_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{expand}}=O\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}c_i\prod_{j=i}^{r}b_j\right)\).

notation.meaning: lifting map for the ith reversed reduction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role and branching-product accounting fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports this lifting-cost model.

children.title: Solution Reconstruction Costs
children.top_down_role: Time, memory, and representation overhead required to recover original-instance solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Reconstruction Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lifting cost when each reduced solution has one reconstructed predecessor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose preprocessing applies \(r\) reductions and stores records \(H_1,\ldots,H_r\). Starting from a kernel solution \(x_r\), reconstruction computes \(x_{i-1}=\lambda_i(x_i,H_i)\) for \(i=r,r-1,\ldots,1\). If evaluating \(\lambda_i\) takes \(\Theta(t_i)\) time and at most \(s_i\) working bits in addition to its materialized input and output, then reconstruction takes \(\Theta\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}t_i\right)\) time. When records are streamed backward and obsolete solutions are discarded, the working space including the current materialized solutions is \(O\!\left(\max_{1\le i\le r}(s_i+|x_i|+|x_{i-1}|)\right)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deterministic reconstruction reverses the reduction history. Its time is the sum of the lifting times, while its streamed working space is governed by the largest lifting workspace and adjacent intermediate solutions.
assumptions_latex: Every record \(H_i\) defines a correct single-valued lifting map \(\lambda_i\).
History records can be accessed in reverse order.
The \(i\)-th lifting evaluation takes \(\Theta(t_i)\) time and at most \(s_i\) additional working bits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{reconstruct}}=\Theta\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}t_i\right)\) and \(S_{\mathrm{reconstruct}}=O\!\left(\max_{1\le i\le r}(s_i+|x_i|+|x_{i-1}|)\right)\).

notation.meaning: solution after the first i reductions

children.title: Reduction-History Storage
children.top_down_role: Storage requirements for retaining the information needed during postprocessing.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-History Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit storage required for reversible preprocessing records.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence of \(r\) reductions, let record \(H_i\) contain a rule identifier chosen from \(m\) rules, an affected-location identifier chosen from a set of size \(n_i\), and a payload of \(p_i\) bits. If the decoder knows the field lengths \(m\), \(n_i\), and \(p_i\), a fixed-field representation uses \(O\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}(\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(n_i+1)\rceil+p_i)\right)\) bits. If each lifting map depends only on its corresponding record and the reconstructed successor solution, this history suffices for reverse-order solution reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With known field widths, each record stores an applied-rule identifier, an affected-location identifier, and a lifting payload. The total history size is the sum of those field lengths.
assumptions_latex: Each reduction is identified among \(m\) rules.
At step \(i\), the affected location is identified among \(n_i\) possibilities and the lifting payload has length \(p_i\) bits.
The decoder knows the field widths or receives equivalent framing metadata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|H|=O\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}(\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(n_i+1)\rceil+p_i)\right)\).

notation.meaning: number of addressable locations at step i

children.title: Postprocessing Dominance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where expansion or reconstruction outweighs the cost of solving the reduced instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Postprocessing Dominance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic criterion for postprocessing to dominate kernel solving.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(n,k)\), \(S(g(k))\), and \(R(n,k)\) denote preprocessing, kernel-solving, and postprocessing times for an input of size \(n\), parameter \(k\), and kernel-size bound \(g(k)\). Postprocessing is asymptotically dominant on a regime \(\mathcal D\) precisely when \(P(n,k)+S(g(k))=o(R(n,k))\) along every unbounded sequence in \(\mathcal D\). Under this condition the end-to-end time \(T=P+S+R\) satisfies \(T(n,k)=\Theta(R(n,k))\) on \(\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Postprocessing dominates exactly when preprocessing plus kernel solving is asymptotically negligible relative to reconstruction or expansion cost.
assumptions_latex: \(P,S,R\) are nonnegative running-time functions.
\(\mathcal D\) specifies the asymptotic input-parameter regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P+S=o(R)\Longrightarrow T=\Theta(R)\) on \(\mathcal D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role and asymptotic implication are mathematically coherent, but the candidate supplies no citation for the proposed postprocessing-dominance terminology or model.

children.title: Weighted Instance Growth
children.top_down_role: Growth caused by weight magnitude, multiplicity, or weight-preserving transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Instance Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding growth caused by integral weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a combinatorial instance have structural encoding length \(L_0\) and integral weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_q\). Under signed binary encoding, its total length is \(L=L_0+\Theta\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{q}(1+\lceil\log_2(|w_i|+1)\rceil)\right)\). Consequently, if \(|w_i|\le W\) for every \(i\), then \(L=L_0+O\!\left(q(1+\log_2(W+1))\right)\); numerical magnitude contributes logarithmically to binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary encoding adds a number of bits proportional to the sum of one plus the logarithm of each absolute weight. For weights bounded by W, this adds O(q(1+log(W+1))) bits.
assumptions_latex: All weights \(w_i\) are integers.
Weights use a signed binary representation.
\(W\ge 0\) and \(|w_i|\le W\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=L_0+\Theta\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{q}(1+\lceil\log_2(|w_i|+1)\rceil)\right)\), and \(L=L_0+O\!\left(q(1+\log_2(W+1))\right)\) when \(|w_i|\le W\).

source_refs.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

children.title: Encoded Instance Growth
children.top_down_role: Growth caused by representation choices and expanded encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoded Instance Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive accounting of structural and numeric encoding lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a transformation maps an encoded instance \(I\) to \(I'\), retains an encoding of \(I\), adds \(a\) structural objects, and adds binary-encoded integers \(z_1,\ldots,z_b\). If the complete encoding of each added structural object, including its incidence data and framing, requires at most \(d\) bits, then \(|I'|=O\!\left(|I|+ad+\sum_{j=1}^{b}(1+\log_2(|z_j|+1))\right)\). Thus a polynomial bound on object count alone does not bound the transformed bit length unless the introduced integers also have polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transformed size includes the complete encodings of new structural objects and the binary lengths of introduced integers; counting objects alone can miss numeric growth.
assumptions_latex: \(I'\) retains an encoding of \(I\).
The complete encoding of each new structural object requires at most \(d\) bits.
The introduced integers \(z_1,\ldots,z_b\) use signed binary encoding.

notation.meaning: bit length of an encoded instance

source_refs.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

children.title: Binary–Unary Encoding Regimes
children.top_down_role: Size sensitivity arising from alternative numerical encoding conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary–Unary Encoding Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of integer magnitudes under binary and unary encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(N\ge1\), a standard binary representation has length \(\ell_2(N)=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\), whereas a unary representation has length \(\ell_1(N)=N\), up to constant-size delimiters. Hence an algorithm polynomial in \(N\) is polynomial in unary input length but may be exponential in binary input length. Conversely, a bound polynomial in \(\ell_2(N)\) is polynomial under either encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unary length is linear in a number's magnitude, while binary length is logarithmic; this distinction separates polynomial and pseudopolynomial running times.
assumptions_latex: \(N\) is a positive integer.
Encoding delimiters have constant size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_1(N)=N\) and \(\ell_2(N)=\lfloor\log_2N\rfloor+1\).

source_refs.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

children.title: Bit-Length Dominance
children.top_down_role: Cases where representation length becomes the controlling practical resource.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Length Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for numeric encodings to dominate total instance size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the encoded length of an instance as \(L=L_{\mathrm{str}}+L_{\mathrm{num}}\), where \(L_{\mathrm{str}}\) encodes its combinatorial structure and \(L_{\mathrm{num}}=\sum_{i=1}^{q}\Theta(1+\log(|z_i|+1))\) encodes its integers in binary. Numeric bit length dominates on a family \(\mathcal F\) when \(L_{\mathrm{str}}=o(L_{\mathrm{num}})\) along every unbounded sequence in \(\mathcal F\). In that regime \(L=\Theta(L_{\mathrm{num}})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numeric bit length dominates when structural encoding is asymptotically negligible compared with the binary lengths of all encoded integers.
assumptions_latex: Instances are represented by separable structural and binary-numeric fields.
Encoding overhead is absorbed into \(L_{\mathrm{str}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{\mathrm{str}}=o(L_{\mathrm{num}})\Longrightarrow L=\Theta(L_{\mathrm{num}})\).

source_refs.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Quality Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime degradation when an available decomposition exceeds optimal width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a decomposition-based algorithm run in time \(T(n,w)=O(n^c f(w))\) on a supplied decomposition of width \(w\), where \(f\) is nondecreasing. If the optimum width is \(w^*\) but preprocessing returns width \(\widehat w\le \alpha w^*+\beta\), then the realized running time is \(O(n^c f(\alpha w^*+\beta))\). In particular, when \(f(w)=b^w\) for \(b>1\), an additive width error \(\Delta\) multiplies the parameter-dependent factor by \(b^\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using a wider-than-optimal decomposition substitutes its width into the dynamic-programming bound; exponential width dependence amplifies even additive errors.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is nondecreasing.
The supplied decomposition has width \(\widehat w\le\alpha w^*+\beta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(n,\widehat w)=O(n^c f(\alpha w^*+\beta))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role and monotonic substitution are coherent, including the exponential effect of an additive width error, but no source supports the decomposition-quality runtime model.

children.title: State Encoding
children.top_down_role: Representation choices for decomposition states and their effects on storage or comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: State Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical bit-string representation of dynamic-programming states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_B\) be a set of raw dynamic-programming states for a decomposition boundary \(B\), let \(\sim_B\) denote semantic equivalence on \(X_B\), and let \(\mathcal S_B=X_B/\!\sim_B\) be the finite set of semantic states. A canonical state encoding is an injective map \(\operatorname{enc}_B:\mathcal S_B\to\{0,1\}^*\) together with a decoder \(\operatorname{dec}_B\) satisfying \(\operatorname{dec}_B(\operatorname{enc}_B(C))=C\) for every \(C\in\mathcal S_B\). A raw state \(x\in X_B\) receives the code \(\operatorname{enc}_B([x]_{\sim_B})\), so two raw states receive the same code exactly when they are semantically equivalent. If \(\ell_B=\max_{C\in\mathcal S_B}|\operatorname{enc}_B(C)|\), then \(|\mathcal S_B|\le 2^{\ell_B+1}-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical encoding injectively maps semantic-state equivalence classes to decodable finite bit strings, so raw states share a code exactly when they are semantically equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(\sim_B\) is an equivalence relation on the raw state set \(X_B\).
The quotient \(\mathcal S_B=X_B/\!\sim_B\) is finite.
Codes are finite binary strings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dec}_B\circ\operatorname{enc}_B=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal S_B}\), and \(|\mathcal S_B|\le 2^{\ell_B+1}-1\).

notation.meaning: raw state set for boundary B
set of semantic-state equivalence classes for boundary B

children.title: State Hashing
children.top_down_role: Hash-based indexing concerns for large collections of decomposition states.

knowledge_statements.title: State Hashing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact hash-table lookup for canonically encoded decomposition states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given canonical state codes \(e=\operatorname{enc}_B(s)\), choose a hash function \(h:\{0,1\}^*\to\{0,\ldots,M-1\}\) and maintain buckets indexed by \(h(e)\). To insert or query \(s\), compute \(e\) and \(h(e)\), then compare \(e\) with every code in that bucket; merge table entries only after exact code equality. If \(h\) is sampled from a universal family, then for distinct codes \(e,e'\), \(\Pr[h(e)=h(e')]\le1/M\). Collision checking makes the procedure exact for every sampled hash function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hash canonical state codes into buckets and confirm exact equality before merging; universal hashing bounds collision probability without making correctness probabilistic.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{enc}_B\) is canonical and injective on semantic states.
Bucket collisions are resolved by exact code comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e=e'\) is required for merging, while \(e\ne e'\Longrightarrow\Pr[h(e)=h(e')]\le1/M\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, exact bucket comparison correctly prevents probabilistic merging errors, and the stated collision bound matches a universal family with range size M. No inspectable source is supplied for the hashing claim or its state-table application.

children.title: State Deduplication
children.top_down_role: Recognition and removal of equivalent or repeated decomposition states.

knowledge_statements.title: State Deduplication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical deduplication of equivalent dynamic-programming states at one decomposition interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite multiset of generated states \(S\), a continuation-preserving equivalence relation \(\equiv\) on \(S\), a canonicalization map \(c:S\to S\) satisfying \(c(s)\equiv s\) and \(c(s)=c(t)\) if and only if \(s\equiv t\), and an injective encoding \(e:c(S)\to\{0,1\}^*\), maintain a dictionary indexed by \(e(c(s))\). For each \(s\in S\), insert \(c(s)\) if its key is absent; otherwise combine its payload with the stored payload using the problem's exact aggregation operator. The output contains one representative of every equivalence class intersecting \(S\), and continuation values are preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonicalize every generated state, merge payloads only for equal canonical representatives, and retain exactly one representative per continuation-equivalence class.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite.
\(\equiv\) preserves every future transition and completion value.
\(c:S\to S\) is constant exactly on equivalence classes.
\(e\) is injective on \(c(S)\), and the payload aggregation operator is exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output contains exactly one representative of each equivalence class intersecting \(S\), without changing attainable completion values.
review_flags: No supplied source with a specific locator supports the algorithm and exactness criterion.

children.title: Collision-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Correctness and performance risks arising from hash collisions or weak state fingerprints.

knowledge_statements.title: Collision-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness boundary separating verified equality handling from unsafe hash-only deduplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:S\to H\) be a state hash and let \(s\not\equiv t\) denote states having different feasible continuations or completion values. Deduplication by hash value alone is exact only when \(h(s)=h(t)\) implies \(s\equiv t\) on every reachable state pair. If a reachable pair satisfies \(h(s)=h(t)\) and \(s\not\equiv t\), then an execution that discards one state may lose a feasible or optimal completion. Collisions are harmless when each equal-hash pair is subsequently compared by a collision-free canonical encoding or an exact equivalence test; hashing then affects performance but not correctness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hash-only merging is safe precisely on reachable states where equal hashes imply continuation equivalence; exact secondary comparison removes this correctness boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is the set of reachable states.
\(\equiv\) is defined by equality of future behavior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An unverified collision between inequivalent reachable states creates a correctness failure boundary for exact deduplication.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly treats collision-safe hashing for exact state-space algorithms.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and mathematical distinction between hash-only merging and exact secondary comparison fit the leaf, but no inspectable citation supports the claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Automata-Construction Blowup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-space cost of explicitly constructing a product automaton used over a decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a decomposition algorithm combines \(r\) finite state components with sizes \(q_1,\ldots,q_r\) by explicit Cartesian-product construction. Before reachability pruning or quotienting, the constructed automaton has at most \(Q=\prod_{i=1}^r q_i\) states. If each state has at most \(d\) outgoing transitions, explicit storage and traversal require \(O(Qd)\) transition records and \(O(Qd)\) time, excluding state-encoding costs. Thus even when every \(q_i\le q\), construction may require \(q^r\) states; parameterized tractability requires this factor to be bounded solely by the designated parameter or avoided through implicit generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit product of component automata can contain the product of their state counts, making construction exponential in the number of components.
assumptions_latex: The construction explicitly materializes reachable and unreachable product tuples before pruning.
Each product state has at most \(d\) stored outgoing transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unpruned construction uses at most \(Q=\prod_{i=1}^r q_i\) states and \(O(Qd)\) time and transition storage.

notation.meaning: number of states in component automaton i

review_flags: The supplied complexity locators do not specifically support product-automaton construction in decomposition algorithms.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits automata-construction blowup. The product-state count is standard, but the O(Qd) construction-time claim additionally depends on constant-cost tuple and transition generation and lacks a supporting locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory-Dominated Exact Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource classification for exact algorithms whose peak state storage governs realizability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an exact algorithm \(A\), let \(T_A(I)\) be its operation count and \(M_A(I)\) its peak number of simultaneously stored machine words on input \(I\). Given an input family \(\mathcal I\) and resource budgets \(\tau(I)\) and \(\mu(I)\), call \(A\) memory-dominated relative to these budgets on \(\mathcal I\) when \(T_A(I)\leq\tau(I)\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\), while \(M_A(I)>\mu(I)\) for at least one \(I\in\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to specified budgets, an exact algorithm is memory-dominated when every input meets its operation budget but at least one input exceeds its peak-memory budget.
assumptions_latex: Time and memory are measured in a fixed word-RAM model.
The budgets \(\tau(I)\) and \(\mu(I)\) are specified for every \(I\in\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Memory dominance identifies peak storage as the violated resource constraint while the operation-count constraint remains feasible throughout \(\mathcal I\).

notation.meaning: operation count of algorithm A on input I
peak stored-word count of algorithm A on input I

review_flags: No supplied source defines this local resource classification.

children.title: Randomness Costs
children.top_down_role: Random-bit demand, sampling overhead, and reliability costs in randomized parameterized methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomness Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-bit, repetition, and failure-probability costs of a Monte Carlo exact solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let one run of a randomized exact solver use at most \(R(n,k)\) unbiased random bits, take time \(T(n,k)\), and produce a verifiably correct answer with probability at least \(p\), where \(0<p<1\). If runs are independent and the first verified answer is accepted, then \(m\) runs use at most \(mR(n,k)\) random bits and \(mT(n,k)\) time, while the probability that every run fails is at most \((1-p)^m\). For \(0<\delta<1\), choosing \(m=\left\lceil\log(1/\delta)/(-\log(1-p))\right\rceil\) makes this failure probability at most \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent repetition multiplies time and random-bit use by the repetition count while reducing failure probability geometrically.
assumptions_latex: Runs use independent unbiased random bits.
A successful output is recognized by a sound and complete exact verifier.
Each run succeeds with probability at least \(p\), where \(0<p<1\).
The target failure probability satisfies \(0<\delta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure probability at most \(\delta\) is achieved with the displayed repetition count and corresponding linear resource overhead.

notation.meaning: target upper bound on total failure probability

review_flags: No supplied source with a specific locator supports this amplification bound in the stated setting.

children.title: Derandomization Costs
children.top_down_role: Time, memory, and construction overhead introduced by deterministic substitutes.

knowledge_statements.title: Derandomization Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time and construction overhead from replacing random seeds by an explicit hitting set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a randomized algorithm uses seeds from \(\{0,1\}^{R(n,k)}\), takes time \(T(n,k)\) per seed, and has at least one successful seed for every input. Let \(H_{n,k}\) be an explicitly enumerable seed set intersecting the successful-seed set of every input of size \(n\) and parameter \(k\). If constructing or initializing its enumeration costs \(C_H(n,k)\), and verifying one output costs \(V(n,k)\), then enumerating every seed, verifying its output, and returning the first verified solution yields a deterministic exact algorithm with time \(O(C_H(n,k)+|H_{n,k}|(T(n,k)+V(n,k)))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit hitting set derandomizes seed choice at a multiplicative execution-and-verification cost equal to its size, plus its construction cost.
assumptions_latex: Every input has a successful seed.
Output verification is deterministic, sound, and complete.
\(H_{n,k}\) intersects every successful-seed set and can be explicitly enumerated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Seed enumeration gives a deterministic exact solver with time \(O(C_H(n,k)+|H_{n,k}|(T(n,k)+V(n,k)))\).

notation.meaning: explicit universal hitting set of seeds
cost of constructing or initializing enumeration of the hitting set

review_flags: No supplied source establishes this hitting-set derandomization model.

children.title: Randomness–Determinism Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Practical regimes balancing randomized efficiency against deterministic guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomness–Determinism Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Seed-family size as the resource interface between randomized and deterministic realizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a seeded exact procedure use seeds of length \(R(n,k)\), have per-seed execution-and-verification time \(T(n,k)\), and accept only verifiably correct outputs. Random seed selection gives a Monte Carlo realization whose success probability is the successful-seed density. Replacing random selection by an explicit hitting family \(H_{n,k}\) gives a deterministic realization with worst-case time \(O(C_H(n,k)+|H_{n,k}|T(n,k))\), where \(C_H(n,k)\) is the construction or enumeration-initialization cost. If \(T(n,k)\), \(C_H(n,k)\), and \(|H_{n,k}|\) are each bounded by a computable function of \(k\) times a polynomial in \(n\), then the deterministic realization is fixed-parameter tractable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random seed selection avoids exhaustive coverage; deterministic coverage replaces it with the size and construction cost of a hitting family, while preserving fixed-parameter tractability when all resulting factors are FPT-bounded.
assumptions_latex: Output verification is deterministic, sound, and complete.
An explicit hitting family exists for every relevant \((n,k)\).
The per-seed procedure and hitting-family overhead satisfy the stated fixed-parameter bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated bounds, hitting-family enumeration transfers reliability from random selection to deterministic coverage without losing fixed-parameter tractability.
review_flags: No supplied source directly documents this parameterized seed-family tradeoff.

children.title: Random-Source Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity to limited independence, weak randomness, or unavailable random sources.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Source Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary when the implemented seed distribution differs from the analyzed random source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_x\subseteq\{0,1\}^R\) be the successful seeds for input \(x\), and suppose correctness analysis assumes the uniform distribution \(U_R\), giving success probability \(|G_x|/2^R\). An implemented source with distribution \(D_x\) instead succeeds with probability \(D_x(G_x)\). Therefore the advertised lower bound \(p\) is justified only if \(D_x(G_x)\ge p\) for every admissible input. No positive guarantee follows solely from seed length or support size: a source may assign zero mass to \(G_x\). Independence-based amplification also fails when repeated seeds are correlated unless the required conditional success bound is preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Success guarantees depend on probability mass assigned to good seeds; bias, missing support, or correlated repetitions can invalidate the analyzed bound.
assumptions_latex: \(G_x\) is the set of seeds producing a correct output on \(x\).
The implementation may use a nonuniform or correlated source.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A random-source guarantee fails whenever the implemented distribution or repetition process does not preserve the required mass on successful seeds.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly addresses adversarial bias or dependence in random sources for exact algorithms.

children.title: Algebraic Field Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of feasibility, reliability, or performance on the selected algebraic field.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Field Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of algebraic algorithm correctness on field characteristic and available elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an algebraic exact algorithm whose correctness requires division by integers in a finite set \(D\subseteq\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}\) and requires specified evaluations of integer polynomials \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\) to be nonzero. After mapping the integers and polynomial evaluations into a field \(F\), the same symbolic computation is valid only if the image of every \(d\in D\) and every required evaluated image of \(P_j\) is nonzero. In particular, changing the characteristic can invalidate a divisor, pivot, determinant, interpolation denominator, or nonvanishing test. Field-independent validity therefore requires these nonvanishing conditions to hold in every field under consideration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Algebraic correctness can change with field characteristic because required divisors, pivots, determinants, denominators, or polynomial evaluations may become zero.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is expressed using field operations.
Correctness depends on the specified divisions and nonvanishing evaluations.
Each required integer and polynomial evaluation has a defined image in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symbolic computation transfers to \(F\) only when every stated nonvanishing condition remains valid in \(F\).

notation.meaning: coefficient field used by the algorithm
finite set of required nonzero integer divisors
integer polynomial with a required nonzero evaluation

children.title: Bit-Complexity Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence on operand length and the cost of finite-precision or exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Complexity Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of arithmetic-operation bounds into bit-operation bounds for exact computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an exact algorithm performs at most \(N\) arithmetic operations on integers or rational encodings whose operands have at most \(B\) bits throughout the computation. If addition, comparison, multiplication, and exact division on \(b\)-bit operands cost at most \(M(b)\) bit operations, then the arithmetic phase costs \(O(NM(B))\) bit operations and uses at least the storage required for its \(B\)-bit operands. Hence an arithmetic-operation bound alone is not a bit-complexity bound: polynomial bit complexity additionally requires a polynomial upper bound on intermediate bit length \(B\) and on conversion, normalization, and coefficient-access costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arithmetic operation counts yield efficient exact implementations only when intermediate operand lengths and per-operation bit costs are also controlled.
assumptions_latex: All intermediate operands have bit length at most \(B\).
Each permitted arithmetic operation costs at most \(M(B)\) bit operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The arithmetic phase has bit cost \(O(NM(B))\); uncontrolled \(B\) can destroy polynomial-time realizability.

notation.meaning: upper bound for one B-bit arithmetic operation

children.title: Field-Size Regimes
children.top_down_role: Implementation behavior across small, extension, or large-field settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Field-Size Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Field-size thresholds for avoiding a finite collection of bad algebraic choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite field, let \(B\subseteq F\) be the set of choices causing one algebraic subroutine to fail, and suppose \(|B|\leq b(n,k)\). Uniform sampling from \(F\) has failure probability \(|B|/|F|\leq b(n,k)/|F|\). Hence, for \(0<\varepsilon\leq1\), one trial has failure probability at most \(\varepsilon\) whenever \(|F|\geq b(n,k)/\varepsilon\). More generally, if \(r\) positions must receive distinct field elements and each position independently forbids at most \(b(n,k)\) elements, greedy selection is guaranteed when \(|F|\geq b(n,k)+r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite field is large enough when its size dominates the number of bad values and the number of distinct choices required by the algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is finite and \(B\subseteq F\).
Sampling is uniform when the probabilistic bound is used.
For the availability bound, \(r\) is a positive integer and each position forbids at most \(b(n,k)\) field elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed field-size inequalities guarantee the corresponding failure-probability or distinct-choice availability requirement.

notation.meaning: set of bad field elements for one trial
upper bound on the number of forbidden elements
number of positions requiring distinct choices

children.title: Arithmetic-Growth Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Performance limits caused by growing coefficients or intermediate arithmetic representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic-Growth Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intermediate coefficient growth as a bottleneck in exact algebraic realizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an exact computation performing \(N\) integer additions and multiplications. If every input has absolute value at most \(2^{B_0}\), define recursively \(B_{t+1}\le B_t+1\) for addition of two \(B_t\)-bit magnitudes and \(B_{t+1}\le 2B_t\) for multiplication. Along a chain of \(m\) unrestricted multiplications, the elementary bound is \(B_m\le 2^mB_0\). Therefore a polynomial arithmetic-operation count does not ensure polynomial bit complexity: without modular reduction, cancellation control, fraction normalization, or an independent height bound, intermediate representation length may grow exponentially in multiplication depth and dominate both time and memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated exact multiplication can make intermediate coefficients exponentially long in multiplication depth, overwhelming a polynomial arithmetic-operation count.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic is exact over integer encodings.
No reduction or independent coefficient-height bound is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A multiplication chain of depth \(m\) can require operands with up to \(2^mB_0\) bits under the stated recurrence.

notation.meaning: upper bound on operand bit length after depth t
